Leadership isn’t just about the job you hold, it’s about being willing to help when others need it. Grateful everyone on board arrived safely."

Minneapolis Chief of Police Brian O'Hara called out the city's "bourgeois liberal mentality" after the death of George Floyd. (Getty Images)

Looking back on the incident, O'Hara said he hopes Americans choose action over standing by when innocent people are in danger.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

"We're coming up on the 25th anniversary of September 11," he said. "I would hope everybody in this country now knows that if things are escalating to the point where there's going to be some kind of violence, I think every citizen that is able to has a duty to try and help to stop it."

He also said airlines should ensure restraints are readily available and that crew members are trained to use them if passengers become violent.

"I think it would be good to make sure that they have restraints that are available, that at least some people are trained in some way to use them safely to get somebody restrained if they needed to," O'Hara said.

As of Thursday afternoon, authorities had not publicly identified the passenger or announced any criminal charges.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Broward Sheriff's Office and the Federal Aviation Administration for additional information and comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Squad-backed ‘Tennessee Three’ lawmaker wins House primary in newly redrawn district
excerpt:
Fox News correspondent Matt Finn has the latest on the competitive seats up for grabs on 'Special Report.'

Squad-backed Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, District 86, part of the trio of lawmakers...
body_text:
Fox News correspondent Matt Finn has the latest on the competitive seats up for grabs on 'Special Report.'

Squad-backed Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, District 86, part of the trio of lawmakers in his state referred to as the "Tennessee Three," won the Democratic primary Thursday in Tennessee's newly redrawn 9th Congressional District.

Pearson defeated state Sen. London Lamar, District 33, community activist Marion LaTroy Alexandria-Williams and attorney Jim Torino. He will face Brent Taylor, the Republican nominee who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, in November with his campaign warchest of millions of dollars he has raised throughout his campaign, significantly outpacing his Democratic opponents.

The Memphis-area state lawmaker entered the primary with the backing of prominent Democrats who are part of the progressive group of lawmakers called "the Squad," including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., and Summer Lee, D-Pa., who all joined Pearson at a campaign rally in Memphis last month.

'SQUAD' MEMBER'S COMEBACK BID THWARTED AS ESTABLISHMENT DEMS NOTCH VICTORY AGAINST SOCIALISTS

Known for his fiery, preacher-style speeches, Pearson has also received support from national left-wing groups including Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, MoveOn and Indivisible.

The so-called "Tennessee Three" lawmakers seen pictured above. From left, Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, D-Memphis, Rep. Gloria Johnson, D-Knoxville, and Rep. Justin Jones, D-Nashville, raise their fists as they walk across Fisk University campus after hearing Vice President Kamala Harris speak, Friday, April 7, 2023, in Nashville, Tennessee.  (AP Photo/George Walker IV)

Pearson rose to national prominence in 2023 as one of the "Tennessee Three" lawmakers who participated in a gun-control protest on the state House floor following the Covenant School shooting in Nashville that killed three young kids and three adults.

Republican lawmakers subsequently expelled Pearson and fellow state Rep. Justin Jones over the protest, though they later regained their seats.

A third Democrat, Gloria Johnson of Knoxville, avoided expulsion by a single vote, according to local media reporting.

Tennessee state Reps. Justin Pearson, D-Memphis, Rep. Justin Jones, D-Nashville, and Rep. Gloria Johnson, D-Knoxville, holding their hands up as they exit the House Chamber doors at Tennessee State Capitol Building in Nashville, Tenn., Monday, April 3, 2023. (Nicole Hester /The Tennessean via AP)

'JUMPING SHIP': HOUSE DEM FINDS EXIT STRATEGY AFTER SCOTUS RULING SHIFTS ADVANTAGE TO GOP

The open-seat primary won by Pearson on Thursday followed a redrawing of Tennessee’s congressional map that divided Memphis among three Republican-leaning districts and prompted longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen, D-Tenn., to retire.

Before the new map, heavily Democratic Memphis was largely kept together in the 9th District, giving Tennessee Democrats one reliable congressional seat in an otherwise deeply Republican state.

U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) questions Special Counsel Jack Smith as he testifies during a hearing before the House Judiciary Committee in the Rayburn House Office Building on Capitol Hill on January 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

Cohen has been the lone Democrat in Tennessee’s nine-member House delegation alongside eight Republicans since 2023, but the new map favors the GOP in all nine districts.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Wisconsin man flies helicopter to Cabela's because the drive was too long
excerpt: Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy reports on the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation into an airspace incident involving President Donald Trump's Marine One helicopter....
body_text:
Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy reports on the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation into an airspace incident involving President Donald Trump's Marine One helicopter. Official reports confirm a commercial plane coming from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport caused a momentary loss of separation with the presidential helicopter.

Look, sometimes you just really need to go to Cabela's.

And when the store is 50 miles away, you have two options: get in the car and sit in traffic like a schmuck, or fire up the helicopter and be there in minutes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

Helicopter ready for departure at heliport. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

The 69-year-old Wisconsin pilot flew from Rosendale to the Cabela’s in Richfield on Saturday evening, landing in a mostly empty section of the store’s parking lot so he could pick up some bowhunting supplies.

Naturally, some busybody saw a helicopter descend outside Cabela’s and called the police.

Washington County sheriff’s deputies arrived to investigate the unusual landing, only to discover there was no emergency, no dramatic getaway and no criminal activity.

Nothing to see here. Just a man who values his time and urgently needed a fresh pack of broadheads.

"So I asked my neighbor friend if he wanted to take a ride to Cabela’s to get some shopping done," Pipping said.

Pipping, who has decades of flying experience, said he called the store before making the approximately 20-minute flight. He also circled the parking lot beforehand to make sure he had enough room to land safely.

Signage is displayed outside a Cabela's Inc. retail store in Greenville, South Carolina, on Tuesday, Oct. 4, 2016. Cabela's agreed to be bought by Bass Pro Shops in a $5.5 billion deal, handing a victory to the activist investor that had been pushing the outdoor-sports equipment retailer to put itself up for sale. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

When asked why he decided to fly rather than make the roughly 45-minute drive, Pipping responded with a question of his own.

"Why would you drive if you can fly there in a helicopter?" he said.

OREGON BALLOT MEASURE THAT WOULD HAVE CRIMINALIZED HUNTING AND FISHING FAILS TO QUALIFY FOR VOTE

Pipping said there were no vehicles near the far end of the massive parking lot, allowing him to land, head inside and complete his shopping without incident.

By the time he returned, however, a deputy was waiting to check out the aircraft.

A small commercial helicopter parked at an airport. (Getty Images)

Pipping was properly licensed, had landed safely and complied with applicable Federal Aviation Administration regulations. He was not arrested or cited.

The sheriff’s office ultimately described the incident as a "unique way to make a shopping trip."

Love all things hunting, fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick Outdoors on Instagram and TikTok!

title: Australia news live: Richard Marles insists Tony Burke’s speech on Labor’s new restrictive immigration policy ‘hasn’t been called off’
excerpt:
Deputy prime minister says Burke’s speech before National Press Club was not cancelled. Follow today’s news live

Marles was asked about home affairs minister Tony Burke’s delayed speech before the Na...
body_text:
Deputy prime minister says Burke’s speech before National Press Club was not cancelled. Follow today’s news live

Marles was asked about home affairs minister Tony Burke’s delayed speech before the National Press Club about migration policies.

The deputy prime minister said the decision was merely a move of date, not a cancellation. Marles said:

double quotation markIt’s not unusual for dates to be moved around in people’s diaries and in terms of presenting speeches of that kind. I think what’s important here in terms of migration policy is complex. It’s one that we’ve been working on since we’ve come to government.

Tony Burke will be talking about that and he’ll be talking about that at the National Press Club at the earliest opportunity.

double quotation markMoving around dates in a diary for senior members of government is very routine. It happens literally all the time. The speech hasn’t been called off. A date has been changed. That literally happens every week. And there’s nothing more to it than that.

Australia’s best sustainable architecture for 2026 – in pictures

This year’s finalists for the National Architecture awards’ sustainability category include a compact Canberra housing development and the largest commercial use of hempcrete in the country.

New Victoria premier pushes on with work-from-home laws

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, who took over as leader after an internal revolt against Jacinta Allan, will continue pursuing the laws she championed, AAP reports.

The legislation would give full-time, part-time and casual workers the right to work from home two days a week on a pro-rata basis where reasonable.

The bill has already passed the Labor-controlled lower house and will soon be debated in the upper house as the November state election approaches.

It has attracted staunch opposition from business lobby groups, which have met with Carroll since his elevation to premier. But a Victorian government spokesperson confirmed on Friday the government’s position had not changed.

Among the more contentious elements of the bill is a requirement for employers to pay any reasonable costs to allow an eligible employee to work remotely. This may include essential equipment and secure access to work systems.

Federal parliament is returning from winter break next week.

Do you have a question you’d like to ask Guardian Australia’s team of political reporters in Canberra? Our political editor, Tom McIlroy, and the team will be answering readers’ questions on the Australian Politics podcast.

Please send us your questions to australianpolitics@theguardian.com.

Can Australia make housing affordable while avoiding a major market crash?

The Reserve Bank has raised interest rates and the property market is in retreat. So far, so normal.

There is a sense that this year’s fall in home prices feels different from previous episodes. The data tells another story.

Over the past four decades there have been seven property market downturns of varying length and depth, according to analysis put together by Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist.

They are often triggered by interest rate hikes, which make home loans more expensive, but they also occur during crises and policy changes.

Police investigating after 23-year-old found dead at rural property with injuries consistent with animal attack

Police are investigating after the body of a man was found with significant injuries in Sydney yesterday, with initial inquiries indicating he may have been attacked by animals prior to his death.

NSW police said emergency services were called to a rural property in the suburb of Eschol Park in south-west Sydney on Wednesday around noon. On arrival, officers found the body of a 23-year-old man.

A crime scene was established and detectives have begun an investigation into the death.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

EV imports more than doubled in June quarter

Electric vehicle imports have also surged as the US-Iran conflict drove up petrol prices and sent motorists flocking to Chinese manufacturers such as BYD, AAP reports.

Battery electric vehicle sales more than doubled in the June quarter to 69,414, data from the Australian Automobile Association showed.

On the other hand, imports of automated data processing (ADP) equipment – including equipment used to fit out AI datacentres – fell by more than a quarter in the three months to June after a surge at the start of 2026.

Fuel diplomacy tanks Australia’s trade surplus

Australia has recorded its lowest quarterly trade surplus in almost a decade as the federal government raced to secure fuel cargoes during the Middle East oil crisis, AAP reports.

The jump in imports narrowed Australia’s goods trade surplus to $1.1bn in the June quarter, the lowest figure since 2017, Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showed on Thursday.

The Albanese government’s deal-making blitz to secure supplies from Australia’s fuel trading partners was evident in country-specific data.

Despite the decline in the quarterly trade surplus, the trade balance increased $4.3bn in the month of June, above forecasts. That was largely driven by a 60% jump in non-monetary gold exports, reversing a 35% decline in May.

Former ABC executive says Race Around the World clip about Rinehart not a breach, but worthy of apology

Alan Sunderland, a former editorial director at the ABC, has said he was not surprised the broadcaster’s ombudsman found an episode of its Race Around the World program did not breach its editorial standards related to harm and offence.

The program included a four-minute documentary that ended with crude and offensive comments about mining magnate Gina Rinehart, including a line about “mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll”. The ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, later apologised for the episode amid Rinehart’s threats of legal action, and the broadcaster edited the footage to remove the offending lines.

Sunderland said there was a “long history of latitude” at the ABC for content, “particularly with satirical entertainment programs where people ascertain that the depiction of violence, whatever it is, was clearly meant to be humorous”:

double quotation markIt is not per se a breach of standards to depict violence where nobody would reasonably in good faith think that it was an actual direct threat of violence.

Still, Sunderland said he believes it was probably right for Marks to apologise:

double quotation markI think the ABC needs to take account of public tastes on this. Public tastes move and shift over questions of what is and isn’t offensive, but I think there was a pretty common acceptance, even from the film-maker herself, that it was inappropriate. And I think they did the right thing to make that call, regardless of whether it breached editorial standards or not.

Marles was asked about home affairs minister Tony Burke’s delayed speech before the National Press Club about migration policies.

The deputy prime minister said the decision was merely a move of date, not a cancellation. Marles said:

double quotation markIt’s not unusual for dates to be moved around in people’s diaries and in terms of presenting speeches of that kind. I think what’s important here in terms of migration policy is complex. It’s one that we’ve been working on since we’ve come to government.

Tony Burke will be talking about that and he’ll be talking about that at the National Press Club at the earliest opportunity.

double quotation markMoving around dates in a diary for senior members of government is very routine. It happens literally all the time. The speech hasn’t been called off. A date has been changed. That literally happens every week. And there’s nothing more to it than that.

Marles maintains gambling reforms about striking a ‘balance’ over ‘complex’ issue

Richard Marles, the deputy prime minister, said the government still intends to get its gambling reforms past parliament despite opposition from the Greens and the Coalition, who both argue that they do not go far enough.

Marles spoke to RN Breakfast, echoing the government line that they are the “strongest reforms in respect of gambling advertising that have ever been put forward”. He went on:

double quotation markI mean, we are doing more in terms of breaking the link between gambling advertising and sport, more in terms of protecting our kids from being exposed to gambling advertising on TV and radio at the times when they would be watching and listening. We’re doing more in terms of supporting BetStop, which helps people who identify to restrict their own gambling habits.

So this is really important legislation and we’ll work with the parties across the parliament to get it passed.

When asked about criticism of the legislation, Marles said gambling was a “complex” issue with differing views.

double quotation markIt’s also an area where you need to strike a balance and we believe we’ve done that … We’re not saying that people should not be able to engage in betting but there needs to be a balance. And it’s important.

Penny Wong says Australia has ‘more work to do’ forging relationships in the Pacific

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is in Fiji today amid a meeting with her counterparts from across the Pacific.

Wong said Australia has been working to rebuild trust and Australia’s reputation in the region, as well as its “strategic position in the Pacific”.

double quotation markWe’ve got work more work to do. We’ve announced that we do want to engage with and negotiate with both Tonga and Solomon Islands. Obviously, there’ll be a lot of work there that we want to do with them in partnership.

Wong also said she hopes China “takes note” of the region-wide opposition to a ballistic missile test Beijing undertook in July.

double quotation markIt was a test which was destabilising and in a region where leaders have said we want an ocean of peace. It’s really important that partners respect that, and we would continue to encourage that respect.

Good morning, and welcome to Friday. It’s Nick Visser here to get us started. Here’s what’s on deck.

Australia has recorded its lowest quarterly trade surplus in nearly a decade amid a long push to secure fuel cargoes during the oil crisis in the Middle East.

Electric vehicle imports have surged, with battery EV sales more than doubling in the June quarter to nearly 70,000.

title: After the floods, hunger: Mozambique’s second disaster
excerpt:
Xai-Xai, Mozambique – Months after floodwaters tore through his neighbourhood, Joacim Pinto still walks past the empty plots where his crops once grew.

The ground that once gave his family food and i...
body_text:
Xai-Xai, Mozambique – Months after floodwaters tore through his neighbourhood, Joacim Pinto still walks past the empty plots where his crops once grew.

The ground that once gave his family food and income now stands as a reminder of what was lost. His livestock disappeared, and the gardens that provided food and security were swallowed by the floods.

But for Pinto, 50, the disaster did not end when the water receded.

For the resident of Xa-Xai, in Mozambique’s southern Gaza province, surviving the floods was only the beginning of the struggle.

“We either die from the floods, or if we survive, hunger takes over,” Pinto tells Al Jazeera.

The floods swept across Mozambique from late December 2025 into early 2026, leaving communities like Pinto’s facing a second crisis: finding enough money to buy food after losing the ability to produce much of it themselves.

“The floods destroyed our wells, pipes, livestock and gardens,” Pinto says. “The price of basic food increased sharply.”

Mozambique is still recovering from one of its most damaging flood seasons in recent years. The disaster affected communities across several central and southern provinces, including Gaza, Maputo, Inhambane, Sofala and Zambezia.

For farming families, the destruction was immediate. Fields disappeared under water, harvests were lost, and roads used to move food between farms and markets were damaged.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), about 275,405 hectares (680,540 acres) of farmland were affected, threatening the livelihoods of approximately 314,783 farmers.

In rural Mozambique, farming is not simply a source of income. It is a household safety net.

Before the floods, Pinto’s garden reduced his dependence on shops and traders. It provided food for his family and helped protect them from sudden price increases.

Now the gardens around his neighbourhood lie empty, and families who once relied on their own harvests must turn to markets where prices have climbed.

The United Nations’ World Food Programme (WFP) warned that flooding has disrupted access to food across many affected areas.

Roads became impassable, markets stopped operating in some communities, and transport costs increased. In places where floodwater cut roads, food could not easily reach people who needed it.

At the same time, local production fell as farmland was damaged.

“So, while the exact inflation rate varies by district, what we see on the ground is significant pressure on food prices driven by a dramatic reduction in supply, alongside a surge in humanitarian needs,” Ana Mato Hombre, WFP Mozambique spokesperson, tells Al Jazeera.

“In many flood-affected areas, food stocks were lost, cropland destroyed and several markets are not functioning at all,” she adds.

Hombre says isolated cases of traders taking advantage of shortages cannot be ruled out, but the main force behind rising prices appears to be the loss of production and disruption of supply routes.

The effects of the floods have travelled far beyond damaged fields.

“Every time we have floods or droughts in the Southern African region, food prices rise because of supply shortages and the high cost of importing food,” says Tafadzwanashe Mabhaudhi, a professor of climate change and food systems at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.

Mabhaudhi, who is originally from the region and has studied climate-related threats to food systems across Southern Africa, says repeated disasters are changing how vulnerable communities survive.

“It also means poorer diets because people cannot access a range of foods,” he tells Al Jazeera.

The latest floods came while communities were still recovering from the severe drought linked to the 2024–2025 El Nino weather pattern, which affected agricultural production across parts of southern Africa.

For families already weakened by drought, another disaster leaves little time to recover.

The crisis has also reached traders trying to keep food moving.

“We had no choice but to add 10 percent in markup to the price of rice, flour, live chicken and other products,” says Shuwa Anolis, a truck driver and food trader in Xai-Xai.

Flooding disrupted major transport routes linking southern and northern Mozambique, pushing up fuel and delivery costs.

“Look at the main highway linking south to north of the country; it was flooded and impassable. Our fuel costs remain high too,” Anolis tells Al Jazeera.

He says the price of prepared chicken increased after the floods because transporting and supplying food became more expensive.

But for families who lost their crops, higher prices add another burden.

Traders are trying to recover rising costs while households that once fed themselves from their own land are struggling to buy what they need.

Mozambique is repeatedly absorbing the costs of climate extremes despite contributing little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country’s exposure is shaped by geography, dependence on agriculture and limited resources to rebuild after disasters.

Mabhaudhi says Mozambique’s position downstream of major river systems also increases its vulnerability because flooding can be influenced by rainfall and land-use activities beyond its borders.

But the impact is not only measured in lost crops and damaged homes.

Repeated disasters are shrinking the time communities have to recover. Families lose crops, begin rebuilding and then face another shock before they have regained their footing.

For Pinto and thousands of other survivors, the disappearance of the floodwaters has not marked the end of the crisis.

The challenge now is rebuilding livelihoods before the next shock arrives.

“The same communities whose crops were devastated by drought are still recovering, and now they have been devastated by floods,” Mabhaudhi says. “There is a limit on people’s ability to cope with back-to-back disasters.”

title: Disneyland, actors' union clash over parental leave, benefits as union negotiates first contract
excerpt:
Flag retreat ceremony honors members of all U.S. military branches daily with an updated look for the 70th anniversary celebration.

Magic United, an affiliate of Actors' Equity representing 1,700 par...
body_text:
Flag retreat ceremony honors members of all U.S. military branches daily with an updated look for the 70th anniversary celebration.

Magic United, an affiliate of Actors' Equity representing 1,700 parade, show and character cast members at Disneyland, and Disney are in the midst of negotiations on a first contract, and they're telling Fox News Digital it's not going smoothly.

While most Disneyland employees have been represented by unions for decades, the Characters and Parades department remained nonunion until workers voted to organize in 2024 amid California’s cost-of-living crisis after the pandemic. This has led to negotiations between the newly formed union and Disney in order to negotiate a first contract both parties can agree on.

Because this is the workers' first union contract, both sides disagree over how to characterize Disney's proposals. Disney argues it is negotiating the initial terms of employment rather than eliminating existing union benefits. The union counters that workers currently receive benefits such as paid parental leave, so excluding them from the first contract would effectively mean employees lose those benefits.

The Los Angeles Times noted that, "Although the union said it has been getting movement on a number of health and safety issues, there are other points in contention, including the amount the company matches for employee contributions to their 401(k) retirement savings plans and a proposal that limits the number of times a worker can give away a shift without managerial approval."

DISNEYLAND MAY SCRAP LONG-STANDING PARK RULE THAT FRUSTRATED VISITORS

The union to represent Disneyland's character and parade performers only formed recently after the COVID-19 pandemic. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital contacted both parties about the ongoing negotiations, recalling founder Walt Disney’s famous anecdote about having founded the Disneyland park as a place where parents and their children can have fun together, asking whether Disney is fulfilling that mission as negotiations continue.

"Disneyland is often presented as ‘the ultimate family-friendly destination,’ but that’s no longer the case for 1,700 Cast Members in the Characters and Parades departments who create Disney magic by bringing beloved characters to life in shows, meet and greets and character dining experiences," a representative for the union responded.

"Disney has proposed eliminating paid parental leave for these workers and in the first year of a contract the company presented a zero percent wage increase – despite a period of high inflation. Orange County, California where Disneyland is located also is rated as one of the costliest places to live in the United States," the spokesperson added.

The representative claimed further that Disneyland "wants to eliminate paid parental leave, cut the number of paid holidays and size of401(k) contributions and make it unnecessarily harder for Character and Parade workers to swap shifts."

Al Vincent Jr., Actors’ Equity’s Executive Director, told the Los Angeles Times in a report about these negotiations, "When you propose to take away paid parental leave from those who work day in and day out to give other families great experiences, that’s not family friendly."

CHEAPEST DAYS TO VISIT DISNEY: HERE'S WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW BEFORE BOOKING YOUR TRIP

Jessica Jakary, a Disneyland Resort spokesperson, told Fox News Digital, "Disneyland Resort values its cast members, offers competitive benefits and is proud of its long history of working collaboratively with the unions that represent them." (David McNew/Getty Images)

Jessica Jakary, a Disneyland Resort spokesperson, has contested these claims, declaring to Fox News Digital, "Disneyland Resort values its cast members, offers competitive benefits and is proud of its long history of working collaboratively with the unions that represent them."

Disney as a company has stated that it is committed to ongoing negotiations with Magic United, noting to Fox News that there appears to be some confusion in the comparison to Walt Disney World in Florida where there are no state disability payments for parental leave like those provided for in California.

Disney has also said to Fox News Digital that it has not proposed to limit the ability to trade shifts, but instead the proposal only limits the number of times a cast member can give away a shift without managerial approval.

Disney also said that Disneyland Resort has proposed wage increases over the term of the agreement, and that while it is not offering an immediate wage increase, it has continued to provide annual increases to this bargaining unit as negotiations progress.

In one example provided, Disney claims that as of December 2025, full-time and part-time cast members in this bargaining unit have received a 4% increase.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Disneyland is in California, one of the most expensive states in America to live in. (iStock)

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

title: Meta fined $567m in largest child safety ruling against social media giant
excerpt:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has seen his company face an increasing number of lawsuits over child safety.

A US judge in New Mexico on Thursday ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure t...
body_text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has seen his company face an increasing number of lawsuits over child safety.

A US judge in New Mexico on Thursday ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure to warn the public about dangers its platforms posed to children, marking the largest ruling against the company over child safety.

Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the social media giant is a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution and that it must put the money in a fund aimed at reducing future harms.

The ruling is in addition to $375m in fines Meta was already ordered to pay in the case, for a total of $942m.

Judge Biedscheid compared Meta to a factory, with advertising and content as its product and "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children to be the pollution that must be abated".

Meta, which owns and operates Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, has been contacted by the BBC for comment.

Regarding the earlier $375m verdict against in the case, Meta had said it intended to appeal the ruling. It was the first time that a state had successfully sued Meta over child safety issues.

The case stems from a 2023 lawsuit brought by attorneys for the State of New Mexico, arguing Meta should be held liable for the way in which its platforms endangered children and exposed them to sexually explicit material and contact with sexual predators.

In the first phase of the trial, Meta was found to have repeatedly violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act as its recommendation algorithms essentially "steered" young users toward harmful content and contacts.

Recommendation algorithms are the tools that Meta uses to automatically curate the content a user sees on its platforms.

In ruling on this second phase of the trial, Judge Biedscheid found that Meta's harms reached the level of "public nuisance", or an issue of health and safety that has become so widespread it is negatively impacting a general public.

In addition to being the largest fine Meta has received over child safety issues, the ruling also appears to be the first time that a social media company has been deemed a public nuisance.

"Just as noxious pollution produced by the factory can harm the common public right to reasonably clean air, the harmful effects of Meta's platforms on children do not stay contained by its platforms and, instead, migrate to the internet as a whole and, perhaps most concerning, to the real world and create a common, societal burden on and harm to the affected children and their families and schools, as well as hospitals and law enforcement," the judge wrote.

Meta told to pay $375m for misleading users over child safety

She spent 16 hours on Instagram in a day. It's up to a jury to decide if Meta is to blame

Meta and TikTok let harmful content rise after evidence outrage drove engagement, say whistleblowers

title: Primary showdown: Polls close in Tennessee as conservative firebrand eyes governor's office
excerpt: Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., analyzes the Democratic strategy to limit President Donald Trump's war powers regarding Iran, calling it a 'delay tactic.' She emphasizes confronting Iran's nuclear amb...
body_text:
Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., analyzes the Democratic strategy to limit President Donald Trump's war powers regarding Iran, calling it a 'delay tactic.' She emphasizes confronting Iran's nuclear ambitions and its role in funding terrorist groups like Hamas. Blackburn also criticizes a Michigan Senate candidate for his anti-Israel comments.

The polls have closed in Tennessee as conservative firebrand Sen. Marsha Blackburn aims to change her work address from Washington D.C., to Nashville.

The former longtime congresswoman and two-term senator with a robust national profile thanks to her regular cable news appearances is considered the front-runner in Thursday's Republican gubernatorial primary, in the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Bill Lee.

The Republican face-off for governor of Tennessee, where Democrats haven't won a gubernatorial election in two decades, takes top billing as the red-leaning southeastern state holds nominating contests for state and federal offices.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee is running for governor in the 2026 race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Bill Lee. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Blackburn is running in a race that also includes four-term Rep. John Rose, who like Blackburn is a staunch Capitol Hill supporter of President Donald Trump, and state Rep. Monty Fritts.

Even though the president handed out endorsements in other GOP gubernatorial primaries this cycle, Trump remained neutral in the Tennessee contest.

"Unfortunately, she’s running for governor. She’s running for governor of Tennessee. I’d love her not to, I begged her," Trump said in January. "‘I said, ‘Marsha, don’t. We don’t want to lose you in the Senate.’"

But the president has said Blackburn would be a good governor, and also noted that Rose has been a staunch loyalist.

Even though she didn't land Trump's endorsement, Blackburn has showcased her support for him.

"As President Trump sends power and authority back to the states, I'm ready to deliver for the people of the Volunteer State and make our state America's conservative leader," she wrote on the eve of the primary in a social media post that included a photo of her and Trump.

Five Democrats, including Memphis City Councilwoman Jerri Green, are bidding for their party's gubernatorial nomination.

Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., is seen inside the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 4, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc.)

Tennessee's other U.S. senator, Republican Bill Hagerty, is unopposed in the GOP primary as he seeks a second six-year term in the Senate.

Five Democrats are vying to challenge Hagerty in the general election. Then-Sen. Al Gore's re-election 36 years ago was the last time a Democrat won a Senate contest in Tennessee.

In U.S. House battles, Memphis voters will cast ballots for their Democratic and Republican nominees using a new GOP-drawn congressional district map that created an extra right-leaning seat and forced longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen to not seek re-election.

Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) walks through the U.S. Capitol on February 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, two-term Republican Rep. Andy Ogles, a major Trump ally in the House who is backed by the president, is facing a stiff primary challenge from Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, who was endorsed earlier this week by Lee. The race has seen a large infusion of money from outside groups.

Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Sam Acho Q&A: Former NFL player and ESPN analyst speaks out on civility and accountability in sports and media
excerpt:
Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Acho is working with the Reagan Foundation Center on Civility & Democracy to promote civility.

Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Ac...
body_text:
Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Acho is working with the Reagan Foundation Center on Civility & Democracy to promote civility.

Former NFL player and current ESPN NFL analyst Sam Acho attended the Ronald Reagan Foundation Center on Civility & Democracy’s inaugural Reagan Civility & Democracy Forum last week.

There, he advocated for improving civility among Americans, especially in sports.

"We talked about civility in sports and how many of the same attributes athletes use can be applied to civil discourse: sportsmanship, winning and losing the right way, and playing within a set of rules," Acho told Fox News Digital.

PATRIOTS LEGEND ROB GRONKOWSKI REVEALS THE IMPACT POLITICS HAS ON LOCKER ROOM DYNAMICS

As a former pro athlete and now a top sports media figure, Acho shared his vision for the role of athletes and sports media in promoting civility across the country, and how Sophie Cunningham fits into it, in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital.

Questions and answers have been shortened for brevity and focus.

Sam Acho No. 74 of the Buffalo Bills looks on during a preseason game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field in Detroit on Aug. 23, 2019. (Getty Images)

Q: What does civil discourse look like to you?

Sam Acho: It can include disagreement. You don’t always have to be on the same page. In football, some people believe in a 3-4 defense; others prefer a 4-3. Some say you have to blitz to get to the quarterback... others believe in playing coverage... but the goal is the same: to win the game.

In society — especially among political leaders — the goal should be to serve the country and make it better... People may disagree about which law or approach is best, but at the end of the day, it’s about wanting the country to be better.

Q: Did conversations about politics and other issues happen in NFL locker rooms?

Sam Acho: Nowhere in the locker room was it not allowed to have certain conversations...

We'd have debates about, um, is it harder to, to be a track athlete or a golfer.

We'd also have political debates. We'd talk about politics, talk about certain rules, certain laws. "Hey, what do we think about what the president said? What do we think about what this governor is trying to do?"

... I remember we were, when Colin Kaepernick was taking a knee and protesting during the national anthem, we weren't shying away from that.

Colin Kaepernick, center, kneeled during the national anthem before an NFL game against the Dallas Cowboys. ( )

Q: Did those conversations ever become uncivil?

Sam Acho: In any family, in any team, in any conversation, you may cross the line, but usually when you cross the line, you either apologize or they apologize, or you try to find a way to make it right.

I'm not, I'm not gonna pretend that we lived in a utopia... But when you cross the line or when you go out of bounds or when you make a mistake, okay, you either apologize, or when you lose, right, you shake hands, you move on, right?

When the conversations did become uncivil, or maybe we had a big disagreement, I didn't drop my ball and walk away. No, I actually went and said, "Oh, we have practice in like 15 minutes." Then we had meetings in two hours. Then we were together at lunch the next day.

Q: How could the NFL and its players, coaches and executives help promote civility?

Sam Acho: I think one thing that athletes have that many other people don't is a platform. A lot of athletes have a platform... And I think one area that quarterbacks, that coaches, that players, that athletes can continue to use is their platform, not only to speak out on issues that matter to them, but also to educate themselves on issues that matter.

And so one area I think that athletes... and coaches and executives can do is to continue to speak up and, and stay educated on topics.

Q: Do you believe using that platform to speak up on topics comes with the risk of promoting uncivil discourse?

Sam Acho: Everything comes with risk. Life comes with risk... But oftentimes it's not really about risk, it's more about... how do you respond to defeat? How do you respond to adversity? How do you respond to, uh, something not going your way?

When I'm on TV... there's a risk that people may disagree with my opinion, but that doesn't mean that I just absolve myself from the conversation. It's understanding the risk... and still moving forward with an educated perspective.

Q: But in general, you would encourage more athletes, especially those with platforms, to make their feelings on certain topics known?

Sam Acho: I would encourage athletes to continue to understand that they are more than just what you do on a field. That's probably my biggest encouragement. Oftentimes... you, as an athlete, you think that, or people tell you that you are what you put on tape.

That you're only that, and you're more than just that. There's our human capital. There's your physical capital. Yes, you train, you eat right, you go to sleep on time to be the best athlete you can be. But there's also your intellectual capital.

KATIE UHLAENDER: ATHLETES RISK PAYING THE PRICE IF PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT IS PASSED

Athletes should know they are more than one dimension of a human being. The same is true for people in politics: You are more than a governor or a senator. You should ask who you are becoming as you make decisions. Are you simply trying to gather as much power as possible, or do you recognize that there is something beyond one election or one vote?

Q: What do you think about Sophie Cunningham’s recent use of her platform?

Sophie Cunningham #8 of the Indiana Fever looks on against the Minnesota Lynx in the fourth quarter at Target Center on August 02, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Lynx defeated the Fever 108-100. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) (David Berding/Getty Images)

Sam Acho: So I'd have to get, I'd have to dial myself back more in to see what kind of what Sophie Cunningham has been saying and not saying, but I will say, I go back to this. Like, as an athlete, you have an opportunity to use your platform and to steward it well. You absolutely do.

And I don't think that athletes should shy away from speaking up for what they believe. I think so many people in society, they speak up for what they believe. And know that, yeah, there's a risk involved for sure. I think that athletes should continue to use and to steward their platform, knowing that you may not be liked you may not be liked, but I think athletes should continue to use their platform and steward it well.

Q: How can sports media figures do a better job of promoting civil discourse?

Sam Acho: It goes back to the idea of platform. A lot of sports media figures, not all, but many were former athletes. So they put down that physical side, now they're using the intellectual side.

And I think it is remembering that even as a sports media, media figure, you do have a platform. Pat McAfee has a huge platform on ESPN. I think about, um, and what he's been able to do with his platform, and then using that to realize that people follow you. People listen to you. People may not agree with everything you say, but you do have a platform, and you want to steward it well.

Your voice, your opinion, those things are yours. So they're yours to steward. They're not yours to say, "Okay, how can I gather as much power, as many followers as I can?" And just waste it. No, you're a steward.

Q: What does it look like to steward a sports media platform poorly?

Sam Acho: There was a game last year, last season, or maybe the season before, and Texas played Georgia. And third quarter of the game or so, late third quarter, there was a call that didn't go Texas's way. Texas was the home team. They were hosting Georgia. And a lot of the fans were upset the referees missed the call. Well, while the referees missed the call, all of a sudden the fans at Texas started to throw cans and, and bottles and things on the field in order to delay the game so that the referees could go and maybe look at the call and try and reverse the call.

And the referees did end up going and changing the call. Texas still lost the game, number one. Number two, it wasn't a good look for, uh, it wasn't a good look for Texas, and I think it's even being willing to say that, right? Not just saying, "Well, look, I went there and I'm a broadcaster and we won or we lost or they got the call right." No, the call was wrong, but you don't go and say, "I'm gonna just throw bottles on the field," and say that that's okay. I think that no matter who you are in sports and sports media and, and no matter what avenue you have, I think it's wise to say, "Hey, that was wrong. He was out of bounds.

"We were out of bounds." And, and realizing that it may cost you the game. And even if you try to, even if you do that thing that was wrong and, and, and, uh, you get the call that goes in your favor, what did you actually win??

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: Some of Doge's $110bn saving reports are wrong or lack evidence, US watchdog finds
excerpt:
Elon Musk (left) was formerly in charge of

Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supporting evid...
body_text:
Elon Musk (left) was formerly in charge of

Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supporting evidence", a watchdog has found.

A report released on Thursday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has given an extensive review of Doge's claims about its so-called Wall of Receipts, which reported savings of $110bn (£82bn) across contracts, grants and leases.

"Several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the report stated.

Asked for comment, a White House official said the administration told the GAO that all employees had to complete ethics training and follow financial disclosure requirements.

Doge, the Department of Government Efficiency, was not an official government department. It launched at the start of President Trump's second term but closed last month. Its Wall of Receipts was a way of showing its purported savings in taxpayer money online.

Elon Musk, the billionaire boss of Tesla and SpaceX who formerly led Doge but left in May 2025, initially promised to save as much as $2tn a year by slashing federal jobs and shuttering government programmes, among other cost-cutting measures.

Even by Doge's own estimates, it fell short of that goal, as its website claims to have saved an estimated $214bn.

"While Doge provided some information about estimated savings, several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the GAO report stated.

It said Doge had not been transparent regarding the methods it used to calculate savings, highlighting it "did not provide sufficient information to verify the method used to calculate 96% of Doge-reported savings".

Among its specific findings was that 108 of the 264 leases identified by Doge for termination were already in the process of ending before the body was established. That accounts for about $15.3m of the total $53.5m in savings Doge claimed.

"The Wall of Receipts does not include an explanation of how the savings from terminated leases were calculated," the GAO said.

Claims were also made about savings that were not achieved, like $1.7bn for ending a defence department contract for IT services. However, the contract was never terminated and thus no savings were achieved, according to the congressional watchdog's report.

"While the Wall of Receipts includes some information about the data and sources underlying reported savings, it does not sufficiently disclose limitations affecting data quality," it assessed.

The GAO audit, which was carried out at the request of Democratic Senators Gary Peters and Richard Blumenthal, covered savings data reported from 20 January  2025 through 7 July 2026.

"Everyone supports rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, but Doge was a slapdash and deceptive effort that misled the American people while doing real damage to the government's ability to serve them," Senator Peters said in a statement on Thursday.

Under Musk, Doge pushed for massive reductions in the federal workforce, as well as the shuttering of programmes and even agencies such as the US Agency for International Development (USAID).

Some of Doge's moves were met with legal fights, or were reversed. When the group's cost-cutting resulted in bird flu officials at the US Department of Agriculture being fired, the Trump administration looked to re-hire them days later.

In a social media post last month announcing its closure, Doge said: "While the formal mission of Doge has come to an end, the mission to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse will continue. Good stewardship of taxpayer dollars and accountable government are not temporary initiatives."

Elon Musk says Doge was 'somewhat successful' but he would not do it again

title: EXCLUSIVE: Michigan House speaker calls for answers over $300M taxpayer-funded Rx Kids program
excerpt: Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall discusses concerns over Michigan's Rx Kids initiative, including taxpayer funding, unrestricted cash payments, eligibility requirements and what he calls a broader gua...
body_text:
Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall discusses concerns over Michigan's Rx Kids initiative, including taxpayer funding, unrestricted cash payments, eligibility requirements and what he calls a broader guaranteed income effort.

The Republican leader of Michigan’s House says a state-funded maternal health initiative has become something far different than lawmakers were promised, accusing Democrats of using more than $300 million in taxpayer funding to advance a broader guaranteed-income agenda.

Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall made the remarks in an interview with Fox News Digital as House Republicans continue scrutinizing Rx Kids, a taxpayer-funded program that provides unrestricted cash payments to pregnant women and new mothers.

Hall argued lawmakers believed they were funding a maternal and prenatal health initiative, not what he described as a broader experiment in guaranteed income.

GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE

Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall discusses his concerns about Michigan's Rx Kids program. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"I think the Democrats kind of slipped this in here under the idea that it was for prenatal care," Hall told Fox News Digital. "Lawmakers did not have the complete picture."

Rx Kids launched in Flint in 2024 and provides expectant mothers with a $1,500 lump-sum payment during pregnancy, followed by $500 monthly payments after the child is born.

According to materials provided to Fox News Digital by Hall’s office, the program has expanded to communities across Michigan with more than $300 million in taxpayer funding.

Rx Kids has promoted the initiative as a maternal and infant health program designed to reduce financial stress for new families. According to podcast interviews and program materials, its leaders have also discussed expanding the model to communities across Michigan and beyond.

EXCLUSIVE: VIDEO SHOWS MICHIGAN LAWMAKER TOURING DAYCARE IN $1.1M TAXPAYER FUNDING PROBE

Hall argued the program lacks the eligibility requirements found in traditional public assistance programs.

"We have a lot of social safety net programs in our country that are working very well," Hall said. "They have eligibility checks. They look at citizenship. They look at income verification.

"Rx Kids, by design, is given to anyone that has a child," he continued. "They don’t look for citizenship. They just pay out anyone that has a child."

Hall’s office also provided Fox News Digital with video of legislative committee testimony in which program officials acknowledged payments had been made to individuals who were not legally present in the United States.

CALIFORNIA ‘BASIC INCOME’ EXPERIMENT FAILS TO PROVIDE ‘FINANCIAL INDEPENDENCE,’ STUDY FINDS

Hall argued taxpayer-funded cash assistance should include income and legal status requirements similar to those used by existing public assistance programs.

"What we prefer are the traditional welfare programs like Medicaid, the food stamp program and the WIC program," Hall said. "They make sure you’re here legally, they make sure you’re not making a lot of money and then they give you the benefit. That’s not what Rx Kids is."

Hall also criticized the program’s unrestricted cash payments, noting recipients are not required to spend the money on diapers, formula, housing or other expenses related to pregnancy or caring for a newborn.

"They give you this free cash and there are no strings attached by definition," Hall said.

MAYORS WANT TO KEEP HANDING OUT FREE CASH AFTER FEDERAL FUNDS DRIED UP

The cover of the Rx Kids playbook describes how communities can replicate the Michigan-based maternal cash assistance program. (rxkids.org)

Hall said caseworkers had told him they had seen recipients use the money for alcohol, drugs and gambling. Fox News Digital has not independently verified those claims.

The speaker also pointed to public comments from Rx Kids leaders that he said reinforced Republican concerns that the initiative is intended to become something larger than a maternal health program.

Hall's office also shared podcast interviews in which Rx Kids co-founder Luke Shaefer discussed the expanded Child Tax Credit and the role he believes Rx Kids can play following the expiration of those federal payments.

In a separate interview, Dr. Mona Hanna, the leader of Rx Kids, discussed her vision of expanding the initiative into a government-scale public program.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED RECOUNTS SMASHING VODKA BOTTLE AFTER BEARD CRITICISM

Hall said those remarks aligned with his assessment of Rx Kids.

"This is a progressive left-wing experiment toward basically a universal income," Hall said. "They’re trying to move the welfare state down that lane."

Hall also questioned the program’s advisory network.

Hall's office also shared archived versions of the Rx Kids website that listed Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan Secretary of State and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson's husband Ryan Friedrichs and Community Change official Dorian Warren as members of the program's advisory circle.

MICHIGAN’S TOP ELECTION OFFICIAL WINS DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR, ADVANCES TO BATTLEGROUND RACE

The advisory circle page was removed from the organization’s website days after lawmakers questioned program leaders during a June 2 Michigan House Oversight Committee hearing.

The timing of the removal does not establish why the page was taken down.

"Our secretary of state’s husband is on the advisory board. Abdul El-Sayed is on the board," Hall said. "It’s like a who’s who of radical left Democrats."

Hall’s office also pointed to an Rx Kids white paper examining voter turnout among recipients and the program’s promotion of Vot-ER, a physician-backed voter registration organization powered by TurboVote.

Materials provided by Hall’s office also identified Hanna as an adviser to Vot-ER.

Hall said those connections and the program’s research into voting behavior deserved additional scrutiny.

"We’re trying to understand why are you so interested in the voting pattern of the people that are receiving your no-strings-attached welfare," Hall said. "We aren’t getting good answers."

Hall said House Republicans did not include additional funding for Rx Kids in Michigan’s newly signed budget, though the program still has access to previously appropriated funds.

TRUMP ADMIN PAUSING OVER $1B IN MEDICAID PAYMENTS TO MINNESOTA, CALIFORNIA OVER FRAUD, COMPLIANCE CONCERNS

Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall, left, stands with Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Hall has criticized the state's Rx Kids program. (Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"The good news is that we cut off funding to this program in the new budget," Hall said. "In the future, we’re going to try to put guardrails around it so that it goes to the people that truly need it."

Rather than eliminating assistance for struggling families, Hall said he wants taxpayer dollars directed toward existing programs that assess financial need and place restrictions on how certain benefits can be spent.

"I think people support those programs," Hall said. "They have eligibility requirements to ensure that you’re not taking advantage of the system."

Fox News Digital reached out to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s office, Rx Kids and Michigan State University for comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Travel restrictions – from Israel and Europe – trap students in Gaza
excerpt:
Mariam al-Najar, a 24-year-old student from Khan Younis in Gaza, was waiting for a message that could change her life.

When an email arrived two weeks after she applied for a scholarship from the Uni...
body_text:
Mariam al-Najar, a 24-year-old student from Khan Younis in Gaza, was waiting for a message that could change her life.

When an email arrived two weeks after she applied for a scholarship from the University of Cassino and Southern Lazio in Italy, she felt, for a brief moment at least, that years of studying had finally paid off.

The university confirmed that she had been offered a place for a master’s degree in economics and management, one of the few times during a long period of despair that Mariam had felt any hope about the future.

“Being accepted was like a ray of light that suddenly appeared and gave me a sense of life and hope again,” she told Al Jazeera. “I was applying for scholarships while feeling deeply hopeless and I never expected to receive an acceptance.”

The scholarship offer was not just an opportunity for Mariam to continue higher studies at a leading university but also offered hope of a new future amid Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza.

But securing a place at the university opened the door to a whole new set of challenges for Mariam.

Italy was a main destination for the evacuation of Palestinian students from the Gaza Strip between 2025 and 2026.

Approximately 229 students were evacuated from Gaza prior to May 2026, with another group of around 40 students joining in June 2026.

Part of the reason for the high demand is attributed to the lower living and tuition costs in Italy compared to many other European countries. In Italy, the annual figure for students is around €10,200 ($11,773), compared with the United Kingdom and 30,000 pounds ($40,408) to 60,000 pounds ($80,820) per year.

For Mariam, these still substantial costs were not the immediate challenge, the difficulty was how to reach Italy amid Israel’s siege on Gaza.

“I did not believe that travel had become guaranteed, because the acceptance was only the beginning of the journey,” she said. “There are still many steps and challenges that need to be overcome.”

Mariam applied for a visa and was approved, before she then contacted several organisations who may have been able to facilitate her journey to Italy. But Israeli restrictions on travel, made even tougher as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, mean that she has not yet been given permission to leave Gaza. That has put her arrival at the university in time for the start of autumn term in doubt.

Every passing day in besieged Gaza brings a sense of lost opportunities for Mariam, particularly as Israel has almost completely destroyed the enclave’s educational sector and infrastructure.

“It feels as though this is not just a journey for education; it has become a major challenge. Many students have had their visa applications rejected more than once and there are obstacles preventing students from travelling and continuing their studies abroad,” she said.

“After years of trying and holding on to hope, losing this opportunity or having my studies postponed has become a nightmare that I fear could come true. This scholarship represents more than just education for me. It is a path towards a future I have tried to reach despite all circumstances.”

Many students in Gaza have faced similar offers to study abroad, but seen their hopes crushed due to difficulties in travel and funding.

“Behind every application and every scholarship, there is a student with a dream who is simply trying not to lose their future,” she said.

“The scholarship is not just an opportunity to study; it is a hope that the years of our resilience and struggle during the war will not turn into a lost dream.”

The Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it works with universities to help facilitate travel for students from Gaza to Italy.

But the main obstacle facing them is not obtaining university admission itself, but navigating a Kafkaesque bureaucracy, both to leave Gaza and to enter Italy, said Professor Giovanna Citti from the University of Bologna.

“The main obstacle facing Palestinian students from Gaza is not obtaining university admission itself, but their ability to leave Gaza and complete the procedures required to reach Italy,” Citti said. “Even after receiving admission, students need authorisation to leave Gaza and, in many cases, they have to transit through Israel and Jordan.”

“Humanitarian corridors required intensive diplomatic negotiations because obtaining exit permits from Gaza is extremely difficult,” Citti added. “The students are academically qualified and highly motivated. The problem is not their ability to study; the problem is creating a clear and reliable pathway for them to reach their universities.”

“The delay in travel procedures has become a major concern for students who have already received scholarships and university places.”

As increasing numbers of students find themselves in similar situations to Mariam, initiatives focused on scholarships and student travel have emerged to address the growing challenge.

One of those is Gaza40+, which has more than 1,200 registered Palestinian students seeking help in continuing their education outside Gaza. Students risk losing their scholarships or university places if they fail to reach the university in time for fixed enrolment deadlines.

More than 500 of these students have already received university offers from institutions across Europe, while others continue receiving support throughout the application and scholarship process. The initiative says registrations continue to increase, with about five to 10 new student and volunteer registrations received each day.

Gaza40+ has helped 120 students leave Gaza to continue their studies abroad since it was formed, in addition to 20 family members who travelled with them.

Despite hundreds of students securing university admissions and scholarships, leaving Gaza remains the biggest obstacle to continuing their education.

Gaza40+ says the absence of a clear and consistent humanitarian pathway to exit Gaza for universities abroad is one of the biggest challenges for Palestinian students.

The initiative says that while some countries had previously provided relatively easier routes for students from Gaza, that was now changing.

In Italy, for example, students were recently informed that they must demonstrate Italian language proficiency before being considered for evacuation from Gaza. While the government says the requirement is essential, it creates another barrier for students already in the heart of one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

“Students are not losing opportunities because of their academic qualifications or their commitment. They are losing them because of circumstances beyond their control,” said Nasser Taha from Gaza40+.

“We need stronger coordination between governments, universities, and international organisations to ensure that Gaza students can reach their universities and do not lose their educational opportunities.”

Gaza40+ says ensuring a pathway for students from Gaza to their studies abroad requires coordination between governments, universities and international organisations.

Doaa Fawzi Hamdan, a student at the University of Bologna, said that scholarship had appeared to provide an opportunity for her to continue her education after three years of disruptions in Gaza.

Despite completing all the required paperwork – and frequent electricity shortages, weak internet connection and forced displacement – she is still waiting for an Italian visa.

“The most difficult part is receiving acceptance from a university but not knowing whether you will be able to reach it on time,” Doaa told Al Jazeera. “We are not asking for special treatment. We only want the opportunity to reach our universities and begin our studies like students everywhere in the world.”

title: ‘No red line’: South Lebanon residents outraged as Israel resumes strikes
excerpt:
As Israel resumes strikes and displacement orders in southern Lebanon, residents of the region are expressing anger and helplessness during ongoing talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials.

For d...
body_text:
As Israel resumes strikes and displacement orders in southern Lebanon, residents of the region are expressing anger and helplessness during ongoing talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials.

For displaced families, Thursday’s latest round of strikes, which injured at least eight people, is further evidence that the June ceasefire has failed to protect them from Israeli military action. The Israeli military sparked this latest wave of panic by issuing a forced evacuation order for the town of Mansouri on Wednesday, marking its first displacement directive in weeks.

“Mansouri is not part of Israel’s occupation zone,” Yousef Shehemi, mayor of the neighboring town of Majdal Zoun, told Al Jazeera’s Zeina Khodr. “But Israel has no red lines—they target where they want. They have not respected any ceasefire.”

Families from Mansouri who fled were still gathered on the outskirts of the town on Thursday, waiting for word that it was safe to return.

Outrage was mounting on the ground as residents watched the Israeli military demolish homes and set fire to farmland, with many expressing little faith that ongoing negotiations between Beirut and Israel will secure their safe return.

Abu Rached, a resident of Majdal Zoun, said the destruction had gone unanswered by Lebanese officials. “Can’t you see what they did to south Lebanon? They’re destroying it, displacing people—even the [Lebanese] army can’t stay in Mansouri,” he told Al Jazeera. “Where are the officials?”

Representatives from Lebanon and Israel met in Rome for another round of negotiations earlier this week, after both governments signed a “framework” intended to secure an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon once Hezbollah is disarmed.

Hezbollah, which is not a part of the ongoing talks, has publicly opposed the deal.

The deal also envisioned “pilot zones” where Israel would pull back and the Lebanese army would move in to ensure there are no weapons outside the control of the state, allowing displaced people to return. But so far, the agreement has not secured any significant Israeli withdrawal in southern Lebanon.

The Israeli military has been systematically wiping out villages in south Lebanon, demolishing buildings and burning olive groves —a push that critics say amounts to an ethnic cleansing campaign.

Still, the region had seen relative calm over the past months. Hostilities renewed this week after an explosive device killed two invading Israeli soldiers, though it is not clear whether it was planted before or after the ceasefire.

Hezbollah did not claim responsibility for the attack.

The Israeli attacks were concentrated in Mansouri but not confined to it.

Further north, in Burj al-Shemali, an Israeli strike hit a residential home, marking the first attack on the town since the ceasefire took effect in June. Almaza Hazim, a resident, described to Al Jazeera the chaos of trying to help a neighboring family caught in the blast.

“Our neighbour was screaming from the explosion. We ran to help them—there were injuries—before another strike destroyed the house,” Hazim said.

title: Cruise line's tougher booking rules ignite backlash over higher deposits and payments
excerpt: Gambling influencer Bobby Rivas, known online as "Bluffin Bob," surprises a Virgin Voyages cabin steward with a $5,000 cash tip after winning at the ship’s casino, sparking emotional reactions from vi...
body_text:
Gambling influencer Bobby Rivas, known online as "Bluffin Bob," surprises a Virgin Voyages cabin steward with a $5,000 cash tip after winning at the ship’s casino, sparking emotional reactions from viewers online.

Princess Cruises is introducing stricter booking policies, including higher deposits and earlier final payment deadlines, fueling mixed reactions among travelers.

Among the biggest changes is an update to the timeline for final payments, the cruise line confirmed in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Beginning with new bookings for sailings departing in 2027 and beyond, we are implementing a 120-day final payment and a modified cancellation fee schedule," the company said.ANGRY CRUISE PASSENGERS BLAST MAJOR LINE OVER SURPRISE DAILY GRATUITY HIKE"These changes bring greater consistency to the booking process and reflect broader industry practices, while also helping ensure that guests have fair access to the staterooms and sailings they want to experience," the statement continued.

The new rules will take effect on Sept. 2 for new bookings on sailings departing Jan. 1, 2027. Guests were notified of the policy changes in an email from the cruise line, according to industry website Cruise Critic.

Princess Cruises is tightening its booking policies by requiring larger deposits and moving final payment deadlines earlier. (iStock)

The cruise line is also increasing standard deposits. Guests booking seven-day cruises in inside, oceanview, balcony and mini-suite staterooms will now pay $300 per person, up from $250, while suite deposits will increase from $500 to $600 per person, according to the review website.

Princess Cruises also noted that reservations will automatically be canceled if final payment is not received by the deadline, though guests will continue receiving payment reminders before the due date, according to reports.

The policy changes have prompted debate among cruise fans on social media. Some travelers said the earlier deadlines will not affect their vacation plans because they typically pay off cruises as soon as possible.

"I pay it all as soon as I book," one person wrote on TikTok. "I get my reservations in that day, and I'm always sail ready."

The new rules will take effect Sept. 2 for new bookings on sailings departing Jan. 1, 2027. (iStock)

Another commenter said, "I don't mind these changes because I like to pay off my trips as fast as I can so that I'm able to begin saving for the next one."

Others, however, questioned why passengers would be required to put down more money earlier in the booking process.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Those deposits are crazy," one commenter wrote.

Another person argued that the earlier payment deadline could create problems for travelers using payment plans.

Princess Cruises' decision to tighten its booking policies has generated mixed reactions from cruise fans on social media. (iStock)

"120 days out for final payment is the worst of all of it!" the commenter wrote. "Especially people who are on payment plans."

The booking changes come as other cruise lines have also introduced policies that have frustrated some travelers.

Fox News Digital previously reported that Celebrity Cruises faced backlash after raising its automatic gratuity charges with little notice, prompting some passengers to say they would tip crew members directly in cash instead.

The cruise line increased its daily automatic gratuities by $1.50 per person across all stateroom categories, raising the charges to between $19.50 and $24.50 per guest, per day.

Many passengers criticized the timing of the announcement, saying they were notified the same day the higher rates took effect.

"At this point, they just need to include gratuities in their fare like the luxury lines do," one Reddit user wrote.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.
