Hong returned as nat...
body_text:
Seoul ‌police have raided the Korea Football Association (KFA) offices ⁠⁠as part of an “obstruction of business” investigation into the appointment of former coach Hong Myung-bo.

Hong returned as national ⁠team coach in 2024 after a previous spell in charge from 2013 to 2014.

His appointment came under scrutiny after the KFA abandoned a months-long search involving foreign candidates ‌and appointed him following a brief meeting.

The issue resurfaced after South Korea’s disappointing FIFA World Cup campaign, which ended in a group-stage exit.

At a parliamentary hearing last month, Hong rejected suggestions by lawmakers that he had received special treatment in his appointment, ⁠while taking responsibility for South Korea’s ⁠failure at the tournament.

South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism said in October 2024 that the KFA breached its own rules in the appointments of Hong and former coach Jurgen Klinsmann, finding that the technical director’s ⁠meeting with Hong did not constitute ⁠a proper interview.

However, it found no evidence of illegal conduct and did not order Hong’s contract to be cancelled.

Police had already been ‌investigating complaints alleging improper interference in Hong’s appointment before the World Cup.

No criminal findings have been announced ‌against ‌Hong or KFA officials.

The KFA did not immediately respond to a request by Al Jazeera for comment.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Illegal immigrant's hit-and-run on 'kind' elderly woman triggers ICE action: 'Could hear screaming'
excerpt: President Donald Trump outlines a major new initiative at the White House aimed at fast-tracking commercial trucking licenses for military veterans. Trump criticizes leftist policies that help grant c...
body_text:
President Donald Trump outlines a major new initiative at the White House aimed at fast-tracking commercial trucking licenses for military veterans. Trump criticizes leftist policies that help grant commercial licenses to undocumented immigrants, claiming they cause deadly crashes on highways, and promises to quickly replace those unauthorized drivers with certified military veterans who deserve these high-paying jobs.

FIRST ON FOX: An illegal immigrant’s alleged hit-and-run that critically injured an elderly woman outside her Miami-Dade home prompted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to urge local authorities to "cooperate with us and not release this criminal from jail."

Seventy-four-year-old Geraldine Byrd, whom neighbors described as "kind" and friendly, is on life support in critical condition after authorities say she was run over by illegal immigrant Tomas Raymundo Brito, according to CBS Miami.

The outlet reported that Brito allegedly struck Byrd twice outside her home early Sunday morning. Byrd had stepped out of her car to open her gate when Brito allegedly struck her vehicle, causing it to spin into Byrd before his truck allegedly struck her again, trapping her underneath the vehicle.

Neighbors were reportedly alerted to the crash by the sound of a loud boom. One neighbor, named Kristina Diaz, told NBC 6 South Florida that "we could hear screaming, we could hear everybody yelling, ‘Where is she? Oh, she’s underneath the car. Call 911.’"

MAN CHARGED IN CRASH THAT KILLED MOTHER AND TWO YOUNG SONS HAS ICE DETAINER, PRIOR DWI CONVICTIONS

Seventy-four-year-old Geraldine Byrd, a woman described as "kind" and friendly by her neighbors, is on life support in critical condition after allegedly being run over by illegal immigrant Tomas Raymundo Brito (right). (Daniel A. Varela/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images; DHS)

The same neighbor told the outlet that Byrd "would always send my daughter gifts for her birthday. So, she was a very kind woman." Speaking in Spanish, another neighbor, Flor Ortiz, told CBS Miami that although she and Byrd "do not speak the same language, but we always greet each other. She is a good person."

After the incident, Brito allegedly got out of the truck and fled the scene. A family member of Byrd’s reportedly chased him down and found him hiding in a shed. After his arrest, Brito reportedly admitted he was the driver and said he drank five beers before the incident.

Byrd was airlifted to a nearby hospital and remains on life support in critical condition, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

Brito was charged with leaving the scene of a crash causing serious bodily injury and driving without a license.

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF TRYING TO DISARM VIRGINIA POLICE OFFICER

Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava, center, gives her opening remarks during a news conference about the Memorial Day weekend mass shootings, Monday, May 31, 2021 at the Fred Taylor Miami-Dade Police Headquarters in Doral, Fla. (Carl Juste/Miami Herald via AP)

Fox News Digital learned that ICE lodged a detainer with the Miami-Dade Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center the same day Brito was arrested.

Brito entered the U.S. illegally at an unknown date and location, according to DHS. He is a Guatemalan national.

"This criminal illegal alien from Guatemala is charged with hit-and-run after a drunk-driving accident that sent a 74-year-old woman to the hospital in critical condition in Miami-Dade County," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"He should have never been allowed in our communities or on our streets," Mullin continued, adding, "ICE is asking officials in Miami-Dade County to cooperate with us and not release this criminal from jail, and to turn him over to ICE custody so we can remove him from our country."

Mullin added that "thanks to the strong leadership of President Donald Trump, ICE is unleashed to go after criminal illegal aliens like this one so that we can make America safe again."

A spokesperson for the Miami-Dade Corrections and Rehabilitation Department confirmed with Fox News Digital that the department had received ICE's request and that Brito is currently in custody.

The spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "Miami-Dade County honors these detainer requests in accordance with the law by holding the individual for the authorized 48-hour period."

The spokesperson said that "if ICE does not take custody of the individual within that timeframe, the individual is released as required by law."

"Miami-Dade County and the Miami-Dade Corrections and Rehabilitation Department comply with all applicable laws regarding immigration detainer requests and do not deny detainer requests submitted by federal authorities," the spokesperson added.

NEW MAINE LAW LIMITS POLICE COOPERATION WITH FEDERAL IMMIGRATION OFFICIALS

US President President Donald Trump (C), Florida Governor Ron DeSantis (R), and Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem (not pictured) tour a migrant detention center, dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz," located at the site of the Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport in Ochopee, Florida on July 1, 2025. President Trump is visiting a migrant detention center in a reptile-infested Florida swamp dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz." Trump will attend the opening of the 5,000-bed facility -- located at an abandoned airfield in the Everglades wetlands -- part of his expansion of deportations of undocumented migrants, his spokeswoman said. (Photo by ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS / AFP) (Photo by ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images) (Getty)

Miami-Dade County is not a sanctuary jurisdiction, and Florida law prohibits sanctuary policies. The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office also participates in ICE's 287(g) program under state law.

Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava, a Democrat, has previously criticized ICE’s "Alligator Alcatraz" detention center, which closed down this June. Upon the center’s closure, Cava released a statement alleging that "people, including some of our own residents," had been "held there without meaningful due process."

She added that "immigrants helped build Miami-Dade County, and our community has always believed that public safety, the rule of law, and respect for human dignity can go hand in hand."

Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Rand Paul predicts Fauci contempt vote will pass, vows swift DOJ referral
excerpt: Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., believes that he has the votes to hold former chief medical advisor to the president, Dr. Anthony Fauci, in contempt for invoking the Fifth Amendment, and he plans to immediatel...
body_text:
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., believes that he has the votes to hold former chief medical advisor to the president, Dr. Anthony Fauci, in contempt for invoking the Fifth Amendment, and he plans to immediately refer him to the DOJ if successful.

Senate Republicans are readying immediate ramifications for Dr. Anthony Fauci's refusal to testify last week in the upper chamber, and the leader of the push believes the votes are there to pull it off.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and his Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs are slated to decide whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress for declining to answer lawmakers’ questions after being subpoenaed to testify, and, instead, invoking the Fifth Amendment on Thursday morning.

"I think there is a very good chance that we will win the vote," Paul told Fox News Digital.

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Anthony Fauci declined to testify in a Senate committee hearing on his role in the U.S. response to COVID-19, invoking his 5th Amendment rights. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images, Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

And if successful, Paul wants to get the Department of Justice (DOJ) involved swiftly.

"The next step will be when we send the referral over directly to the Department of Justice," he said.

Paul unveiled the contempt resolution on Tuesday, which stipulated that once reported from committee, it would be sent to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia.

The Kentucky Republican has spent years challenging Fauci, who previously served as the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) director and played a major role in the country’s policy and messaging on COVID-19 during the pandemic.

WATCH: RAND PAUL SAYS THERE'S ONE THING AMERICANS HAVE NEVER HEARD FROM FAUCI

He’s charged that Fauci should be thrown in prison and sought to compel him to admit that the virus sprang from a lab leak in Wuhan, China, in connection to risky research allegedly funded under his direction.

Last week’s hearing was meant to be the ultimate battle between the two and the pinnacle of Paul’s yearslong crusade against Fauci. But that didn’t happen when Fauci, under advice from his lawyers, pleaded the Fifth Amendment well over 100 times during the hearing.

"Although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government, and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," Fauci said.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Those became the last words that the former chief medical advisor to the president uttered in the hearing beyond invoking his constitutional rights.

That prompted Paul to tee up a vote on contempt charges against him in a bid to compel Fauci to speak. The lawmaker also cast doubt on whether Fauci’s invocation of the Fifth Amendment comported with his sweeping pardon from former President Joe Biden on his way out of office.

Biden granted Fauci a full and unconditional pardon for all actions taken between Jan. 1, 2014, and Jan. 19, 2025.

Former President Joe Biden speaks about foreign policy during a speech at the State Department in Washington on Jan. 13, 2024. (Susan Walsh/AP Photo)

"I think there's another legal question that the courts may have to decide upon, and that is whether or not a presidential pardon offers you complete immunity," Paul said as the hearing closed.

When asked to expand on the legal question looming over Fauci’s pardon, Paul declined. "It’s a good legal discussion, and we will make those legal points to DOJ in sending the referral over," Paul said.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Sudan war threatens ancient Meroe pyramids, a UNESCO Heritage Site
excerpt: Sudan’s war is endangering the ancient pyramids of Meroe, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as fighting and a lack of security have brought all preservation work to a halt and left the fragile structures ...
body_text:
Sudan’s war is endangering the ancient pyramids of Meroe, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as fighting and a lack of security have brought all preservation work to a halt and left the fragile structures exposed to the elements.

“The site may face a disaster, and collapses are possible,” archaeologist Mahmoud Suleiman said, warning that the more than three-year conflict has prevented experts from carrying out basic maintenance.

Located about 200km (125 miles) north of Khartoum, Meroe is home to more than 200 narrow, steep-sided pyramids built between 800 BC and 350 AD as tombs for rulers of the Kingdom of Kush.

Guards said windblown sand and encroaching vegetation are accelerating their decay. “The sand has thickened heavily on the pyramids and even inside the temples, and the grass grows thick,” guard Mustafa Ahmed said.

“The pyramids have deteriorated greatly, and stones have begun to fall.”

Antiquities inspector Mohamed Mubarak said salt released from accumulated sand is attacking the “inherently fragile” stones, eroding ancient inscriptions.

Suleiman said climate change, the dispersal of Sudan’s archaeological workforce and the halt of foreign missions have all contributed to “significant deterioration”.

UNESCO has warned that more than 100 cultural sites have been damaged and at least 22 museums looted or destroyed since the war began in April 2023.

title: US-Israel war on Iran upends Europe’s summer holiday travel patterns
excerpt:
London, United Kingdom – Nadia Waleed had set off from London with her husband and three daughters for a holiday in Bali, before continuing on to Pakistan, with stopovers in Dubai.

“A family holiday ...
body_text:
London, United Kingdom – Nadia Waleed had set off from London with her husband and three daughters for a holiday in Bali, before continuing on to Pakistan, with stopovers in Dubai.

“A family holiday with multiple flights and stopovers is stressful at the best of times, but the situation in Iran resulted in multiple last minute changes in flight schedules by [the Emirates] airline,” she told Al Jazeera about her trip this summer.

Days before flying, her return flight schedule had changed. A three-hour stopover in Dubai was now extended to 18 hours.

“A two-hour-long phone marathon ensued whereby we managed to get earlier return flights from Pakistan which reduced the layover duration,” she said.

But the next day, one family member’s schedule was changed again – their return flight was pushed back by a month.

“We have also had emails informing us of changes in flight details during our holiday by one hour, requiring rearranging of taxis and pickups,” she said.

Her experience is a small, personal illustration of a larger disruption.

The United States-Israel war on Iran has forced airlines to abandon huge stretches of airspace, sending commercial traffic on longer, costlier detours and upending the plans of families, retirees and honeymooners.

At Trailfinders, a UK travel company, the shockwaves arrived in bulk.

“The Middle East conflict meant Trailfinders had thousands of bookings to rearrange or cancel,” said Nikki Davies of the agency, pointing to Dubai, Qatar and Abu Dhabi, destinations in their own right but also crucial transit points for travellers heading on to Australia and Asia.

Once the UK’s Foreign Office advised against travel to the region, which invalidated insurance if ignored, the clients postponed in droves.

That advisory has since been lifted, and Davies described “incredible pent-up demand” for travel through the Gulf again.

But the disruption appears to have shifted where people choose to travel to.

“Europe is proving extremely popular as it’s closer to home and the standout destinations are Italy, Spain, Greece and Norway,” she said.

TUI, Europe’s largest tour operator, is seeing the same shift at scale.

“Traditionally, 75 percent of the European travellers at TUI book their summer holidays in Europe,” said TUI spokesperson Aage Dunhaupt. “This trend for package holidays is even stronger this year and shows that holidaymakers flock to the all-inclusive and protected package holidays.”

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency this week told airlines to avoid Jordanian airspace after renewed attacks, extending its existing warning against Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and Oman until August 31.

British Airways has suspended flights to Dubai, Doha, Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv, and will permanently drop its London-Jeddah route. Its twice-daily London-Riyadh service will be cut to once a day when it resumes in August. Virgin Atlantic has suspended its London-Dubai route through the coming winter season.

For independent travel agent Assra Satti, the anxiety showed up in the fine print. A family booking a July holiday to Vietnam via Istanbul wanted written guarantees before committing, wondering if they would be rerouted or reimbursed should the war disrupt their flights.

Satti secured written confirmation of both options, and the family flew as planned. As the holiday approached, the same clients expressed concern about a rumour circulating on social media that jet fuel surcharges might land them with an unexpected bill after booking. Satti’s advice to nervous clients has been to book everything as a single protected package, even at a slightly higher price, “because then the whole holiday is protected”.

The mechanics of avoiding conflict airspace are counted in tonnes of fuel and hours in the air, according to Moiz Hamid, a pilot with Pakistan International Airlines.

He says rerouted flights typically add an extra one to two hours flying west, and burn an additional 2,500 to 7,000kg (5,500-15,500lb) of fuel depending on the aircraft, a cost some airlines offset by cutting cargo payload.

The rerouting has also brought congested frequencies, GPS jamming and heavier workloads for pilots and controllers alike.

“Flying a longer, safer alternate route does come with its own risk, the biggest factor being unfamiliarity,” Hamid says. “In normal situations you’re not flying through certain areas, but in these unusual circumstances you have to be rerouted through areas that would be deemed safe by your company, your operator and your regulator. The fatigue does go up, the extended workload does go up.”

Hamid pointed to the downing of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 in December 2024, blamed on navigational errors from military jamming, as a reminder of the stakes when aircraft stray off course.

The ripple effects also reach destinations with no direct stake in the conflict.

UK-based tourism operator Jean-Marc Flambert said that for Sri Lanka, 77 of the 87 weekly flights connecting Europe to the island run through the Middle East, and nearly all of them were disrupted.

“It was almost like COVID in the initial stages,” he said.

Bookings for this summer are down 20 to 30 percent industry-wide, a blow that lands hardest on those who depend on tourism.

Flambert recalled a fisherman turning up at his hotel with a catch, but nobody was there to eat.

“What does a fisherman do? He’d just dig a hole and chuck it.”

Families with young children, he said, have been the most likely to cancel outright, while young couples and retirees have proved far more willing to take the risk of a longer layover or a missed connection.

It is a small mercy for operators like his, patching together new routes through Thailand, Singapore and India to keep clients coming.

Based in London, Flambert is personally weighing that calculation this summer. He has booked a family holiday to Tanzania through Emirates, and has been holding off paying the hotel for as long as he can.

“What if something happens?” he said. “We’ve not done a package, so obviously if the airline changes and the hotel is still there, we’re going to lose our hotel money.”

His children are aged 15 and 18, “old enough to manage”, so he is prepared to take the risk.

“If I get stuck in Dubai for three days, I have friends in Dubai, I’ll just go and stay at a friend’s house, it’s not a big deal.”

But he is clear about where the real cost lands.

“If you lose $500, it’s going to hurt, but it’s not going to kill you,” he said. “The affected countries are feeling that. So let’s be a little bit empathetic.”

title: Messi scores his first goals since World Cup as Inter Miami beat San Luis
excerpt:
Lionel Messi scored his first two goals since the World Cup and took the career scoring lead in the Leagues Cup as Inter Miami overcame an early deficit to beat Atletico de San Luis 4-2.

The match at...
body_text:
Lionel Messi scored his first two goals since the World Cup and took the career scoring lead in the Leagues Cup as Inter Miami overcame an early deficit to beat Atletico de San Luis 4-2.

The match at Nu Stadium on a rainy Wednesday night was delayed 30 minutes in the second half due to lightning in the area.

Messi scored in the 11th and the 44th minutes. He has 14 goals in 12 Leagues Cup matches – one ahead of Los Angeles FC’s Denis Bouanga for most in the tournament’s four-year history.

Telasco Segovia and defender Micael also scored, and Noah Allen had three assists as Inter Miami extended its unbeaten streak to eight matches.

Messi returned to Miami’s starting lineup in his second match since the World Cup, where he led Argentina to their second straight final appearance before La Albiceleste lost 1-0 to Spain.

The 39-year-old played 37 minutes as a substitute in a 2-2 draw with the Columbus Crew on Saturday.

After being held off the scoresheet against Columbus, it didn’t take Messi long to make an impact on Wednesday. He fired a long cross from Allen past Andres Sanchez to equalise after David Rodriguez put San Luis ahead with a header four minutes into the match.

Messi finished from close range later in the first half and assisted on Micael’s header in stoppage time.

Messi led Miami to the Leagues Cup title in 2023 shortly after his arrival to the club. Inter Miami reached the final again last year, losing 3-0 to Seattle in a match that ended with a brawl involving Luis Suarez.

The veteran forward appeared to spit towards a member of the Sounders’ staff and grabbed at least one Seattle player by the neck during the melee, resulting in a six-match tournament suspension.

That means Suarez, who has seven goals in the past four matches, was not available on Wednesday and will not play in this year’s tournament.

title: New York gubernatorial candidate urges 9/11 attendees to turn away from Mamdani during ceremony
excerpt: 9/11 families are calling for NYC Mayor Mamdani to be banned from the 25th-anniversary ceremony in September. Giovanni Galante, who lost his wife Grace, organized a petition citing Mamdani's public re...
body_text:
9/11 families are calling for NYC Mayor Mamdani to be banned from the 25th-anniversary ceremony in September. Giovanni Galante, who lost his wife Grace, organized a petition citing Mamdani's public record and alleged minimization of 9/11 attacks.

Bruce Blakeman, the Republican candidate in New York's gubernatorial race, said Wednesday that attendees at this year's Sept. 11 memorial ceremony should turn their backs on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani if he attends.

"I would equate this to a wake. You don't go to a wake if you're not welcome," Blakeman, whose nephew was killed in the South Tower on Sept. 11, 2001, and who currently serves as Nassau County executive, told reporters.

"I think it's completely appropriate if family members ask him not to come, but if he does come, I think there's a respectful and peaceful way to protest that and I would suggest that people turn their back on the mayor," he said.

FIREFIGHTER BROTHER OF 9/11 VICTIM INCENSED BY 'RADICAL' MUSLIMS WINNING KEY DEM PRIMARIES

Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, right, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Blakeman called for a silent protest if Mamdani attends this year's Sept. 11 memorial ceremony. (Steve Pfost/Newsday RM via Getty Images; Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

Blakeman argued Mamdani's refusal to condemn the phrase "globalize the intifada" should disqualify him from attending the ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.

"He's not welcome there because he has yet to say anything in opposition to the global intifada. As a matter of fact, it seems like he supports that phrase, which is part of the reason why we had the tragedy we had on 9/11," Blakeman said.

Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

The mayor has said he still plans to attend the ceremony.

9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during an announcement on municipal grocery stores at a Campaign for Hunger community food distribution center in Brooklyn on July 27, 2026. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I will proudly honor the families, the survivors, the first responders forever impacted by that horrific terror attack by standing alongside them at this year's 9/11 commemoration — reaffirming that we will never forget the solemn day..." Mamdani said last week.

His comments came after relatives of Sept. 11 victims launched a petition urging the National September 11 Memorial & Museum to bar Mamdani from attending the ceremony in Lower Manhattan.

"Concerns have been raised about Mr. Mamdani's public positions, associations, and responses to rhetoric that many perceive as hostile to these shared values," the Change.org petition states.

"Given these concerns, we respectfully ask that the organizers carefully consider whether Mr. Mamdani's participation would align with the intention of the ceremony and the expectations of the families most directly affected by the tragedy."

JEWISH LEADERS FAULT MAMDANI RHETORIC AS UPPER WEST SIDE STABBING, HATE CRIME PROBE CONTINUES

Bruce Blakeman, Nassau County executive and Republican candidate for New York governor, who is running to unseat Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and has secured President Donald Trump's endorsement. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

A spokesperson for the 9/11 Memorial & Museum previously told Fox News Digital that the organization has "intentionally worked to keep the commemoration free of politics because remembering those we lost on 9/11 should never be a partisan issue."

"Government officials from across the political spectrum, including every sitting president, governor, and mayor since 9/11, have attended the ceremony simply to bear witness — they do not deliver remarks and are asked to remain in a designated area," the spokesperson added.

Former New York Gov. George Pataki was also asked Wednesday whether Mamdani should attend the ceremony.

"It's my nature to be inclusive, and that is my instinct, but Sept. 11 is different. So, I may have comments on that," Pataki said, according to the New York Post.

The 9/11 Memorial in the financial district of Lower Manhattan, New York at the site of World Trade Center. (iStock)

Fox News Digital's Charles Creitz contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: ‘Orange elephant in the room’: Pauline Hanson’s political rise is inspiring racism, inquiry hears
excerpt:
Former AFL inclusion manager tells inquiry One Nation leader’s conduct is encouraging people to use ‘similar behaviour and words’

The rise of One Nation is fuelling racism, a federal parliamentary in...
body_text:
Former AFL inclusion manager tells inquiry One Nation leader’s conduct is encouraging people to use ‘similar behaviour and words’

The rise of One Nation is fuelling racism, a federal parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at First Nations people has been told, with high‑profile Indigenous journalists warning the inquiry that 1970s‑style racism “is back”.

The inquiry is holding public hearings in Melbourne this week, hearing evidence from prominent personalities and sporting groups about their experiences of racism, discrimination, violence and harm across Australia.

Independent Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe asked Tanya Hosch, former inclusion and social policy manager at the AFL and senior consultation with Kind Enterprises, if Hanson’s “rise was increasing racism” referring to the One Nation leader as the “orange elephant in the room”.

Hosch told the committee that while she had not personally met the politician, she believed the rise of One Nation and the controversial senator “expressed racism” through her public speech and rhetoric.

“I believe many of the things that she says have racist intent and express racism. I do believe that it does encourage people to use similar behaviour and words and actions and I think that is pretty well-documented.”

National Indigenous Television’s national Indigenous editor and host of current affairs program The Point, John-Paul Janke told the inquiry that racism, online hate and discrimination had flourished after the failed Voice to Parliament referendum in 2023.

Janke said that, while he has seen improvements over his nearly 40 year professional career, he’d also noticed a steep escalation in online abuse and violence targeting Indigenous peoples.

“I have witnessed an alarming escalation of online racial slurs, of delegitimising First Nations history and expertise, coordinated online pile ons, and sustained abuse aimed at First Nations voices.”

Janke, a Wuthathi and Meriam man from the Torres Strait Islands said in his work speaking with Indigenous people from remote, regional and metropolitan areas – all had witnessed a rise in racism and hate.

“Online racism is now becoming in-person violence. They are worried that it is escalating. Janke said. “I am a father of four boys, and the racism that I grew up with in the 1970s is back.”

“The names that I was called in the 1970s in far-north Queensland, sadly, is being used against my children today. When when will it stop?”

Janke, along with Channel 10 journalist and presenter Narelda Jacobs and former Channel 9 morning presenter, Brooke Boney also gave detailed evidence to the inquiry.

They spoke about the increasingly virulent rise of racism, online hatred and the challenges of reporting on First Nations issues in the Australian mainstream media landscape, including recommending cultural awareness training in newsrooms and ensuring and advocating for respectful coverage.

Jacobs, a Noongar woman from Western Australia said that conservative media can also fuel negative perceptions of First Nations people with very little regulation within the sector to address concerns.

“There is very little accountability when it comes to media outlets sprouting hate and and racism, there are no consequences if you do lodge a complaint,” Jacobs told the inquiry.

“It’s seen by those media organisations as engagement that fuels their purpose, they continue publishing articles or opinion pieces, because it sells.”

title: Florida man allegedly attacked sister with machete while she was sleeping next to toddler daughter
excerpt: New York City crime policies face intense scrutiny after 12-year-old Jacob Freytes is killed by a stray bullet in the Bronx. Mother Migdalia Martinez and sister Angelica Coriano join 'Fox & Friends' t...
body_text:
New York City crime policies face intense scrutiny after 12-year-old Jacob Freytes is killed by a stray bullet in the Bronx. Mother Migdalia Martinez and sister Angelica Coriano join 'Fox & Friends' to speak out, demanding justice and slamming the suspect's lengthy arrest record. Martinez warns that career criminals currently feel more safe than ever before.

A Florida man is accused of slashing his sister with a machete while she was sleeping in bed next to her 1-year-old daughter, according to officials.

Ruben Altidore, 36, repeatedly hacked at his sister in her bedroom in an unsuccessful attempt to kill her on Monday in Margate, which is located about 40 miles north of Miami, according to an arrest report per WPLG.

"Oh my God, why aren’t you dead yet?" he shouted during the attack, according to the arrest report.

Altidore was arrested on Monday in connection with the attack. He was charged with attempted felony murder, aggravated child abuse and violation of probation, according to jail records.

BELOVED TEACHER KILLED AS SHE SLEPT, DAUGHTER STABBED IN ATTACK AS MOTIVE REMAINS UNCLEAR: DA

Ruben Altidore, 36, is accused of repeatedly hacking at his sister with a machete in her bedroom. (Broward County Sheriff's Office)

His sister survived the attack but suffered serious injuries.

She suffered a 10-inch wound that reached the bone on the back of her right thigh, a four-inch laceration to the back of her right hand with the possible amputation of at least four fingers, a near amputation of her left index finger and thumb and a cut to her left palm with a near amputation of her left thumb, according to investigators.

The victim’s 1-year-old daughter was found after the attack lying in the bed covered in blood, though investigators said the child was not injured.

The woman eventually managed to escape and ran to a neighbor for help, WPLG reported, adding that her piercing screams were captured on home surveillance video.

MAN FACING FEDERAL CHARGES AFTER ATLANTA TRAIN PASSENGER STABBED ABOUT 20 TIMES, FBI INVESTIGATING

Ruben Altidore was being held without bond at the Broward County Main Jail. (Getty Images)

"My [brother] is trying to kill me," the woman reportedly screamed as investigators arrived at the scene, according to the police report.

A cousin of the victim also told investigators that Altidore attacked his sister with a machete, and a neighbor reported hearing the victim screaming after she ran outside following the attack.

"She ran to the middle of the street and then ran to my front door where she was asking for help," neighbor Luis Pereria told WPLG. "Apparently she was sleeping when this all happened. I was just baffled by it. How can you do that?"

Investigators found a large amount of blood inside the victim’s bedroom that was tracked into the hallway, to a bathroom door and outside the home.

Ruben Altidore was charged with attempted felony murder, aggravated child abuse and violation of probation. (Broward County Sheriff's Office)

A machete sheath was discovered in the kitchen, and a machete was found under a bed with what appeared to be "red smudges," investigators said.

Altidore was taken to the Broward County Main Jail and is being held without bond.

A motive for the attack remains unclear at this time.

title: Pakistan beat West Indies to end 8 away Test losing streak and draw series
excerpt:
Pakistan ended its eight-match losing streak away from home in cricket Tests with a resounding eight-wicket victory against the West Indies to level the series.

First innings century-maker Abdullah S...
body_text:
Pakistan ended its eight-match losing streak away from home in cricket Tests with a resounding eight-wicket victory against the West Indies to level the series.

First innings century-maker Abdullah Shafique and Babar Azam, in his first series since being reappointed as captain, led Pakistan to 77-2 with unbeaten knocks of 24 runs each as the visitors achieved victory shortly after lunch on Day Four of the second Test on Wednesday.

Babar knocked off the target by hitting back-to-back sixes against left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican, whose six-wicket haul in the first innings had limited Pakistan’s lead to 43 runs.

West Indies won the first Test by 90 runs at Tarouba. In the second Test, spinners Sajid Khan and Ali Usman utilized favourable conditions on a wearing wicket of Queen’s Park Oval to ensure Pakistan remained unbeaten in a Test series against the West Indies since 2000.

Pakistan lost the wickets of Imam-ul-Haq, brilliantly snapped up by Justin Greaves in the slips cordon for 9 in Jayden Seales’ first over Wednesday, and Azan Awais was bowled by Shamar Joseph for 18 before Shafique and Babar sealed the win inside four days.

Earlier, West Indies had set up a modest target of 75 runs after it got bowled out for 117 with off-break bowler Sajid (4-32) and left-arm spinner Usman (4-39) sharing eight wickets between them.

Opening batter Brandon King could not bat in West Indies’ second innings due to a back injury sustained on Day Three when he ran out Babar with a spectacular direct throw from short cover.

Resuming on 106-3 – only 60 runs ahead – the resistance of West Indies’ tailenders ended quickly, with Usman picking up the wickets of Kemar Roach and Joseph.

Greaves, the last recognised batter, played on to seamer Mohammad Ali’s delivery back onto his stumps after adding just two runs to his total as he attempted a cross-batted shot, but got a big inside edge.

Pakistan’s last Test win away from home came against Sri Lanka in 2023 during Babar’s first tenure as captain, before Shan Masood led the side for nearly three years during which Pakistan lost 3-0 in Australia; 2-0 in South Africa; and 2-0 in Bangladesh.

Masood was eventually relieved of the captaincy after Pakistan’s dismal run in red-ball cricket, but the return of Babar as skipper saw Pakistan lose the first test at Tarouba last week, in Pakistan’s eighth loss away from home in three years.

title: Australian politician admits to sending text saying ‘my job is boring’ during a hearing
excerpt:
Mark Parton defends sending text message but denies he sent it to a sex worker, saying he is a ‘multi-tasker from hell’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An Australian poli...
body_text:
Mark Parton defends sending text message but denies he sent it to a sex worker, saying he is a ‘multi-tasker from hell’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An Australian politician has admitted sending a text message that read “fuck, my job is boring” during a parliamentary hearing , but denied an allegation that he sent it to a sex worker.

Mark Parton, the leader of the opposition in the Australian Capital Territory, made the admission after an anonymous complaint referred to the Legislative Assembly’s commissioner for standards alleged that last week’s text was sent to a sex worker.

The Canberra Times first reported the text exchange between Parton and an unidentified person, with an image published on Wednesday showing Parton sending a photo taken from his seat at the committee table, followed by the messages: “fuck, my job is boring. Wanna swap.”

At a press conference on Thursday morning, the Liberal leader said the standards commissioner had told him the allegations had been dismissed and no investigation would be launched.

“The three reasons that [the standards commissioner] can choose to not investigate a complaint are A: that there is insufficient evidence, B: that it is a frivolous or vexatious complaint, or C: that it’s politically motivated,” Parton said.

“The commissioner didn’t give me advice as to which one of those three, but I think you can decide which one or all of the above.”

The standards commissioner was contacted for comment.

Asked three times by a reporter whether the allegations were true, Parton initially referred to the complaint’s dismissal and said he did not regard the matter as being in the public interest before conceding he sent the text.

“Did you send a text message that said, ‘fuck, my job is boring’?” a reporter asked.

Parton continued to deny the text was sent to a sex worker. Asked whether he had ever engaged with sex workers, he declined to answer, saying he did not believe “the question was in the public interest”.

“I’m not going to entertain questions that are completely removed from that … I’m just not going there,” Parton said.

The text was sent during a budget estimates hearing on Friday about plans to redevelop Telstra Tower in consultation with the local Ngunnawal Indigenous community. Asked whether it was appropriate to send personal texts during the hearing, Parton described himself as “a multi-tasker from hell”.

“I think those of you who’ve known me for long enough would know that I’ve got an off-the-cuff larrikin communication style. I understand that most people’s perception of budget estimates hearings is that they’re pretty boring,” he said.

“We’re also humans … people have the ability to send messages to people on their private devices that have got nothing to do with the public wealth.”

Parton ruled out resigning over the saga, saying he still believed he had “the full backing” of his party room, despite describing members as “dismayed” and “a little disappointed”.

“We’ve had a series of conversations overnight. My understanding is that that’s still the case … If indeed there’s a critical mass that wants to go another way, so be it. But I don’t believe that’s what’s going to occur here,” he said.

In a statement on Wednesday night, a spokesperson for Parton said the matter had been referred to police. Parton said on Thursday that the matter was under investigation as a harassment complaint.

The ACT chief minister, Andrew Barr, said he was “not seeking to score political points” over the situation and that estimates hearings were an “important part of parliamentary accountability”.

“The hearings run for approximately 75 hours over two weeks, and hundreds of officials attend to assist the Assembly in its scrutiny of government administration and expenditure,” he said.

“If the Leader of the Opposition considers the process boring, perhaps that is an argument for examining the format in the future, rather than a reflection of the importance of the work being undertaken.”

title: Alan Jones’s alleged victim denies ‘fabricating’ claims against broadcaster during robust cross-examination
excerpt:
Former 2UE and 2GB radio broadcaster is facing 22 charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily new...
body_text:
Former 2UE and 2GB radio broadcaster is facing 22 charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A former student sports star has denied in a Sydney court that he “fabricated” indecent assault allegations against broadcaster Alan Jones after he lost his police job and fell on “extremely hard times”.

Jones’s defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC on Wednesday suggested to complainant J during cross-examination that he had a financial motive to report his alleged indecent assaults 20 years after the incidents.

The former police officer, now in his 40s, had earlier told Sydney’s Downing Centre local court that Jones had touched him sexually when he was a teenager. J was being financially supported by the broadcaster at the time.

J told the court earlier this week that Jones gifted him a Nokia mobile phone, a Nissan car and a stipend which rose from $350 to $600 a week over a nine-year period.

“Your evidence in relation to payments into your account from Belford [company] and the increase in payments has been you trying to assert Jones had an ulterior motive for making payments to you?” Bashir asked the former athlete.

J replied: “No, I wasn’t trying to assert that.”

Bashir continued: “Do you accept that those payments were for the purpose of assisting you for your training and competition and living expenses?”

The cross-examination of J could not immediately be reported as it was subject to an interim non-publication order. But judge Glenn Walsh lifted the order on Thursday afternoon.

Jones is facing 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges. He has pleaded not guilty.

The court heard on Wednesday that J resigned from the police after he was convicted of assault and found to have breached the force’s code of conduct.

Bashir put to him that he lost his income of $120,000 a year and had to pay child support and rent, and had to move in with a relative. J denied during cross-examination that he had a gambling problem.

Challenged by the judge about the relevance of J’s financial problems to his complaint about the alleged indecent assaults by Jones, Bashir said: “A complaint like this, if successful, is a stepping stone to civil proceedings. I will be putting that to him.”

“It is an opportunity to then go on to make a claim and an opportunity to cast himself in a different light after he lost his job,” Jones’s barrister told the court.

J earlier this week told the court he had decided to go to NSW police about his alleged assaults after seeing in the media that Jones had been arrested and charged in November 2024.

Bashir said on Wednesday during cross-examination: “You had from that moment decided to fabricate that Mr Jones sexually touched you as a young teen?”

“When you sent the email [to police] in November 2024, you did so as part of a decision to fabricate claims Jones sexually touched you as a teen?” Bashir asked.“No, I wasn’t planning to fabricate anything,” complainant J replied.

Bashir said J hadn’t raised the alleged incidents when he was charged with drink driving in the mid-2000s, or when he was charged with assault in the early 2020s or when he was subsequently facing termination from the force.

J agreed he did not raise the allegations at those times.

Asked whether he saw Jones’s arrest as a “life-changing opportunity”, J said he was not after financial compensation and only wanted justice.

“I’ve been clear on this,” he told the court. “I don’t want anything from this. I won’t accept [money]. I don’t want anything but proper justice in relation to this matter.”

Bashir alleged that J gave the police false statements about when Jones had gifted him the phone and car. The court heard that J originally told police Jones gave him the phone when he was 14 or 15, but he was in fact 18.

J agreed after being shown documents that Jones gave him the car when he turned 18 and had left school, and not when he turned 17, as he had previously told the court.

“At the time I provided the details, I thought that was accurate,” J said on Wednesday.

Bashir suggested J’s claim that Jones increased his weekly stipend after Jones said he had “been a good boy” was also a fabrication. She said his stipend was increased by Jones when he had success in his sport.

Bashir: “Do you accept those payments, to your knowledge, were for the purpose of assisting you with training, competition and living expenses?”

“Yes. He did pay me to assist with training and competing … I don’t know if that was the reason for the increase in the payments,” J told the court.

Bashir then said: “It’s the case, isn’t it, that you are recasting these payments as something sinister when in fact your understanding at the time was that they were anything but?”

Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations were either baseless or distorted the truth.

Bashir on Monday argued that the alleged victims in the case were egged on to complain by media rivals, and their reliability and credibility were questionable.

title: Outrage as Ugandan football captain murdered in street gang attack
excerpt:
David Owori was attacked by suspected robbers outside his home in Kampala, police say

Ugandans are mourning the death of one of the country's best-known footballers after he was beaten to death by su...
body_text:
David Owori was attacked by suspected robbers outside his home in Kampala, police say

Ugandans are mourning the death of one of the country's best-known footballers after he was beaten to death by suspected robbers near his home in the capital, Kampala.

Police said David Owori was fatally assaulted after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings, prompting an outpouring of grief and renewed public anger over violent crime in Uganda.

The 27-year-old captained Sports Club (SC) Villa, the Uganda Premier League record champions, where he played both as a right-back and midfielder. He also represented the country's Cranes national team.

"We have lost more than a player - we have lost a leader, brother and friend," SC Villa said in a statement.

Witnesses said a group of attackers hit the footballer with paving stones on Tuesday night before robbing Owori of his belongings and fleeing, leaving him unconscious.

SC Villa spokesperson Asan Kasingye told journalists that Owori was targeted just outside his home in Makindye, a Kampala suburb.

"The player was ambushed by thugs as he approached his home, leaving him with life-threatening injuries before he was rushed to the medical facility," Kasingye said.

Owori was rushed to a nearby medical clinic and then transferred to a private facility in the city, but he died of his injuries on Wednesday.

Local police spokesperson Rachael Kawala said detectives were pursuing leads to identify those responsible.

"The scene of the incident has been documented and processed to ensure that all relevant evidence is collected and preserved," Kawala added.

Owori's murder has sent shockwaves across Uganda, with the football community, fans, teammates and politicians demanding justice.

Tributes are continuing to pour in for the defender, who was popularly known as Colgate.

The Federation of Uganda Football Associations (FUFA) described Owori as "a true leader on and off the pitch".

"David was not just a footballer. He was both a leader and an inspiration to a generation," it said in a statement.

Uganda Cranes said the team had lost a football star who "carried the hopes of a nation".

Parliament on Wednesday observed a minute of silence in honour of Owori, and called for quick investigations.

The versatile player, renowned for his tactical discipline and ability to feature across midfield, returned to SC Villa in 2023 for a second spell, becoming one of the club's longest-serving players.

He helped lead the record Ugandan champions to their first league title in 20 years  securing a 17th top-flight crown in 2024.

His influence on and off the pitch earned him a contract extension until January 2027 with the team.

Owori also featured for Uganda's national team during the 2021 Africa Cup of nations qualifying campaign and was regarded as a strong contender for future call-ups to the Cranes.

His death has triggered anger on social media, with many Ugandans questioning the level of violent crime in Kampala and calling for tougher action against criminals.

The killing comes just weeks after the death of another Ugandan sports star - rugby international Sydney Gongodyo, who was also fatally attacked by a mob in Kampala

title: Healey urged to be bold on borrowing in first test of Burnham’s growth pledge
excerpt:
Some want the chancellor to exploit newly flexible fiscal rules – others want a more creative approach, such as borrowing from markets

With just 12 weeks to go until his first budget, new chancellor ...
body_text:
Some want the chancellor to exploit newly flexible fiscal rules – others want a more creative approach, such as borrowing from markets

With just 12 weeks to go until his first budget, new chancellor John Healey is seeking ways to ramp up public investment, without busting the Treasury’s fiscal rules – and some economists are urging him to be bold.

As he settles into No 11 Downing Street, the former defence secretary’s most immediate challenges concern day-to-day government spending.

These include the need to pay for Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on energy bills and to fill the £5bn funding gap in the defence investment plan left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves – which helped prompt Healey’s resignation earlier this year.

Healey could opt to meet these costs through tax changes – with a bank windfall levy back on the agenda, for example – or by ordering Whitehall departments to penny-pinch elsewhere.

It will help that Reeves bequeathed him significant “headroom” against the rules, £24bn at the time of her spring forecast, which is unlikely to have been completely eroded by the impact of the Iran war.

But separately from these short-term pressures, Healey’s boss has made clear that he wants to see a step-change in long-term investment in infrastructure and housing, to meet his promise of growth in every postcode.

One way to fund some of that additional investment may be to exploit what Burnham called “any flexibility” in the existing fiscal rules. The chancellor told the Times there was “scope for more and more rapid investment”.

Reeves, now a humble backbencher, made a historic change to the way debt is defined under those rules. It means extra borrowing doesn’t count against the Treasury’s target if the government uses it to acquire a financial asset. That can mean a stake in a company, or a loan, for example.

Reeves used the new definition, known in Treasury parlance as public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL – pronounced “persnuffle”), to promise a significant increase in public borrowing, but economists have argued for some time that the Treasury could go further.

A recent paper by the Resolution Foundation thinktank argued that the “PuFins” – public financial institutions, which include the National Wealth Fund, British Business Bank and National Housing Bank – could borrow up to an additional £9bn a year, without breaching the fiscal rules.

The Starmer government had already expanded these bodies, giving them additional capital, but the thinktank urged Burnham to go further.

Lord Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist who has been mooted as a possible Burnham adviser, has also suggested there could be scope within the rules to borrow more for infrastructure projects – and suggested creating a new independent agency to assess which should be supported.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) cautions that the question of whether there is flexibility within the rules may not be the best one to ask.

“People are getting a little bit hung up on the fiscal rules. I think they should stick to them, for credibility reasons. But if the government increases borrowing, it is still borrowing: it will still put up borrowing costs and increase debt, creating more problems for the future.

“The real, meatier question is: ‘What is the substantive case for that investment? Is that a good thing to be investing in?’” she adds.

Some experts argue for a more creative approach, however. Thomas Aubrey, of the Bennett school of public policy at Cambridge University, says: “If you really want to move the needle, which seems to be what Andy Burnham is implying in speeches, then the PSNFL stuff is just not going to be enough.”

Instead, he argues that public corporations, such as the development corporation for Greater Cambridge that Reeves announced earlier this year, should be allowed to borrow directly from markets. “You could do that with energy, water, large-scale public infrastructure projects, housing,. The UK is one of the only major economies that doesn’t have a deep market for public corporation debt.”

Interest rates would be higher than for direct government borrowing, he argues, where there is a Treasury guarantee – but the trade-off would be significantly more scope for long-term investment.

And he argues the buyers of such debt, including pension funds keen to match their liabilities, would be distinct from those that now buy government bonds, or gilts – so the Treasury would not be cannibalising existing demand.

“There is no shortage of capital for projects with detailed costings, credible revenue forecasts and hypothecated income streams,” he argued in a recent policy note for the Centre for Cities thinktank.

The UK’s borrowing costs are already higher than many other large economies, and Treasury officials would likely caution Healey against anything that might unsettle the gilt markets.

Aubrey suggests other Whitehall departments have previously shown interest in allowing public corporations to borrow – but it has always been blocked by the Treasury, which would have to agree to classify their debts as separate from government borrowing.

The approach urged by Aubrey chimes with proposals from Burnham-adjacent thinktank Mainstream. The PM’s right-hand woman Louise Haigh also pointed to proposals for public corporations to be allowed to borrow directly, in a piece she wrote for leftwing publication Renewal, earlier this year.

How to boost investment is just one of a slew of economic questions facing Healey and the prime minister in the next few critical months, but it is perhaps the one most central to Burnham’s projects of devolution and reindustrialisation – and an early test of how radical the new administration will be.

title: Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups
excerpt:
Investigation by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and Legal Agenda shows Israel deliberately attacked Amal Khalil and colleague Zeinab Faraj knowing they were civilians

An Israeli strike that killed Leban...
body_text:
Investigation by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and Legal Agenda shows Israel deliberately attacked Amal Khalil and colleague Zeinab Faraj knowing they were civilians

An Israeli strike that killed Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and injured her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April was a war crime, three rights organisations said on Thursday.

Investigations from Human Rights Watch (HRW), Amnesty International and Legal Agenda showed that Israel deliberately and directly attacked Khalil and Faraj, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. The organisations called for the attacks to be investigated as war crimes, while HRW called for states to halt arm sales to Israel and put targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing crimes.

Deliberate attacks on civilians, which both journalists were, is a war crime. Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office.

The reports also indicated that Israel delayed Lebanese ambulances from reaching Khalil and Faraj for hours – at one pointing dropping stun grenades on Lebanese Red Cross workers and firing on their ambulances.

The delay in rescue might have led to Khalil’s death, as hospital reports indicate that she might have still been alive hours after an Israeli strike toppled a building on top of her and Faraj.

“The evidence is clear that the Israeli military knew, or should have, that Faraj and Khalil were civilians, but attacked them anyway, and then prevented paramedics from rescuing them for hours,” said Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch.

Israel said it “regrets any harm caused to journalists,” and that the journalists were killed “as part of a series of events” during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed. There was about two hours between the initial strike that killed the two men Israel said were in Hezbollah, and a second strike that targeted a building the journalists were sheltering in.

Amal Khalil was a 42-year-old journalist working for al-Akhbar, a Lebanese newspaper, while Zeinab Faraj was a 21-year-old freelance camerawoman and photojournalist. Both had been active in covering the war in Lebanon over the last three years.

On 22 April 2026, the pair drove to the village of al-Tiri, south Lebanon, to verify reports that Israeli troops had left the area. They drove behind a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, a municipal official of the city of Bint Jbeil, as well as Mohammed Hourani, a friend of the mayor.

Al-Tiri was in what Israel calls its “security zone” in southern Lebanon, which its troops occupy. Amnesty said that despite the Israeli military calling it a military zone and barring people from going there, it is still required to distinguish between civilians and combatants.

At 2.25pm, after entering al-Tiri, the car carrying Bazzi and Hournai was struck, killing the men. Khalil called the Lebanese civil defence and requested assistance.

The civil defence drove to the entry of the village, where they were told to stop at a military checkpoint while they waited for authorisation from the Israeli military to enter the village safely.

Rescue crews operating in areas of south Lebanon where fighting is taking place or which the Israeli military occupies must coordinate with the “mechanism”, a deconfliction channel, to get safe passage. Among others, the Israeli military must give approval for requests for civil defence to get safe passage.

By 5pm, the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon had given a safe route for civil defence to follow to enter the town, but Israel had not yet given its approval.

While waiting for the civil defence to arrive, Faraj and Khalil left their car and sought shelter elsewhere. Israeli quadcopters circled low overhead while the two journalists waited, Faraj said.

“The drones came extremely close through the roof, less than a metre from my face and Amal’s,” she said.

At 3.31pm, a member of the Lebanese civil defence called Khalil and urged her to get into her car and drive out of the village, as he had not yet received permission from the mechanism to enter the village. Around nine minutes later, Israel struck the journalists’ car, injuring both women.

“Glass and debris flew towards us. My ear felt like it burst. She [Amal Khalil] was bleeding heavily from the nose and head and had shrapnel wounds in her arm and thigh; she couldn’t move her leg,” Farj said.

The two women crawled into a nearby building for shelter. They both continued calling people, asking for assistance, but were told they could not be rescued until authorisation was given from the mechanism.

At 4.25pm, Israel conducted a third strike, bombing the building where they were sheltering, collapsing it and burying both women under the rubble.

At 5pm, permission was given to the Lebanese Red Cross to enter the village. They were able to evacuate Faraj, who had a fractured skull, severe injuries to her right leg and eye, and a crushed hand. Rescuers could not rescue Khalil, who was trapped under rubble.

The rescuers came under attack by an Israeli quadcopter, which dropped a stun grenade near them. Witnesses also said they heard bursts of gunfire during the evacuations, and HRW reviewed photographs of bulletholes in the ambulances consistent with small arms fire.

The rescuers were forced to withdraw with only Faraj.

The Israeli military finally granted the request for rescue crews to re-enter the town at 8.15pm. Khalil’s body was recovered at 11pm. 
 An examination of her body at the nearby Tebnine hospital showed that she probably died at 7pm – two-and-a-half hours after she was struck for the last time. She was trapped under the rubble during that time, waiting to be rescued, while the Israeli military prevented rescue crews from saving her life.

All three organisations have demanded accountability for Khalil’s killing, and described it as part of a larger pattern of impunity by the Israeli military towards civilians.

“The impunity enjoyed by Israeli forces for the killing of journalists and other civilians in Lebanon over the past three years has enabled the Israeli military to continue with its unlawful airstrikes, including direct attacks on civilians,” said Heba Morayef, director for the Middle East and north Africa at Amnesty International.

“It is well past time that the international community impose a comprehensive arms embargo on Israel,” Morayef added.

title: Indian journalist Tarun Tejpal convicted in rape case
excerpt:
Tarun Tejpal, a well-known journalist and author, will be sentenced later on Thursday

An Indian court has found former Tehelka magazine editor Tarun Tejpal guilty of raping a former colleague, overtu...
body_text:
Tarun Tejpal, a well-known journalist and author, will be sentenced later on Thursday

An Indian court has found former Tehelka magazine editor Tarun Tejpal guilty of raping a former colleague, overturning his 2021 acquittal in a decade-old sexual assault case.

The Goa bench of the Bombay High Court said it was convicting Tejpal under sections of Indian law pertaining to rape and sexual harassment, legal website LiveLaw reported.

Tejpal, who has consistently denied the accusations against him, can appeal against the verdict in a higher court.

Tejpal's accuser, who cannot be named under Indian law, had alleged that he assaulted her in an elevator at a Tehelka event in Goa in November 2013.

He was arrested and spent seven months in jail until the Supreme Court granted him bail.

In 2021, a trial court in Goa threw out all the charges against him. The Goa government had appealed against the judgment.

Appearing for the Goa government, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta urged the high court to impose the maximum sentence on Tejpal.

"This court must give a clear message to society that when a girl says no, it means no. A no means a no," Livelaw quoted him as saying.

"All I can say is I am 62. I believe I am a political victim. I am a father of two daughters. I have a wife. All we can say is we will go up and appeal. My lawyer wants me to request you to be lenient," legal website Bar and Bench quoted Tejpal as telling the court.

title: Texts suggest Angus Taylor ‘paid money to the Reformers … or was refusing to’, Icac inquiry hears
excerpt:
Jean-Claude Perrottet, brother of former NSW premier, asked about messages referencing federal opposition leader and factional group Reformers

Icac’s spotlight has shone on Dominic Perrottet’s brothe...
body_text:
Jean-Claude Perrottet, brother of former NSW premier, asked about messages referencing federal opposition leader and factional group Reformers

Icac’s spotlight has shone on Dominic Perrottet’s brother – and it won’t be the last we hear from his family

New South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has been shown text messages which suggest Angus Taylor “had paid some money to the Reformers … or was refusing to”, according to the lawyer assisting the inquiry.

Taylor, the federal opposition leader, is not named in Icac’s allegations and has previously denied making payments to the hard-right factional group the Reformers.

Jean-Claude Perrottet, a member, was on Thursday read text messages sent by Reformer cofounder Christian Ellis in September 2021. Ellis says the group has “zero dollars at the moment” in one message.

Jean-Claude asks why and Ellis replies: “Because Michael O’Hara hates the vax campaign, and Angus Taylor hates Rob.”

The counsel assisting Icac, Juliet Curtin, asked: “That seems to be suggesting that Mr Taylor had paid some money to the Reformers too, doesn’t it, or was refusing to?”

Jean-Claude replied: “It sounds like that’s the suggestion.” Curtin then said: “Do you know anything about that?”

“Look, I’ve heard it come up [at the inquiry], but until that came up, I hadn’t recalled that at all,” the younger brother of the former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet said.

Dominic Perrottet is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of wrongdoing.

The inquiry has previously heard evidence, including from Reformers cofounder Robert Assaf, that hotelier Michael O’Hara threatened to end an arrangement in which he paid lobbying company Beckington for Reformers factional work after the group adopted an anti-vaccination stance.

Jean-Claude, earlier on Thursday, told the corruption inquiry he did not know why he received monthly payments of $5,000 from a lobbying company alleged to have accepted prohibited political donations.

The corruption watchdog is investigating whether the Reformers solicited or accepted illegal donations for the recruitment or renewal of members to the Liberal party.

That practice, known as branch stacking, is not illegal. On Wednesday, Jean-Claude, 29, told the inquiry he had done factional work while employed as an electorate officer by NSW Liberal upper house member Damien Tudehope.

On Thursday, he was questioned about his time with the Reformers after his departure from Tudehope’s ministerial office in 2019.

Curtin asked about invoices for four monthly payments of $5,000 and one payment of $5,500 from registered lobbying company Beckington between April and August 2021. Jean-Claude Perrottet at the time was employmed at Medallion Financial on a base salary of $55,000.

The inquiry has previously heard that Beckington, set up by Ellis and fellow Reformer Jeremy Greenwood in 2019, received payments from prohibited donor and hotelier O’Hara for factional work after issuing fake invoices for consulting advice.

Asked about the “substantial injections of cash” into his account, Jean-Claude said: “I’m honestly trying to do my best here. I honestly don’t recall why I might have done some work for them [Beckington].”

“I don’t know. I mean, it could have been for work. I mean, maybe, maybe Christian owed me money. I don’t know,” Jean-Claude told the inquiry.

The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson SC, asked if his inability to remember why he had been paid was due to “the possibility that in fact you weren’t doing any work of a consulting nature or marketing nature for Mr Ellis in 2021”.

“It may be,” Jean-Claude Perrottet said. “I mean, Christian [Ellis] may have owed me money. Like we’re all, you got to understand, we’re all mates and 20-year-olds.”

Curtin later read messages between him and Ellis that suggested the two had discussed how he should include GST in his invoice.

In a message from Ellis after Jean-Claude Perrottet had asked him for payment, Ellis wrote: “Alright. But it’s 5k, not five and a half, you sneaky man.”

Ellis wrote to Jean-Claude Perrottet: “O’Hara pays GST, but it’s included in the five”. Curtin put it to him that the money O’Hara was paying to Beckington was being used to pay him. “I honestly don’t recall whether that’s the case,” he said.

Jean-Claude Perrottet, whom the commission had previously heard travelled to Fiji to avoid summons to appear at a parliamentary inquiry in 2023, said he “was going through a very stressful time” at the start of that year.

On Thursday, Icac heard that the late former federal Liberal vice-president Teena McQueen may have paid money to support Reformers work.

Reformers associate Dylan Whitelaw had previously told the inquiry McQueen would “pay for a bar tab” for Reformers events. Assaf previously gave evidence that McQueen had provided a venue for training sessions and a call centre for recruitment.

“I think … we used Teena McQueen’s boardroom, God rest her soul,” Assaf told Icac.

On Thursday, Jean-Claude was read messages between Reformers which suggested McQueen may have donated $500 directly to the group via McInerney, who has been named in Icac’s allegations. Jean-Claude said he did not know if McQueen donated to the group.

The watchdog revealed its witnesses for next week, including Greenwood, who has been named in two allegations.

The corruption watchdog is examining an allegation that between 2020 and 2023 Liberal figures, including Greenwood, Ellis and another Perrottet brother, Charles, solicited or accepted donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company, Toplace, in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Nassif.

McInerney was expected to give evidence next week. Icac is investigating an allegation that prohibited donations were made by the schools governing body, arranged and approved by McInerney, including through Beckington and a lobbying company controlled by Greenwood, JPG Advisory.

Last week, the inquiry heard that a screenshot of a message from Dallas McInerney, the then chief executive of Catholic Schools NSW, was sent to Reformers members in which McInerney said he planned to “shake down Angus for 10k” during a breakfast meeting with ministers.

The message was allegedly sent in March 2021 when Taylor was energy minister in the Morrison government.

Dylan Whitelaw, another Reformers associate, was read a later-intercepted text message in which he claimed McInerney had told him he had secured a commitment from Taylor for a “15k injection and a 3k monthly donation!”

Whitelaw couldn’t recall sending the message and told the inquiry he would be “very surprised” if Taylor made any contribution. McInerney, who is a factional ally of Taylor, will appear at the inquiry next week.

Contacted for comment on Thursday, Taylor’s office pointed to previous statements made by the Liberal leader: “I have already made my position clear. No payments were made. The commission has made no allegation that I engaged in any wrongdoing or unlawful conduct. It would be wrong and misleading to suggest otherwise.”

title: Trump administration refunds $100bn in tariffs struck down by Supreme Court
excerpt: United States President Donald Trump’s administration has refunded about $100bn in tariffs since the nation’s top court ruled against its use of emergency powers to impose duties on dozens of trade pa...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has refunded about $100bn in tariffs since the nation’s top court ruled against its use of emergency powers to impose duties on dozens of trade partners, according to customs officials.

The Trump administration collected about $166bn from US importers before the US Supreme Court struck down a large portion of the president’s tariff regime in a 6-3 ruling in February.

In a court filing on Tuesday, the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) disclosed that it had returned more than three-quarters of $128.68bn in tariff revenues earmarked as “potential and certified refunds”.

“CBP’s financial accounting system receives updates from Treasury that indicate these CBP certified refunds are being regularly dispersed,” Brandon Lord, executive director of CBP’s Trade Policy and Programs directorate, said in the filing with the US Court of International Trade.

In its ruling, the US Supreme Court found that Trump exceeded his authority when he invoked the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose fentanyl-related tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China, and broader “reciprocal” tariffs on more than 90 countries.

Trump angrily denounced the ruling at the time, branding the six justices who sided against him “fools” and “lapdogs” for the Democratic Party.

The ruling did not nullify Trump’s tariffs on specific industries invoked under the 1962 Trade Expansion Act, leaving intact duties on goods including steel, automobiles and copper.

Following the Supreme Court’s decision, the US Court of International Trade in March ruled that companies affected by the invalidated tariffs should be refunded.

Trump has continued to roll out new tariffs since the Supreme Court’s ruling.

Last month, his administration announced levies of 10-12.5 percent on imports from dozens of countries that officials claim have not taken sufficient action to combat forced labour.

On Monday, a group of 25 US states, including New York, California, Arizona and Colorado, filed a legal challenge against the latest tariffs, calling the measures a pretext to re-impose the duties struck down in February.

title: Retired NFL standout Roddy White suggests Ryan Clark's outspokenness may have played role in ESPN exit
excerpt:
Dan Dakich gives his reaction to Ryan Clark being laid off by ESPN on Monday while he was live on air.

ESPN’s latest round of layoffs last week included former NFL players-turned-TV analysts Ryan Cla...
body_text:
Dan Dakich gives his reaction to Ryan Clark being laid off by ESPN on Monday while he was live on air.

ESPN’s latest round of layoffs last week included former NFL players-turned-TV analysts Ryan Clark and Cam Newton, as well as reporter Tom Pelissero, who had joined the company from NFL Network. Clark’s exit drew particular attention after more than a decade with the network.

The moves come as ESPN prepares for one of its most significant NFL coverage seasons yet, a run that will culminate with the network’s first Super Bowl broadcast.

Front Office Sports reported that former All-Pro wide receiver Steve Smith is expected to have an expanded role on ESPN studio programming. ESPN confirmed Monday that Jason McCourty will join "Monday Night Countdown," appearing to step into the opening created by Ryan Clark’s layoff. McCourty joined ESPN in 2024 and is now exclusive to the network after leaving his CBS game analyst role earlier this year.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Ryan Clark of ESPN's "Monday Night Football Countdown" before the NFC Wild Card Playoff game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Los Angeles Rams at State Farm Stadium on Jan. 13, 2025, in Glendale, Arizona. (Ric Tapia/Getty Images)

Former NFL wide receiver Roddy White is among the latest sports figures to weigh in. White, who faced Clark during their playing careers, said Clark’s abrupt ESPN exit stood out because of how highly he regarded the former analyst’s work.

"I think Ryan Clark is exceptional at his job," he said. "It's unfortunate that he got released by ESPN because he is so good at what he does. Usually, guys who are that good don't lose their jobs."

White also pointed to Clark’s outspokenness on issues beyond football, suggesting it may have been a factor in the separation.

Atlanta Falcons wide receiver Roddy White (84) warms up before an NFL game against the Baltimore Ravens at Georgia Dome on Sept. 3, 2015, in Atlanta, Georgia. (Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)

"Clark speaks up on a lot of issues outside of football. He is always standing up for the Black community and being on our side. I think this, and his opinionated nature, may have cost him his job because ESPN, as a network, doesn't want people touching on politics and community-related topics. They just want everything to be sports-related."

5 OPTIONS TO REPLACE RYAN CLARK ON ESPN'S SUPER BOWL HALFTIME SHOW

White finished his 11-year career with the Atlanta Falcons with 10,863 regular-season receiving yards.

Clark had been one of ESPN’s more visible NFL voices, regularly appearing on "NFL Live," "First Take," "Get Up" and "SportsCenter." In 2023, at the 44th Annual Sports Emmy Awards, he took home the Sports Emmy in the Outstanding Personality/Studio Analyst category for his work across ESPN platforms.

Ryan Clark of ESPN's "Monday Night Countdown" on set before the game between the Miami Dolphins and the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on Nov. 11, 2024 in Inglewood, California. (Ric Tapia/Getty Images)

Clark had also been a fixture on the "Countdown" desk alongside Scott Van Pelt since 2023. His layoff, however, drew added scrutiny because it reportedly happened during an "NFL Live" broadcast, prompting questions about how the network handled the move.

In 2021, Clark launched "The Pivot Podcast" with former NFL players Fred Taylor and Channing Crowder. He has also hosted "Inside the NFL" since 2023.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X, and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.
