title: Pete Buttigieg distances himself from Biden amid 2028 talk, suggests 'Build Back Better' doesn't work
excerpt:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg criticized former President Joe Biden's 2020 presidential campaign slogan during an interview with Politico.

Former Transportation Secretary and potenti...
body_text:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg criticized former President Joe Biden's 2020 presidential campaign slogan during an interview with Politico.

Former Transportation Secretary and potential 2028 presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg appeared to distance himself from former President Joe Biden and rejected the idea of a "return to normal" during a Politico interview Tuesday.

"I'm trying to purge my vocabulary of anything with the prefix 're-' in it, anything with the word back in it," Buttigieg told columnist Jonathan Martin. "I don't think now is the time to be talking about 'Build Back Better.' Build better, yes. I don't even want to talk about back."

Martin pointed out that "Build Back Better" was Biden's 2020 presidential campaign slogan and asked if that meant he believed the party has changed in the last six years.

JAMES CARVILLE ARGUES ONE KEY MISTAKE FROM BIDEN HAS LEFT DEMOCRATS IN DISARRAY

Pete Buttigieg, left, served as Transportation Secretary under former President Joe Biden, right, during his administration. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

"Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, if that could have worked, it would have worked," Buttigieg said.

Overall, Buttigieg rejected the idea of pushing a "return to normal" message that was the staple of Biden's original campaign.

"But to me, the most important thing is — are we demonstrating a readiness to be focused on building what’s next or are we basically preaching some version of 'return to normal'? 'Return to normal,' in my view, won’t work."

"One way to say I’m not a 'return to normal' is to present the idea that looks furthest left, because that makes you, in a certain way, seem bold. I don’t think it’s the only way to be bold. And so, I think it is really important to not let it lapse into a 'left versus center' thing, when the most important question to me is, are we going to try to sell some version of a previous status quo?" Buttigieg said.

BUTTIGIEG REVEALS HOW HE'D ADVISE DEMOCRATS ON KEY ISSUES IF HE COULD TIME TRAVEL BACK TO 2020

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg criticized the "Build Back Better" mindset in a Politico interview. (Janie Osborne/Getty Images)

The former Biden official also "couldn't say" the former president was a mentor to him, though he referred to him as a "good man" and a "good boss."

"I wasn't close enough to him to say that," Buttigieg said. "But I would say that he, again, after I competed against him, and he beat me and everybody else in that primary, he gave me a tremendous opportunity to do a lot of work that I cared about, that was meaningful, that I'm proud of ... I learned a lot from him, but I wouldn't say I was close enough to him that I claim that."

Fox News Digital reached out to Biden's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Buttigieg's comments came after a University of New Hampshire Granite State Poll published last month showed him neck-and-neck with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., in a potential 2028 match-up, though he has yet to fully commit to another presidential run.

KAMALA HARRIS LEAVES BIDEN OFF LIST OF TOP THREE 'MOST EFFECTIVE' PRESIDENTS

A recent poll placed former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg just behind Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. (Nikos Frazier/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images)

In light of this, Buttigieg has doubled down on far-left proposals such as eliminating the Electoral College or expanding the Supreme Court while downplaying concerns over the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and its candidates.

"I think one of the reasons why you see people who run on a promise of shaking it up, whether it's a DSA candidate on the left or whether it’s someone like Donald Trump, is because people can tell that the system we have is not just showing its age — it's letting us down," Buttigieg said on "America Reports."

The comment drew criticism from Fox News political analyst Reince Priebus, who served as RNC chairman and White House chief of staff to President Donald Trump in his first term, warning that Democrats like Buttigieg are aligning with people on "the wrong side of normal."

"The opponent — the Democrats from where Pete Buttigieg is at — is aligning itself with people that are far outside the mainstream. They're on the wrong side of normal, and he didn't really address that when he was pressed," Priebus said on "America Reports." "And that's the big question for him."

Fox News' Madison Colombo contributed to this report.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

title: Dems in the hot seat for skipping crucial hearing on radical group hiding in US: 'Embarrassment'
excerpt: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called the empty seats on the Democratic side of the dais an "embarrassment" and accused his absent colleagues of refusing to confront evidence about the Muslim Brotherhood’s a...
body_text:
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called the empty seats on the Democratic side of the dais an "embarrassment" and accused his absent colleagues of refusing to confront evidence about the Muslim Brotherhood’s alleged network in the United States.

Democratic lawmakers were missing during Wednesday's Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing as they skipped a hearing on the Muslim Brotherhood’s alleged network inside the United States, drawing a blistering rebuke from Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas.

"You may notice that there are empty chairs on the Democrat side of the dais," Cruz said as he opened the hearing by pointing out that  every Democratic member of the subcommittee refused to attend. "The American people should ask themselves why not a single member of the minority decided that a hearing on terrorism was worth their time? It is an embarrassment."

Cruz tied the Democrats’ boycott to Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory, arguing that the timing helped explain why no Democratic members attended. Cruz accused the party of embracing a candidate who had campaigned alongside left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

Cruz cited Piker’s past statement that "America deserved 9/11" and asked the witnesses what El-Sayed’s rise said about the direction of the Democratic Party.

HASAN PIKER UNLOADS ON 'ISLAMOPHOBIC PIECES OF S---' DEMOCRATS AS EL-SAYED FACES PARTY UNITY TEST

"Abdul El-Sayed, the son-in-law of a leading member of several Brotherhood groups, won Michigan’s Democrat primary for U.S. Senate. Perfect timing for this hearing, probably explains why no Democrats are here and none intend to attend," Cruz said. "Because their campaign is now openly embracing terrorist organizations waging war on America."

(From left to right) Democratic Party Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Peter Welch of Vermont, Mazie Hirono of Hawaii, Alex Padilla of California and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Muslim Brotherhood supporters near the Jordanian border with the West Bank from 2021 can be seen in the background. (Getty Images)

The five Democratic members of the subcommittee — Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Mazie Hirono of Hawaii, Alex Padilla of California and Peter Welch of Vermont — announced beforehand that they would not attend. In a joint statement, the senators accused Cruz of staging a "political creepshow" that scapegoated Muslim Americans.

"Scapegoating Muslims may be a Texas Republican strategist’s idea of ‘solid gold’ to whip up their voters, but Democrats have no intention of indulging this political creepshow, particularly after the recent violence targeting places of faith," they said. "Our focus is the costs families face thanks to rampant, non-stop Trump corruption."

Blumenthal separately told reporters Wednesday that Democrats refused to attend because the hearing "could well be used as an anti-Muslim, Islamophobia kind of show trial."

MICHIGAN SENATE RACE: EL-SAYED’S TIES TO EXTREMIST FUEL ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH VOTERS

The Connecticut Democrat added that he planned to meet with members of the Muslim community who shared concerns about the Muslim Brotherhood, "which appears to be a terrorist organization," while advocating for "tolerance and inclusion."

US Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) speaks during a press conference at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on January 24, 2023. (MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)

The offices of Whitehouse and Welch referred Fox News Digital to the joint statement when asked why the senators chose to boycott rather than attend and challenge the witnesses directly. The offices of Hirono and Padilla had not responded by publication time.

Cruz and the hearing’s witnesses rejected the Democrats’ characterization of the proceeding as an attack on Muslims generally.

Lara Burns, a retired FBI special agent who helped lead a terrorism-financing investigation against what was once the largest Muslim charity in the United States, the Holy Land Foundation, warned that Americans should not disregard evidence because it is politically controversial.

A surfaced OIG report shows FBI agents were urged to avoid communications with CAIR, the Council on American-Islamic Relations. (Getty Images)

"For decades, narratives have been intentionally seeded into public discourse that portray terrorist organizations as resistance movements," Burns testified before arguing Americans cannot "ignore evidence introduced in federal court simply because that evidence is politically uncomfortable."

"The history of this network is not in question," she added. "It was made public decades ago, but few paid attention. Now is the time to pay attention and understand the facts."

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: The Left wants Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham to shut up and dribble when it comes to trans sports
excerpt: Riley Gaines breaks down the latest controversy surrounding the WNBA, the Seattle Storm, Sophie Cunningham, and young fans who showed support for protecting women’s sports at a Fever vs. Storm game. R...
body_text:
Riley Gaines breaks down the latest controversy surrounding the WNBA, the Seattle Storm, Sophie Cunningham, and young fans who showed support for protecting women’s sports at a Fever vs. Storm game. Riley discusses why she believes the league is alienating families and female athletes, how Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham have become central figures in the broader women’s sports debate, and what the incident says about leadership, fan culture, and fairness. She also reacts to the WNBA’s response, Sophie Cunningham’s public statement, and a separate controversy involving Angel Reese, Paige Bueckers, and questions around league rules and competitive integrity. This episode focuses on women’s sports, the future of the WNBA, free expression from fans, and why Riley believes female athletes deserve better from the institutions built to support them.

All of a sudden, it is liberal members of the sports media who want athletes like Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham to stick to sports.

"Caitlin Clark just wants to shut up and dribble, and it's time we respect that," far-left sportswriter Dan Wolken wrote in a Yahoo column this week.

The column is in reference to Clark declining to comment on Cunningham's recent remarks about wanting to keep biological males out of female athletics.

"I think for us, it's not really a discussion we have in our locker room," Clark said when asked about Cunningham's comments. "I think that's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions, but our focus is on basketball. That's what we talk about and how we can get wins, and obviously we didn't do that tonight."

On the surface, we agree with the left's newfound stance on Caitlin Clark.

Clark does not owe anyone a comment on transgender participation in sports or any other issue unrelated to basketball. She has spent her entire life preparing to become a professional basketball player. She has no obligation to become the public face of any cultural issue.

The problem is that many of the very people suddenly insisting Clark should be left alone spent the past three seasons refusing to leave her alone.

Caitlin Clark No. 22 of the Indiana Fever shoots during a game against the Minnesota Lynx on Aug. 2, 2026, at Target Center in Minneapolis, Minn. (NBAE via Getty Images)

ELLE DUNCAN BLAMES CAITLIN CLARK, HER FANS FOR MEDIA SMEAR CAMPAIGN WHILE IGNORING FACTS

The same commentators now criticizing conservatives for asking Clark about transgender athletes repeatedly demanded that she address what they described as the racism and homophobia directed at the WNBA's Black and lesbian players following her arrival in the league.

Just last week, former ESPN host Elle Duncan called for Clark to do exactly that.

"I would love for it to be very clear to the people who think they are her fans but are using her, if she would say, 'Stop that s---. I don't want it. I'm tired of it,'" Duncan said on The Sports Gossip Show podcast. "As opposed to what we've seen, which is, 'The media makes up these narratives. The media makes up this discourse.'"

Hill, David Dennis Jr., Cari Champion, Ros Gold-Onwude, Dan Le Batard and countless others made similar demands. They wanted Clark to legitimize their manufactured crisis.

Notice that Wolken never argued the media should respect Clark's then.

Now, they all want her to shut up and dribble.

Sophie Cunningham (left) and Caitlin Clark (right) cheer on their teammates from the Indiana Fever bench during a WNBA game. (Kamil Krzaczynski)

DAN LE BATARD CLAIMS ESPN IS RUN BY MCAFEE AND 'WHITE PEOPLE' AFTER LAYOFFS, SLANDERS OUTKICK IN UNHINGED RANT

Next, let's try to have the type of conversation that few have managed to have about Caitlin Clark. A nuanced one.

The conservatives involved in this debate do not come away looking particularly strong either. It's fair to ask Clark about transgender athletes, given the attention the issue has received over the past week. However, calling her a "coward" for declining to answer reeks of the same entitlement conservatives often accuse the left of displaying.

"Caitlin Clark might be the biggest coward in the history of sports," Daily Wire commentator Matt Walsh said. "She refuses to say anything about the anti-white racism she has been subjected to since coming into the league. She punts on the trans question, which is the easiest question you could ever be asked. No spine."

Meanwhile, Awful Announcing is enjoying the spectacle, gloating that "Conservative media ate Caitlin Clark up. Now they're spitting her out."

We understand why some people believe Clark should simply say that biological males should not compete in women's sports. For one, that position is hardly fringe. According to Pew Research, roughly 78% of Americans agree. That includes Democrats, Republicans, and independents.

The WNBA exists because sports are separated by sex. There would be no WNBA if men's and women's athletics were not separate. Howard Bryant's comparison this week between Cunningham's comments and Colin Kaepernick's protests was both ignorant and desperate.

Still, the topic of transgender athletes has become deeply divisive in American politics. Therefore, it is entirely understandable that Clark would rather stay out of it entirely.

Caitlin Clark addressed the women's sports transgender athletes controversy after the Fever's loss, saying it's for leagues and governing bodies to find solutions with their athletes. (Getty Images)

Cunningham is not a villain for sharing that view. Clark is also not a coward for declining to discuss it. Both statements can be true at once.

As has so often been the case throughout her WNBA career, Caitlin Clark once again looks like the only adult in the room.

While everyone around her manufactures outrage, she continues to handle herself like a professional.

Amid the toxic discourse, Clark has put together one of the greatest seven-game stretches in WNBA history, averaging 26.1 points and 8.6 assists per game.

Caitlin Clark is one of the few star athletes in America today who just wants to play ball. No amount of political pressure will change that.

As hard as it is for some to fathom, Caitlin Clark isn't interested in the culture war. She just wants to play basketball.

title: US officials push back on reports of dangerously low munitions supplies
excerpt: The White House and Pentagon have pushed back on a slate of recent reports indicating that supplies of both offensive and defensive weapons have dropped dangerously low after five months of war on Ira...
body_text:
The White House and Pentagon have pushed back on a slate of recent reports indicating that supplies of both offensive and defensive weapons have dropped dangerously low after five months of war on Iran.

Experts have said that low supplies of air defence interceptors, particularly those used in Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) air defence systems, may pose a particular threat to US forces, with knock-on effects for allies in the region and beyond.

But in a statement provided to Al Jazeera on Tuesday by the White House, President Donald Trump pushed back on claims the US faced deficiencies in its current supply.

“We have far more munitions than anyone in the world, and far more than we need, despite the fact that an unprecedented amount was given away by Crooked Joe Biden and the Biden Administration to Ukraine and Europe at no cost, in one of many of their extremely dumb moves,” Trump said. He was referencing the Patriot interceptor transfers to Ukraine under former President Joe Biden following Russia’s invasion.

Trump pointed to new efforts to scale up weapons production, although experts have questioned whether supplies of air defence missiles could indeed be scaled up in a timely fashion.

“And as we build up, we will start issuing more to our allies in Europe and elsewhere,” Trump said.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell also maintained that the US was not in dire straits on the issue.

“America’s military is the most powerful in the world and has everything it needs to execute at the time and place of the President’s choosing,” Parnell said in a statement to Al Jazeera.

“We have executed multiple successful operations across combatant commands while ensuring the US military possesses a deep arsenal of capabilities to protect our people and our interests.”

Several reports on Monday indicated that the situation may be more pronounced than US officials have publicly said.

CNN, for instance, reported that the US military had depleted 80 percent of the THAAD interceptors it had prior to the war and about half of its Patriot interceptors. Sources described the levels as “dangerously low”.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth swiftly contested the 80 percent figure and the characterisation of the threat it posed, posting “not true” and “shame on you” on X on Monday.

In an analysis published by the Washington, DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) on July 27, the think tank calculated that, as of that date, the military had just more than a third of its Patriot interceptors left and about half of its THAAD interceptors.

CSIS has assessed that it would take at least three years, even with a recent flurry of funding, to bring supplies to pre-war levels.

The Reuters news agency and CBS News separately reported that the military has used the majority of its Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM).

Unlike the Patriot and THAAD interceptors, the highly accurate long-range missiles are used in offensive attacks. Two sources told Reuters that “virtually all” the missiles, which cost about $1m each, had been used.

No Trump administration official has publicly acknowledged any threats posed by munition shortages, despite the fact the administration has requested $95bn in its Fiscal Year 2027 defence budget and $21bn in a supplemental funding request to replenish its stores.

Multiple media reports have indicated that Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has repeatedly raised concerns behind closed doors. The New York Times reported in late July that concerns over weapons supplies were at least one factor in Trump’s decision to back away from an even greater escalation that month.

That came after a memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Washington and Tehran that had brought a halt to fighting in June collapsed, leading to nearly two weeks of attacks from both sides.

Experts say shortages in both offensive and defensive weapons could leave US forces less secure.

Shortages of offensive ATACMs and PrSM degrade the army’s ability to launch strikes from afar, requiring closer-range attacks that are more likely to put forces in peril, according to Mark Cancian, a retired US Marine Corps colonel and senior adviser with CSIS.

“For ATACMS and PrSM, if you run low or out, then you would have to use some other mechanism, and that would be air-delivered or sea-delivered, so you’re talking probably Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles (JASSM) or Tomahawk to strike a deep target, or having aircraft fly over enemy territory,” Cancian said.

“It’s more dangerous, and you really have to beat down any air defence system,” he added.

The shortages of air defence interceptors, however, are “much more serious”, Cancian said.

“When we talk about missile defence… we don’t have that many left, and there are no good substitutes,” Cancian said. “If we run out of Patriots, then the missiles get through.”

Such concerns were underscored by a July 17 attack on the Muwaffaq Salti airbase in Jordan, in which three US soldiers were killed when Iranian missiles were able to slip through US military and Jordanian air defence systems.

To be sure, after five months of war, Iran’s military capabilities remain unclear, but it is unlikely Tehran would be able to fully exhaust remaining US interceptors in the short term, Cancian assessed.

However, with the current level of US stockpiles, every interception of an Iranian strike weakens US deterrence capabilities against military powers like China.

“Every missile that’s used is one fewer that’s available to deter China”, Cancian said, “and we are now at a point where the joint staff are really very nervous about that”.

Meanwhile, NBC News, among other US media, has reported that the military has already taken a more judicious approach to intercepting Iranian attacks deemed unlikely to cause major harm. The strategy can help to preserve interceptors, but can also increase the chances of miscalculation.

The reported US air defence shortages also raise concerns for Washington’s allies.

The US sells patriot missiles and, to a lesser degree, THAAD interceptors, to allies in the Middle East.

In May, the Trump administration announced an additional $25bn in Patriot interceptor sales and related services to Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar. It has also long provided the weapons to Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel.

There have already been reported delays in offensive weapons deliveries to US allies in Europe and Asia, although no air defence delays have yet been reported to allies in the Middle East.

“That will almost certainly change”, Cancian said, “and the US will endeavour to hold more of the interceptor back to replenish our own stockpiles”.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has been warning of a dwindling supply of Patriot interceptors to block Russian attacks. He has repeatedly sought US approval to produce the weapons in Ukraine, a permission only Japan and Germany currently have.

On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said that allies have supplied Kyiv with far fewer air defence interceptors in 2026, accounting for just a third of the deliveries from the same period last year.

Even with an influx of funding, Cancian said the near-term shortages of US interceptors will not be swiftly resolved.

“Money will not be a problem,” he said. “The problem is time.”

Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

The former Disney Channel star found herself at the center of a headline-making scandal when she accused a hacker of attempting to blackmail her with private nude photos. Thorne ultimately beat the alleged extortionist to the punch by releasing the images herself.

"I just did an honest Twitter post," Thorne recalled during an appearance on "Call Her Daddy." "I just kind of set it out as ... you're not gonna keep taking this from me, so here it is."

FORMER DISNEY STAR BELLA THORNE STUNS IN GREEN SEQUIN BIKINI DURING BEACH DAY WITH FIANCÉ

Bella Thorne said the public backlash following her 2019 nude photo blackmail ordeal "really, really broke me" during an appearance on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast. (Vittorio Zunino Celotto/Getty Images)

Thorne said she shared the images to take control of the situation before the alleged blackmailer could release them. The decision sparked a wave of backlash that the "Shake It Up" star said left her emotionally devastated.

"And you know, I think the worst part of that was people saying, 'Well, you did this. You are faking it. You just wanna show us your t--s. You want us so badly to see your private parts that that's why you're doing it. You want it.' And that to me, like, really broke me then. That like, really, really broke me," Thorne told host Alexandra Cooper.

The now 28-year-old actress recalled filming an Instagram story where she was "completely ... broken and so upset, just mad."

Bella Thorne rose to fame as CeCe Jones on the Disney Channel hit series "Shake It Up," starring alongside Zendaya from 2010 to 2013. (Bob D'Amico/Disney Channel)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

The ordeal eventually took an unexpected turn when Thorne said she received a call from the FBI.

"And then I get like a call one day, and it's the FBI, and they're like, 'Hey, you know, we've seen this thing. We think it's our guy and, like, can we come over? Can we get all the data? Can we see what this is?' And they came over to my house," Thorne recalled. "So now I have like a house full of FBI, which is like the craziest thing."

Bella Thorne said she later worked with the FBI for more than a year after investigators contacted her about the alleged blackmail case. (Gary Miller/Getty Images for Glass House Brands)

Bella Thorne said the screenshots she shared with investigators ultimately helped authorities identify the alleged suspect. (Alberto Rodriguez/Penske Media)

Thorne said she worked closely with the FBI for more than a year, sharing all the information she had. She said investigators ultimately identified the suspect by matching his writing style.

"So if I had not posted those screenshots ... they wouldn't have caught him," she said. "Or maybe they would've caught him later, but they wouldn't have had that direct source."

She said sharing the screenshots ultimately helped investigators build their case.

"And that's how they knew, is because of the screenshots," Thorne added. "Because it's his exact writing, and they're like, 'This is his MO. It's the same guy, it has to be.'"

body_text:
Video shows the moment riders were left hanging upside down after an apparent malfunction on the Wipe Out ride at the Ocean City Boardwalk in New Jersey. Credit: Caitlin Gulli via Storyful

Visitors looking for thrills at a popular boardwalk got more than they bargained for after a ride unexpectedly ground to a halt, forcing passengers to wait in a situation few would want to find themselves in.

Video shared on Instagram appears to show the Wipe Out ride at the Ocean City Boardwalk stopped mid-cycle with riders suspended upside down as concerned spectators gathered below.

In the clip, women can be heard yelling as one bystander tries to reassure those trapped on the ride.

EIGHT RIDERS LEFT DANGLING ATOP 100-FOOT ROLLER COASTER FOR OVER THREE HOURS AT TEXAS AMUSEMENT PARK

Riders were left hanging upside down after the Wipe Out ride malfunctioned at the Ocean City, New Jersey, boardwalk. (@caitlingulli/TikTok)

"You're alright honey! You're alright!" one person can be heard shouting.

The video quickly sparked a wave of reactions on social media, with many viewers expressing relief that the ride's safety restraints appeared to do their job despite the frightening ordeal.

"On a positive note: whoever designed the safety harnesses should get a MASSIVE raise," one Instagram user wrote.

SIX FLAGS GUESTS STRANDED 245 FEET IN AIR AFTER POWER OUTAGE FORCES COASTER EVACUATION

Visitors enjoy an evening on the Ocean City Boardwalk in Ocean City, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Drago/Getty Image)

Others said the incident reminded them of similar experiences.

"My cousins were stuck on a ride in Ocean City 20 years ago. Still happening," another commenter wrote.

DISNEY WORLD GUEST WITH HEART CONDITION DIES OF CARDIAC EMERGENCY AFTER ICONIC RIDE

The Ferris wheel at the Ocean City Boardwalk is seen at sunset. (Photo by Al Drago/Getty Images)

Some viewers tried to lighten the mood, with one writing, "You are in fact not alright honey, you're upside down for way longer than you should be."

It was not immediately clear what caused the apparent malfunction, how long riders remained suspended, or whether anyone was injured.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Ocean City Fire Department, Ocean City Police Department, the ride's operator and the New Jersey Department of Community Affairs for comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

News Corp has delivered a strong rise in revenue across its global business, despite weakness in its news division, marked by a slide in digital subscribers at its Australian mastheads.

The Rupert Murdoch family-backed business reported a 7% lift in full-year revenue to $US9bn, according to financials released this morning, driven by strong results in its business news-focused Dow Jones unit, book publishing and digital real estate assets.

Its well known news media division, however, weighed on results, with advertising revenue falling 2% during the financial year to 30 June. The company’s global newspaper stable includes the Sun and the Times in London, the New York Post and The Australian, and many other mastheads.

Digital subscribers at News Corp Australia slid from 1,166,000 to 1,162,000 during the year, according to the company’s internal data.

News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson used the results to hit out at AI models that “pilfer and profit from our work” without compensation.

“We will pursue those pilferers, and companies that are clients of these crass kleptomaniacs should know they are patently in possession of stolen goods,” Thomson said.

News Corp already has commercial agreements in place with OpenAI and Meta.

Thomson claimed that “without our journalists, our authors, our data, our brands and our professional expertise, users would be drowning in a slimy sea of AI slop”.

Man, woman dead after hours-long siege lockdown in regional Queensland

An hours-long siege ended in tragedy after a man and woman were found dead in an outback home, AAP reports.

Several streets in Charleville, 600km west of Toowoomba in Queensland, were thrust into lockdown after police were called to investigate reports of a serious assault at the home around 6pm on Wednesday.

Residents in a three-street block were forced to retreat into their homes for nearly eight hours as specialist police surrounded the area. The emergency public safety declaration was revoked just before 2am on Thursday.

A 45-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman were found dead in the home.

A crime scene was set up and a report is being prepared for the coroner. Police will hold a press conference on the matter later this morning.

A New South Wales man has been charged for allegedly threatening violence towards a female MP in social media posts earlier this week.

Officials said the man allegedly made a number of posts towards the parliamentarian, making alleged threats of violence, threats to damage property and statements that they intended to find the victim in public and cause her harm.

After an investigation, police arrested the man, 43, in Tascott on the NSW Central Coast on Wednesday.

He was charged with the use of a carriage service to threaten serious harm. He was refused bail and will appear before court today.

The government has asked the consumer watchdog to draw up some national safety standards to crack down on the sale of unsafe ebikes in Australia.

Ebike incidents have escalated in recent years (as their use has also skyrocketed). NSW recorded 226 injuries related to ebikes in 2024. In the first seven months of 2025, that had already to surged to 233 injuries plus four deaths.

The government says new rules will ensure the standards are the same across all states and territories and will apply to the sale of ebikes, e-scooters and e-skateboards. High-powered and high-speed devices linked to serious injuries and deaths won’t be allowed to be sold.

The transport minister, Catherine King, says:

double quotation markThis standard will give Australians the confidence that the products being sold are legal and fit for purpose, and will help keep Australians safe.

Almost 600 childcare services were shut down in the latest quarter, a twentyfold increase on the same quarter last year, as federal, state and territory governments crack down on dodgy and underperforming providers.

State and territory regulators took action against 589 services and cancelled their approval to operate – meaning they lost access to childcare subsidy funding and cannot legally run. Though, not all of those services were currently operating.

The government says state and territory regulators also took 1,538 compliance actions in the March quarter – which puts providers on notice if they are not meeting standards. It was double the number of notices compared with the same time last year.

Governments have been under significant pressure to lift safety and standards across the childcare sector following allegations of child sexual abuse and safety breaches.

double quotation markEnforcement action is at record highs. The percentage of services meeting the national quality and safety standards is at the highest level ever as well.

We have also introduced legislation to cut funding to centres that aren’t up to scratch … This is a good sign. But there is more to do.

title: Fifa admits mistakes but Infantino remains president
excerpt:
Gianni Infantino was first elected Fifa president in 2016

Gianni Infantino will remain as Fifa president after he received the backing of senior executives in a meeting in Morocco, despite world foot...
body_text:
Gianni Infantino was first elected Fifa president in 2016

Gianni Infantino will remain as Fifa president after he received the backing of senior executives in a meeting in Morocco, despite world football's governing body admitting "mistakes" have been made.

Infantino summoned members of the management board to Fifa's Africa office in Rabat on Wednesday following mounting criticism of his aborted attempt to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investors, with the organisation releasing a statement of support four hours after the meeting ended.

European football's governing body Uefa said at the weekend that it has lost confidence in Infantino, calling the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal a "shabby, back room, opaque deal".

Much criticism has come from within Fifa, including secretary general Mattias Grofstrom, who was at Wednesday's meeting. In an internal memo sent to Fifa staff on Tuesday, he wrote that the situation is "a sad and reproachable series of events".

However, in a statement following the meeting, Grofstrom and the managament board "reaffirmed their full support" for Infantino as president.

Infantino had offered Fifa's 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed a proposal for private investment in its tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups, through a new subsidiary, FFE.

Fifa said that during Wednesday's meeting "mistakes" regarding FFE were "acknowledged", saying it was "not the intention" for the Fifa council and members association to "feel excluded from the process and that the process should have been handled differently".

The governing body added it "acknowledged that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media" - with the Times breaking the story of Infantino's plan on 28 July.

Fifa said it had written to the council and members association to apologise for these errors "with a commitment to ensure they do not happen again", adding it will now conduct a review.

However, the statement also said the organisation "will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation".

Earlier, Fifa denied a story in the Times that Infantino had promised Morocco it will host the 2030 World Cup final in exchange for its support.

Fifa said it was a "false and misleading" claim and that a decision on where to hold the final, with the tournament also hosted by Spain and Portugal, will be made "in due course".

Arrivals for the emergency Fifa meeting in Morocco

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Infantino calls executive meeting as criticism mounts

Infantino opponents threaten 'non co-operation' with Fifa

Infantino will hope that this begins to draw a line under the latest, and perhaps biggest, controversy that has beset his 10-year tenure.

However, this show of support from Fifa executives followed yet more stinging criticism of the Swiss.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, whose country hosted the recent World Cup with the United States and Mexico, said he no longer had confidence in Infantino.

Former Barcelona, Real Madrid and Portugal winger Luis Figo, who ran for the Fifa presidency against Infantino's predecessor Sepp Blatter in 2015 before withdrawing, called on him to immediately resign.

Figo said: "Infantino has debased the office that he promised to elevate.

"It is too late to save his dignity but it is not too late to save football."

But Infantino, 56, looks set to fight for re-election for a fourth term.

Rivals have until 18 November to put their names forward to stand against him, with the election to be held at the Fifa Congress in Morocco in March 2027.

A candidate requires 106 votes from Fifa's 211 members to win.

Uefa, however, may well have other ideas.

At the weekend, European football's governing body said it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership and threatened legal action against Fifa.

Earlier this week several member associations - including Wales, with England set to follow suit - withdrew support for his re-election.

Fifa also said that although "mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the Fifa regulatory framework".

It is unlikely that such statements and the approval of a group of executives will dampen Uefa's anger.

title: Miranda Kerr's ultra-specific diet includes venison for breakfast, no eggs or seed oils
excerpt: Health and wellness expert Jillian Michaels warns against the viral healthmaxxing trend and the danger of 'health FOMO' on social media. She criticizes young women for taking health advice from influe...
body_text:
Health and wellness expert Jillian Michaels warns against the viral healthmaxxing trend and the danger of 'health FOMO' on social media. She criticizes young women for taking health advice from influencers who 'don't know what they're talking about,' contrasting them with medically trained doctors.

Miranda Kerr recently detailed her ultra healthy, if a bit unique, diet, which includes eating venison for breakfast and cutting out eggs altogether.

"I love food, but when I got sick, I had to learn even more that food is medicine," the former Victoria’s Secret Angel told Kristin Cavallari on her "Let’s be Honest" podcast. "So, I love to have nutritious and delicious foods that feed my soul, but, at the same time, I don’t crave like unhealthy food anymore because I know how detrimental that can be to my body on the inside, not even about what it looks like on the outside, but on the inside.

"I want to have vitality and energy and that’s kind of why I eat healthy."

Two years ago, Kerr revealed she was diagnosed with proctitis, a form of irritable bowl syndrome, when she was pregnant with her second son six years earlier.

MIRANDA KERR RECALLS FIRST MEETING EX ORLANDO BLOOM'S FIANCEE KATY PERRY: 'WE JUST IMMEDIATELY GOT ALONG'

Miranda Kerr has an unusual diet. (Getty Images)

She told Get the Gloss at the time she drank a liter of celery juice a day, which is known to be an anti-inflammatory, and said she is now in remission.

The 43-year-old supermodel told Cavallari she wants to be able to run around with her grandkids someday, "be baking them cakes like my grandma did for me" and feel healthy "for as long as" she can.

"‘Cause I think that’s more important than what you look like," she argued. "It’s so much more important that you feel that vitality, and that’s why I say that my non-negotiables are meditation. Like, I’m doing that instead of working out, I guess you could say, with the busy life that I have right now, but that’s the choice that I make because that’s what feeds me."

She said other people might be "really fed" by going for a run in the morning, for example.

"Each to their own. You have to find what elevates you, what de-stresses you," she said.

She also loves dance parties with her kids.

Kerr shares Flynn, 15, with ex-husband Orlando Bloom and Hart, 8, Myles, 6, and Pierre, 2, with her husband, Snapchat founder Evan Spiegel.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

She said she’s been drinking Noni juice, which she calls a "superfood superfruit," in the morning for 30 years since she was 13.

"What I love about it is it’s full of antioxidants, and it has a lot of vitamins and minerals."

The supermodel said she eats meats like venison and turkey. (Getty Images for Christian Dior)

She said she drinks a 30-millimeter shot, and her youngest child has some as well, but she admitted her teenager is "not into it."

Kerr then has a marshmallow tea "because that’s good for the gut lining. S,o I get the marshmallow leaf, and then I put it and brew it in hot water."

That's followed by a few tablespoons of coconut yogurt with honey and a bite of a banana.

"I do all of this before I have my coffee. I get to my coffee, and my coffee is my moment where I’m in bliss," she admitted.

Her Fabula brand coffee, which she said is mold- and lead-free, includes coconut milk from high-end grocery store Erewhon and maple syrup.

"I do proteins, like meats like venison, bison, lamb, turkey. I eat all the meats that aren’t mass-produced for the reasons that we all know," she explained.

MIRANDA KERR'S HUSBAND, EVAN SPIEGEL, PRAISES HER 'VERY DIFFERENT' CO-PARENTING RELATIONSHIP WITH ORLANDO BLOOM

"I’m not much of a fruit girl, to be honest, but I will have a banana, and I also think a banana is a great snack to go," she said. "I do love mangoes."

She also stays away from dairy and wheat, "and I’m very specific about the oils, so only cooking with coconut oil or avocado oil. No seed oils."

Kerr said she does tallow sometimes, "mostly for the kids." She also tries to get them to eat sourdough because they refuse to eat gluten-free bread.

Miranda Kerr attends the Met Gala with husband Evan Spiegel. (FilmMagic)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Lots of squash, carrots and parsnips are also on the menu.

"And I do have a little bit of salmon but not too much because of the mercury that’s in salmon," she said.

The model said she used to "live on sushi" when she lived in New York, but she doesn't eat it anymore because of the possibility of parasites.

"I do love caviar," she admitted. "Caviar’s good. There’s no parasites there."

As far as sweets, she likes carob, and she and her younger kids have tea parties where they drink lemon balm tea with carob.

"I do like chocolate, and, so, I also will make, like, a carob hot chocolate with coconut milk, maple syrup, carob. It’s really good," she added.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: US man arrested at Trump’s golf course charged with multiple felonies
excerpt: A California man who was arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course while pretending to be part of the security detail preparing for the US president’s visit has been charged with several...
body_text:
A California man who was arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course while pretending to be part of the security detail preparing for the US president’s visit has been charged with several felonies, including the possession of a large-capacity magazine as well as a stash of illegal weapons found in his car and home.

Jeanine John Taele, 38, was arrested on Sunday at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes, two days before the president was set to visit the town for a Republican National Committee dinner.

Taele pleaded not guilty to all the charges on Monday, with bail set at $250,000, though he had already appeared in court on a state weapons and second-degree robbery charge for an unrelated, earlier incident.

He was due in court on Wednesday on a federal weapons charge, but the hearing was cancelled. According to a spokesperson from the US attorney’s office, Taele is being held at a downtown LA jail and is not yet in federal custody.

Taele was first seen on the president’s property on Friday, walking throughout the course wearing an earpiece and taking photos and videos of federal agents’ activities as they conducted a security assessment, according to a federal criminal complaint filed with the California Central District Court.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said a search of his pick-up truck in the club car park turned up a loaded 9mm pistol, binoculars, and a badge that read “security protection agent”, according to federal prosecutors.

On Monday, law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey and found an unregistered short-barreled rifle and other firearms, magazines, ammunition, body armour, and notebooks with “concerning statements”, federal authorities said. No details about the statements were released.

The 38-year-old was a corporal in the US Marines. He was deployed to Iraq in 2008 and Afghanistan in 2010, and worked as a warehouse clerk, according to the US Marine Corps. He earned numerous commendations, including an award for good conduct during his service from 2008 to 2016.

In brief remarks about Taele’s arrest to Fox News on Tuesday, Trump said that “only consequential presidents” are targeted and that he was “definitely consequential”, which brought him “a little solace”.

title: Search for Amelia Earhart's long-lost plane reignites with ambitious new expedition
excerpt:
Air and Space Museum’s Amelia Earhart expert Dorothy Cochrane speaks with Fox News Digital about the theories surrounding the famed aviator's disappearance.

Researchers are gearing up to resume their...
body_text:
Air and Space Museum’s Amelia Earhart expert Dorothy Cochrane speaks with Fox News Digital about the theories surrounding the famed aviator's disappearance.

Researchers are gearing up to resume their search for Amelia Earhart's lost plane in the Pacific Ocean after setbacks delayed the search.

Purdue University officials said in a recent statement that researchers will travel to Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific to investigate the Taraia Object, a satellite-imaged anomaly believed by some to be Earhart's lost Lockheed Electra.

The expedition, called the Taraia Object Expedition, will depart on Oct. 7.

AMELIA EARHART MYSTERY EXPEDITION HALTED AS RESEARCHERS SEEK ANSWERS ON MISSING PLANE

"The expedition seeks to help complete the historic journey that ended with her disappearance 89 years ago," officials said.

The expedition is based on researchers' belief that Earhart's plane came down near Nikumaroro, known as the Nikumaroro Hypothesis.

Researchers are preparing to travel to Nikumaroro Island in October as part of a new expedition to search for the long-missing aircraft of Amelia Earhart. (U.S. National Archives)

Supporters of the theory believe that Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan became stranded on the remote island after failing to reach Howland Island — possibly dying as castaways.

Earhart disappeared on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first female pilot to fly around the world.

NEWLY RELEASED AMELIA EARHART DOCUMENTS REVEAL VIVID DETAILS OF JAPAN'S ROLE IN SEARCH FOR DOOMED AVIATOR

She and Noonan lost contact during one of the final legs of their journey, going missing after leaving Lae, New Guinea, en route to Howland Island.

Supporters of the Nikumaroro hypothesis believe Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan became stranded after failing to reach Howland Island. An image of Nikumaroro Island is seen above. (Google Maps)

She was 39 years old at the time and one of the most famous people in the world.

The upcoming expedition was announced last year but was delayed while officials awaited approval from the government of Kiribati. The country's cabinet has since approved the mission.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Richard Pettigrew, founder and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, which is leading the expedition, said that he is "grateful for the patience and enthusiasm of everyone who has followed this journey with us."

Pilot Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, are shown with a map of the Pacific that shows the planned route of their last flight. (Getty)

"The evidence supporting the Nikumaroro Hypothesis remains compelling, and the only way to answer this question is to go to Nikumaroro, inspect the Taraia Object firsthand and follow the evidence wherever it leads," Pettigrew said in a statement.

Fox News Digital reached out to Purdue University for comment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The story of Earhart's disappearance has captivated Americans for decades and has been the subject of ongoing research.

Earhart disappeared on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first female pilot to fly around the world. (Getty)

Last year, the National Archives released over 4,600 pages of previously unsealed government records related to Earhart's 1937 disappearance, including her final known radio transmissions.

More recently, pilot Justin Myers said he identified a possible image of Earhart's missing Lockheed Electra in Google Earth imagery of Nikumaroro.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

Tom Hanks and wife Rita Wilson walked the Pre-Grammy GALA red carpet discussing what they believe is the success to a great relationship, after being married for 34 years.

Rita Wilson is sharing the marriage advice her mom gave that didn't sit right with her.

During a recent appearance on Michelle Obama's podcast, "In My Opinion," the 69-year-old actress spoke about the outdated marriage advice her mom gave her before she met and married Tom Hanks.

"I was engaged before I got engaged to my husband. If I had married that person, I would have been divorced within a year," she said. "I thought that was what you were supposed to do at a certain age. I actually thought, because I had never really fallen in love with anyone, that I would be okay."

While engaged to that man, Wilson said she asked her mom for advice, telling her: "I don't know though. Should I marry him? I'm not really in love with him," and getting a surprising response in return.

Wilson shared she was engaged prior to meeting Tom Hanks and the marriage advice her mom gave her. (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)

'SHAMELESS' STAR EMMY ROSSUM REVEALS SECRET MARRIAGE AT 21 AFTER BOYFRIEND'S ALLEGED SHOCKING ULTIMATUM

"She said, 'Don't worry, you grow to love him.' I was like, 'Mom, that's not my generation,'" she said. "Her generation was like, 'Is he a good man? Will he provide?' There wasn't any of this, 'I have to be madly in love.' My parents were married for 59 years, so whatever they figured out, they figured out. But I still wanted to hold out for that falling in love thing."

Ultimately, Wilson did not go through with marrying the first man, knowing "marriage would not have sustained that relationship," and found love with Hanks after they reunited on set of "Volunteers" in 1984, later tying the knot in 1988.

The "Now and Then" actress told Obama, and her co-host and brother, Craig Robinson, that when she "finally met Tom and fell in love with" Hanks, she had the feeling that "this is very, very different than what I had before."

When it comes to being a mom, Wilson said she wasn't sure she wanted to have children, but knew she "didn't wanna have children with the wrong people or person."

Wilson said seeing what a good father Hanks was encouraged her to want kids. (Dave Benett/WireImage)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"Tom had two children," she said. "I already saw that he could be a good dad. So I was like, okay, good, that's helpful. A little example here."

Hanks was already a father to Colin and Elizabeth, who he shares with his ex-wife, Samantha Lewes, and later welcomed sons Chet and Truman with Wilson.

Of his children, Colin and Chet have followed in Hanks and Wilson's footsteps, with Elizabeth pursuing a career and an author and journalist, under the pen name E.A. Hanks, and Truman focusing on other aspects of filmmaking.

Most recently, Chet has found success starring in "Running Point" alongside Kate Hudson, and Colin has appeared in a number of successful projects, including "Life In Pieces," "Fargo," "American Crime Story" and others.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Chet Hanks shared that he asks his dad for career advice all the time. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

"I’ve always asked him for advice when it comes to acting and he’s always given me really great advice," Chet told Page Six in September 2024. "He just said, ‘If you just know your lines, and you show up on time, and you’re nice to everybody, that gets you a long way.'"

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

title: Viagra could do more than advertised as study reveals surprising health superpower
excerpt: Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — ma...
body_text:
Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may be associated with a lower risk of cancer recurrence and potentially new diagnoses.

Viagra could do more than give men a boost in the bedroom, as new research suggests it may have benefits for cancer patients.

The prescription medication, which is manufactured and distributed by Viatris, is commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction by increasing blood flow during sexual stimulation.

It was originally developed to treat high blood pressure and chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart before researchers discovered its unexpected effect on erectile function during clinical trials.

PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS

A new study published by the American Association for Cancer Research found that the pill may have properties that can prevent cancer from spreading.

Researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, led by Dr. Yarden Ariav in the lab of Professor Ayelet Erez, found that Viagra’s active ingredient — sildenafil, a PDE5 inhibitor — may restrict cancer metastasis, or the formation of new tumors.

Viagra’s active ingredient, sildenafil, may restrict cancer cells from spreading, a new study suggests.

The team, which included scientists at the U.S. National Cancer Institute, analyzed human and mouse cancer cells, genetic experiments and 20 years of health data from five million members of Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest nonprofit healthcare provider and health insurer. They also examined how genes, proteins, fats, cholesterol and cellular energy interact.

The analysis revealed that sildenafil limits the cancer cell’s ability to make use of cholesterol, which is an important mechanism in how the cell breaks away from the primary tumor and migrates throughout the body, according to a press release from the American Committee for the Weizmann Institute of Science.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Sildenafil was found to block an enzyme called phosphodiesterase type 5, or PDE5, and increase the signaling molecule called cGMP, which dilates blood vessels – the feature that has made Viagra a successful treatment for erectile dysfunction.

According to the researchers, cGMP also binds to a protein that transports cholesterol within cells, reducing the cholesterol available for essential cellular functions. Cancer cells are "particularly vulnerable to this reduction in cholesterol supply," they noted.

Viagra was originally developed to treat high blood pressure and chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart before researchers discovered its unexpected effect on erectile function during clinical trials. (Alex Segre/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Based on their findings, the researchers suggested that combining Viagra-related drugs with statins, which lower cholesterol, could help slow the spread of cancer by reducing tumor cells' access to both existing and newly produced cholesterol.

"We have uncovered a new biological pathway that links a well-known signaling molecule to cholesterol regulation within cells and shown how this pathway can be harnessed to interfere with the ability of cancer cells to form metastases," Erez, senior researcher and dean of Weizmann’s Miriam and Aaron Gutwirth Medical School, commented in a statement.

Combining drugs from the Viagra family with statins – a class of drugs responsible for reducing cholesterol production in the body – may be even more effective in restricting the spread of cancer, the researchers suggested. (iStock)

"Beyond their therapeutic promise, our findings highlight that cancer biology is shaped not only by mutations in tumor cells, but also by the patient’s metabolic state and by medications they are already taking for other conditions."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The researcher added that this study "underscores the importance of treating the whole patient – not just the cancer – when tailoring the most effective therapy."

The study’s use of mouse models could pose a limitation to the final implications, as cancer treatment may not always translate similarly to humans, the researchers acknowledged.

The human evidence is also observational, which reveals an association instead of a proven cause and effect.

Fox News Digital reached out to the study authors and the medication's manufacturer for comment.

Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Senate confirms Trump pick Erica Schwartz as new CDC director
excerpt:
Schwartz, president’s third pick to lead top US public health agency, confirmed in 51-44 Senate vote

Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control a...
body_text:
Schwartz, president’s third pick to lead top US public health agency, confirmed in 51-44 Senate vote

Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director ‌of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a rare win for the Trump administration after a string of failed attempts to fill senior health posts.

Schwartz was confirmed by a ⁠51-44 vote that broke largely along party lines, with Tim Kaine of Virginia the sole Democrat to support her nomination.

Donald Trump’s third pick to run ​the CDC, Schwartz is set to take the reins of the agency after a tumultuous period of leadership turnover, and amid public concern over an outbreak of cyclosporiasis and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s hesitancy towards vaccines.

At her confirmation hearing last month, senators pressed Schwartz on whether she would stand firm against any attempts by the health secretary to erode the scientific consensus around vaccines. She replied that she “will never betray the science” but generally deflected questions about how she would manage the relationship with Kennedy.

“We need a CDC director that will ⁠actually stand up to crazy, stupid things being said that undermine faith in immunization,” said Bill Cassidy, the committee’s Republican chair and a physician.

Schwartz replied that Kennedy “will absolutely allow me to be CDC director”, and Cassidy later announced his support for her nomination.

“There are challenges facing Americans’ health today. I will work with her to face those challenges and regain trust in the CDC,” Cassidy said after the Senate confirmed her.

A navy veteran, Schwartz served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, after positions in the United States Public Health Service where she was detailed to the Coast Guard, eventually becoming the force’s chief medical officer.

Trump’s first nominee to lead the CDC, David Weldon, a former Florida congressman, was withdrawn by the White House in March 2025 just before his confirmation hearing.

Schwartz will be the first permanent CDC ​director since Susan Monarez, Trump’s second pick, who was fired by Kennedy last year after less than a month over a clash on vaccine policy.
