A Kansas mother of four is reportedly recovering after a suspected spider bite led to surgery, serious infections and ...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Kansas mother of four is reportedly recovering after a suspected spider bite led to surgery, serious infections and a weeks-long hospital stay.

Britagne Miller, of Goddard — about 14 miles west of Wichita — said she was sitting around a campfire with her husband and children at Cheney Lake on May 28, when several spiders crawled on her and apparently bit her, according to local outlets KAKE and FOX Kansas.

Four days later, the area around one bite on her calf became swollen and painful, prompting her to seek medical care, FOX Kansas reported.

"This one kept swelling and swelling, and it was like, you know, a fire stir that's metal," Miller told KAKE. "It was like shooting down my leg into my foot, and it felt like it was being stabbed."

GIANT GOLDEN SPIDERS COULD SPREAD THIS SUMMER; EXPERTS DOWNPLAY HEALTH RISK

Britagne Miller said she was sitting around a campfire with her husband and children on May 28 when several spiders crawled on her and apparently bit her. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)

Miller was admitted to Wesley Hospital in Wichita on June 4 and underwent surgery, according to KAKE and a GoFundMe created by her husband, Jake Miller.

Her treatment was complicated by existing blood-clotting disorders, liver problems and allergies to certain medications, KAKE reported.

Miller later developed infections. Doctors also determined that she was suffering from end-stage liver failure and warned her family that her condition could be fatal, according to KAKE.

Miller, who chose to continue treatment rather than enter hospice care, said she remembers little from her time in intensive care, according to the outlet.

BULL BISON SENDS YELLOWSTONE VISITOR FLIPPING THROUGH THE AIR IN CAMPGROUND ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO

Britagne Miller said she remembers little from her time in intensive care. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)

She was released from the hospital on July 11, and is continuing her recovery at home.

Miller now requires home health care, physical therapy and regular visits with specialists. She also hopes to receive a liver transplant but is not yet eligible to be placed on the transplant list, according to KAKE and the GoFundMe.

Doctors have not confirmed what kind of spider bit her, KAKE reported.

Dr. Raymond Cloyd, a horticultural entomologist at Kansas State University, told KAKE that the brown recluse and black widow are two venomous spiders commonly found in Kansas.

TEXAS TEEN BITTEN BY BARRACUDA IN POPULAR VACATION SPOT AFTER BRACELET GLINTS IN WATER

Britagne Miller was released from the hospital on July 11, and is continuing her recovery at home. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)

Cloyd advised sealing cracks and using caution with boxes, shoes and other undisturbed items, KAKE reported.

"We know there is still a long road ahead, but we are holding on to hope that one day this season will be behind us, and she will be able to continue doing what she loves most — being a mom, and someday a grandmother," the GoFundMe states.

The Miller family could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for additional comment.

Sophia Compton is a Writer at Fox News Digital. Sophia was previously a business reporter covering finance, energy and tourism and has experience as a TV news producer. She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud
excerpt:
Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília

Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp ...
body_text:
Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília

Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election.

The Trump administration stopped short of expelling Viotti, a former senior United Nations official. But Washington warned that further diplomatic action remains possible if Brasília continues to withhold its approval for would-be ambassador Daniel Perez, a Florida Republican and close ally of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.

“We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” a state department spokesperson said.

The ambassador’s visa could be restored if Brazil accepts Perez’s appointment. “This is a reciprocal action,” the spokesperson said. “Should the ambassador leave the country, she would need to reapply for a visa.”

The dispute has become entangled with Brazil’s increasingly bitter election campaign, in which Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and a close political ally of Trump.

Brasília swiftly condemned the US action as part of a deliberate campaign to influence the election. Lula’s office said: “Today’s decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons.”

Brazil also accused the US of breaching diplomatic norms by announcing Perez’s nomination before seeking Brasília’s consent. The Brazilian government said its consideration of the appointment was still under way, and that it had been made clear no decision would be taken before the first round of the election, on 4 October.

The Trump administration argues that Brazil has no right to interfere with the president’s choice of US ambassador to the country.

“President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world,” the state department said. “We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes.”

The latest confrontation follows Brazil’s refusal last month to issue visas to Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, and one of his senior aides.

The US officials had planned to visit Brasília from 27 to 30 July for meetings with government officials, religious leaders and others about election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression.

Washington described the trip as routine, and rejected Brazilian claims that it was intended to interfere in the election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” the state department said at the time.

Brasília has stood by its decision, saying the officials intended to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electronic voting system in what it called an “unacceptable attempt to interfere in the national political process”.

The row is particularly sensitive because Jair Bolsonaro and his supporters have spent years alleging, without evidence, that Brazil’s electronic voting system is vulnerable to fraud. He has been barred from standing for office and was convicted over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election.

The diplomatic confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, whose governments have sharply diverged over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region.

Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. The Brazilian president has blamed Rubio for some of the administration’s actions against his government, although he has sought to avoid a direct personal confrontation with Trump, and has said the two men got on well when they first met.

Economic pressure has added to the tensions. The Trump administration has imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, citing what it says are unfair trade practices and failures to prevent forced labour. Lula’s government has rejected the allegations, and accused Trump’s administration of trying to help Bolsonaro’s political family.

The US has also classified Brazil’s two biggest drug-trafficking organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a move opposed by Lula’s government.

Yet the state department insists that it still wants to restore a normal relationship with Brasília. “We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues,” a senior US official said.

title: Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed
excerpt:
Assessment of more than 2,000 native species warns nearly one in five at high risk of deadly H5N1, including parrots, fur seals and quolls

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Sign...
body_text:
Assessment of more than 2,000 native species warns nearly one in five at high risk of deadly H5N1, including parrots, fur seals and quolls

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

Almost 400 native Australian bird and mammal species have been assessed as being at a high risk – or worse – from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, a federal government assessment has revealed.

Some of Australia’s most beloved animals – including species of penguins, fur seals, quolls, dolphins, more than 300 birds and the Tasmanian devil – are considered at least high risk from the virus, meaning they could suffer “severe reduction in population size or viability” or worse if it reached them.

Five species are considered at extreme risk, meaning “unlikely to survive where the virus occurs”.

These are all birds that breed in single islands or groups of islands, such as the endangered Christmas Island frigatebird and the critically endangered herald petrel, which only breeds on Raine Island in the far north of the Great Barrier Reef.

More than 80 endangered and critically endangered species are also considered to be facing at least a high risk from an infection, suggesting that the H5N1 strain of bird flu will push them further towards extinction.

The federal government released the results of the assessment of more than 2,000 native species, carried out with Charles Darwin University and BirdLife Australia, on Tuesday evening. Nearly one in five have been rated as facing extreme, very high or high risk.

Australia’s three resident seals – the Australian fur seal, the New Zealand fur seal and the Australian sea lion – are all considered at very high risk. The Tasmanian devil and the eastern quoll, both assessed as high risk, are the land mammals at greatest threat.

The extent of the analysis and the number of species considered at high risk underlines expert fears for the threat to local wildlife.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

Prof John Woinarski, a leading conservation scientist at Charles Darwin University who helped devise the analysis, said: “This has sketched out a more bleak picture than perhaps we considered previously.

“We are going to get major consequences for many species and our bird and mammal diversity is likely to suffer substantial impacts from this disease.”

Prof Hugh Possingham of the University of Queensland, a lead councillor at the Biodiversity Council, said the analysis was “a good first cut” but it should have been released two years ago.

“A year ago we needed a priority action list and we should have been taking action then because everyone knew that it was coming,” he said.

Kate Millar, the chief executive of BirdLife Australia, said while the list of species at high risk or worse was “long” and “incredibly confronting” it also meant Australia could “prioritise and take action protecting the species most at risk”.

Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said the “list of doom” revealed “the true extent of the disaster facing Australian wildlife”.

He said it demanded a “serious response” from the government “but instead we have had cuts to on ground environment programs nationally”.

“Almost one in five Australian mammals and birds has been rated by the government as at risk of severe population reductions or even extinction,” he said. “This includes quolls, parrots, seals and pelicans.”

The council is among several conservation groups calling for the government to fund a $200m package to scale up on ground efforts to protect wildlife, including feral animal controls.

The government has said it has committed $113m to prepare for bird flu, including $47m “to accelerate protective action” for threatened species and biodiversity.

Jess Abrahams, national nature campaigner at the Australian Conservation Foundation, said: “Australia is already in the midst of an extinction crisis and we need to be prepared for just how harrowing this could get.

“Australians love nature and we all need to be emotionally prepared for the onslaught that could occur and know what to do if they come across a sick, dying or dead animal.”

The H5N1 virus has killed millions of birds and mammals since it spread from Europe in 2021 to every continent on the planet.

Australia was the final continent to be breached six weeks ago, when infected Antarctic and subantarctic migratory seabirds were found dead and sick in Western Australia and South Australia.

The virus has now been confirmed in more than 100 individual birds and air surveillance has recorded the first mass mortality event from the disease, in South Australia. Detections have also been confirmed in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland.

title: Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv kills one and injures others
excerpt:
Russia has attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and drones, killing one person and leaving at least 12 others injured after strikes across Kyiv and the surrounding area, authorities say.

The head...
body_text:
Russia has attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and drones, killing one person and leaving at least 12 others injured after strikes across Kyiv and the surrounding area, authorities say.

The head of Kyiv's military administration, Timur Tkachenko, said the "enemy is once again massively attacking the Kyiv region" and has hit residential buildings and warehouses.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said there were fears people could be trapped under rubble after strikes on the centre of the city.

Russia has intensified attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, and Wednesday's assault air raid alerts remained in place for more than an hour as waves of ballistic missiles hit the city and its outskirts.

Tkachenko said "the consequences of the enemy attack are being recorded in the Bucha, Brovary, and Fastiv districts of the region".

"I urge everyone - do not ignore air raid sirens. Take care of yourselves, your loved ones, and your family," he added.

Kyiv's military administration has reported one woman killed and at least 12 other people wounded in the attacks.

The latest strikes on Kyiv come after Ukraine has increased its attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure, including power facilities.

It has also repeatedly targeted depots of the Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries. Five people were killed and 10 wounded in the Moscow region on Tuesday morning in the most recent strikes on Wildberries warehouses.

The day before, Russian officials say seven people were killed and 58 injured in a drone attack on a busy beach in the southern Krasnodar region as tourists look on.

Ukraine, meanwhile, expressed outrage over a video showing a man chased by a drone in Kherson, calling it a deliberate "hunt" and "safari" targeting civilians.

Both sides have denied deliberately targeting civilians.

Ukraine has urged allies for more US-made Patriot missile interceptors to defend against Russian ballistic attacks.

Russia says seven killed and 40 injured by Ukrainian drone hitting busy beach

Ukraine says major Russian oil refinery and airfield hit, as Moscow reports eight deaths

title: Federal appeals court clears way for DeSantis-backed law restricting children at some drag shows
excerpt:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announces Meta's compliance with Florida's 2024 law banning social media access for kids under 14.

A divided federal appeals court cleared the way for Florida ...
body_text:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announces Meta's compliance with Florida's 2024 law banning social media access for kids under 14.

A divided federal appeals court cleared the way for Florida to enforce a Gov. Ron DeSantis-backed law restricting children from certain sexually explicit live performances, including drag performances the state argues are obscene for minors.

The full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit ruled Tuesday 8-5 that Orlando restaurant Hamburger Mary’s had not shown it was likely to succeed in its First and Fourteenth Amendment challenge to Florida’s Protection of Children Act.

The court vacated the preliminary injunction in full and sent the case back to the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida for further proceedings. The ruling clears the way for enforcement, though Hamburger Mary’s could still seek additional review.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier celebrated the decision in a post on X.

DESANTIS SHUTS DOWN FLORIDA SCHOOL'S 'DRAG & DONUTS' EVENT FEATURING DRAG QUEEN 'MOMMA' ASHLEY ROSE: REPORT

Florida AG James Uthmeier, center, touted Tuesday's decision in a post on X. (Rich Pope/Getty Images, File)

"Huge victory for our team at the 11th Circuit! After 3 years of litigation, the full court affirmed the constitutionality of Florida’s ban on children attending sexualized drag shows," Uthmeier wrote.

The law makes it a misdemeanor to "knowingly admit a child to an adult live performance," according to the court’s opinion.

The law defines an "adult live performance" as a live show that "depicts or simulates nudity, sexual conduct, sexual excitement, or specific sexual activities ... lewd conduct, or the lewd exposure of prosthetic or imitation genitals or breasts" and that also predominantly appeals to a "prurient, shameful, or morbid interest," is "patently offensive" for the age of the child present and, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value for that child's age.

Writing for the court, Judge Andrew Brasher called the law "a straightforward regulation of obscenity."

"Preventing children from attending adult live performances obscene for them is rationally related to Florida’s interest in safeguarding the well-being of minors," Brasher wrote.

TIKTOK IN LEGAL HOT SEAT AS STATE ACCUSES APP OF EXPOSING KIDS TO HARMFUL CONTENT WHILE MISLEADING PARENTS

A drag performer in Miami. (Getty Images, File)

The majority rejected Hamburger Mary’s arguments that the terms "lewd" and "the age of the child present" made the law unconstitutionally vague or overly broad.

Brasher wrote that Florida Supreme Court precedent limits the meaning of "lewd" to sexual conduct. He also wrote that all three parts of the law’s obscenity test must be met before a performance is prohibited.

The majority also ruled that using an age-variable standard did not make the law unconstitutional on its face.

Eight judges agreed that Hamburger Mary’s was unlikely to succeed on the merits of its constitutional claims. Six judges joined Brasher's opinion in full, while Judges Kevin Newsom and Britt Grant joined all but the section addressing universal injunctions.

Grant wrote separately that the court did not need to rule on the scope of the injunction after deciding that Hamburger Mary’s was unlikely to succeed on the merits.

FIRED SCHOOL COUNSELOR LOSES AGAIN AFTER FREE SPEECH FIGHT OVER GENDER-THEMED BOOKS IN HIS OFFICE

A drag queen performs onstage in Miami. (Getty Images, File)

Judge Robin Rosenbaum argued that the law forces venues to guess which performances are suitable for children of different ages while exposing operators to criminal penalties, fines and the possible loss of a business license.

"Today our Court embraces mess-around-and-find-out (‘MAFO’) First Amendment jurisprudence," Rosenbaum wrote.

She argued that the law could chill protected speech by forcing businesses to risk prosecution before learning how officials would apply it.

Rosenbaum also argued that the statute effectively imposes strict liability over a child’s age and could expose violators to jail, fines and the loss of a business license.

US MONITORING ‘CONCERNING’ UK PROSECUTION OF RETIRED PASTOR WHO PREACHED JOHN 3:16 NEAR HOSPITAL

People take in a drag performance in Orlando, Fla. (Getty Images, File)

She wrote that the law "wields a Titanic-sized iceberg of chilling power against protected speech."

Judge Nancy Abudu filed a separate dissent focused on the law’s legislative history.

Abudu argued that comments from the law’s supporters, along with warnings from legislative staff, supported Hamburger Mary’s claim that the measure would chill protected drag performances.

The majority rejected that argument, writing that courts generally do not strike down an otherwise constitutional law based on an alleged improper legislative motive.

INDIANA REPUBLICAN SENATOR MOVES TO BLOCK KIDS FROM ACCESSING PORN ONLINE

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks with reporters at the Florida State Capitol in Tallahassee. (Matias J. Ocner/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images, File)

The majority also wrote that nothing in the law targets performances simply because they feature drag.

Hamburger Mary’s filed the lawsuit in 2023 after Florida enacted the measure.

The restaurant said it had previously hosted Sunday drag performances advertised as family-friendly but canceled those shows and barred minors from its other performances because it feared enforcement.

A federal district judge initially issued a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of the law. A divided three-judge panel of the 11th Circuit affirmed that decision before the full court agreed to rehear the case.

DeSantis' and Uthmeier's offices, as well as the ACLU of Florida, did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: CDC reportedly expands US cyclosporiasis outbreak to 15 states
excerpt:
Six additional states caught up in investigation after Michigan reported first two US deaths linked to disease

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reportedly expanded the largest known...
body_text:
Six additional states caught up in investigation after Michigan reported first two US deaths linked to disease

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reportedly expanded the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak to 15 states.

The alleged expansion includes the addition of six states, according to the Washington Post, which cited three people familiar with the matter. Those states include Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina, according to a fourth person familiar who spoke to the paper.

A spokesperson from Arkansas’s health department confirmed the outbreak expansion to the Guardian, saying in a statement: “Arkansas is one of the states the CDC is adding to the multi-state outbreak for cyclosporiasis.”

The Guardian has contacted the CDC and the health departments of Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina.

As of 28 July, the CDC had recorded 6,707 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis, along with approximately 11,500 suspected cases awaiting confirmation. Cases have been reported in 45 states since May, although most of the suspected cases have been concentrated in Michigan and Ohio.

The disease is a form of food poisoning originating from Cyclospora cayetanensis, a microscopic parasite that causes symptoms including diarrhea, appetite loss, bloating, extreme fatigue, low-grade fever, stomach cramps, nausea and vomiting.

Cyclosporiasis spreads through the fecal-oral route, most commonly by consuming contaminated food or water. Symptoms typically begin about a week after infection, and without treatment can last anywhere from a few days to a month or longer, according to the CDC. Those with symptoms are advised to stay well hydrated.

Although the Food and Drug Administration is still investigating six cyclosporiasis outbreaks, it has identified iceberg lettuce produced by Taylor Farms de Mexico as the source of one outbreak. In response, Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled lettuce distributed to restaurants in 27 states and grocery stores in 15 states.

On 24 July, the CDC announced that the outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce had expanded to four additional states – Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania. As of that date, illnesses associated with the outbreak had been reported in nine states: Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

Michigan – the state hardest hit by the outbreak, with health officials reporting 11,234 outbreak-linked cases – on Monday reported the first two US deaths linked to the disease since the outbreak began.

The CDC has warned the public to not eat recalled Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce, and to contact healthcare providers if cyclosporiasis symptoms are experienced.

title: Armed man arrested at Trump’s LA golf course ahead of president’s visit
excerpt:
A man carrying a loaded handgun and hollow-point ammunition has been arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf club, days before a scheduled visit by the US president, local authorities said.

...
body_text:
A man carrying a loaded handgun and hollow-point ammunition has been arrested at Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf club, days before a scheduled visit by the US president, local authorities said.

The man, arrested on Sunday at the Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes, was identified by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as 38-year-old Jeanine John Taele. The department said he had been seen photographing and filming the grounds while appearing to monitor security preparations ahead of Trump’s scheduled appearance at a Republican Party fundraising dinner on Tuesday.

Deputies said they found a 16-round magazine loaded with ammunition in his pocket, and later recovered a loaded pistol with a round chambered, along with a second loaded magazine, from his vehicle in the golf course car park.

Officials said Taele had already been under investigation by the El Segundo Police Department over a separate robbery case.

On Monday, detectives working with the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force searched Taele’s Downey home, where they said they recovered an illegally modified rifle, a second pistol, body armour, high-capacity magazines, bulk ammunition and other radio signal devices and notebooks containing what officials described only as “concerning statements”.

The sheriff’s department said it had not identified any credible threat to the public and that Taele is being held without bail while prosecutors weigh charges.

Trump’s visit is part of a broader campaign swing through California and Nevada ahead of the November midterm elections.

title: 'Squad' socialist scores re-election nod as radical wave continues to sweep party
excerpt:
Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist, achieved a significant primary victory in Colorado, unseating a 29-year congressional incumbent, Diana DeGette.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., one of Co...
body_text:
Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist, achieved a significant primary victory in Colorado, unseating a 29-year congressional incumbent, Diana DeGette.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., one of Congress’ most outspoken progressives and a member of the "Squad," won the 12th Congressional District's Democratic primary Tuesday evening, teeing up her re-election for a fifth term.

Tlaib’s primary victory against Michigan state lawmaker Shanelle Jackson and Inkster Mayor Byron Nolen continues a string of victories for progressives as the Democratic Party’s far-left wing enjoys pronounced primary election success that has strengthened the hand of its coalition. It has also widened the range of positions held by their candidates.

When Tlaib and fellow Squad members joined the House of Representatives in 2019, their campaigns stood out for their far-left views. Tlaib and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., in particular, stood out because of their membership in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Eight years later, the DSA has backed Tlaib again.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., yells during a State of the Union address in the House Chamber of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., Feb. 24, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"For years, Rashida has been a strong voice in the halls of the Capitol, unapologetically standing up for the working class everywhere. Fighting for affordable housing, for clean air and water, for an end to the genocide in Gaza, and so much more – Rashida is a beacon of hope and courage for those in her district and across the world," the group said in a statement.

The group has also vastly expanded its influence beyond established figures like Tlaib.

From primary candidates in New York like socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier and her victory over incumbent Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., the veteran chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, to Melat Kiros, another socialist in Colorado, unseating 30-year incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Colo., progressives have expanded their influence over the party.

It’s a stark reversal of the party’s finger-pointing in the wake of disappointing 2020 congressional election results where Democrats were left with slimmer majorities in the House and Senate.

DYING FORMER CONGRESSMAN BARNEY FRANK TELLS DEMOCRATS THEIR FAR-LEFT MESSAGING IS COSTING THEM VOTERS

Democratic congressional candidate Melat Kiros speaks to supporters at an election night watch party after winning the Colorado primary June 30, 2026 in Denver, Colo. Kiros defeated incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Colo., in the Democratic primary. (Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images)

"Don’t say socialism ever again. We need to get back to the basics," then-Rep. Abigail Spanberger, D-Va., said at the time.

But Tlaib, along with other progressives in the party, pushed back, arguing that their platforms would set the future tone of the party. In a widely circulated memo on Nov. 10, 2020, they made the case that progressives would appeal to an expanded voter base.

"We need a new generation of leadership grounded in a multiracial, working-class experience and background," the memo urged.

"As we speak, congressional Democrats are debating why they underperformed and some have been quick to blame progressives. There is no denying Republicans levied salient rhetorical attacks against Democrats, but these will continue to happen as they do every cycle."

Tlaib, in comments to Politico at the time, argued the platform would appeal to a kind of populist streak in the Democratic Party, similar to the populism she saw present in Trump’s appeal among the GOP.

FAR-LEFT SURGE: MAMDANI-BACKED CANDIDATES OUST DEM ESTABLISHMENT INCUMBENTS

Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., speaks with union activists about free speech on college campuses at the Capitol in Washington, May 23, 2024. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)

"If we truly want to unify our country, we have to really respect every single voice. We say that so willingly when we talk about Trump supporters, but we don't say that willingly for my Black and Brown neighbors and for LGBTQ neighbors or marginalized people," Tlaib said.

Having once again secured the Democratic nomination in 2026, Tlaib will advance to the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, where she is heavily favored to win. She last won re-election against Republican challenger James Hooper in a 69.7% to 25.4% victory in 2024.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump-backed Bronze Star veteran secures party nod in must-win district
excerpt:
Captain Mike Bouchard, candidate for Michigan's 10th Congressional District, spoke to Fox News Digital ahead of Veteran's Day.

Bronze Star veteran and Republican congressional candidate Michael Bouch...
body_text:
Captain Mike Bouchard, candidate for Michigan's 10th Congressional District, spoke to Fox News Digital ahead of Veteran's Day.

Bronze Star veteran and Republican congressional candidate Michael Bouchard won a GOP primary on Tuesday evening in a bid to represent Michigan’s 10th Congressional District after receiving an endorsement from President Donald Trump.

Republicans are hoping Bouchard’s storied credentials and message of righting the country’s direction are enough to carry the district as the GOP looks to hold onto its slim majority in the U.S. House of Representatives.

But the district is far from a guarantee.

DEMOCRATS TARGET MORE GOP HOUSE SEATS AFTER SOCIALIST VICTORIES ROCK LEFT-WING PRIMARIES

Michael Bouchard, a Bronze Star recipient and candidate for Congress in Michigan's 10th congressional district, poses in a campaign video. (Michael Bouchard for Congress)

Incumbent Rep. John James, R-Mich., last won reelection in 2024 in a 51.1% to 45.0% victory over Democratic challenger Carl Marlinga, a judge and former prosecutor.

The cycle before that, James beat out Marlinga by a narrow 48.8% to 48.3% win in 2022.

James, who enjoyed the benefit of incumbency, announced he would vacate the seat and instead pursue a gubernatorial bid, calling it a way to secure Michigan’s prosperity for future generations.

"My family, like countless others, came to our great state for the better opportunities our manufacturing and automotive industries offered and to live the American dream," James said in a statement.

Bouchard is highlighting his time in the military as a member of the 82nd and the 101st Airborne Divisions. He was deployed to Iraq as well as the U.S. southern border. Like James, who also has a military background, Bouchard was awarded a Bronze Star for his service with the joint task force against ISIS.

Bouchard, a political newcomer who hasn’t held office previously, is pitching himself as a continued part of the country's shift away from the direction of the previous administration.

ARMY VET, TRUCKING EXECUTIVE RAVES OVER TRUMP PLAN TO BOLSTER BLUE COLLAR INDUSTRY BY FAST-TRACKING VETERANS

Republican gubernatorial candidate in Michigan, Rep. John James, R-Mich., speaks during a breakfast at Fireside Grill & Patio on Aug. 3, 2026 in Novi, Michigan. James will face off against businessman Perry Johnson in the Republican primary on Tuesday August 4. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"Under President Trump, I led missions on the southern border; back then we got the job done. But on day one, Joe Biden shut us all down; he opened the border," Bouchard said in a campaign video.

"Human trafficking, drug smuggling, known terrorists walked right in," he continued. "The Army taught me that weak leadership has consequences and I’m ready to lead America back."

On his website, Bouchard has highlighted fostering American manufacturing, finishing the southern border wall and increasing parental participation in education systems.

Trump issued an endorsement of Bouchard in a post to Truth Social earlier this year.

"A third-generation Michigander, brave U.S. Army veteran and Bronze Star recipient Mike has served his state and nation with distinction and will bring that same fighting spirit to the U.S. Congress," Trump wrote.

"Mike Bouchard has my complete and total endorsement to be the next representative from Michigan’s 10th congressional district," he added.

DEM PRIMARY ERUPTS AS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE DISMISSES RIVAL AS ‘CELEBRITY CANDIDATE’

U.S. President Donald Trump walks to a waiting Air Force One at the Hagerstown Regional Airport on July 31, 2026 in Hagerstown, Maryland. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Notably, Bouchard has also attracted endorsements from other key congressional figures, such as U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich.

Having cleared the Republican primary, Bouchard will head to the Nov. 3 general election.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Tennessee coach unloads on NCAA's 'bulls–t', after star linebacker suspended for outdated rule
excerpt:
Dan Dakich torches the NCAA for suspending Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for a plane ticket.

KNOXVILLE, TN - After the NCAA decided it was going to suspend Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for t...
body_text:
Dan Dakich torches the NCAA for suspending Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for a plane ticket.

KNOXVILLE, TN - After the NCAA decided it was going to suspend Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for the opening two games of the upcoming season, his head coach did not hesitate to call out the organization for the current rule structure.

Following the 2025 season, Carter decided it was time to pursue his NFL dreams by declaring for the draft and hiring a professional agent to start the process. It was at that moment that the Tennessee linebacker lost his collegiate eligibility according to the antiquated rules currently in place.

Because Carter also accepted a $427 plane ticket from his professional agent to attend a training session, which is when the linebacker first discovered that he had suffered a foot injury that would prevent him from fully reaching his potential of being drafted high.

NCAA ROCKED BY COLORADO JUDGE'S 2022 CLASS ELIGIBILITY RULING THAT COULD RESHAPE COLLEGE SPORTS THIS YEAR

Linebacker Arion Carter of the Tennessee Volunteers speaks at SEC Football Media Day at Tampa Marriott Water Street on July 20, 2026, in Tampa, Fla. (Getty Images)

In reality, Arion would have lost millions because of the injury, so he decided the best course of action was a return to college, which transpired just weeks after he first initially announced his decision to go pro.

Carter also paid back the $427 and the school self-reported the 'violation' to the NCAA.

After informing Tennessee that he wanted to return, the question whether the Vols had a roster spot for him. So, he entered the transfer portal for a quick stop, before rejoining the Tennessee football program.

Speaking on Tuesday before the Vols open Fall camp, head coach Josh Heupel did not mince words on the NCAA's punishment of a 2-game suspension for the linebacker.

"He's done everything the right way..The ruling that came out from the NCAA of a 2-game suspension I truly believe is bullshit," Heupel fiercely noted. "You look at the landscape of college football, the rules of NIL and everything, I think the ruling is completely outdated. I am disappointed for him, and for us, with the result of that ruling."

NCAA suspends Tennessee linebacker for $427 plane ticket, as college sports hands out millions in NIL

Tennessee head coach Josh Heupel, center, and defensive lineman James Pearce Jr. (27) celebrate with their team after defeating Oklahoma during an NCAA college football game Saturday, Sept. 21, 2024, in Norman, Okla. (AP Photo/Alonzo Adams)

What did the NCAA have to say in response to upholding a 2-game suspension for Arion Carter?

"NCAA rules are clear: student-athletes may not sign with agents to pursue NFL Draft opportunities, and this student-athlete knowingly violated those longstanding rules. When student-athletes violate NCAA rules, the school declares them ineligible and works with the national office to determine requirements for reinstatement, which can include repayment and/or withholding from competition."

The problem is that there is no way back for an athlete if they decided to declare for the draft, but potentially get hurt in the early training process before all-star games, and also before winter workouts are set to begin in college.

The whole process is laughable when it comes to what is actually transpiring in college athletics right now.

There are schools using agents to circumvent that rev-share cap so athletes can make millions, while high school prospects are signing are agreeing to terms with schools that include private airfare travel for the player themself and their family.

Ted Cruz urges Senate to stay in Washington until Protect College Sports Act passes this week

Right now, college athletes are making millions of dollars for their schools, and the NCAA, but a rule that is outdated is preventing a football player from garnering national exposure like Carter would when Tennessee plays Georgia Tech in a primetime game during the second week.

"AC at the end of last chose to enter his name in the NFL Draft process in the middle of January, right before the deadline where you have to make the final declaration," Josh Heupel noted. "He found out he needed a medical procedure that was gonna require surgery. He made the choice, and the right choice for him, to come back to college football.

"He was upfront and honest, and paid back the four-hundred-dollar flight. He's done everything, and handled everything, the right way. Very truthful, and upfront about everything. I think it's unfortunate that a young man that represents everything inside of this game the right way is faced with that ruling."

Arion Carter No. 7 of the Tennessee Volunteers celebrates a third-down stop during a game against Alabama at Neyland Stadium on Oct. 19, 2024, in Knoxville, Tenn. (Getty Images)

Now, even though he is a leader on the Tennessee football team, Arion Carter will miss the opening games of the 2026 season.

The young man could have sued the NCAA, and probably won pretty easily, and this would have been another court case the organization would have had to deal with.

But, Carter is going about his business in preparation for the season and handling it with grace.

There are plenty of people who don't agree with the NCAA upholding a suspension, and the Tennessee administration is high on the list. And most likely, college football fans across the country.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

title: Trump admin trucking crackdown lands 51 immigration detentions, 36 English language proficiency violations
excerpt:
Program streamlines CDL licensing for veterans with military driving experience as administration touts crackdown on illegal immigrant commercial drivers.

President Donald Trump's administration anno...
body_text:
Program streamlines CDL licensing for veterans with military driving experience as administration touts crackdown on illegal immigrant commercial drivers.

President Donald Trump's administration announced the results of a crackdown on illegal immigration in the trucking industry on Tuesday.

The Department of Transportation (DOT) began the crackdown, Operation Highway Shield, in Florida earlier this year. The DOT has since expanded the effort to multiple states in the Midwest, including Illinois, Indiana, Iowa and Ohio, Fox News has learned.

Officials carried out 3,487 enforcement stops during the operation that resulted in 766 unsafe commercial vehicles or drivers placed out of service, 51 immigration detentions, 47 criminal charges filed, 39 incarcerations, 36 English Language Proficiency (ELP) violations, and three cargo theft recoveries totaling roughly $1 million in stolen freight.

TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS

A state trooper inspects a truck on the highway. (Fox News Channel)

The Trump administration maintains that federal immigration and commercial driving enforcement remains a top priority.

Fox News previously broke news about the ramped-up enforcement efforts in Florida in March. Florida Troopers said that up to half of truckers at some weigh stations cannot meet English proficiency requirements.

"I try to concentrate on the [signs] they have to read," Master Trooper Craig Lents said at the time. "If you are going down the road at 70 miles per hour, and you see that sign, you only see it for a split second."

In another encounter caught on video, a trooper asked a trucker what a road sign meant.

VIRGINIA BUS CRASH THAT KILLED FIVE INVOLVED DRIVER WHO DOESN'T SPEAK ENGLISH, SEAN DUFFY SAYS

A state trooper gives an unidentified truck driver an English and safety test at a truck stop alongside the freeway. (Fox News Channel)

The trooper then asked what drivers should do if they saw the sign, to which the trucker replied, "No," again.

The Trump administration has noted that federal English requirements have been on the books for years.

"It's been the law for a long period of time," said Derek Barrs, Federal Motor Carrier Safety administrator. "It's a safety issue. … If there was a crash or something like that, I would want to make sure that driver would know how to respond — slow down for upcoming traffic or a crash that has happened up ahead."

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCK DRIVER FROM INDIA ARRESTED IN DEADLY CALIFORNIA HIT-AND-RUN AFTER BIDEN RELEASE

President Donald Trump's administration has vowed crackdowns on illegal immigrants in commercial driving. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

Authorities explained that being unable to speak or read English is extremely dangerous, as truckers are driving by important road signs at high speeds while carrying hundreds of tons.

The enforcement push comes after a string of deadly crashes nationwide involving drivers the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claims were in the U.S. illegally or operating with commercial drivers' licenses (CDLs) they should never have had.

title: Iran’s unseen supreme leader becomes weapon in escalating power struggle, experts say
excerpt:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reportedly submitted a letter of resignation to the Office of the Supreme Leader on ‘Fox News Live.’

Iran’s rival political factions are increasingly invoking ...
body_text:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reportedly submitted a letter of resignation to the Office of the Supreme Leader on ‘Fox News Live.’

Iran’s rival political factions are increasingly invoking the authority of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to attack their opponents and protect their own positions, even as questions persist over whether he is actively governing the country, according to an Iran expert.

The internal struggle surfaced in two reports published by Iran International concerning Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s relationship with the new supreme leader.

In the first report, senior cleric Mohammad-Bagher Kharrazi, a relative of the Khamenei family by marriage, claimed Pezeshkian had repeatedly threatened to resign and was warned that his next resignation would be accepted.

IRAN EXPERT BRANDS ISLAMIC CENTER OF ENGLAND IRAN'S 'UK OFFICE,' URGES IMMEDIATE CLOSURE

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian speaks with Fox News Channel's Martha MacCallum during an interview on September 25, 2025 in New York City. (John Lamparski/Getty Images)

"If he resigns one more time, I will approve it," Kharrazi quoted Khamenei as saying.

Pezeshkian’s office strongly deniedthe account. Mehdi Tabatabaei, the president’s deputy for communications and information, called the allegation "baseless and an outright lie," while another presidential advisor said Kharrazi had no contact with the supreme leader and was known for telling "strange stories."

Hours later, Iran International published a second report alleging Pezeshkian had met Mojtaba Khamenei only once, inside a vehicle with tinted windows at an undisclosed location in Tehran.

According to the outlet’s unnamed sources, the encounter lasted several minutes, the two men could not see each other and Pezeshkian was not permitted to shake Khamenei’s hand. The report alleged that the president later questioned whether the voice he heard had actually belonged to the supreme leader.

IRAN’S GOOD COP, BAD COP GAME IMPLODES AS EXPERTS WARN REGIME VIEWS US AS 'EVIL'

Reformist candidate for the Iran's presidential election Masoud Pezeshkian waves as he arrives to vote at a polling station in Shahr-e-Qods near Tehran, Iran, on July 5, 2024. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)

The claims have not been independently verified. Pezeshkian previously described a substantially different encounter, saying publicly that he had spent approximately two and a half hours with Khamenei in a cordial atmosphere.

Kasra Aarabi, director of IRGC research at United Against Nuclear Iran, said the competing claims surrounding Pezeshkian and Mojtaba Khamenei reflected a deeper struggle inside what he described as an "Islamist oligarchic mafia system."

Under Ali Khamenei, Aarabi said, the supreme leader functioned as the system’s "godfather," arbitrating among rival Islamist factions and guaranteeing their access to power and money. His removal created a vacuum that Mojtaba Khamenei’s appointment was intended to fill, but the new supreme leader’s prolonged public absence has left rival factions uncertain about who is actually in charge.

"The very essence of this mafia system is built on a godfather," Aarabi said. "If the godfather is absent, whether because he is severely incapacitated or nonexistent, that vacuum … re-emerges between the various Islamist oligarchic clans."

Aarabi said those factions are not primarily divided by ideology.

"They’re not competing over ideology," he said. "They’re competing over raw power and economic interests."

In that environment, Aarabi said, Mojtaba Khamenei’s name has become a political instrument that competing factions can invoke to legitimize themselves, constrain their rivals or justify decisions whose true source remains unclear.

WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

People hold placards with an image of Iran's new supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei with late Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, during a gathering to support Mojtaba Khamenei, amid the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, in Tehran, Iran, March 9, 2026. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) Via Reuters)

"Mojtaba’s name is the glue that’s holding the system together right now," Aarabi said. "Each of these clans invokes his name to justify its existence, legitimize its position, and consolidate its place within this fragile system."

Exiled Iranian journalist Mehdi Ghadimi described the resignation claims as part of a recurring political strategy used by reformist administrations.

"This is a familiar cycle," Ghadimi said. "Whenever they feel that their usefulness to the supreme leader has come to an end, they start circulating these resignation rumors in an effort to build public sympathy and improve their image before being pushed aside."

Ghadimi said similar rumors surrounded former presidents Mohammad Khatami and Hassan Rouhani during the final years of their administrations. He argued that reformist-aligned media channels often continue circulating resignation claims even after a president’s office formally denies them, allowing officials later to portray themselves as having challenged the supreme leader.

On Mojtaba Khamenei’s status, Ghadimi went further than Aarabi, saying he did not believe there was "a functioning person by that name who is capable of thinking, making decisions or speaking."

"Either he is dead, or he is being kept alive in an extremely unstable and severely deteriorated condition," Ghadimi said.

Aarabi said the two reports illustrate that dynamic. A cleric opposed to or unaligned with Pezeshkian invoked Mojtaba Khamenei’s authority to weaken the president by claiming his next resignation would be accepted, while figures around Pezeshkian pushed back with an account portraying the president as having met directly with the supreme leader.

Mojtaba Khamenei has not appeared in any publicly released video or audio recording since succeeding his father, according to Iran International. Iranian officials have offered conflicting accounts about how often senior government figures have met him.

Aarabi cautioned that using Khamenei’s name as a source of authority will become increasingly difficult if his public absence continues.

A composite image shows several Iranian leaders named in the State Department’s Rewards for Justice program offering up to $10 million for information on key figures tied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), including Mojtaba Khamenei, top left. (State Department / Rewards for Justice; Khoshiran / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images)

"There’s only so many times you can use someone’s name without any proof of life that they actually exist," Aarabi said. "The longer Mojtaba is absent, the more questions develop over whether he is alive or able. And as soon as that doubt increases, you will see this infighting increase."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Devastating LA wildfire sparked by utility company tower, long-awaited report finds
excerpt:
Investigators pin blame for Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and ruined thousands of homes, on ‘electrical arcing events’ at out-of-service tower

The deadly 2025 Eaton fire in the Los Angeles area ...
body_text:
Investigators pin blame for Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and ruined thousands of homes, on ‘electrical arcing events’ at out-of-service tower

The deadly 2025 Eaton fire in the Los Angeles area was caused by equipment belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison, fire officials said in a report released on Tuesday.

Los Angeles county fire officials found that the cause of the fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses was a tower that was not in service, according to the report.

“After 18 months of thorough review of all evidence, alongside retained electrical and metallurgical experts, the investigation concluded that the cause of the wildfire conflagration was due to the electrical arcing events that took place on the out-of-service Southern California Edison (SCE) tower,” the agency said in a statement.

It took firefighters nearly a month to extinguish the blaze, which scorched 22 sq miles (57 sq km).

Kathleen Dunleavy, a spokesperson for Southern California Edison, said the utility has received the report and is reviewing it.

“We have taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the very beginning,” Dunleavy said. She said SCE previously acknowledged “it was likely our equipment was associated with the ignition of the Eaton fire”.

She said the utility continues to support the community as it recovers.

SoCal Edison has claimed in lawsuits earlier this year that Los Angeles county agencies failed to send timely evacuation warnings to residents in east and west Altadena. Eighteen of the 19 people who died in the fire lived in west Altadena.

The utility also has claimed water agencies, including Pasadena Water and Power, did not provide enough water as the fire spread, leaving firefighters with limited resources. Los Angeles county declined to comment about the latest court filings.

The Los Angeles county arson fire investigation unit jointly conducted the investigation with California department of forestry and fire protection. It found electrical arcing on the utility’s out-of-service tower sparked the dry brush below and that the utility was responsible for maintaining and operating its electrical lines and equipment “in a manner that would minimize the risk of catastrophic wildfire posed by them.”

The blaze was sparked during extreme weather conditions that included high temperatures, low humidity and powerful winds. Two “electrical arcing events” occurred in quick succession, causing an unknown burning material to fall from the tower to the ground below, according to the report.

Within 12 seconds, dry grass and brush was ignited and the fire swiftly developed “into a conflagration engulfing the areas of the San Gabriel Mountains, Altadena, Pasadena, Sierra Madre and La Cañada Flintridge”, the report said. It took more than two weeks to fully contain the wildfire.

The report cites an interview with a Pasadena resident who called 911 on 7 January after spotting flames across the canyon from his home’s rear window. The caller described it “as a 10in x 10in fire at the base of a high-voltage electrical tower”, the report said.

The Eaton fire burned at the same time as the Palisades fire, the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles to date and among the five worst in California’s history. The blaze killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 homes and buildings in Pacific Palisades. The fire ripped through hillside neighborhoods, destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views.

The man accused of sparking the Palisades fire will be tried again this fall after his first federal arson case ended in a mistrial in June. Prosecutors said Jonathan Rinderknecht used a barbecue lighter on 1 January 2025 to spark a blaze that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up 7 January.

title: Social media reacts to tennis star Aryna Sabalenka's comments on WTA transgender rules
excerpt: Fox News discusses the Supreme Court's decision to uphold transgender sports bans. Former NCAA All-American Riley Gaines states it's 'insane' to challenge biological sex in sports, asserting boys shou...
body_text:
Fox News discusses the Supreme Court's decision to uphold transgender sports bans. Former NCAA All-American Riley Gaines states it's 'insane' to challenge biological sex in sports, asserting boys should not compete in girls' sports. She calls the opposing movement 'misogynistic,' advocating for female athletes' rights and fair competition, a view echoed by Education Secretary Linda McMahon. This highlights the contentious issue in women's sports.

Aryna Sabalenka has stirred up quite a bit of discourse on social media over the last 24 hours, and it had nothing to do with what she wore in her latest match.

The number one women's tennis player in the world went on record Monday saying that she's in favor of the WTA's new transgender eligibility policy, which includes a genetic screening requirement.

The Belarusian star was asked about it during her Canadian Open press conference in Montreal, and she did not hold back, calling it a necessary step and saying, "It's really important to keep the fairness in our tour."

SOFTBALL HALL OF FAMER SENDS BLUNT WARNING TO THOSE DEFENDING INCLUSION OF BIOLOGICAL MALES IN FEMALE SPORTS

While most applauded Sabalenka for her take as well as the WTA for trying to keep their league fair, not everyone on social media was thrilled.

Aryna Sabalenka celebrates winning match point against Anastasia Pavlyuchenkova in the women's singles quarterfinal during day 10 of the 2025 Australian Open at Melbourne Park on Jan. 21, 2025, in Melbourne, Australia. (Getty Images)

As they did with the Sophie Cunningham/WNBA trans debate, plenty of people on social media chose to bury their heads in the sand, saying that biological men in women's sports isn't a real problem.

Others resorted to the "old standby" of leftists everywhere: When all other arguments fail, just call your opponent a "bigot" and a "transphobe."

While a very loud, vocal minority took to social media to try to shout Sabalenka down, plenty more were on her side, pointing out that more star athletes need to be emboldened to voice their opinions on the matter, especially for something as rooted in common sense as "men shouldn't play women's sports."

WRITER ARRESTED FOR ALLEGEDLY BEATING WIFE CALLS SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM 'ANTI-TRANS, ANTI-BLACK' IN WILD OP-ED

As someone on X mentioned, it's amazing that we even need to be having these conversations, let alone heaping praise on people for saying something that less than two decades ago was a nearly universally accepted fact.

Anyone pointing out that there are no biological men competing in women's professional tennis is either being intentionally obtuse or they're missing the forest for the trees so badly they should be considered legally blind.

Biological males are infiltrating girls' sports, specifically at the youth and high school level, at remarkably high levels.

'Save Girls Sports' activists at a rally in California on Saturday, May 9, 2026 (OutKick's Alejandro Avilla)

Several of my OutKick coworkers have even documented a few of these cases.

TRANS ATHLETE WINS NEW YORK STATE GIRLS' SHOT PUT TITLE, BEATING SECOND PLACE BY MORE THAN 2 FEET

The WTA is just doing what should be done in this situation: being proactive.

And these leftists know exactly what they are doing, too.

It's why people like West Wilson will say that there aren't any biological males in the WNBA but will conveniently leave out youth and high school sports, all the while a WNBA coach wears a shirt that says "Trans Kids Belong."

Aryna Sabalenka returns a shot against Cristina Bucsa of Spain during their women's singles fourth-round match on Day Eight of the 2025 US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in the Flushing neighborhood of Queens, New York City, on Aug. 31, 2025. (Getty Images)

As the goalposts continue to move, sane people continue to scratch their heads.

CHERYL REEVE SENDS CLEAR MESSAGE TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM WITH ‘TRANS KIDS BELONG’ SHIRT DURING FEVER-LYNX GAME

Thankfully, stars like Sabalenka and Sophie Cunningham have the courage to speak out, and hopefully more will follow their lead.

title: University of Maryland ‘teacher of the year’ detained by ICE in Texas
excerpt:
DHS said pharmacy instructor Berhanu Kibret overstayed visa and arrested him at Dallas-Fort Worth airport

An instructor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore who only just received a “teacher of t...
body_text:
DHS said pharmacy instructor Berhanu Kibret overstayed visa and arrested him at Dallas-Fort Worth airport

An instructor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore who only just received a “teacher of the year” award has been arrested by federal immigration agents under the command of the Trump administration.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials detained Berhanu Kibret, an instructor at the university’s pharmacy school, at the Dallas-Fort Worth airport in Texas, according to multiple news reports. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed Kibret’s arrest, citing an expired visa – but it stopped short of providing a location.

In a statement, the University of Maryland said Kibret was arrested while returning from a meeting of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, where he received a “teacher of the year” award.

“Dr Kibret has a valid work authorization, so it is our hope that any issues surrounding his status will be quickly resolved and that he will be permitted to continue his work at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy,” the institution added, according to CBS.

Kibret’s research focuses on how the brain’s cannabinoid system influences mental health, brain disease and the effects of addictive drugs, the university’s website says. He obtained bachelor’s and master’s degrees in science as well as a PhD in Ethiopia – and he completed his postdoctoral fellowship at William Paterson University in Wayne, New Jersey.

Calling Kibret a “highly valued member of the University of Maryland, Baltimore community”, the school said it was “greatly troubled” by his arrest.

The university added: “He is an effective and beloved teacher, and a highly regarded colleague. His detention has generated not only great sympathy for his plight, but also a heightened sense of apprehension here on campus.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the DHS said ICE arrested Kibret after he entered the US on 21 June 2021 on a visa set to expire on 31 May 2024.

“Against our nation’s laws, he overstayed his visa and failed to depart,” the DHS statement said. “He will remain in ICE custody pending his immigration proceedings.”

The Guardian has reached out to the University of Maryland, Baltimore for additional comment.

Arrests such as that of Kibret have drawn criticism, particularly in light of the Trump administration’s repeated pledge to focus on targeting the “worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens” for arrest and deportation.

A Guardian analysis published in February found that 77% of people placed into deportation proceedings for the first time after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 had no criminal convictions.

Kibret’s arrest came after ICE in July detained and later released a Johns Hopkins researcher at the Baltimore/Washington international airport.

Federal authorities detained Fatima Ameaka, a Cameroonian citizen with a doctorate in pharmacy who works at Johns Hopkins University’s Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Speaking to several outlets during Ameaka’s detention, a Johns Hopkins spokesperson described her as a “respected member of our community”.

“The university understands the fear and concern this instills in members of our community,” the spokesperson added. “Dr Ameaka was traveling in a personal capacity, and though we cannot comment on the specifics of her situation, we want to assure our community that the university is actively working to provide support for Dr Ameaka, including ensuring she has access to legal representation.”

Documents reviewed by ABC indicated that Ameaka held a work authorization valid through 2029 and had a pending asylum case.

Nonetheless, as ABC reported, the DHS had initially said of Ameaka: “In violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her visa. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

Ameaka’s attorney on Sunday confirmed that she had been released from ICE detention.

title: Trump keeps calling Thune despite public fight over SAVE America Act
excerpt:
President Donald Trump didn’t fully back Senate Majority Leader John Thune, telling reporters in the Oval Office,

FIRST ON FOX: The reports of President Donald Trump and Senate Majority Leader John T...
body_text:
President Donald Trump didn’t fully back Senate Majority Leader John Thune, telling reporters in the Oval Office,

FIRST ON FOX: The reports of President Donald Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune's dead working relationship have been greatly exaggerated, the South Dakota Republican leader told Fox News Digital.

"I've heard from him twice this morning already. He called me over the weekend, and so there, you know, we talk, I don't bother him, I'm not calling him every day," Thune said in an interview.

Last week, Trump said, "We're going to find out," whether Thune was the man for the job to lead Senate Republicans, casting doubt on a critical relationship between him and the Senate’s top Republican.

TRUMP QUESTIONS THUNE'S LEADERSHIP AS SAVE AMERICA ACT STALLS

Reports of Senate Majority Leader John Thune and President Donald Trump's relationship deteriorating are greatly exaggerated, Thune told Fox News Digital. In fact, they have spoken several times over the last few days since Trump's "we'll see" comment about his future as Republican leader. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images ;)

The tension stems from the SAVE America Act floundering in the Senate, and Trump’s desire to see the election integrity package passed by any means necessary.

Thune doesn’t see Trump’s comment as a personal slight, however. Both he and the president "want to get to the same place. We have, sometimes, disagreements about how best to get there."

"Most of mine are constrained by what's achievable in an institution like the Senate that has procedural roadblocks to do almost anything," Thune said.

"We have those candid conversations, but I'm not worried about that relationship," he continued. "I know he's going to push as hard as he can. That's his business model, is to just keep pushing, pushing, pushing to get people to go as far as they can go."

SENATE FACES 'COME-TO-JESUS' MOMENT ON TRUMP'S ELECTION PRIORITY UNDER GOP'S NEW PLAN

There is a voracious appetite among Trump, Senate Republicans and their base to see the SAVE America Act passed. One that Thune hears everyday, either online or within his own conference.

It’s dominated the oxygen inside the Capitol and beyond its walls, and the pressure comes as the Senate is sprinting to finish work on key items, like preventing a government shutdown and confirming dozens of Trump’s nominees.

"There are good days and bad days," Thune said. "And around here, probably lately more bad days than good days, but you know you just kind of, like I said, keep your head down, do the work."

But passing the SAVE America Act is the most elusive item for Republicans, given the current make up of the Senate.

While there are a cohort of Republicans who are voting against it, Thune made the point that every single Senate Democrat has shut it down each of the five times that it’s been brought to the floor in a variety of configurations.

And Thune is one of the Republicans that wants the bill passed — he’s an original co-sponsor of the SAVE Act, the precursor to the current version of the SAVE America Act. The avenue of cutting Democrats out of the equation and ramming through aspects of the bill through budget reconciliation exists, which Thune is interested in pursuing.

But then comes the problem of generating 50 votes to support that, and keeping those votes together to shut down "crazy democratic amendments."

GOP RIFT GROWS AS THUNE HITS BRAKES ON TRUMP'S ELECTION BILL TO AVERT SHUTDOWN

Thune's job helming the Senate majority is to do the math on what can be accomplished in an institution that’s "designed" to be difficult. And the votes still aren’t adding up.

"I keep asking the question, am I the only one in this town that can count to 50? Because it seems like these questions recur and there are a lot of people out there who haven't seemed to internalize the fact that there aren't Democrats that are going to flip and vote for this," Thune said.

"And there aren't 50 Republicans that are going to vote to nuke the filibuster. Those are two facts that are indisputable and unchangeable."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., argued that Democrats were continuing their push to keep DHS closed because it was "politically advantageous." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Thune’s position is, by extension, an embodiment of the Senate in many ways.

Unlike the House, legislation and agendas can’t be rammed through without a bipartisan agreement to blast through the filibuster. And senators' concerns and desires encompass an entire state, not just a sliver of a state’s population.

Through several interviews with Fox News Digital, he’s instilled that part of his job is to listen and take consensus on what does and doesn’t work, deliberating on the best path for a deliverable outcome.

"This place was supposed to be difficult, so that no dictator could master it, and I think that's kind of the role of the Senate in our system and our democracy," Thune said.

"It's important to keep that in perspective, but it's frustrating as heck when you're somebody who likes to get things done, likes to get results, and you've got procedural roadblocks holding things up as we try to wind down and get some things done," he continued.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Ex-Olympian weighing ‘all options’ after reflecting pool charges dropped
excerpt:
David Hearn has ‘number of potential remedies’ after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage, attorney says

An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Li...
body_text:
David Hearn has ‘number of potential remedies’ after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage, attorney says

An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has said that “all options are on table” for legal recourse after prosecutors recently abandoned the case abruptly.

David Hearn “has a number of potential remedies” after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage now attributed to faulty work by a contractor, attorney Steven Levin said in a statement. Levin added that those could include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses”, and requests for investigations by various government entities, including Congress.

Hearn, 67, was arrested on 19 June and faced one felony count of property destruction – a charge that could have resulted in a 10-year prison sentence and a $1,000 fine – which he denied.

The charge came after Donald Trump’s administration spent $14m to change the reflecting pool’s color. A new pool liner almost immediately began to peel off, and the president blamed vandals. Four people were arrested, but only Hearn was charged with a felony.

On Friday, Trump’s justice department moved to dismiss the charge against Hearn, saying in a filing that the damage to the pool liner was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor” who worked on it.

In a 20-page court filing in Washington DC superior court on Friday, prosecutors said they had received information about a “rush to complete the project” prior to events associated with the celebration of the US’s semiquincentennial on Fourth of July.

Washington DC’s US attorney, Jeanine Pirro, said that her office – which handles cases in the city’s superior court – had received key documents from the federal department of the interior after the indictment was filed. Those documents “indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the reflecting pool,” Pirro wrote in Friday’s court filing.

The resulting decision to drop the charge against Hearn set off a dispute within Trump’s administration. The president said Pirro had “choked” and “folded like an umbrella” leading to speculation that she might be fired from her post. Trump has continued to blame vandalism for problems with the pool makeover.

On Monday, the president ducked questions about Pirro’s charge dismissal but maintained his criticism of her, saying “I disagree 100% with [her]”. Pirro was spotted at the White House hours after Trump’s comments on Monday.

Attorneys for Hearn have previously said the government “owes Mr Hearn an apology”.

“The Trump administration’s case against Davey Hearn should have never been brought,” his attorneys, including Levin, said on social media. “Its dismissal … does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong.”

Hearn told the Associated Press that he had been detained by the national guard and US park police for five hours after stopping by the reflecting pool during a bike ride. He acknowledged that he briefly touched a part on the liner attached to the side and told NBC News the pool’s condition “was the same after I stepped away from the water as it was before I got there”.

Lawyers for Hearn have also called on prosecutors to disclose the legal instructions they gave to grand jurors about the elements of the criminal charge handed up against him.

“The grand jury transcripts disclosed to the defense thus far contain other irregularities that reflect a misleading presentation to the grand jury and a need for review of the entire grand jury record in this matter,” Hearn’s attorneys wrote.

Hearn’s opportunities for legal recourse against the federal government may come only after his attorneys petition the court to dismiss the case “with prejudice”, meaning that it could not be refiled. The justice department dropped the charge “without prejudice”, meaning that it can be refiled.

“We are responding with our own motion to dismiss with prejudice so that he is not longer at risk of being harassed by the government further,” Levin said on Tuesday. “Once that is resolved Mr Hearn will focus on what comes next.

In a statement to the Wall Street Journal, Hearn’s attorney Norm Eisen said the team plan to go on the offensive against the government: “All legal remedies are on the table going forward to respond to the miscarriage of justice,” Eisen said.
