Got a tech question? Get Kurt’s free CyberGuy Newsletter, share your voice, a story idea or comment at CyberGuy.com.

title: Gatwick airport to open second runway after legal challenge fails
excerpt:
£2.2bn project will allow about 100,000 more flights a year to use Britain’s second busiest airport

Gatwick airport is to start development of its second runway after campaigners lost a legal challen...
body_text:
£2.2bn project will allow about 100,000 more flights a year to use Britain’s second busiest airport

Gatwick airport is to start development of its second runway after campaigners lost a legal challenge to the plans.

The court of appeal on Tuesday dismissed a bid by local campaign groups to challenge an earlier high court ruling that the scheme could proceed.

The £2.2bn project, approved by the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, in September, will allow about 100,000 more flights a year to use Britain’s second busiest airport.

Pierre-Hugues Schmit, the Gatwick chief executive, said the airport was “very pleased that this ruling brings to an end an eight-year planning and legal process which has carefully tested and scrutinised every aspect of our expansion plans on multiple occasions”.

The plans will involve the West Sussex airport slightly repositioning its emergency runway and using it routinely for short-haul passenger aircraft. It is now among the busiest single-runway airports in the world, and hopes to have the second runway in operation as early as 2030.

The government declared the court ruling a “major milestone for Gatwick and for local communities”.

Alexander said: “Around 13 million more passengers and 100,000 more flights will give holidaymakers greater choice and strengthen global links to help make the UK one of the most attractive places in the world to invest.

“We’ll back expansion that supports growth and our climate goals. To drive forward sustainable change, we’re also investing more than £219m for green fuel production to cut emissions from flying and secure the future of aviation.”

Campaigners had sought a judicial review of the Department for Transport’s decision to approve the plans, arguing that the government had not properly assessed the scheme’s climate impact.

One of the applicants, Peter Barclay, the chair of Gatwick Area Conservation Campaign, said he was disappointed with the ruling. He said: “It is time for governments to wake up and realise that saying yes to the expansion of any and every airport will not kickstart the economy … It will further lock in aviation’s climate, noise and air pollution impacts, increase congestion on roads and public transport and blight local communities.”

Meanwhile, Luton Rising, the council-owned company behind Luton airport, announced that all legal challenges to its expansion plans had now been cleared. The supreme court has dismissed any final possibility of appealing against a high court ruling last November upholding Alexander’s signoff on plans to increase the airport’s annual capacity from 19 million to 32 million passengers by the mid-2040s.

The airport owner said it would create up to 11,000 new jobs and generate up to an additional £1.5bn in annual economic activity, and pledged strict controls on noise and carbon emissions, air quality and surface access to the airport.

title: Washington state Democrat who flipped pro-Trump district faces tough primary
excerpt:
Incumbent Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate who owns an auto repair shop, hopes to retain congressional seat

The two-term Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is heading into one of the...
body_text:
Incumbent Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate who owns an auto repair shop, hopes to retain congressional seat

The two-term Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is heading into one of the country’s most closely watched contests on Tuesday after national recognition for flipping a Republican seat in 2022.

Representing Washington state’s third district, Gluesenkamp Perez finds herself squeezed between Democrat and progressive Brent Hennrich and Republican state senator John Braun on her right. There are six other candidates on a single crowded ballot and the top two finishers will advance to the November general election regardless of party.

Democrats are favored to win the House of Representatives in November’s midterm election, but highly contested seats like Gluesenkamp Perez’s will be crucial to securing a majority, and expanding the margin.

Republican Jaime Herrera Beutler won Washington’s third district in 2010 and held it for six terms, until Gluesenkamp Perez narrowly beat Trump-endorsed Joe Kent in 2022. Trump has carried the district in all three of his presidential runs, most recently by about three points, and yet in 2024 Gluesenkamp Perez ran roughly seven points ahead of her party’s presidential nominee.

Logging, mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life in much of the area and Gluesenkamp Perez’s success has stemmed from her appeal to moderates and rural voters. An auto repair shop owner, she won over many in south-west Washington, including Republicans who considered Kent too extreme.

“We like her a lot,” said Laura Oltmann, 41, a resident and supporter who describes herself as a conservative. Kent did not embody conservatism, Oltmann said.

But through Gluesenkamp Perez’s two terms, frustration has built among her own party, growing when Democrats saw her siding with Republicans on major legislation. Hennrich, who is challenging her in the primary, ran for the same seat in 2022 before standing down, but decided to run again. “I stepped out of this race to unify Democrats to help get Marie through, so we could get rid of our six-term incumbent, Jaime Herrera Beutler,” he said.

“[Gluesenkamp Perez] has turned out to be just an absolute epic failure for Democrats.”

Hennrich is not alone. Several local Democratic organizations inside the district have broken with her. “She ran as a Democrat and inspired a lot of people, and she won, and we thought she was going to be what we wanted her to be. But everybody’s disappointed,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity.

Kirkpatrick traces that disappointment to Gluesenkamp Perez’s votes for the Save Act, Trump’s effort to overhaul elections, as well as for a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity, and federal funding tied to the war in Iran. She claims the congresswoman has also stopped talking to her own party’s local officers.

Thea Zahn, the chair of the 20th legislative district, agreed. “What majority are you going for?” she said. “Are you going for a majority that believes in Democratic values, or a majority that will fail over and over again when it comes down to it, when you really need people to stand up and say this is what we believe in?”

“If she gets to the primary, I will be one of them. I won’t vote for Marie. I will never vote for Marie Perez again,” Zahn added.

The congresswoman’s defenders make a different argument: that the district’s partisan lean leaves her little room, and that the seat matters more than any single vote.

“The reality is we live in a Republican district. It is Republican,” said Terri Niles, who chairs the 17th Legislative District Democrats and spoke in a personal capacity. “I’ve knocked on tens of thousands of doors.”

Niles argues that none of Gluesenkamp Perez’s contentious votes actually resulted in legislation passing, and that the calculation for Democrats is simpler than her critics allow. “The most important thing everybody should keep in mind is that flipping the House is our goal,” she said. “That should be the most important thing for every Democrat out there.”

The Democratic infighting comes at a precarious moment. An Emerson College poll conducted in mid-July for the Northwest Progressive Institute found Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican Braun tied. Braun, the Republican leader in the Washington senate, has become one of the GOP’s top congressional recruits, earning Donald Trump’s endorsement in April and the backing of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

“We could hand a truly 100% Maga candidate a congressional seat for life,” said Tim Probst, a local Democratic party leader. “Because once he gets in there, he’s not getting out.”

title: A rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only train
excerpt:
This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways

The 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil P...
body_text:
This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways

The 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil Patel’s week. “I’ve never gotten a seat. I always stand up even when I get here early,” says the 22-year-old, struggling to keep his balance while the gangway underneath sways from side to side.

Painfully for Patel, who is commuting back and forth to the capital for a computer science internship, it’s the first leg of a three-hour journey home to Walsall. He grabs the back of a chair to remain steady but says he’s just thankful that the train has left on time – and that it’s even on the move at all.

“There’s been a couple of times where everyone’s boarded and then the train’s been cancelled and we all had to get off,” he says. On another occasion, his journey home took five hours because this service was delayed, meaning he missed a connecting train.

This rush-hour service, operated by London Northwestern Railway (LNR), is the busiest commuter-only journey in England and Wales, according to figures by the Department for Transport.

Overall, it’s the second busiest commute, the No 1 being a morning Thameslink service from Bedford to Three Bridges – which passes through three international hubs: St Pancras International, and Luton and Gatwick airports.

We decided to join commuters getting the packed, two-hour-plus service on Thursday evening. According to the DfT, the service had a load factor – how many people are on a train compared with its maximum capacity – of 170% when the analysis was carried out last autumn. LNR says the number of seats on the service has increased from 460 to 812 since the data was gathered.

There is the familiar scrum moving towards the train after the platform is announced, an infamous tradition at Euston station. At first it seems as if this crop of commuters has lucked out, as it isn’t overly busy. But as the clock approaches 5.46pm, the carriages begin to heave with people.

Some fan themselves to keep the summer heat at bay. When the train is finally on the move, most gangways are cluttered with unlucky commuters unable to snag a seat. Some stand but others sit, bearing the rough and tumble of the shifting metal surface underneath.

Among them is Daniel Garrill, 23, who regularly gets this service. “I know I’m going to be sitting in some dodgy spot,” the data analyst says, having never got a seat during the week.

He travels between London and Manchester at least twice a week, meaning he has to bring a suitcase – which is tricky because there’s “nowhere to put your bag either”. He has to keep fiddling with his luggage to ensure it doesn’t escape down the carriage.

On the other side of the gangway is Akshay Vaghela, 31, who is commuting to Rugby. He says he is forced to stand half the time, and more often than not is “resigned to finding a seat on the floor”. This train is particularly busy because it is cheaper than the shorter Avanti service also heading to Crewe.

“I’ve gotten used to it because I know what booking this service means. It’s a free-for-all for the seats, otherwise you’re standing,” he says. Despite the train being kitted out with air conditioning, Vaghela says it’s still “stuffy, hot and sweaty” because there are so many people on it. “Unless you’ve got water, you’re struggling until you get home,” he says.

There is a chance things might not stay this way. Andy Burnham, newly installed as prime minister, has had rail operators in his sights for a while, making headlines for calling out poor performers while mayor of Greater Manchester.

He has previously said nationalising railways is a “no brainer” and launched the Bee Network as mayor, which brought privatised bus and tram networks into the local government’s control and capped fares at £2. Rail services across Greater Manchester will start to join the network by the end of the year.

He faced a rude reminder of the state of our railways last month. After his election as MP for Makerfield, he took a 10.54am Avanti West Coast train from Manchester to Euston. The service was delayed by 21 minutes, making him eligible to claim compensation.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also faced a bumpy train journey, saying she sat on the floor of a packed service from London Paddington to her constituency in Swindon.

Burnham hinted in May that there could be a swifter move towards rail renationalisation – a number of operators were brought under state control while Keir Starmer was prime minister – saying it would “reduce train fares and make them affordable to people again”.

Vaghela is optimistic that Burnham will enforce some change. He says “priority routes like this one which connect main parts of the country should be looked at”, especially because “everyone’s paying the same price and some people get seats and others don’t, there’s a disparity there”.

As we advance further down the carriages, we squeeze past commuters packed together by the platform doors, sidestep buggies and grab on to windows, poles or even fellow passengers to avoid tumbling to the floor.

Standing among a group of commuters in a packed gangway is retiree Andy Simms, 65. He has a lucky escape, only having to bear the service for half an hour. He’s getting off at the first stop: Milton Keynes Central.

Simms isn’t too bothered about the packed train. “It’s fine but busy,” he says, though he admits: “If you’re doing this every day it must be very annoying, especially if you’re paying for a season ticket.”

Overall, he thinks trains are better than he remembers. “Things used to be a lot worse on trains back in my youth. It was scruffy, dirty and violent,” he says.

On the prospect of Burnham making changes to the rail system, he’d rather he keep his focus elsewhere. “I think social care is more important than train journeys. I’d rather he fix that than this,” he says, while holding on to a pole behind for balance.

An LNR spokesperson said: “Our services to and from Euston are extremely popular, which is why we have made a major £1bn investment in new trains to provide extra space for our customers.

“Since this data was gathered we have added hundreds of extra seats to this particular service, increasing its capacity by 77% and significantly reducing its load factor to provide more comfortable journeys for passengers.”

title: New stars, fading appeal: Has the Hollywood Walk of Fame lost its luster?
excerpt:
Production vendors are sounding the alarm on the 'decimation' of the film industry in California.

Even as new inductees arrive, some Tinseltown historians say the legendary Hollywood Walk of Fame has...
body_text:
Production vendors are sounding the alarm on the 'decimation' of the film industry in California.

Even as new inductees arrive, some Tinseltown historians say the legendary Hollywood Walk of Fame has lost its luster.

The iconic strip that began with a groundbreaking ceremony in 1960 and now spans 15 blocks of Hollywood Boulevard and three blocks of Vine Street has experienced physical neglect.

Many of the 2,852 five-pointed brass and terrazzo stars honoring entertainment industry achievements are dirty, cracked and covered in grime. They sit in Hollywood’s commercial center full of discount souvenir shops, panhandlers and pushy vendors. Trash and unpleasant odors are common, while the general overall condition of the boulevard leaves the area feeling neglected and far from glamorous.

Christina Applegate attends a ceremony honoring Christina Applegate with a star on the Hollywood Walk Of Fame on Nov. 14, 2022, in Los Angeles, California. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for Netflix)

CHRISTIAN SLATER OPENS UP ABOUT ‘WEIRD’ REALITY OF FAME AFTER 5 DECADES IN HOLLYWOOD

"It’s really tough today because of what Hollywood has become… there’s very aggressive people on the street," author and pop culture historian Chris Epting told Fox News Digital. "Unfortunately, Hollywood’s been allowed to fall into a really sad state. It’s outright dangerous in many parts."

Epting, who remembers going to the Walk of Fame as far back as the 1970s when he was a kid, noted that when Hollywood as a place began falling apart, it took the Walk of Fame right along with it.

"There’s no way to separate the two," he added. "I think a lot of people lament the fact that part of Hollywood — really most of Hollywood — is not that friendly or inviting the way it once was and the stars on the sidewalk pay that price as well."

Epting, who co-authored the 2017 memoir "Change of Seasons: A Memoir" with musician John Oates of the R&B band Hall & Oates, recalled being with Oates the day he and Hall received their star right in front of the Musicians Institute.

"It’s kind of cool to be part of their little world, the day they got theirs," Epting said, noting that sometimes stars are put in certain places on the famous walkway. For instance, Jay Leno requested that his star be placed at the exact corner where he had twice been arrested for vagrancy early in his comedy career.

Ricky Gervais poses at the ceremony honoring Ricky Gervais with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on May 30, 2025, in Hollywood, California. (Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images)

"I don’t think many people go out looking for it like they used to, but I think that if they could help the area out a little bit, that would probably help people reconnect with the Walk."

Meanwhile, new inductees are named by the Walk of Fame Selection Committee with roughly 33 honorees selected each year from hundreds of submissions.

Last month, Actress Ming-Na Wen and singer/songwriter Sheila E., both Walk of Famers, joined Hollywood Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Ron Frierson, to announce the Class of 2027 honorees from Funko Hollywood retail store.

AVRIL LAVIGNE HONORED WITH A STAR ON THE HOLLYWOOD WALK OF FAME: ‘I FEEL VERY BLESSED AND GRATEFUL’

Flowers cover the Walk of Fame star for Rob Reiner Monday, Dec. 15, 2025, in the Hollywood section of Los Angeles. (Damian Dovarganes/AP Photo)

Among the new group of entertainment professionals chosen from the overall categories of Motion Pictures, Television, Live Theatre/Live Performance, Radio, Recording, and Sports Entertainment include actors Idris Elba, Sam Elliott, sisters Elle and Dakota Fanning and Kate Hudson.

Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos rounded out the Motion Pictures category, while actors David Alan Grier, Lisa Kudrow, Pedro Pascal and Adam Scott were among those selected in the TV category. Waylon Jennings (posthumously), The Ramones, Smashing Pumpkins and others made the cut in the Recording category.

"… These 32 extraordinary individuals have each made a lasting impact on audiences around the world through their talent, creativity, and dedication to their craft," Walk of Fame Selection Chairman Peter Roth said in a statement. "We are honored to recognize their remarkable contributions and look forward to celebrating them as they take their place in Hollywood history."

According to the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce, the Hollywood Walk of Fame attracts an estimated 10 million visitors annually. More recent mobility data, however, has the estimate closer to 5 to 6 million visitors each year.

Look at celebrities who have received stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, in Hollywood, California, on April 26, 2023.  (iStock)

Still, Hollywood historian and storyteller Scott Michaels, known for creating Dearly Departed Tours, an LA tour company that looks at the dark side of Hollywood history, blames much of the Walk of Fame’s decline on the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce, arguing its focus has shifted toward revenue rather than preservation.

Michaels, who was a member of the Chamber for a few years, noted that these days it costs $85,000 to receive a star on the celebrity promenade, while at one time the price tag was just $2,000.

Now, many star ceremonies, which still draw crowds, are scheduled to purposefully coincide with their latest movie or album release. And even corporate brands can receive stars on the Walk.

And because stars are considered historic landmarks never to be removed, certain disgraced figures or minor reality TV names permanently remain.

"There was a time when the Hollywood Walk of Fame was a true honor," Michaels told Fox News Digital, noting that stepping just below the famous celebrity hands and footprints at Grauman’s Chinese Theatre, visitors once experienced the shiny brass-and-terrazzo stars embedded in the sidewalk outside.

Since then, a large silver statue called "The Four Ladies" marking the beginning of the Walk of Fame at the corner of LaBrea and Hollywood Boulevard saw the small bronze of Marilyn Monroe at the very top of it stolen (after a thief sawed it off and took it). Marilyn was recovered, but Michaels noted six years later it’s never been reinstalled.

A pedestrian walks past the "Four Ladies of Hollywood" gazebo on Hollywood Boulevard in Los Angeles, on Wednesday, June 19, 2019. (AP Photo/Richard Vogel)

In August 2025, a van slammed into the statue of the "four trailblazing ladies of color" and heavily damaged pioneering actress Anna May Wong, known as the first Chinese American movie star.

A year later, the damaged likeness of Wong has yet to be fully restored.

While the Chamber may not be necessarily responsible for the statue, it likely had its cooperation on design and approval, Michaels said.

The statue is the "gateway" to the Walk of Fame with tourists often posing in front of it.

Marilyn Monroe's star on the Walk of Fame. (Scott Michaels)

Fox News Digital reached out to the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce multiple times for comment.

The 1.3 mile famous boulevard has also generated negative headlines in recent years, including the time actress/singer Miley Cyrus claimed she landed in the hospital with a brutal infection after filming a scene on the Walk of Fame. Another incident involved a homeless man dumping a bucket of feces on a woman’s head.

A few years back, when Michaels petitioned to move Marilyn Monroe’s star from in front of the McDonald’s a few blocks from Grauman’s Chinese Theatre to in front of the theater because he was "sick of seeing her star being covered in s---, piss and trash," his request fell on deaf ears.

Michaels said the Chamber representative’s response was simply, "Who will pay for it?"

'EXORCIST' STAR LINDA BLAIR 'UNKNOWINGLY' WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD

(L-R) Harper Vivienne Ann Lockwood, Lisa Marie Presley, Priscilla Presley, Riley Keough, and Finley Aaron Love Lockwood attend the Handprint Ceremony honoring Three Generations of Presley's at TCL Chinese Theatre on June 21, 2022, in Hollywood, California.  (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic/Getty Images)

Yet, Michaels noted, well over 100 images of Monroe are plastered in shops, on shirts and signs, all visible from the street.

"Vendors are out of control. You can now sell dry fetid sausages without a food grade or inspection, in front of actual licensed restaurants. But try to open a restaurant," Michaels quipped, about the state of the boulevard.

Chuck Suhayda, former board member of the Hollywood Neighborhood Council, told Fox News Digital there was a time when a lot of money was spent keeping the Walk clean and up to date on repairs. He credited that to the Chamber’s Economic Workforce Development department, various agencies like the Hollywood Boulevard Commercial and Entertainment District and "the very effective Community Redevelopment Agency installed in Hollywood under previous California Gov. Jerry Brown."

MASKED BURGLARY CREWS TERRORIZING RITZY NEIGHBORHOODS SHOW 'THEY'RE DOING THEIR HOMEWORK,' VETERAN COP WARNS

Suhayda recalled that historically, security firm Andrews International provided the local Business Improvement District security patrol services on Hollywood Boulevard.

"Cameras were all up and down Hollywood Blvd," Suhayda said, noting that Hollywood is and has been considered "ground zero" for terrorist attacks in an area that extends from the 101 freeway to La Brea Avenue.

Yet, despite the decline, Epting still holds fondness for the iconic boulevard in his heart.

(L-R) Seth Gabel, Bryce Dallas Howard, Director Ron Howard, Cheryl Howard, Reed Cross Howard (R) and family attend Ron Howard's star ceremony on the Hollywood Walk of Fame on Dec. 10, 2015, in Hollywood, California.  (Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images)

"I was always curious about what celebs were actually there when their star was unveiled," he said, recalling a time in the late ‘80s when he took his visiting aunt from New York to see the famous promenade and wound up seeing a real-life star too.

"She kept saying that along with the stars she wanted to see a celeb too," Epting recalled. "And I said, ‘Well, that’s the last place in the world you would ever go see celebrities’."

"So we’re crossing the street by the Chinese Theater as I say, ‘Aunt Lee, for the last time, you don’t see celebrities come to Hollywood!’ And then a head turns around of a gentleman passing us, and he goes, ‘Well, I don’t know if that’s altogether accurate young man’ and it was Jack Lemmon."

"We both laughed, and it was this charming little moment between sort of all three of us," he recalled.

Tourists take pictures of the Hollywood sign from a shopping complex along Hollywood Boulevard in Hollywood, California, Aug. 3, 2017. ( )

"But that said, I do hope they figure out a way to make the area more accommodating, more inviting and more engaging because the Walk is, you know, it’s a nice bit of history… it’s kind of like the Hollywood sign. It may just be a sign, but it’s there for so long. It does get sort of engrained in your brain, just like those coral-colored stars on the boulevard."

title: MARK PENN: Socialist Mamdani sold a tax on billionaires. Regulars homeowners could pay the price
excerpt:
‘Mornings with Maria’ panelists discuss Bill Ackman's warning that the new NYC pied-à-terre tax will lead to capital flight and lower overall tax revenues as wealthy residents flee luxury properties.
...
body_text:
‘Mornings with Maria’ panelists discuss Bill Ackman's warning that the new NYC pied-à-terre tax will lead to capital flight and lower overall tax revenues as wealthy residents flee luxury properties.

It sounded simple and even kind of warmly populist in nature — a small tax on "pied-à-terre" properties in New York City. But the more you dig into it, as with all things from Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the more you see it as part of a far more devious plan that could destabilize the New York City housing market and cost middle-class people their homes and savings.

Gotta love whoever pulled this French name into implying the tax would just fall on a few very rich people — no more than 31,000. That was pure deception.

Think about it for a moment: Why tax nonresident property owners? Because they don’t vote in the city. By design, the policy targets non-resident property owners who lack a vote in local elections, shifting municipal tax burdens onto individuals who have no direct voice at the ballot box. And then the city uses money extracted from non-voting property owners to plug general budget deficits and fund broader municipal initiatives. Who knows – perhaps the money will even wind up funding residents who are in New York City illegally.

MAMDANI EXTENDS DEADLINE FOR NYC HOMEOWNERS TO SEEK EXEMPTION FROM NEW PIED-À-TERRE TAX

Because the Department of Finance’s initial roll sent notices to 960,000 property entries, primary residents are now forced to navigate bureaucratic hurdles to prove their exemption. The statute had a little-noticed provision that co-ops and condos qualify for the tax if the NYC Department of Finance computers identify their assessed value over $1 million. Presto chango — hundreds of thousands of New York homeowners were caught up in the initial mailing. And the surcharge on non-primary residences can reach up to 5% or more of market value annually.

So now add $50,000 a year in costs to a million-dollar non-primary condo. What are those owners going to do? Hit the sell, sell, sell button.  Imposing steep surcharges on secondary condo owners could chill the broader housing market, reduce demand from out-of-town buyers, and ultimately drag down property values across the board. In the end, local homeowners will pay the price through diminished equity. It’s simple economics.

And if you do live in NYC as a primary resident, you now have to prove it. Because the city did not properly screen out existing voters or primary taxpayers beforehand, they are making residents file documents such as their federal tax returns just to clear their names. If you live elsewhere in New York State but keep a place in the city, or if you own two apartments in the city, you are also caught in this net.

LIBERAL PODCASTER SAYS HE WAS 'DOXED' BY MAMDANI'S 'WANTED POSTER' OF PROPERTY OWNERS

And never mind that out-of-town property holders were already paying taxes here even though they use few if any city services. No use of schools, no clogging of traffic, reduced sanitation. They would have an argument to be taxed less, not more. And perhaps they can go to court arguing that the tax is discriminatory since it applies to a class of people without a rational basis related to municipal service usage. It potentially violates the equal protection and commerce clauses.

CLINTON, OBAMA-ERA DEMOCRATIC HEAVYWEIGHTS PENN AND EMANUEL RIP NYC'S MAMDANI OVER TAXES, ISRAEL, BLAST DSA

This is how creeping socialism works: Politicians advertise that they are going after only those greedy out-of-town billionaires, while creating a sprawling administrative property database that exposes personal details of thousands of everyday homeowners and forces residents to surrender tax returns just to defend their homes.

And before you know it, what was billed as "tax the rich" hits you and your family.

Mark J. Penn is the chairman and CEO of Stagwell Inc. and chairman of the Harris Poll. He is a Fox News contributor.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may help protect against a deadly disease, doctor says
excerpt: Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications may be associated with a lower risk...
body_text:
Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, confirmed research has suggested that glucagon-like peptide-1 medications may be associated with a lower risk of cancer recurrence.

GLP-1 medications have transformed diabetes and obesity treatment, but emerging research suggests their benefits could extend far beyond those purposes — potentially even aiding in cancer prevention and survival.

Dr. Loren Rourke, a Texas-based board-certified breast cancer surgeon, author and speaker, said growing research suggests glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications — including Ozempic and Wegovy — may be associated with a lower risk of cancer diagnoses and recurrence.

She pointed to findings presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting in Chicago, where researchers reported an association between GLP-1 use and lower breast cancer recurrence rates, as well as a potential role in preventing the disease.

MILLIONS COULD GAIN EASIER ACCESS TO POPULAR PEPTIDES AFTER FDA PANEL VOTE

However, she noted that the evidence remains observational and can’t prove that the drugs reduce cancer risk.

Emerging research suggests that GLP-1 medications could aid in cancer prevention and survival. (iStock)

"So these aren’t studies that, unfortunately, patients can latch onto, call their doctor and say, ‘I want to get on a GLP-1 right now to reduce my risk of breast cancer or make my breast cancer better,’" Rourke told Fox News Digital. "However, what it did do was shine the light on GLP-1s and that relationship."

The main reason that GLP-1s may aid in cancer prevention, according to Rourke, is that the drugs promote weight loss and reduce chronic inflammation.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"GLP-1s cause a decrease in your BMI. They cause weight reduction," she told Fox News Digital. "We know that a lower BMI equals a better prognosis with breast cancer."

In particular, post-menopausal women who are struggling with weight gain could get an extra benefit, the doctor said. (iStock)

"So if the secondary effect of taking a GLP-1 means you’re going to lose weight, then that’s a benefit, because we know you’re going to do better with breast cancer."

Diabetes and obesity medications can also lower estrogen production associated with excess body fat, the surgeon noted.

"The more fat you have, the higher your estrogen production," Rourke said. "You’re kind of bathing your body in estrogen, so to speak. So it intuitively makes sense that we are seeing this correlation or association."

GLP-1s also decrease the inflammatory state in which cancer thrives, the surgeon noted.

"The more fat we have, the higher your estrogen production."

"So if it’s fixing the overall chronic inflammation of the body, that’s going to help for a lot of reasons," she said.

"I think this is going to extend beyond breast cancer, but we need to get that scientific proof of a direct cause — is this just an association or a correlation?"

Rourke emphasized that researchers have not yet proven that GLP-1 medications directly affect breast cancer cells.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"But this study has now garnered enough attention, interest and scientific hypotheses that the work is getting started for the randomized controlled trials that we’re all waiting for — and then we can act upon those."

The main reason that GLP-1s may aid in cancer prevention is that the drugs promote weight loss and reduce chronic inflammation, according to a doctor. (iStock)

To patients who are considering starting GLP-1s, Rourke offered the following advice.

"My bottom-line message on this one is, if you have an elevated BMI, you’re trying to lose weight, you’ve tried a healthy diet, you’ve tried to exercise, and you’re not winning that fight, consider GLP-1s, and you’re going to get a secondary benefit."

In particular, post-menopausal women who are struggling with weight gain could get an extra benefit, Rourke added, but she urges them to "call their doctor and have that one-on-one conversation."

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

President Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer Todd Blanche appears on track to become the next US attorney general after two Republican senators drop their opposition to his nomination.

The Senate Judiciary Committee is due to meet for a vote this morning on Blanche’s nomination following last week’s delay.

Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis had sought concessions from the Department of Justice and White House relating to President Donald Trump’s settlement agreement with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

Cornyn and Tillis had refused to back Blanche’s bid for the permanent post without official confirmation killing the fund meant to compensate people who believe they were unfairly prosecuted by the Justice Department.

Blanche’s written order, issued late Sunday, came after the days of negotiations between the Justice Department and the Republican senators who are leaving Capitol Hill when their terms end in January.

“We want to express our gratitude to Mr Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon,” Cornyn, of Texas, and Tillis, of North Carolina, said in a statement.

Blanche has repeatedly said that the Justice Department was scrapping plans for the fund, which sparked bipartisan outcry over the possibility that violent rioters who attacked police at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021, could be considered for payments.

But skeptical lawmakers said they were concerned that could be revived without a commitment in writing, especially because Trump has continued to defend the idea.

Trump declined to call for Rep Max Miller’s resignation following allegations of domestic abuse from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. Trump said he has always known Miller as “a good person” and called the situation “a very sad thing.”

In an 89-4 vote, the Senate voted to take up a measure that would temporarily keep the government funded and help avoid a shutdown in the fall. The measure, known as a continuing resolution, would maintain government funding at current levels through 11 December, with some adjustments for specific programs. The Senate is slated to debate the funding bill and move it closer to a final vote.

A coalition of 25 US states sued the Trump administration over new tariffs pegged at 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes struck down by the supreme court in February. The states are asking the US Court of International Trade to halt the tariffs, declare them unlawful and order refunds of duties that have already been paid. More here.

Trump accused US attorney Jeanine Pirro of having “folded like an umbrella” amid reports that he was considering removing her from her post. Trump criticized Pirro on Monday after she dropped vandalism charges against a former Olympian accused of damaging the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. More here.

The Democratic party faces a crucial test of its direction today as voters in the midwestern swing state of Michigan decide whether to nominate for US Senate a progressive candidate advocating for universal healthcare or an-establishment-backed moderate.

The state’s Democratic primary is the latest high-profile battle over the party’s future, as it seeks to chart a course back to power in Washington following Donald Trump’s victory in 2024.

Leftwing candidates have surged in Democratic primaries in solidly blue areas across the country in recent months.

Some congressional primary races in Michigan will also offer a sense of where the party is headed as it looks to take back control of US Congress from the Republicans.

Progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old former public health official, has led in recent polls against his moderate rival, US representative Haley Stevens, a 43-year-old who first came to Congress after flipping a red seat.

A flood of more than $40m in outside spending has come into the race to support Stevens or attack El-Sayed, including from groups associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), a pro-Israel lobby.

The winner of Tuesday’s Democratic primary will face Mike Rogers, a former congressman from the state who was also the Republican nominee for US Senate in 2024, when he lost to Elissa Slotkin.

The Michigan US Senate seat is critical for Democrats in their dark-horse quest to retake the upper chamber, where Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats.

title: WATCH: GOP senator unloads on 'creature of Washington' challenger in critical Senate showdown
excerpt:
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital Sherrod Brown's decades-long Washington record remains his biggest liability as the high-stakes Senate race heats up.

MARYSVILLE, OH - The Ohio Senate r...
body_text:
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital Sherrod Brown's decades-long Washington record remains his biggest liability as the high-stakes Senate race heats up.

MARYSVILLE, OH - The Ohio Senate race could very well decide the balance of power in the U.S. Senate in November and incumbent Republican Jon Husted is making the case that the reasons his Democratic opponent was voted out of office two years ago are still relevant today.

"He’s spent 32 years in Washington and he's got nothing to show for it, the voters over here in Ohio know it," Husted told Fox News Digital at the annual Summer Farm Fest on Sunday when asked about his race against former Dem. Sen. Sherrod Brown.

"That's why they sent him packing two years ago. He was defeated by Bernie Moreno by over 200,000 votes. This is all he's done. He's been in an elected office since 1974. He hasn't done anything in the private sector. He's just been a creature of Washington and I think the voters finally are tired of it. That's why they sent him packing. I don't think they're gonna have any enthusiasm for rehiring him for a job that he failed at."

After representing Ohio in the Senate for almost two decades after years of serving in the House of Representatives, Brown was defeated by Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 in a blistering campaign that was one of the most expensive in U.S. history. Moreno consistently tied Brown to the unpopular positions of then-President Joe Biden, and Husted told Fox News Digital those concerns still exist, particularly on immigration.

FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

Fox News Digital spoke to Republican Sen. Jon Husted about his race against challenger Sherrod Brown in a closely watched Senate campaign. (Fox News Digital/Getty)

"We had basically an invasion of 11 million people," Husted said. "He supported amnesty for them. He supported Social Security payments for illegals, healthcare for illegals, COVID checks for illegals. The sanctuary cities he supported led to crime, fentanyl, human trafficking in our state, and it's been terrible and the voters know this."

"They know that he failed them. They know when he goes off to Washington with his comrades that he votes like a liberal, that he's too liberal for Ohio, that he has a track record of voting with Bernie Sanders and Kamala Harris and Joe Biden, and that's out of step with where Ohio is."

Over the last few weeks, Brown has blanketed the airwaves with ads criticizing Husted on data centers, a hot-button issue in Ohio, arguing that Husted’s support of data centers over the years has resulted in higher energy prices for consumers.

Husted, who was appointed to the Senate in January 2025 after the departure of now-Vice President JD Vance, pushed back on that assertion when asked about the ads.

"He had 32 years in Congress, he did nothing about it, and I, in my, just briefly over a year there, have legislation to require data centers to build their own power, to pay their own way, and to give the benefits of their presence to the citizens of those local communities, rather than the way that Sherrod Brown has done it, where he's failed," Husted explained.

DEM SENATE CANDIDATE SHERROD BROWN CLAIMS HE SUPPORTS 'CLOSING THE BORDER'; GOP SAYS RECORD PROVES OTHERWISE

Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat from Ohio, during a campaign event at the Steubenville City Building in Steubenville, Ohio, US, on Friday, Oct. 11, 2024. (Justin Merriman/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Husted continued, "This is the problem with the guy, is that he does nothing, and then a problem comes out, and he says, blame that person… He didn't do anything about it. He never does anything about it. He just waits for problems to happen. And then he says, well, it's the other person's fault. It's time to hold him accountable."

Husted made the case that the policies Brown supported in Congress led to the high energy rates the country is seeing now.

"He spent 32 years in Washington and didn't do anything except raise our electricity prices because he and the radical climate change agenda shut 23 power plants in Ohio," Husted said. "If we had those 23 power plants today, we wouldn't have high energy prices."

Husted continued, "Him voting for Obamacare, which has doubled the price of health care insurance in the state of Ohio and around the country. He needs to be held to account for his failed policies."

While Ohio has been historically known as a bellwether swing state, President Donald Trump won the state convincingly in 2016, 2020, and 2024, shifting the Buckeye State to a reliably red stronghold. However, recent polling, including a Fox News poll in June, shows Husted trailing Brown as Republicans battle the historical headwinds of the party in power struggling in midterm elections.

Brown, recruited back into politics in part by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, is looking to flip one of the four seats Democrats need to regain control of the Senate, with Ohio among the party's top pickup opportunities alongside Alaska, Maine and North Carolina.

Senator Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, during a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Feb. 13, 2025. (Getty Images)

With less than 100 days to go until the midterms, Husted says that Brown’s record will be front and center.

"Just showing the contrast between 32 years of failure from Sherrod Brown and the fact that I'm an Ohio guy, I've fought for Ohioans, I've helped in state government to turn this state in the right direction," Husted said. "We now have more jobs than we've ever had in our state's history, the lowest unemployment rate, frankly, than we ever had in our states' history. And we don't need to send this guy back to Washington, Sherrod Brown, to continue the failed policies that have harmed the country and harmed our state. We need a guy like me who will fight for Ohio."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Brown campaign for comment.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Guatemala volcano eruption sends lava spewing into the air
excerpt:
Watch: Lava spews into the air as volcano erupts in Guatemala

The eruption of the Fuego volcano in Guatemala has triggered the evacuation of at least two villages on its slopes.

Fuego, one of the mo...
body_text:
Watch: Lava spews into the air as volcano erupts in Guatemala

The eruption of the Fuego volcano in Guatemala has triggered the evacuation of at least two villages on its slopes.

Fuego, one of the most active volcanoes in the Western Hemisphere, started spewing lava and ash on Monday.

Pyroclastic currents - rivers of gas, volcanic ash and rock fragments - continued to flow down Fuego's south-eastern slope early on Tuesday, the government agency which monitors its activity said.

Disaster management agency Conred issued a nationwide orange alert, the second highest, and warned locals to be prepared as the eruptions could create further pyroclastic flows and billowing ash clouds.

Conred urged people to keep their windows and doors closed and lessons have been cancelled in schools close to the volcano.

Fuego is located just 16km (10 miles) west of Antigua, a city popular with tourists, who travel to the Unesco World Heritage Site to admire its colonial-era architecture.

The active stratovolcano has also become popular with hikers.

Conred warned visitors and locals alike to refrain from approaching or remaining in areas at risk, in particular on the volcano's slopes.

More than 200 people were killed when Fuego erupted in 2018, many of them caught in the fast-flowing pyroclastic flows which raced down the Las Lajas ravine.

title: ‘One last chance’: The times Trump threatened Iran, said deal imminent
excerpt:
Just over one month into the war on Iran, US President Donald Trump made an apocalyptic threat that raised the alarm in Washington and Middle Eastern capitals alike, attached to a tight deadline.

If ...
body_text:
Just over one month into the war on Iran, US President Donald Trump made an apocalyptic threat that raised the alarm in Washington and Middle Eastern capitals alike, attached to a tight deadline.

If Iran didn’t immediately reopen the critical Strait of Hormuz, Trump warned on April 7, “a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”.

Tehran didn’t blink. And with two hours to the deadline, Trump walked back the threat and instead announced a two-week ceasefire, brokered by Islamabad.

Since then, the US president has repeated this pattern multiple times. It goes like this: Trump ups the ante, shaking up the markets, and then dials it back down at the 11th hour, apparently hoping this strategy will influence negotiations.

On Monday, Trump again insisted that negotiations were close to ending the war – and, yet again, gave “duplicitous” Iran “one last chance” to make a deal or suffer catastrophic strikes.

For its part, Tehran denies any ongoing talks with the US, saying it is only talking to Oman about how to manage the Hormuz strait, the closure of which has caused oil prices to soar amid havoc in energy markets around the world.

The war is now in its 23rd week, with no end to hostilities in sight, and both Washington and Tehran are more entangled than before, with additional variables in the conflict that could determine its direction.

So, how many times has Trump given Iran “one last chance” to make a deal or suffer the consequences, before walking his threat back? And how many times have we heard from the US president that a deal is just around the corner?

There have been several times since February 28, when the US and Israel launched their first joint attacks on Iran, that Trump has threatened an attack but did not follow through.

Less than a month into the war, Trump threatened Tehran over its closure of the Strait of Hormuz, saying the US would strike Iran’s power plants if the critical waterway was not reopened. Two days later, he postponed the strikes for five days, citing “progress” in talks.

As the delayed deadline neared on March 26, Trump delayed the strikes again, this time for 10 days, claiming that Tehran requested it.

Then came the April 7 threat that a whole “civilisation will die”, before Trump called off those strikes and announced a two-week ceasefire, to give Iran a chance to reach a peace deal.

No deal emerged. And then, after threatening to strike Iran “harder”, and in the final hours of the ceasefire, on April 21, Trump announced an indefinite ceasefire, saying Pakistani mediators had asked him to do so.

With those talks making no progress, Trump returned to his threats to strike Iran on May 17, saying “nothing will be left” of Iran if Tehran did not make a deal with the US.

But the next day, Trump again told reporters that he had decided to “put it off for a little while, hopefully maybe forever, but possibly for a little while, because we’ve had very big discussions with Iran”.

By May 27, US strikes were back on after negotiations faltered, once again.

On June 11, after two days of back-and-forth strikes, Trump threatened the US would take “total control” of Iran’s oil and gas industries. But then, a few hours later, he posted on social media, claiming there had been a breakthrough in negotiations and called off the attacks.

On June 17, the US and Iran signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), announcing a ceasefire and a 60-day period to complete negotiations for a lasting peace. Within days, that had fallen apart over the glaring gaps in the two sides’ positions over the contents of the MoU, triggered mainly by who had control of the Strait of Hormuz – and both sides returned to tit-for-tat, widening strikes.

On July 27, Trump halted the strikes, claiming the “perimeters of a deal” had been agreed to, but noting that Washington “is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II”.

On Monday this week, Trump told reporters again that negotiations were close to ending the war and that this was Iran’s “last chance before decapitation”. The US has not followed up on this latest threat yet.

Iran denies it is talking to the US, although it may be holding indirect talks via mediators, analysts say.

Trump has insisted that Iran is “desperate” to cut a deal, or that a deal is imminent, multiple times since the start of the war.

Two days after launching the first attacks on Tehran on February 28, which the US initially appeared to believe would be a quick operation, Trump seemingly conceded it might take a bit longer when he said at the White House: “We projected four to five weeks [to end Iran war], but we can go far longer than that.”

The US president changed tack again on March 9, when he told CBS that “the war is very complete, pretty much”, and that the US military operation was “way ahead of schedule”.

Later the same day, he shifted his stance again, saying the war is “both complete and just beginning”. And later that day again, he said: “We’ve already won in many ways, but we haven’t won enough.”

On March 23, Trump told reporters outside Air Force One that “major points of agreement, I would say – almost all points of agreement” had been reached with Iran. Tehran was denying that it was party to negotiations at this point.

Two days after that, Trump repeated that Iran wanted to “make a deal so badly”. The next day, he also told a cabinet meeting that Iran was “begging to make a deal”.

On April 7, Trump said, again, that Washington was “very close to a deal” with Iran, before threatening to blow up a “whole civilisation”, but then walked back on that to announce a ceasefire the next day.

Over the following days, throughout April, Trump reiterated that the war was, in fact, pretty much over. But it continued.

Trump repeatedly claimed on separate occasions that Iran had “agreed to everything”, that “I think we will get a deal in the next day or two”, and that “I don’t think there’s too many significant differences” between the US and Iranian positions.

On May 23, Trump said the administration was “getting a lot closer” to a deal, which was “largely negotiated, [and] subject to finalisation”.

On June 8, Trump called for “total victory” in the next two weeks and claimed Iran was “willing to give us everything”. Still, no peace deal has materialised and the conflict began again in July.

On Monday this week, Trump again told reporters that Iran was “desperate” for a deal and warned Tehran it had “one last chance” before “decapitation” to make an agreement. Iran denies it is even holding talks with the US, saying that it is only speaking with Oman about management of the Strait of Hormuz.

title: More than 150 migrants rescued after boat catches fire in Channel
excerpt:
Border Force pictured escorting migrants to the UK after being rescued in the Channel in March

More than 150 migrants have been rescued after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire...
body_text:
Border Force pictured escorting migrants to the UK after being rescued in the Channel in March

More than 150 migrants have been rescued after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire on Tuesday morning, French authorities have said.

The boat was attempting to cross to the UK when its engine caught fire, according to the French maritime prefecture of the Channel and North Sea.

It said 157 people have been rescued and are being taken to port in Boulogne-sur-Mer. There are no reports of anyone having been injured or killed.

It comes just a day after Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged his government will be "relentless" in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.

French authorities said the boat left France on Monday night.

Overnight "five people on board the vessel required rescue... the remaining people on board refused the assistance offered by the French patrol boats", the French maritime prefecture said.

"Determined to reach the United Kingdom, migrants crossing the Channel in small boats refused assistance offered by French emergency service, accepting it only in situations of extreme emergency," it said in a statement.

Because of the "structural fragility" of boats used to cross the Channel, it said they decided not to intervene further at that stage.

But this morning the engine caught fire and the "vessel's integrity deteriorated very rapidly".

Rescue boats went to the scene from France and the UK, including the RNLI Eastbourne lifeboat and the UK Border Force vessels BSC Contender and BSC Courageous.

Two French boats rescued 103 migrants and the British boats rescued 54.

All of them are being taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer for treatment, where they are expected to arrive there at 12:30 local time (11:30 BST) on Tuesday.

Earlier, the UK Coastguard said: "A vessel caught fire earlier this morning whilst in the French search and rescue region. UK vessels and a lifeboat are assisting."

Between 1 January and 1 August 2026, a total of 14,526 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 42% of asylum applications between April 2025 to March 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 2 August 2025 to 1 August 2026 carried an average of 67 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from April 2025 to March 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,000 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,535 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from April 2025 to March 2026. This was down by 22% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Political discussions around the UK's policies on illegal migration have resurfaced since tens of thousands of migrants swam into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Thursday.

During a visit to Dover on Monday, Andy Burnham said progress had been made in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.

The prime minister said "people want to see this issue addressed".

He added that enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs have been doubled on both sides of the Channel, but "a system that offers safe routes for people" needs to be built as well.

The Conservatives said that Labour had not delivered on its promises on migration, while Reform UK said if in government it would deploy the navy to ward off crossings.
