title: Calls for UK bank tax to fund cost of living help as HSBC profits hit £7.5bn
excerpt:
Levy could raise £19bn to help pay for Andy Burnham’s support for those struggling with bills, say campaigners

Campaigners have renewed calls for a windfall tax on UK banks that could raise £19bn tow...
body_text:
Levy could raise £19bn to help pay for Andy Burnham’s support for those struggling with bills, say campaigners

Campaigners have renewed calls for a windfall tax on UK banks that could raise £19bn towards Andy Burnham’s cost of living agenda, after HSBC raked in $10.1bn (£7.5bn) worth of profits in the second quarter of the year.

Bosses at HSBC reported on Tuesday that profits rose 60% year on year in the three months to the end of June, helped by fees from wealth management and insurance business, as well as higher interest rates, which allow the bank to charge more for loans and mortgages.

The HSBC chief executive, Georges Elhedery, said he would consider increasing banker bonuses on the back of the strong results and planned to restart a share buy-back programme that had been on pause since last year.

It brings collective profits for the four largest banks – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – to £29.2bn over the first six months of the year, putting lenders back in the crosshairs of campaigners, including Positive Money and the Trades Union Congress, who are calling for a fresh tax on the lucrative industry.

The campaign group Positive Money said bank bosses had pledged nearly half of their profits – a total of £13.7bn – to shareholders through dividends and share buy-backs, proving they could easily shoulder a tax that they calculated could ultimately raise £19bn towards the government’s spending plans at the October budget.

Positive Money said the government could replicate Spain’s levy, targeting any UK revenues above £800m with a 38% tax, in line with the energy profits levy introduced for oil and gas companies announced by the Tory government in 2022.

They said the resulting £19bn would be enough to cover the cost of Andy Burnham’s VAT cut from electricity bills (worth £850m), the £2 cap on bus fares (worth £500m) and the business rates cut for pubs, clubs and music venues (worth £100m) more than 13 times over.

“Previous governments have allowed the powerful banking lobby to persuade them against taxing these record-breaking profits in recent years, despite overwhelming public support for the policy,” said the co-director of Positive Money, Sara Hall.

“We’re calling on Andy Burnham to break with his predecessors by resisting the demands of City lobbyists and reclaiming these lost billions with a windfall tax on bank profits, the proceeds of which could be used to fund truly life-changing support for the households and businesses struggling to pay their bills right now.”

Banking bosses have been cautious when asked about their views on a fresh tax rise. They told journalists over the past week that they were encouraged by Burnham’s economic vision, but stressed that their ability to lend money to businesses was crucial for the new prime minister’s growth ambitions. “UK growth requires strong banks,” Elhedery said.

But advocates of a tax remain undeterred, and the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “There is now a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can easily afford to pay more tax. While higher interest rates have meant mortgage misery and bigger bills for the rest of us, the big banks have been rolling in it.”

Joanne O’Neill, the co-director of advocacy and influencing at ActionAid UK, said the government should also take “meaningful action” to hold UK banks to account for their impact on the climate and human rights.

“ActionAid research has shown how HSBC funnelled billions into fossil fuels and industrial agriculture companies between 2021 and 2023, helping to fuel environmental destruction. And since then it has watered down its climate commitments, further shirking its responsibility to help bring about the just transition we need,” O’Neill said, adding that banks should face a “polluters pay tax” that fairly reflected their responsibility for financing and causing climate harm.
  Metro Bank followed its big four competitors in reporting bumper profits for the first half of the year. The challenger bank reported a 38% jump in pre-tax profits on Tuesday morning to £60.7m over the first six months of 2026, after a jump in corporate, SME and specialist mortgage lending, as Metro tried to corner “underserved markets” to boost profits.
  While the strong rise in profits will add weight to calls for a UK windfall tax, Metro would probably escape Positive Money’s proposals. The bank reported about £241.5m in underlying net interest income for the first six months of the year, and if repeated, would keep its full-year figure below the campaigner’s £800m threshold.

title: Italy suspends free movement with Spain: Is Schengen in crisis after Ceuta?
excerpt:
On July 30, days after more than 60,000 people crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco, Italy announced it was reintroducing border controls with Spain.

Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesus V...
body_text:
On July 30, days after more than 60,000 people crossed into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco, Italy announced it was reintroducing border controls with Spain.

Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesus Vivas, told broadcaster Telecinco that between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in the enclave, as the vast majority have returned. At least 72 people died in the crossing.

Because Italy and Spain do not share a land border, the measure affects people travelling between the two countries by air and sea.

“In Italy, a lot of the media coverage was saying [Italian Prime Minister Giorgia] Meloni is suspending Schengen, or that Spain should be removed from Schengen,” Davide Colombi, a researcher in the Justice and Home Affairs unit at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), told Al Jazeera. “Neither of those options is actually available … you cannot kick a country out of Schengen.”

The Schengen Agreement, signed in 1985 and put into force a decade later, abolished passport checks at the internal borders of its 29 member states, creating one of the world’s largest zones of free movement.

Colombi explained that suspending Schengen “doesn’t necessarily mean anything”.

“One member state cannot suspend Schengen. What it can do is temporarily reintroduce internal border controls,” he said.

Such controls are, in fact, a well-worn feature of the passport-free zone.

According to the Asylum Information Database (AIDA), run by the European Council on Refugees and Exiles (ECRE), at least six member states – Austria, Denmark, France, Germany, Norway and Sweden – have kept some form of internal controls almost continuously since 2015, and nine states maintained them throughout 2025.

Europe’s refugee crisis peaked in 2015, when more than a million people arrived in the European Union. Germany reinstated border controls with Austria after roughly 40,000 arrivals in one weekend; Austria, France, Sweden, Norway and Denmark soon followed.

But Italy’s move represents “the first time that a country has unilaterally reinstated Schengen border controls based on a large number of arrivals in a country with which it doesn’t share internal borders,” said Eleonora Testi, ECRE’s senior legal officer.

Colombi was more direct about the practical logic. “There is no realistic possibility for anybody from Ceuta to arrive in Italy,” he said.

Neither analyst sees the measure as a response to Ceuta itself so much as a template to demonstrate that a member state can invoke Schengen’s emergency provisions over a crisis unfolding in another territory, for reasons that are more political than operational.

“Italy’s reintroduction of border controls with Spain is nothing more than political theatre. It’s a savvy manipulation of EU law to show that the government is ‘tough on migration’, while effectively only causing problems to tourists and other people travelling from Spain to Italy [on a Schengen visa],” said Chiara Catelli, advocacy officer at the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants (PICUM).

Within days, 22 EU member states signed a joint letter aligning with Italy’s position.

Testi contrasted this with the EU’s treatment of a comparable case, when Poland suspended the right to claim asylum at its border with Belarus in March 2025, in what AIDA described as a clear breach of EU and international law. There was no equivalent show of member-state solidarity – instead, an EU regulation was proposed to help Warsaw manage the crisis.

“There is a different response in this case,” Testi said, “probably because of the general political positions that Spain has held in comparison to most other European member states.”

At a time when most European countries shift towards tougher border and asylum measures, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialist government in Spain has pursued a comparatively liberal migration policy, leaning on economic integration and legal pathways rather than deterrence. Recently, Madrid invited undocumented people to apply for legalisation, allowing them to work – and more than a million did so.

For Colombi, Ceuta is not where Schengen’s unravelling began.

“The domino effect started back in 2015, and it’s been facilitated by the European Commission not doing anything about it,” he said.

Germany reintroduced controls with Poland in 2023 and again in 2025. Italy itself has maintained controls on its border with Slovenia. In June 2026, the commission issued formal opinions urging the nine states with controls in place over 12 months to phase them out – guidance that appears to have had little practical effect.

“If you have the one body that is supposed to enforce and implement EU law not enforcing EU law,” Colombi said, “it basically leaves all member states doing whatever they want … responding to their national electorate based on fears that they themselves have created.”

That is the crux of the existential argument.

The European Pact on Migration and Asylum, meant to distribute responsibility more fairly across the bloc, became applicable on June 12, barely six weeks before Italy’s move tested the scenario it was designed to manage.

“We’ve heard the narrative that the pact works, but only if arrivals are kept low … an asylum system has to function even in times of emergency,” said Testi.

The political wrangling over migration comes at a critical time. Elections are due in 2027 in Italy, Spain and France.

“Depending on how the political tide changes … there might be centre-to-right-wing to extreme right-wing governments in all of Europe,” she said, and with them, less appetite for solidarity when the next country – “it could be Greece next time, it could be Bulgaria” – faces a surge of arrivals.

What led to the deadly Ceuta crossings – Moroccan pressure, a Spanish court ruling on deportations, or Spain’s regularisation policy – has been debated.

Jorge Tamames of Madrid’s Elcano Royal Institute called it “first and foremost a security, diplomatic, and humanitarian challenge, not a migratory one”.

But whatever caused the Ceuta crisis, the response is what CEPS and ECRE regard as the real test of the bloc’s cohesion.

“Schengen is not in crisis because of what’s happening within the EU,” Colombi said. “It’s how member states and the commission are dealing with these issues that is actually dismantling Schengen, dismantling freedom of movement for everybody … migration is not the existential threat it’s portrayed to be.”

He said the real threat to the EU is what happens when member states discover that invoking Schengen’s emergency powers against each other, for political reasons, carries no real cost.

title: Dinghy carrying 157 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire
excerpt:
Passengers rescued by French and British vessels and some being taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer in France

A dinghy carrying 157 people has capsized in the Channel after its engine caught fire at sea.

They...
body_text:
Passengers rescued by French and British vessels and some being taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer in France

A dinghy carrying 157 people has capsized in the Channel after its engine caught fire at sea.

They were rescued from the water by French vessels aided by two British Border Security Command boats and a RLNI lifeboat, and are being taken to Boulogne-sur-Mer, French authorities said.

Some 54 of the people were taken to France on the British vessels.

It comes a day after Reform UK proposed using the Royal Navy to return migrants to France or Belgium under a plan called “operation fortress”.

Responding to the incident, the party’s leader, Nigel Farage said: “We must put a stop to this. Our plan will saves lives.”

title: Former Vikings captain Jack Brewer calls out Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve for 'trans kids belong' shirt
excerpt:
‘The Five’ discuss a WNBA coach seemingly taking a shot at Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham over her stance on transgender athletes in women's sports.

Former Minnesota Vikings captain Jack Brew...
body_text:
‘The Five’ discuss a WNBA coach seemingly taking a shot at Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham over her stance on transgender athletes in women's sports.

Former Minnesota Vikings captain Jack Brewer witnessed a clash of cultures in his state this past weekend.

Ahead of Sunday's WNBA game between the Minnesota Lynx and Indiana Fever, the third organized rally in support of Sophie Cunningham's support for protecting women's sports pitted women's rights activists against pro-trans counter-protesters outside the Target Center.

Inside the arena, Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve was seen wearing a shirt that read "trans kids belong."

CHERYL REEVE SENDS CLEAR MESSAGE TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM WITH ‘TRANS KIDS BELONG’ SHIRT DURING FEVER-LYNX GAME

Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve reacts to play against the Indiana Fever in the first quarter at Target Center in Minneapolis, Minn., on Aug. 2, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"The Lynx have a rich history in that state. That team was established the year I got to Minnesota, and I remember watching them. To now see a coach representing that team in this way is sad. It is sad to think that young girls in Minnesota are coming to games and watching teams promote something like that. It is ridiculous to think that a grown woman would go so hard in support of men playing against women and entering women’s locker rooms," Brewer said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

"This coach is promoting the idea that children who should be receiving psychiatric treatment... should instead be affirmed. It is disgusting and sad. These people are sick and need help. We should be praying for them and finding treatment for them. Instead, people like this coach in Minnesota are promoting these types of atrocities. It is a terrible thing."

Brewer added that the visual was personal to him as a father, and someone with ties to Minnesota. Brewer began his career with the Vikings in 2002 after playing football at the University of Minnesota from 1998-2001.

"As a father and someone whose family is deeply connected to Minnesota sports, I have an eight-year-old daughter who plays highly competitive tennis and competitive soccer. She also plays and trains in Minnesota. We go to Minnesota during the summers. Her cousins, grandparents, aunts and uncles are there. My nieces and nephews are there. I went to school in Minnesota, my family lives there, and my cousins coach various sports there. I am involved in sports in that state. It is embarrassing," Brewer said.

Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve and Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham. (Getty Images)

In addition to Reeve, three other WNBA coaches have come under scrutiny for their responses to questions about women's sports in the last week alone.

Golden State Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase, Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White and Portland Fire coach Alex Sarama all declined to back protecting women's sports at pre-game press conference this past weekend.

STORM CO-OWNER SUSPENDED AFTER INCIDENT WITH SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS AS STAR BREAKS SILENCE ON CONTROVERSY

Meanwhile, Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton was suspended and fined after allegedly berating two young Cunningham fans who were sitting courtside for celebrating Cunningham's stance on women's sports.

Brewer sent a message to the WNBA's other leaders with advice on how to proceed.

"My advice to other coaches, owners and teams is to speak the truth. Every coach who loves God, loves this country and wants to protect women needs to speak out against coaches who are that ignorant. You should not be able to promote something like that without being held accountable. You should be held accountable for your actions," he said.

Brewer also criticized the league for its handling of Caitlin Clark.

"They cannot stand up for the white girl, even though the white girl sells more jerseys than the other players in the league. They cannot admit that the white girl is worth protecting. Caitlin Clark should be the face of the WNBA. She should be to the WNBA what Michael Jordan was to the NBA. Caitlin Clark is the reason people watch the WNBA."Her image should become the logo of the WNBA because she is the reason the league has become popular. I remember watching the WNBA in its early stages," Brewer said.

"There was hardly anybody in the crowd, and they had to let people attend for free. Now stadiums are half-full and, in some cases, nearly sold out."It is sad that the league will not fully support its star player because she does not fit the race-and-gender ideology they want to portray through victimhood. She is not a victim, so she does not fit their victimhood mentality. That is why she gets no love from the teams of the WNBA. It is terrible."

Brewer is backing Clark and Cunningham, and hopes the rest of the WNBA and its fans can rally behind them.

"Caitlin Clark’s impact on the WNBA cannot be denied. Caitlin Clark is the Jerry West of the WNBA. They need to make her the logo and emblem of the league, whether they want to agree with it or not. She has defined the game. There will be greater players than Caitlin Clark, just as there have been greater players than Jerry West. But Caitlin Clark, like Jerry West, made the sport popular at this particular time and juncture," he said.

"They need to give this girl her flowers while she is doing it."That is also why Sophie Cunningham is so popular. She is standing up for herself and standing up for Caitlin Clark. I love her for that, and I have her back. I do not care what Black girls, Black men or anyone else has to say. I am a Sophie Cunningham fan. I do not agree with everything about her, and I think she can be too provocative and show her body too much, but I still pray for her. I like that she stands up for herself, and I like that she has Caitlin Clark’s back, because so do I."

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: Why Trump Media's sale of fast access to market-moving social posts is controversial
excerpt:
Why is Trump Media selling early access to Trump's Truth Social posts?

When Donald Trump speaks, financial traders are among the keenest listeners.

From trade wars to military wars, anything the US ...
body_text:
Why is Trump Media selling early access to Trump's Truth Social posts?

When Donald Trump speaks, financial traders are among the keenest listeners.

From trade wars to military wars, anything the US president says can shift markets, and so teams of traders - as well as a host of automated computer systems - monitor his statements to perform trades within seconds.

Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG) now wants to charge for such market-moving information put out on its Truth Social platform. It has launched a paid service to give Wall Street firms and institutional investors the "fastest access" to the social media site's most influential accounts.

TMTG has not directly said the service includes the account of the president himself, but with some 13 million followers - the most on the site - it's fair to say that his posts would be among, if not the, most influential.

However, the move has prompted a series of legal questions and ethical musings, including whether it is right that a company - of which the president's family remains the majority shareholder - stands to profit from his own public statements.

The service launched by TMTG is called Truth API. It is a new data feed that provides real-time access to posts in "milliseconds" from the "highest-ranking Truth Social accounts".

The service was anticipated to become available to institutional customers on 1 August. The Financial Times reported, external that customers could be charged as much as $100,000 a month for high-speed access, but TMTG has not confirmed the figure.

TMTG says it expects it to create a steady source of new revenue for the firm, which is currently loss-making.

While anyone can pay for the service, it is mainly designed for so-called high-frequency and algorithmic trading firms - those TMTG states are "most impacted by the cost of a delay in information".

For these firms, financial trading is automated. Electronic systems using algorithms buy and sell much faster and at a greater scale than humans, according to Charles Schwab. It is a case of "blink, and you'll miss it", the investment bank says.

"Such systems are often designed to make just a tiny profit on each transaction, but through sheer speed and volume, they can generate large returns for their firms," it adds.

Trump Media to sell instant access to 'market-moving' social posts

There has been a wall of silence in terms of who has signed up to the service so far.

TMTG says it had customers register in advance of the launch date, but has not revealed how many.

Joe Saluzzi, co-founder of Themis Trading, told the BBC that Truth API was "worthless" to trading firms, including his own, which did not have the complex systems already set up to perform transactions at "nanosecond level fast".

He suggests high-frequency trading firms (HFTs) would be among the most likely to sign up, not only because of the money-making potential, but also because they'll be thinking "if I don't do it, somebody else will".

"This is not for retail [investors], this is not even for sophisticated institutional investors," he says. "This data feed is for high-speed traders who have the systems in place and have spent millions and millions of dollars building the systems."

The BBC contacted some of the major US investment banks and high-frequency trading firms, from Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan to Citadel Securities and Jane Street to ask if they had, or planned to, sign up.

All either declined to comment or did not respond.

"Nobody wants to talk about this stuff," says Saluzzi.

Political opponents of Trump have criticised the service. Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Adam Schiff have written to the US securities regulator to ask if it will investigate whether Truth API breaks the law.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has confirmed receipt of the letter, but has declined to comment on whether it will investigate.

The potential for insider trading to occur has also been raised. The practice, which is illegal, involves people making market trades or bets based on information that is not available to the general public.

A spokesperson for TMTG said in response to the letter sent to the SEC that Senate Democrats "continue to mischaracterise Truth API either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information - or, quite possibly, both".

TMTG has also said "the Senators must have invented a new theory of 'insider trading' based on publicly available information".

Whether or not information being provided by the service is public or non-public appears to be the key test.

Richard Painter, former ethics lawyer to President George W Bush, told the BBC he believes it could be classed as insider trading to sell material and official US government information, prior to it being public knowledge, on the platform.

"If I were commissioner of the SEC, I would threaten to resign unless they put a stop to this plan or promise that no posts... that have to do with US government business [will be included]," he says.

Saluzzi, though, points out that many other data providers, news organisations and stock exchanges currently operate similar services, providing a "precedent" for TMTG.

However, he adds: "There's a different story when it comes to ethics."

Trump, who owns about 41% of Trump Media through a trust his children oversee, does stand to profit from the service.

"This appears to be an outrageous abuse of the President's office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders," Warren and Schiff said in their letter to SEC.

title: Holy Land battle: Solomon's Pools become flashpoint in fight over Israel's biblical heritage
excerpt: Aerial video captures the sprawling 2,000-year-old reservoirs that once supplied Jerusalem with water and are now at the center of a dispute over preservation, heritage and sovereignty. (Video by Yeho...
body_text:
Aerial video captures the sprawling 2,000-year-old reservoirs that once supplied Jerusalem with water and are now at the center of a dispute over preservation, heritage and sovereignty. (Video by Yehoshua Sigala.)

Built more than 2,000 years ago to supply Jerusalem with water, Solomon's Pools have become the center of a modern political dispute, with officials from the nearby Israeli town of Efrat accusing the Palestinian Authority of allowing the historic site to deteriorate after it was placed under Ramallah's jurisdiction following the 1993 Oslo Accords.

Most archaeologists date the construction of Solomon's Pools, three ancient reservoirs located between Efrat and Bethlehem, south of Israel's capital, to the Hasmonean period in the second century B.C. The reservoirs were built to supply water to Jerusalem during the Second Temple period. Herod the Great (37–4 B.C.) later expanded the system to provide water to his palace-fortress at Herodium.

"Solomon's Pools are not only the history of the Jewish people in the Land of Israel and the source of Jerusalem's living water, but also the future of Efrat in our ability to exercise our sovereignty, preserve Efrat's development space and sustain tourism for all religions in the area between Jerusalem and Hebron," Dovi Shefler, mayor of Efrat, told Fox News Digital.

EXCLUSIVE: ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG BLASTS MAMDANI, PRAISES TRUMP, SOUNDS ALARM ON IRAN

An aerial photograph shows a water reservoir at the historic site of Solomon's Pools.  (Hazem Bader/AFP Via Getty Images)

The three reservoirs collectively hold approximately 288,000 cubic meters of water, or more than 10 million cubic feet. They are fed by the Arrub and el-Biyar aqueducts, which, together with rainwater, historically supplied Jerusalem with water year-round. During the British Mandate, the pools underwent significant renovations and became known as "Jerusalem's beach" until the Oslo Accords.

Under the agreements, the West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C. Solomon's Pools are located in Area A, which falls under Palestinian civil and security control.

Yonatan Marcus, chief of staff of the Efrat Municipality, told Fox News Digital that during the negotiations, then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin maintained that the pools would remain under Israeli control, alongside other archaeological sites of major Judeo-Christian significance such as Rachel's Tomb in Bethlehem.

However, during the mapping process, he said, the words "Solomon's Pools" remained within Area C on zoomed-out maps, while the reservoirs themselves ultimately mistakenly fell inside Area A.

TRUMP’S MASSIVE GOP FAITH BLOC RAISES RED FLAG ON IRAN DEAL: TRUST HIM, NOT HIS TEAM

Marcus said under Palestinian Authority control, things changed for the worse. "When you visit today, you can see that the place is neglected. Much of it has been destroyed. There are signs everywhere in Arabic stating that swimming is not permitted because the pools are filled with sewage water," he said.

He added that the sewage contamination was not natural, with wastewater deliberately diverted into the pools, replacing the fresh water that flowed there until the Oslo Accords. He said this occurred despite the PLO's commitment under the agreement to protect historical sites in Area A.

"Our main goal is to protect these magnificent pools. It's not just about Jewish history; it's about Judeo-Christian history and whoever believes in the people of the Bible who walked here," he said.

He described the reservoirs as the largest archaeological pools in Israel, saying they occupy a strategic location between the Western Wall and the Cave of the Patriarchs and Matriarchs along Route 60, known as the Biblical Highway.

Although the pools are located in Area A, Marcus said visits by Israelis take place only on coordinated tours secured by the IDF's Judea and Samaria Division, as permitted under the Oslo Accords.

He noted that visits by Israeli officials, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have prompted improvements, saying the Palestinian Authority removed about 200 bags of garbage from the site following years of neglect.

CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

Panoramic view of the Old City of Jerusalem, Israel, viewed from Haas Avenue in late afternoon. (Planet One Images/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"If the pressure of our coming here is going to make them take care of the site, then wonderful. In the end, our goal is for it to be preserved," he said.

Ahmad Fattouh, a spokesman for Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas's Fatah faction, rejected the allegations.

"It's absolutely audacious that the leadership of the colonial settlement of Efrat claims to be concerned about the condition of Burak Sulaymān's pools when they are the very reason behind its declining water levels," Fattouh told Fox News Digital. He said Israeli locals diverted the springs that feed the pools and argued that the Palestinian Authority has restored the site and developed it as a tourist destination.

Fattouh also accused Israeli officials of using the issue to justify taking control of the site, saying Smotrich's visit showed that the pools were not completely dry, contrary to claims by Efrat officials.

Solomon's Pools, a series of ancient reservoirs south of Jerusalem near Bethlehem, have supplied water to Jerusalem for centuries and are at the center of an ongoing dispute over heritage, sovereignty and preservation. (Yonatan Marcus/Efrat municipality )

Yishai Fleisher, international spokesman for Hebron, said the pools are akin to rediscovering a lost part of the Jewish Temple, as they supplied Jerusalem with water for some 2,000 years.

He said preserving the site begins with attracting visitors, producing educational videos, improving access along the new road from northern Efrat, hosting senior Israeli officials and establishing a permanent presence with cameras, patrols and farms.

"Since the story started breaking, the P.A. is trying to build a mosque there. The goal of the P.A. is to stop Israeli presence in Judea and Samaria and the Land of Israel. They are not about developing anything for its own sake," Fleisher claimed to Fox News Digital.

Fleisher, who is an influential voice among the Israeli right, called for a radical change in policy. "What we really have to do is dismantle the P.A. and assert sovereignty over Judea and Samaria. In the meantime, the line should be redrawn so that Solomon's Pools, which are essentially archaeological sites, are placed under Israeli control in Area C," he said.

Amelie Botbol is a freelance field reporter based in Tel Aviv, Israel, who reports on Israel-related news.

title: Mother of PC Harper ‘bitterly disappointed’ that son’s killers remain eligible for early release – UK politics live
excerpt:
Government revises plans to tackle prison overcrowding amid pressure from MPs and victims but domestic abusers and killers could still be released early

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage ...
body_text:
Government revises plans to tackle prison overcrowding amid pressure from MPs and victims but domestic abusers and killers could still be released early

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. The mother of PC Andrew Harper said her family are “bitterly disappointed” that her son’s killers remain eligible for early release after the government revised plans to tackle the overcrowding crisis in prisons.

Following pressure from victims, MPs and frontline prison officers, rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded from the scheme for England and Wales, the government said on Monday.

But domestic abusers and killers will still be eligible for early release, including two men jailed for their role in the death of PC Harper, who sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019.

“Quite frankly, we shouldn’t be in this position,” Debbie Adlam, PC Harper’s mother, told BBC Breakfast.

She said it was “completely right” that rapists and paedophiles are not going to be released under the government’s latest plans, but added “they shouldn’t have been considered in the first place”.

This article includes content hosted on platform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Adlam said she was “devastated” that two of her son’s killers remain eligible for early release. She told the programme:

double quotation markIt feels like we’re letting Andrew down again. We’ve been through the justice system, we thought we’d done as best as we could. Now we’re standing up to fight again … so I just feel really let down, for Andrew’s sake as well as ours.

The justice secretary, Alex Norris, told Sky News this morning that the latest changes to the early release scheme would see 5,000 prisoners released over 10 months, down from 6,000.

He said the government won’t need further emergency release schemes as sentencing changes would provide “long-term security” for prison capacity.

Writing in the Telegraph, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he asked the justice secretary to consider the early release of more female prisoners, “given the lower risk they generally pose” in order to prevent further overcrowding.

Burnham said he had “pushed to the very limits of what is possible” but was unable to exempt more criminals from the early release scheme without the prison system “collapsing within months”.

PC Harper’s wife, Lissie Harper, has expressed anger at the prospect that two of her late husband’s killers could be released early, calling it “an affront to justice” and “an utter betrayal”. The justice secretary said he understood the family’s “anger” and offered an apology.

double quotation markWere we not to make these changes, then we would run out of prison places in this October or November.

I know that’s difficult. I know that’s created harm, and it’s not Lissie Harper’s fault, and I’m sorry that she’s been put into this situation as a result, I genuinely am.

Prisoners serving time for some sexual or violent offences where the automatic release stage is set at two-thirds will become eligible for release at the halfway point, provided they have not committed serious breaches of prison rules, as my colleagues note in this story.

This applies to two of PC Harper’s killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter. Henry Long, the main perpetrator, will not be subject to early release.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said on Tuesday that he would delay the planned early release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales by a month until October.

It follows the suspension of Keir Starmer’s plans to release up to 6,000 offenders from prison early in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.

Burnham suspended the scheme in his second week as PM after coming under intense pressure from MPs, victims, campaigners and frontline prison officers to halt the early release of serious sexual and violent offenders.

That’s why we’re making significant changes: offenders who have been sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and other grooming offences will be excluded from the changes.

The domestic abuse commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, said the decision to exclude those who have abused their partners was “wrong” and “puts victims’ lives at risk”.

title: Hungary comes ‘within millimetres’ of shutting down nuclear power plant amid drought crisis – Europe live
excerpt:
PM Péter Magyar says country nearly forced into decision as extreme heat and low water levels in Danube pose challenges in region

Hungary has come “within millimetres” of having to shut down its nucl...
body_text:
PM Péter Magyar says country nearly forced into decision as extreme heat and low water levels in Danube pose challenges in region

Hungary has come “within millimetres” of having to shut down its nuclear power plant  overnight, prime minister Péter Magyar said, as low water levels in the Danube continue to pose challenges for countries in south-eastern Europe.

“Around 1:30 a.m. we were a few millimetres away from completely shutting down the Paks Power Plant, but then the water level stopped falling and by morning it had risen 1.5 centimetres. The last turbine is currently operating safely,” Magyar said on social media.

The plant already operates at a reduced capacity of just over 10% after the Danube fell to a record low, making it impossible to cool it properly.

Energy minister István Kapitány said on Tuesday that a number of energy saving measures succeeded in lowering energy consumption to keep the grid secure.

A number of businesses have made significant adjustments to their normal ways of working to save energy consumption during the peak hours. For example, a grocery chain Lidl changed its baking shifts, and turned off its drink fridges – despite temperatures expected to get close to 40C. Electric car chargers in their parkings can only be used until 5pm, HVG reported.

Over in Romania, the government celebrated that a two-centimetre rise in water levels after yesterday’s spectacular controlled explosion, intended to divert the flow of the Danube to help cool its Cernavodă nuclear plant.

The plant manager told local media that it should help keep the plant running during the next few days, but more interventions are planned today, with plans to sink old barges to further divert the flow of water.

Temperatures are set to surpass 40C in large parts of Romania today, again.

Elsewhere, I will keep an eye on the much-awaited meeting of EU interior ministers who will discuss last week’s migration crisis in Ceuta amid questions about the EU’s relationship with Morocco and the steps needed to secure the bloc’s external borders.

They are meeting at 10am Brussels time, and we should hear from the EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, in the early afternoon.

I will bring you all the latest lines here.

It’s Tuesday, 4 August 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Over in Brussels, after a weekend of backbiting over the response to the mass border crossings in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, EU ministers will seek to present a more unified front – and signal tougher security at Europe’s frontiers.

EU home affairs ministers are meeting at 10.30 CET via video conference to assess the bloc’s response to the arrival – and quick departure – of tens of thousands of people at the Spanish territory in north Africa. Around 100 people are estimated to have died on both sides of the Spanish-Moroccan border.

Ministers are not expected to take decisions, but EU sources think they will give a broad endorsement to the measures outlined by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen on Monday, intended to ensure stronger border protection “at critical points” of the EU’s external border.

Von der Leyen wants to double down on five areas: strengthening cooperation with non-EU countries to prevent migration; stronger external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; and boosting returns of people with no right to stay.

At a meeting of senior EU diplomats on Monday, several countries stressed the importance of preventing sudden movements of people, calling for greater use of intelligence and monitoring of disinformation and misinformation.

While Madrid’s envoy voiced his government’s frustration with the response from some member states, others rejected suggestions that they had failed to show solidarity over the sudden influx of arrivals.

A number of member states said they were ready to help and reflected on their own experience: Poland and Lithuania referred to the instrumentalisation of people on the move by the Belarusian dictatorship, while Italy and Greece spoke of their dealings with sudden arrivals of large numbers of people. But despite the warm words, many governments remain critical of Spain’s plan to regularise 500,000 undocumented migrants, which has triggered nearly 1.2m applications.

“There is some concern that the regularisation of 1.2m people can be used to paint a picture that the door is open.”

title: Five dead in Moscow region as Ukraine continues warehouse strikes
excerpt:
Ukraine has developed drones, picture here in July 2026, capable of striking deep inside Russia

At least five people were killed and 10 more injured in a Ukrainian drone strike on a warehouse close t...
body_text:
Ukraine has developed drones, picture here in July 2026, capable of striking deep inside Russia

At least five people were killed and 10 more injured in a Ukrainian drone strike on a warehouse close to Moscow overnight on Tuesday, the region's governor has said.

The official did not specify what had been targeted but Ukraine has been carrying out strikes on facilities operated by Wildberries in recent weeks, often dubbed the "Russian Amazon".

Kyiv says the depots are used to supply the Russian military, which Moscow denies.

Local officials also said Wildberries warehouses were targeted in the St Petersburg and Tver regions overnight.

Russia also launched strikes against parts of Ukraine, killing at least four and injuring several people.

Russia's defence ministry said it had intercepted and destroyed 320 drones overnight.

Moscow region governor Andrei Vorobyov said an industrial site in Novoselki, Chekhov - about 69km (43 miles) south of the Kremlin - was attacked, triggering a fire at a warehouse.

He wrote on Telegram that seven of the 10 people injured were in a moderate condition, with one in a serious condition.

Ukrainian media reported that the site of the Moscow strike was linked to Wildberries.

The company has not commented publicly but confirmed its facility in St Petersburg was hit.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said an 89-year-old woman was killed and two girls, aged two and 12, were among seven injured in a Russian strike on the southern port city of Mykolaiv overnight.

A woman and two girls, aged five and 10, were killed in a strike on a residential area in Sumy, and another four people were injured, it said.

Russian strikes also injured two people in the city of Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, while a food warehouse was set on fire in Dnipro, according to the State Emergency Service.

Russia says seven killed and 40 injured by Ukrainian drone hitting busy beach

title: NSW Liberal admits to leaking confidential report to young conservative powerbrokers, inquiry hears
excerpt:
NSW shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, tells inquiry Jean-Claude Perrottet had a talent for recruiting

The leader of the opposition in the New South Wales upper house has admitted to leaking a...
body_text:
NSW shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, tells inquiry Jean-Claude Perrottet had a talent for recruiting

The leader of the opposition in the New South Wales upper house has admitted to leaking a confidential draft report from a 2023 parliamentary inquiry to a member of a group of young conservative Liberal powerbrokers now under investigation by the corruption watchdog, an inquiry has heard.

On Tuesday, Damien Tudehope, the NSW shadow attorney general and Liberal leader in the upper house, gave evidence as part of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny.

The inquiry is investigating allegations the Reformers solicited or accepted illegal donations to recruit or renew members to the party, a practice known as branch stacking, which is not itself illegal.

Tudehope, who has stood aside from his shadow cabinet roles during the inquiry, is not named in any allegations by Icac.

On Tuesday afternoon, counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC, asked Tudehope about a parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe. Tudehope had been the leader of the government in the upper house, under then-Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, until February 2023.

Tudehope was asked if he could recall coming into possession of a confidential draft copy of the inquiry’s report in that month. He said he could not, but was aware of the obligation to keep a draft parliamentary report confidential.

He was shown an email in which he had sent the report as an attachment to Reformer Jeremy Greenwood. Dwyer asked: “Did you send that report in draft to Mr Greenwood?”

The inquiry has heard that Reformers Greenwood, Christian Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of Dominic Perrottet, avoided appearing at the inquiry. Under questioning from Dwyer, Tudehope claimed to have had discussions on Jean-Claude’s whereabouts with Dominic Perrottet.

“I did have a discussion with Dom at one stage, and it was a very casual discussion ... I just said, ‘Where is Jean-Claude?’ And he said he didn’t know. But then, in a subsequent discussion, I think he may have told me he was in Fiji,” he said.

Jean-Claude Perrottet has previously denied any wrongdoing. At the time of the parliamentary inquiry, Dominic Perrottet, who is not accused of any wrongdoing, rejected allegations his borther had tried to orchestrate a branch-stacking operation to unseat federal Coalition MP Alex Hawke, saying “leave my family out of it”.

On Tuesday, Icac heard evidence from businessman Frits Maré, the key witness at the parliamentary inquiry, about a 2020 meeting in which Perrottet and Christian Ellis asked him to contribute $50,000 to an operation to unseat Hawke.

Tudehope, whose name has been mentioned frequently during the first two weeks of hearings, gave evidence about the time Jean-Claude Perrottet and Christian Ellis spent in his electorate and ministerial offices.

He admitted that Jean-Claude Perrottet had a “talent” for recruiting and renewing new members to the party, which he said was essential for any Liberal member looking to hold their seat at preselection.

“[Jean-Claude] had a fairly wide connection of friends, which he was able to marshal together and exploit. Which is well, I won’t say exploit, but sort of get to do things for him.”

Jean-Claude worked in Tudehope’s electorate office in 2018 and in his parliamentary office in 2019, when Tudehope was minister for finance.

Asked about a 2018 message in which Jean-Claude wrote to other Reformers that “Scott and Damien are afraid”. Recognising “Scott” as the former head of his electorate office, Tudehope said he did not recall raising concerns or being aware that Jean-Claude may have been using his hours as an electorate officer in recruiting Liberal members, although it may have “potentially arisen”.

Tudehope described a later incident in which his chief of staff “blew up” about a newspaper article about staffers spending ministerial hours on recruitment against their code of conduct.

The inquiry heard that Ellis was only employed as a staffer in Tudehope’s ministerial office for three months before being terminated in July 2019. Tudehope said that the article “was probably the precipitating event” for Ellis’s dismissal.

The Reformers, who were part of same the conservative right faction as Tudehope, wanted more conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia. Tudehope, who admitted to speaking at multiple Reformers recruitment events, defended himself as “a warrior for social issues for the party”.

After being shown evidence of a bank transfer and one message from Jean-Claude in which he wrote that “Damien” had paid for a venue for an event, and another – “Damien got it” – which suggested he had contributed $5,000 for a Reformers table at a right faction event, Tudehope admitted he may have made payments to the Reformers.

His son, James Tudehope, is not named in allegations but has declined a request to give evidence to Icac after moving to New Zealand earlier this year.

Tudehope told the inquiry on Tuesday that his son, while an employee of Catholic Schools NSW, had raised concerns “at a Sunday lunch” about payments allegedly being made by the schools governing body to Beckington, a lobbying company controlled by Ellis.

“He said to me that, ‘I’m being pressured to pay an invoice for Christian Ellis, and I just don’t think we should be paying it’.”

Tudehope’s former business partner , hotelier Michael O’Hara, is alleged to have made political donations to the Reformers, prohibited because of his involvement in the liquor and gambling industries.

Under questioning from counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, Tudehope accepted that he introduced Reformers Ellis and Robert Assaf to O’Hara and that he was aware O’Hara was “generous” and would be likely to support their factional work financially.

But like O’Hara, the inquiry’s first witness last week, Tudehope disputed whether payments to the Reformers, who were not a registered party, would count as political donations.

“If you think that I would expose a friend of mine to that level of scrutiny that he was exposed to, 83 years of age with stage ... four cancer, do you think that I would have done that in circumstances where I knew that he would be a prohibited donor for the purposes of the Electoral Funding Act? Not on your life.”

Before Tudehope’s evidence on Tuesday afternoon, the NSW Liberal Leader, Kellie Sloane, told reporters at a morning press conference she believed there was a “pathway back” for Tudehope to her frontbench.

title: UFC’s Allan Nascimento dead aged 34 after apparent heart attack
excerpt:
Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) fighter Allan Nascimento has died at the age of 34 after suffering an apparent heart attack in his sleep.

The mixed martial art (MMA) body posted the news about t...
body_text:
Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) fighter Allan Nascimento has died at the age of 34 after suffering an apparent heart attack in his sleep.

The mixed martial art (MMA) body posted the news about the Brazilian’s passing late Monday on their website.

“This morning, Monday, August 3rd, our beloved fighter and exemplary flyweight, Allan Nascimento, was found unresponsive after suffering an apparent heart attack in his sleep,” the UFC statement read.

“Despite the efforts of the responding medical team, he was pronounced deceased at the scene.

“Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Allan’s family, friends, teammates, and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time.”

Nascimento, who remained a Sao Paulo resident throughout his life, leaves behind a wife and two children.

The last fight for the flyweight came in June, when he was defeated by Mitch Raposo in a split decision.

Nascimento fought out of Chute Boxe in Brazil and had a UFC record of four wins and two defeats, with an overall MMA record of 22 wins and seven defeats.

“We have lost a warrior, friend, dedicated competitor and extraordinary human being,” Chute Boxe said in a statement.

“[He] earned the respect and admiration of all who had the privilege of knowing him,” they said on Instagram.

“Allan inspired on and off the mats with his determination, humility, respect and fighting spirit.

“Your presence will be missed immeasurable, rest in peace Allan, your name, your story and your legacy will live forever through our star.”

title: Charity cyclist, 82, dies a day after 3,300 mile ride across Australia
excerpt:
Bob Montgomery completed the charity ride with his grandson

An 82-year-old bike rider who cycled 3,300 miles (5,300km) across Australia to raise money for charity has died a day after completing the ...
body_text:
Bob Montgomery completed the charity ride with his grandson

An 82-year-old bike rider who cycled 3,300 miles (5,300km) across Australia to raise money for charity has died a day after completing the challenge.

Bob Montgomery's death was "unexpected" but "peaceful", his family said in a statement on social media, just a day after he had finished what he had dubbed "One Last Ride" from Broome in Western Australia to Bowral, south-west of Sydney.

He and his 18-year-old grandson had raised about A$105,000 ($74,000; £55,000) for a motor neurone disease (MND) charity with the six-week ride.

It was his sixth fundraising ride in support of MND NSW, the statement said, adding that it was "a cause that was deeply personal to him".

His wife of 59 years, Jenny was by his side during his "peaceful passing", his family said, adding that he was "still passionately sharing his message only hours before his passing."

Montgomery and his grandson Tom Malcolm had arrived in Bowral on Sunday to "roaring applause" from his local community, the national broadcaster ABC reported.

He told ABC he had been motivated by meeting people along the way and enjoying a "beer or two" at each stopover.

"There's so many stories and so many people we met along the way who put their hands into their pockets to throw some cash in, which is fantastic," Montgomery was quoted as saying.

Bob Montgomery's "One Last Ride" saw him cycle from Broome in Western Australia to Bowral, south-west of Sydney

He had been inspired to take on the challenge after losing a cousin to MND and had raised almost A$300,000 on his previous rides. "I have seen family and friends suffer. It's heart breaking," he wrote on his fundraising page.

Malcolm had continued onto Sydney on Monday where the family had gathered once again to celebrate.

But shortly after the party, Montgomery suffered a medical episode, MND NSW chief executive Liam O'Meara said.

O'Meara said he was "deeply saddened" by Montgomery's death, calling him a "cherished friend and tireless supporter of MND NSW".

title: Washington man arrested on arson charge tied to devastating Spokane wildfire
excerpt:
Fox News’ Sarah Alegre reports on wildfires across Spokane County, Washington, destroying hundreds of structures and forcing thousands of residents to evacuate on ‘Special Report.’

A Washington state...
body_text:
Fox News’ Sarah Alegre reports on wildfires across Spokane County, Washington, destroying hundreds of structures and forcing thousands of residents to evacuate on ‘Special Report.’

A Washington state man was arrested Monday on a first-degree arson charge in connection with the Old Trails Fire, one of several wildfires that have destroyed hundreds of structures and forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate the Spokane area, authorities said.

Aaron F. Farinacci, 37, was taken into custody after Spokane County Sheriff’s Office detectives and Washington Department of Natural Resources investigators developed probable cause to arrest him, according to the sheriff’s office.

Citizen tips and information from Airway Heights police officers and Spokane County sheriff’s deputies who responded to the initial call and conducted evacuations helped lead investigators to Farinacci, the sheriff’s office said.

Authorities described Farinacci as a convicted felon from Arizona but said they had found no documented criminal history involving fires.

Investigators have not connected Farinacci to the two other major blazes burning in the area, the Autumn Lane and Fairview fires, officials said.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Aaron Farinacci, 37, was charged with first-degree arson. (Spokane County Sheriff’s Office)

"We will be looking into any other crimes Mr. Farinacci may have committed in the past," Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels said during a news briefing.

Nowels said first-degree arson was the charge supported by probable cause at that stage of the investigation and cautioned that the case could change as authorities gathered additional evidence.

Detectives obtained an arrest warrant for Farinacci and a search warrant for his residence in the 2800 block of West Elliott Drive, according to the sheriff’s office.

Deputies served the warrant Monday and arrested Farinacci without incident. Authorities said detectives found a butane lighter and waterproof matches while detaining and searching him.

SPENCER PRATT REACTS TO SPOKANE DEVASTATION WITH BLUNT WILDFIRE WARNING AND MESSAGE OF FAITH

Firefighters respond to wildfires near Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue / FOX Weather)

Farinacci was booked into the Spokane County Jail and was being held on $1 million bond.

The Old Trails Fire was first reported Saturday near North Old Trails Road and West Euclid Road. It became the largest of three destructive fires burning around Spokane and remained uncontained Monday, according to authorities and wire reports.

Wildfires rage in Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue)

The three fires had collectively destroyed at least 700 structures and prompted evacuation orders affecting approximately 67,000 people as of Monday, according to The Associated Press. More than 1,000 firefighters were battling the blazes.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a statewide wildfire emergency Saturday amid drought, unusually high temperatures and strong winds. The declaration also imposed a statewide prohibition on most outdoor and agricultural burning through Sept. 30.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Trump wants ‘fair treatment’ in fight over Labor’s levy on tech giants to pay for news, US trade group warns
excerpt:
National Foreign Trade Council ‘disappointed’ at move to expand News Bargaining Incentive but Australian experts say government is not going far enough

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest ...
body_text:
National Foreign Trade Council ‘disappointed’ at move to expand News Bargaining Incentive but Australian experts say government is not going far enough

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A major US trade body has rubbished the Albanese government’s plan to make more big tech platforms pay for Australian journalism, issuing a veiled warning about how Donald Trump may respond to the “deteriorating trend”.

The National Foreign Trade Council said it was “disappointed” at the Australian government’s move to expand its News Bargaining Incentive (NBI) to take in Microsoft’s LinkedIn, amid trade tensions between Washington and Canberra including newly increased tariffs on Australian goods.

But competition experts in Australia say the government has not gone far enough in helping support news outlets whose content is being exploited by platforms such as Facebook and Google, and that the exclusion of AI platforms was a major flaw.

“I hope they move on the AI issue and give us that clarity,” said the former ACCC chair Rod Sims.

“I’d like to see a bit of urgency. The potential lack of ambition, and not every [media outlet] getting a deal, certainly worries me.”

The proposed NBI, which the Albanese government seeks to legislate in coming months, would require tech giants to compensate media outlets for the news on their platforms, either through making commercial deals or paying a higher levy.

It initially included Google, TikTok and Meta; Monday’s announcement that the NBI would include professional networking sites – previously carved out from the plan – and increase the cost charge but reduce the cost base, was hailed by Labor as a fairer model.

But Tiffany Smith, the vice-president of global trade policy at the National Foreign Trade Council, criticised the move.

“We remain disappointed that Australia continues to push forward with a news bargaining incentive that now covers an even broader spectrum of US companies,” she told Guardian Australia.

The NFTC is a major American trade lobby, with members including affected companies Meta, Microsoft and Google; other tech companies such as Amazon, Apple and Samsung; and major firms like BP, Coca-Cola, Ford, Toyota, Shell and Visa.

“The Trump administration has made it clear that it is fully committed to the fair treatment of American companies abroad. We call on the Australian government to reconsider this measure, which adds to a broader deteriorating trend in the tax and investment climate in Australia,” Smith said.

But Sims, a former boss of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and a supporter of the NBI, said the government wasn’t doing enough to support news.

Under the plan, big tech platforms would have to make at least six individual deals with news publishers – up from a previous four – to avoid paying the levy, set at a higher rate.

The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, who is leading the process, said on Monday that Australian media would expect to receive “$200 million to $250 million” in total under the arrangements.

Sims said he was pleased the NBI was progressing, and would scrap the carve out for professional networking sites, but said more money should be raised to support journalism – noting $250m was the figure raised under the former News Media Bargaining Code, legislated by the Coalition half a decade ago, and which only included Meta and Google.

Sims said the government should be aiming higher than that, more in the realm of $300m plus, with more companies included and inflation added.

“There’s a lack of ambition, and simple arithmetic here,” Sims said.

News Corp’s Australian chair, Michael Miller, claimed the government’s changes “gut the incentive for tech platforms to strike fair deals with Australian media”, saying the rules “need strengthening, not softening”.

“On an already uneven playing field, getting this wrong won’t just hurt Australian media. It will erode the quality and independence of news every Australian relies on,” he said.

The changes were also criticised by the Coalition and Greens, making the NBI’s pathway through parliament unclear when the legislation is introduced in coming weeks.

Sims was critical that AI platforms deriving value from Australian news would not be captured – even those incorporated into NBI-exposed companies, such as Google’s Gemini. He also worried that many outlets would miss out on benefit, with big tech companies only obliged to make six deals minimum.

“It just means not everybody will get a deal, in fact most won’t … some outlets in public interest journalism won’t get some. That’s a real concern,” he said.

Another former ACCC chair, Allan Fels, said it was positive the government was making progress, but worried the scheme didn’t go far enough to “extract more from the platforms” for Australian journalism.

A Microsoft spokesperson said the company “shares the Government’s objective of promoting a sustainable Australian news ecosystem” and said it would continue “constructive engagement with Government, publishers and industry stakeholders to support high-quality journalism, innovation and economic growth”.

title: Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption when killed, jury told
excerpt:
Journalist’s son says his mother was examining leak from Electrogas, part owned by Yorgen Fenech who is on trial

Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption by the businessman Yorge...
body_text:
Journalist’s son says his mother was examining leak from Electrogas, part owned by Yorgen Fenech who is on trial

Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption by the businessman Yorgen Fenech and members of Malta’s government when she was killed, a jury has heard.

The heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes, Fenech is on trial for murder, accused of commissioning and paying for Caruana Galizia’s killing in a car bombing in October 2017.

The journalist’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia, a software engineer who was part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers investigation into offshore companies, took the stand on Monday.

He described being drawn in to helping his mother with her work, saying that as more facts came to light, it seemed to him a “portal” had opened and he could “see into hell”.

In 2015, Matthew said, he was working on the Panama Papers leak, uploading millions of files into a database that reporters were using to investigate tax havens.

While processing the files, he said, he found information directly relevant to Malta. “I had to share what I was seeing with my mother. I believed it was too important.”

Over time, material from the leak and Daphne’s own sources produced evidence that Malta’s then energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies soon after entering office. A firm of accountants was helping them to open bank accounts in the name of those companies, Matthew said.

The jury was shown a comment left by Daphne in early 2017 under a newspaper article about the minister and the chief of staff. She wrote: “How unbelievably corrupt they are – and worse still, they were not tempted into corruption when they were already jaded in power, but actually got into power with the express purpose of being corrupt. It was their roadmap.”

At the time of her death in 2017, Matthew said, he had been helping his mother process another leak, consisting of thousands of emails stored in the servers of a company called Electrogas, partly owned by Fenech. One of the Muscat government’s flagship projects after winning the 2013 general election had been to privatise a key part of Malta’s electricity infrastructure. The contract had been won by Electrogas.

“I was receiving this info, I couldn’t believe it, it was like a portal opened up and I could see into hell,” Matthew said. The defence objected, saying the witness was offering an opinion.

Asked if Daphne had discussed the tendering process with him, Matthew said she had.

“Factually, what did your mother tell you about the tendering process?” the prosecutor asked. Matthew replied: “That it was corrupt.” The judge interjected to remind the witness that this was an opinion, not a fact.

Asked what he had seen in the emails, Matthew said: “When I started receiving the data and put it in a system to make it searchable, I could see that Yorgen Fenech was at the centre of everything. He was featured in countless emails.”

Matthew said the Electrogas leak was ongoing the day his mother was killed. He said she had wanted to gather a group of journalists together to examine the data, in a collaboration similar to the one that had produced the Panama Papers. He had contacted the Guardian to begin work on the project, but his mother was killed a few months later.

“We never got to do it, and in fact when I see these emails my heart beats fast because I’m taken back to that time when I was with my mother planning on what to do,” he told the court.

After the murder, Matthew set up the Daphne Project, working with a wider group of publications, including the Guardian and Reuters, to continue investigating Electrogas and try to uncover who was behind his mother’s killing.

The reporting uncovered evidence that suggested Fenech had intended to pay bribes in order to secure the power station concession, provoking international condemnation and a European parliament investigation. Fenech, Mizzi and Schembri reject any suggestion of corruption.

The allegations were not repeated on Monday, after the judge ordered the testimony to focus only on what could be supported by documents shown in court.

The prosecution’s questioning ended with a description by Matthew of the day his mother died. They were working together at home and she had prepared a mozzarella and tomato salad. She then left in her car to go to the bank.

“I was working on some software and I heard an explosion. I opened the door, I felt the blood drain away … I started walking faster and faster towards the tower of smoke,” he said.

“First I saw fire on the road – the road was on fire. I saw pieces of metal and flesh. My eyes followed the smoke and I saw a huge ball of fire. I ran towards it. The horn was going off, it wouldn’t stop. I saw a shadow in the car and I remember saying ‘that’s my mum’.”

He told the court he had set aside everything to ensure those responsible were held to account, leaving his job, ending his career and returning to Malta. “We had to make it our mission, which we did. It came at enormous personal cost.”

Fenech, who is on trial for complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, denies the charges. The trial continues.

Transcript and translation by Amphora Media

title: BP profits more than double as Iran war sends oil prices soaring
excerpt:
Energy company’s $5.73bn quarterly profits come after Shell posted second highest quarterly earnings on record

BP has reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Uk...
body_text:
Energy company’s $5.73bn quarterly profits come after Shell posted second highest quarterly earnings on record

BP has reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Ukraine because of rising oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East crisis.

The oil company’s quarterly profits more than doubled to $5.73bn (£4.27bn) in the three months to the end of June, up $2.5bn from the quarter before, as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt energy exports from the Gulf.

Despite the company’s better than expected profits, its new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, said there was “more to do” because BP was “not making the most” of its potential.

O’Neill is expected to undertake an overhaul of the 117-year-old company, including an exit from the North Sea after six decades of production from the UK’s oil and gas basin.

O’Neill told CNBC on Tuesday morning that she had held a conversation with Andy Burnham, and that the new PM had “reinforced his desire to work closely with business” and be pragmatic”.

“The UK is still using a huge amount of oil and natural gas every single day, and we ought to be using our domestic resources first instead of buying those resources from a third party,” O’Neill added.

“You know, I think the new prime minister has come in with a focus on being pragmatic, and with a focus on understanding how communities around the nation can benefit from developing local economic outcomes.”

Burnham was warned last week he could face the first revolt of his premiership over his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas.

BP revealed its climbing profits days after Shell posted its second-highest quarterly earnings on record after months of market volatility caused by the Middle East crisis.

Europe’s largest oil company doubled its net profit to almost $10bn in the three months to June, the highest since its record earnings in the months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The Middle East crisis has also helped the Saudi ⁠oil company Aramco to a ⁠44% rise in ​net profits to $32.69bn in ​the three ​months ​ending on ​30 June, despite disruptions in ‌the strait of Hormuz, owing to higher ​sales revenue for refined and chemical products and crude oil.

The windfall profits for the world’s biggest oil and gas companies have faced criticism. Households and businesses are struggling with rising energy bills, and millions have been affected by severe heatwaves across Europe, which are made more likely and more severe by the fossil-fuel-driven climate crisis.

Donald Trump has said Chevron and ExxonMobil, which also reported sharp profit increases this week, are “making too much money” and should return some of their profits back to the public.

Rosie Downes, head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “Clearly not everyone is feeling the pain of the energy crisis. While BP banks another round of enormous profits, millions of households are paying the price through sky-high energy bills and a climate crisis accelerating rapidly out of control with increasingly severe heatwaves, wildfires and droughts.”

title: Metro Bank customer fights for £14,000 refund after AI-linked fraud
excerpt:
Lender was told money was being taken without authorisation, with cash used to buy credits for Claude chatbot

A Metro Bank customer has told of his fight to get more than £14,000 back after its syste...
body_text:
Lender was told money was being taken without authorisation, with cash used to buy credits for Claude chatbot

A Metro Bank customer has told of his fight to get more than £14,000 back after its systems failed to stop a fraud involving the AI chatbot Claude.

Zoli Rutter, a businessman from Sussex, had a total of £14,244 taken from his bank account. The scam involved fraudsters buying credits to use Claude.

When Metro Bank messaged Rutter to ask whether an attempted transaction was legitimate, he replied “no”, but the criminals were able to make a series of subsequent transactions of between £90 and £200.

The fraud is the latest to be linked to Anthropic, the company behind the Claude family of AI tools.

In May, a Claude user based in the US told Guardian Money about how gift cards to use the chatbot had been bought using his financial details. Other users shared similar stories on Reddit.

Claude has been in the news a lot lately. Last week, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) appeared to endorse Claude when it said Anthropic would provide access to the tool for firms taking part in a hi-tech FCA initiative (which lets financial companies safely experiment with advanced AI) in order “to help speed up their development work”.

However, this week it was revealed that some people’s conversations with Claude were publicly available online.

Rutter had been paying about £15 a month to use the chatbot for a few months when the scam happened.

He had been using the new technology to track and analyse business invoices.

The fraudsters used the Metro Bank debit card linked to his Anthropic account to make the payments and buy credits for the platform.

On 19 June, Metro Bank spotted a suspicious transaction for £90.90 and texted Rutter to ask whether he had authorised it. When he texted back to say that he had not, he received another text to say his account would be frozen. However, just the suspect transaction was blocked and not his account.

Fraudulent transactions then continued. While some were blocked, says the bank, many were not. Metro eventually froze his card the day after the scam started, but by then, more than £14,000 worth of payments had gone through.

A spokesperson for the bank says that owing to the “complex nature of the fraud, regretfully some payments were processed” before it blocked the card fully.

After Guardian Money got in touch, Metro Bank temporarily refunded Rutter while a chargeback refund was sought from Anthropic.

In a statement, the bank said: “This is a concerning case involving a third party that the customer had made previous genuine payments to and provided card details [to], which were then used to make a series of purchases without Mr Rutter’s knowledge.

“We recognise how worrying and frustrating [the] experience has been for Mr Rutter. Metro Bank has refunded Mr Rutter while we progress a chargeback dispute request with Anthropic to refund the money that had been taken.”

It added: “We would encourage customers to contact their bank as soon as they notice any unusual transactions or are aware of any compromise to accounts where their financial details are stored.”

Anthropic says a coordinated gang had used Rutter’s cards to buy credits to use Claude. It says it has no evidence that the compromised card details had come from its own systems. The user behind the fraud has been banned, it adds.

Anthropic says anyone who has been charged for a fraudulent purchase should contact its support site and the charges will be refunded.

Rutter has since been refunded by Anthropic, and the temporary refund from Metro Bank is due to be taken back by the bank.

Metro Bank told him in a letter that he had not received the service it expected its customers to get, and it offered him £300 by way of compensation.

Rutter says he intends to make a complaint about what happened to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

The bank says it has taken steps to prevent delays in cards being blocked.

Anyone who has been affected by an unauthorised card fraud is advised to contact their bank immediately and ask for a refund. They may then be asked to fill out forms detailing what happened.The FCA says the refund should be in a customer’s account by the end of the next business day.

title: Palestine weekly: Israel kills dozens in Gaza after Hamas disarmament deal
excerpt: United States President Donald Trump announced “a historic agreement” on July 30 for the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza, framed as the long-awaited move into the second phase of t...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump announced “a historic agreement” on July 30 for the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza, framed as the long-awaited move into the second phase of the October 2025 “ceasefire” deal.

The agreement was negotiated through the Board of Peace, established by Trump to oversee post-war reconstruction and governance of Gaza.

However, Hamas negotiator Ghazi Hamad told Al Jazeera the Palestinian group would not implement the deal unless Israel fulfilled its obligations, which include halting attacks and withdrawing troops.

A spokesperson for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, meanwhile, said Israeli forces would not withdraw until Hamas was fully disarmed.

With that fundamental deadlock unresolved, Israeli attacks on Gaza, which have characterised the 10-month “ceasefire”, continued, arguably with even greater intensity. Within days of the announcement of the “historic agreement”, Israeli strikes killed at least 19 Palestinians in a single day, bringing the weekend death toll in Gaza to 26.
