"As this is an active and ongoing investigation, DACC is not able to answer specific questions about this case at this time," the department said, adding that it is committed to ensuring kennel operations meet legal requirements and provide humane care.

TMZ, which first reported the search, said Blair was present during the inspection and cooperated with authorities. No dogs were removed from the property, according to the outlet.

Linda Blair "unknowingly" stepped away from acting to launch her Worldheart Foundation in 2003. (Getty Images)

In a video accompanying her Instagram post, Blair reiterated that the visit centered on administrative issues rather than the animals' condition.

"Today we got a really big surprise visit," she said in the video. "And as it turns out, there is nothing but some paperwork and some new diagrams and things."

"Wanted to check in and let you know I am fine. The animals are fine. And we just have some paperwork that has to be dealt with. And that's all this was all about. I don't know why mail isn't used more often to notify somebody. Just saying," she said, while also encouraging supporters to donate to the Linda Blair WorldHeart Foundation — the nonprofit she founded in 2003 to rescue and rehabilitate abused, neglected, and abandoned animals.

She ended her video by reiterating how she and the animals are doing, saying, "I wanna let you know I'm ok and so are the animals. Thank you so much."

Representatives for Blair and the Los Angeles County Department of Animal Care and Control did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

title: Holdouts for Trump’s attorney general pick say they will advance his nomination to the full Senate – US politics live
excerpt:
Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis say that formal order withdrawing ‘anti-weaponization fund’ has addressed their concerns

Blanche formally rescinds Trump’s $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization f...
body_text:
Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis say that formal order withdrawing ‘anti-weaponization fund’ has addressed their concerns

Blanche formally rescinds Trump’s $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization fund’

Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, two key holdouts on Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination – now say they will vote to advance him to the full Senate.

The outgoing lawmakers, who have repeatedly clashed with Trump over the past year, said their concerns were resolved after “successful negotiation of a legally enforceable document” that formally ends the $1.8bn “anti‑weaponization fund” and makes clear that Trump and his family will not receive indefinite protection from audits of future tax filings. Both issues had been deal‑breakers for Cornyn and Tillis. In the document Blanche released on Sunday, the acting attorney general did say that the sweeping immunity offered to the president and his family for their past conduct does not change.

“We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund. Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the Treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share,” the pair wrote in a statement. “We look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate judiciary committee soon.”

The panel is set to vote on Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday.

On Truth Social today, Donald Trump has railed against polling which shows his approval rating stuck in the low end. According to a recent survey by AP-Norc, only 33% of Americans said they approved of the president’s job performance – slightly below where he stood at this point in his first term.

“My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been,” he wrote.

“Why wouldn’t they be with the biggest tax cuts and employment numbers EVER, the biggest outside Investment in America in World history, a totally secure Border, a giant Victory in Venezuela, the Denuclearization of Iran, unparalleled respect and success throughout the World, and much more? Don’t believe the Radical Left’s Fake Poll numbers.”

Republican senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, two key holdouts on Todd Blanche’s attorney general nomination – now say they will vote to advance him to the full Senate.

The outgoing lawmakers, who have repeatedly clashed with Trump over the past year, said their concerns were resolved after “successful negotiation of a legally enforceable document” that formally ends the $1.8bn “anti‑weaponization fund” and makes clear that Trump and his family will not receive indefinite protection from audits of future tax filings. Both issues had been deal‑breakers for Cornyn and Tillis. In the document Blanche released on Sunday, the acting attorney general did say that the sweeping immunity offered to the president and his family for their past conduct does not change.

“We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund. Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the Treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share,” the pair wrote in a statement. “We look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate judiciary committee soon.”

The panel is set to vote on Blanche’s nomination on Tuesday.

On Tuesday, we’ll bring you the latest from Michigan where voters will head to the polls for competitive primaries in Senate and House races.

The most closely watched competition is the Democratic primary for the US Senate, where congresswoman Haley Stevens is up against former public health official Abdul El-Sayed. They’re vying to ultimately win the seat of outgoing senator Gary Peters in November. The race has now turned into a proxy battle for the future of the Democratic party. Establishment-backed Stevens has received support from party leaders and her race has been buoyed by millions from the pro-Israel lobby. Meanwhile the insurgent El-Sayed has built a strong grassroots movement and is endorsed by progressives lawmakers in the Democratic caucus.

There are also several competitive House primaries tomorrow –mirroring the same choice in the Senate race – where more moderate Democratic candidates will face off against progressives who reflect the changing face of the party.

Kay Granger, a former Republican representative, who was the first woman to win a US House seat from Texas, has died at age 83.

Granger served in the house from 1997-2025, and was the first female chair of the House appropriations committee. Before her role in federal office, she was the first woman elected mayor of Fort Worth, Texas.

In a tribute on social media, Republican House speaker Mike Johnson said that Granger “broke barriers for women in public service”.

My colleague Ramon Antonio Vargas previously reported that Granger largely disappeared from the public eye after she announced her plans to retire when her term ended in early 2025.

Granger’s son later reportedly told the Dallas Morning News that Granger was “having some dementia issues” and had moved into an independent senior living center with a memory care community on the same property. However, he disputed that she was being treated at the memory care community and said she was a resident of the independent living side of the property.

Homeland security officials under the Trump administration have quietly attempted to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in US immigrant detention to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, a Guardian investigation has found.

In 2025 and 2026, officials had definitely performed the procedures on at least three detained immigrants and probably subjected two more to the forced treatment – widely considered torture by human rights groups. The other five people gave in and broke their hunger strike at the last minute as force-feeding procedures loomed.

The government has not publicly acknowledged the practice of involuntary medical procedures on striking detainees, as the number of people detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) increases nationwide.

More people have gone on hunger strike in ICE detention centers to protest against conditions and demand resolutions to legal cases.

The investigation, based on hundreds of pages of court records and interviews with multiple sources, reveals a clearer picture of the federal government’s response to hunger strikes within secretive ICE facilities.

In the cases reviewed by the Guardian, the involuntary procedures included force-feeding, where medical staff coercively insert a tube through a hunger striker’s nose and down their throat then pump in nutritional shakes – an agonizing and traumatizing procedure that experts say can cause significant harm to the nose, esophagus and body organs. Other procedures included intravenous forced hydration, involuntary blood draws and the collection of urine samples.

Read the breakdown of the Guardian’s investigation here:

A reminder that my colleagues are covering the latest out of the Middle East at our dedicated live blog. This includes the latest drop in oil prices, since Trump walked back his threats to strike Iran on Sunday.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading 5% lower at $83.50 a barrel by mid-morning, after falling as low as $81.55 a barrel.

As we reported earlier, Republican senator Bernie Moreno has now publicly called for Representative Max Miller, his ex-son-in-law, to step down from Congress amid allegations of domestic and child abuse.

Trump, when asked about the allegations on Sunday on Air Force One, said he was “looking at” the claims against Miller.

“I’m gonna look at it. I mean, so far, it’s accusations,” the president added.

Miller and Emily Moreno, were in the middle of an acrimonious custody battle this year, when Miller filed a defamation against his former wife earlier this year.

On Sunday, Miller posted a video on social media, and continued to deny the allegations.

“I categorically deny abusing my former wife,” the Republican congressman said.

Donald Trump will be in Washington today. He’ll spend most of the day in meetings, but we’ll hear from him at 1.30pm ET when he signs an executive order in the Oval Office.

We’ll bring you the latest lines as that gets under way.

President Donald Trump said new talks to wind down the war in Iran will start Monday afternoon, after announcing he is holding off on new massive strikes he had threatened to unleash on the country.

The talks will seek to end the conflict and revive stalled cargo traffic through the strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway through which about a fifth of all traded oil and natural gas passed before the war.

Iranian state media quoted the country’s foreign ministry as saying Tehran was not currently holding negotiations with the United States.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated against measles, as the surge in infections has reached numbers not seen in the past 35 years.

Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning.

His remark came as the incidence of measles crossed a milestone – the US has now officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing the total tally in 2025 of 2,289.

Taken together, the past two years have seen more measles infections in the US than the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time a greater number of measles cases were recorded in a single year was in 1991.

Kennedy’s statement was extracted from him by Dana Bash, CNN’s host, who invited him to use his “bully pulpit” to talk directly to parents as the new school year approached. She urged him to tell families that they should vaccinate for measles “because it is safe and it will help them save their children’s lives”.

The pastor of a historically Black church on St Louis’s north side, Rodrick Burton has watched with bewilderment as the congressional race in his district has drawn national attention not about the bloodshed in his community, but rather in Gaza.

“As a pastor who’s had eight members murdered, violence over there is terrible,” Burton said of the conflict in the Middle East.

“We have to deal with the problems right in our metropolitan area,” Burton added. “While there’s kinship and stuff … you’re talking about blood overseas, blood on the TV. We got blood right here in our metropolitan area.”

In Tuesday’s Democratic congressional primary, voters in Missouri’s deep-blue first congressional district will decide whether to give pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell a second term, or replace him with Cori Bush, a former progressive congresswoman who accuses Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza. Along with a heated primary in Michigan, the contest has become a proxy battle over the Democratic party’s role in supporting Israel’s military before the November midterm elections, which will determine which party holds the majority in both chambers of Congress.

After losing to Bell two years ago, Bush is vying for her seat back, and a Super Pac linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) has so far spent more than $3m to try to keep her out.

In recent weeks, Democratic voters in New York City and Denver ousted incumbents in favor of candidates who promised they would take a hard line against support for Israel. In Congress, large shares of Democrats have voted for unsuccessful efforts to block arms sales to the country’s security forces, and progressives hope that a win by Bush will underscore their movement’s momentum.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Acting US attorney general Todd Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Donald Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization fund” to compensate his political allies.

The move follows weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general.

While Blanche has repeatedly said publicly that the fund was dead, the justice department had resisted formally confirming that in writing. That had drawn concern from lawmakers that it could be revived in some form, especially after Trump expressed continued support for the idea.

A spokesperson for Texas Senator John Cornyn, one of the senators holding up Blanche’s nomination, confirmed the agreement. The other GOP senator, North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis, did not have immediate comment.

The announcement comes ahead of a Senate judiciary committee vote on Blanche, which is scheduled for Tuesday.

“My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche said in a post on X. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order.”

The order says that “although the acting attorney general has repeatedly advised Congress through testimony, including under oath, as well as in written responses, that the Fund is not moving forward, and the Department has repeatedly represented to district courts that the Fund is not moving forward, today’s Order officially rescinds the May 18, 2026 Order.”

The document released by Blanche on Sunday night also limits the scope of another provision of the settlement that provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits. It clarifies that the tax audit immunity agreement “applies only retroactively” to claims open at the time of the settlement and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings.

Donald Trump has said he cancelled planned military strikes against Iran on the basis of “rapidly” reaching a deal on its nuclear programme and the full reopening of the strait of Hormuz. The president paused the strikes in expectation of a breakthrough and in response to requests from Iran and other countries in the region, he claimed on his Truth Social platform on Saturday.

Marcy Kaptur is being treated ⁠for non-life-threatening injuries after a car crash in Toledo, ⁠Ohio, on Sunday, ⁠the ​Democratic US representative’s office said. Kaptur, 80, was a passenger ⁠in the vehicle and on her way to church, her office ⁠said. Toledo police did not ​respond to ‌a request from Reuters for ‌comment.

Republican senator Bernie Moreno on Sunday publicly called for Representative Max Miller, his ex son-in-law, to step down from Congress amid allegations of domestic and child abuse. As recently as Friday, the Ohio senator had avoided giving his opinion directly on accusations made by his daughter, Emily Moreno, against the congressman.

The family of a Haitian immigrant who froze to death in early March at a bus shelter in Pittsburgh after she was dropped off in the city by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is poised to file a lawsuit this month against the United States and “multiple other governmental and non-governmental entities”, the Guardian has learned.

Technology is fun. I wrote this article once already, and something happened wh...
body_text:
The "NFL on FOX" crew broke down the San Francisco 49ers' 23-19 win over he Philadelphia Eagles in the Wild Card Round.

Technology is fun. I wrote this article once already, and something happened where it disappeared altogether. I really don’t know what the issue is or was, but maybe the second time I dissect the San Francisco 49ers' upcoming season will be even more exciting than the first time.

This was a team that I struggled to bet on or against last season. When I was betting they would lose, they came out with some miracle game. When I bet they would win, they looked like they had never played football before. I can still admit that the squad was impressive despite navigating a wide range of injuries. They were 12-5 for the season and got a 5-3 record from their backup quarterback, Mac Jones. Every loss they took in the regular season was against a postseason team, with the exception of Tampa Bay. They did win the first game of the postseason, taking out the reigning Super Bowl champion Eagles. Then disaster struck against the Seahawks. They gave up a game-opening kickoff return for a touchdown. Then turned the ball over on downs, leading to a Seattle field goal. A fumble and another Seattle touchdown put them down 17-0 after the first quarter. The second half was even worse in many ways. They turned the ball over on downs, then had an interception, turnover on downs, fumble, punt, and then ran three meaningless plays to end the game.

49ERS BRING BACK DEEBO SAMUEL TO FILL VOID LEFT BY RICKY PEARSALL'S KNEE INJURY: REPORT

San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle (85) greets his wife Claire Kittle before a preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on Aug. 23, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Chris Unger/Getty Images)

The team that deals with many injuries at many positions took a shot with someone uber talented, but also coming off of an injury-marred season. Mike Evans, who played only eight games last season, is now their primary receiver. If he is healthy, which he has been most of his career, he will be a difference-maker. They also added Christian Kirk, providing quarterback Brock Purdy with some solid options. It seems like they assumed offense was the priority, considering they also drafted a wide receiver in the second round. Their main addition on defense was Osa Odighizuwa; if he can replicate his season from last year, this should be an even tougher defense.

Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers looks to pass against the Dallas Cowboys during the first quarter in the NFC Divisional Playoff game at Levi's Stadium on January 22, 2023 in Santa Clara, California. (Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images)

49ERS HAVE SUCCEEDED WITH TALENT ACQUISITIONS BUT FAILED AT ADDITION BY SUBTRACTION OF BRANDON AIYUK

The biggest issue I have with the 49ers is that they don’t ever seem to be healthy. There is a ton of talent on this roster, but if you look at the names on paper and those who are actually available, there is a large gap. Christian McCaffrey is one of the best backs in the league, but he misses games fairly regularly. Brock Purdy consistently misses games. Nick Bosa and Fred Warner both played fewer than 10 games last season. George Kittle is on the PUP list to start the year. Ricky Pearsall has some issues with his knee again as well. Healthy, they are elite, but that’s going to be a major question mark for this team all season.

San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan watches from the sideline during the second half of an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Tampa, Florida, on Oct. 12, 2025. (AP Photo/Chris O'Meara)

Their head coach, Kyle Shanahan, has been great at getting the most out of his team regardless of who is on the field. However, I have some concerns that as these players age, they may not be able to go as far as long. No team will be healthy the whole season, but some of these guys are more consistently off the field than they are on the field. At 9.5 games, I don’t love taking the over – even though I think it hits, but you’re playing it at -145 or higher. Instead, I think we bet that there are going to be pieces missing and the Rams and Seahawks will still be better. I’ll take San Francisco to miss the playoffs at +122 if I had to take anything. Most likely I’ll just stay away.

title: Paris prosecutor investigates alleged bullying in government departments after suicide attempt
excerpt:
Internal inquiries also opened after two suicides and two attempted suicides of staff in departments connected to PM’s office

The Paris state prosecutor has opened a preliminary inquiry into alleged ...
body_text:
Internal inquiries also opened after two suicides and two attempted suicides of staff in departments connected to PM’s office

The Paris state prosecutor has opened a preliminary inquiry into alleged workplace bullying after the attempted suicide of a staff member in a department connected to the French prime minister’s office, France Inter radio has revealed.

The public radio station reported on Monday that two government workers in different departments had ended their lives in the past year, and two others had attempted suicide. The radio station said complaints of alleged workplace bullying had been made.

A complaint had been made by a staff representative to the Paris prosecutor in June over alleged bullying in certain government departments, the station said. The prosecutor has opened a preliminary inquiry. A document seen by France Inter and AFP said a complaint had been made that “presumed institutional bullying” had allegedly led a staff member to attempt to end their life.

Three internal government inquiries have also been opened into specific cases and broader workplace wellbeing.

The allegations of workplace bullying relate to a group of dozens of government departments and missions working under the umbrella of services of the prime minister.

The staff member at the centre of the prosecutor’s preliminary inquiry worked in a service that handled issues related to correspondence for the prime minister’s office, France Inter reported.

The woman’s lawyer, Christelle Mazza, told the radio station: “My client had been made [to feel] invisible. She was no longer invited to attend meetings, had been taken off the staff list, treated as if she was no one. She was mocked and jeered at as if it was playground bullying, [she was] ostracised.”

The lawyer said difficulties for staff had been compounded by the instability of governments after Emmanuel Macron dissolved the national assembly and called a snap election in June 2024.

In the two years from June 2024 to June 2026, there were four prime ministers: Gabriel Attal in a caretaker role, Michel Barnier, François Bayrou and Sébastien Lecornu.

No wrongdoing was alleged of the prime ministers.

In a statement, two senior officials in the department of services of the prime minister expressed full respect and support to colleagues and families after the suicides and attempted suicides. They said psychological welfare was “a constant priority” for the prime minister’s services and a specialist audit on workplace wellbeing would be conducted.

One case of attempted suicide was investigated and found not to be connected to the government service, they said. Another case of attempted suicide was at the centre of an administrative inquiry after allegations of bullying. For the two deaths by suicide, “investigations are under way in close cooperation with trade union staff representatives”, they said.

The officials added: “None of the people concerned worked directly with the prime minister or in his office.”

title: Trump's AG pick off life support after key Republican rebels relent
excerpt: President Donald Trump defended the Anti-Weaponization Fund and bashed Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, for opposing his nomination of Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche as permanent attorney general duri...
body_text:
President Donald Trump defended the Anti-Weaponization Fund and bashed Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, for opposing his nomination of Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche as permanent attorney general during his Friday Cabinet meeting at Camp David.

Two key Republican rebels are dropping their resistance against President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Justice Department.

Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., have for weeks dug their heels into the ground against confirming acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to fully take over the position. They have been trying to extract concessions from the administration in exchange for their votes.

And those concessions came on Sunday as Blanche’s first key test fast approaches. After warring with Trump and Blanche’s confirmation nearly being withdrawn, the duo are now ready to support the president’s pick to replace former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

A split image of President Trump, Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas (Eddie Seal/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images; Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc.)

"We want to express our gratitude to Mr. Blanche and his staff for working with us on this, and we look forward to voting to advance his nomination out of the Senate Judiciary Committee soon," they said in a joint statement.

Cornyn and Tillis had two primary objectives: ensure, in explicit writing, that the nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund would return, and that Trump’s audit immunity would not extend beyond him and the defendants listed in his lawsuit against the IRS.

Blanche announced on Sunday that the anti-weaponization fund was getting the permanent boot, and that the audit protection was just going to be narrowly tailored to Trump and his family.

DOJ BARS IRS FROM AUDITING TRUMP’S PRIOR TAX RETURNS IN SETTLEMENT ORDER SIGNED BY BLANCHE

Cornyn and Tillis said that they "are pleased" with the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) formal order to deal with both issues, and noted that doing so addressed "concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share."

Both issues came from the settlement deal Trump and his family reached with the IRS earlier this year that Blanche helped to roll out.

And both lawmakers are needed to advance Blanche out of committee and onto the Senate floor, given that if either one of them balked against the nominee, he would fail and be stuck in limbo.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON CORNYN, TIES AG NOMINATION FIGHT TO BITTER TEXAS PRIMARY

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appears at a confirmation hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., July 15, 2026. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)

Cornyn and Tillis both sparred with Trump over the last few days leading up to this moment.

Trump declared that he would withdraw Blanche’s nomination if neither of them broke their resistance. He reupped the pressure over the weekend when he announced that if Blanche’s confirmation continues to stumble or fail, he would revive the anti-weaponization fund and pressure Congress to codify it.

He declared on Truth Social that, "I will keep Todd as Acting AG, and push hard to get the Anti-Weaponization Bill," passed through Congress.

And Tillis countered that Trump "clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against."

"It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal," Tillis said over the weekend. "Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday."

With the issues appearing to be resolved, the committee vote on Blanche is moving full steam ahead.

Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, rescheduled the vote for Tuesday after nixing last week’s hearing. A spokesperson for Grassley said that his top goal is to see "Todd Blanche’s nomination to be successful."

"Grassley would like to see Blanche confirmed before the August recess as he has an excellent record restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe," they said.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Kmart sells out of low-cost rival to Meta camera glasses across Australia amid warnings of ‘privacy nightmare’
excerpt:
Expert says people face being filmed without their consent as $89 Anko smartglasses sell out in stores and online

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Kmart has sold out of An...
body_text:
Expert says people face being filmed without their consent as $89 Anko smartglasses sell out in stores and online

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Kmart has sold out of Anko-branded $89 camera glasses across Australia, which a digital rights expert says presents a “privacy nightmare” as people face being filmed without their consent.

As of Monday, the clear-lens, black-rimmed glasses, which can capture images and record high-definition videos, were sold out at Kmart stores across Australia and online.

The price point at $89 is significantly cheaper than the Meta Ray-Bans that the Anko brand glasses are styled on, which sell from $337.

The Anko glasses run on HeyCyan software, which allows the wearer to play music, answer calls, use an AI assistant, and transfer photos and videos from the device.

The software is used in a range of low-budget camera glasses, from online retailers including Amazon and Temu. Reddit users report that the software is sluggish compared to the software in the Meta Ray-Bans.

Meta has faced significant pushback from privacy advocates since launching the glasses – which some people have dubbed “pervert glasses” – for their ability to record people in public.

Meta’s glasses have a light on to indicate the wearer is recording, but there have been reports of users covertly recording in public, and reports that moderators employed by Meta review intimate footage from the glasses, including of people using the toilet and having sex.

The company last month rolled out an update that disables the camera if the LED light is interfered with, and also reportedly began removing videos from its platform of wearers using the device to harass strangers in public.

New York courts, the US air force and a hacker convention have all reportedly banned people from wearing the glasses.

Meta has said it has sold more than 7m of its glasses worldwide, and has recruited celebrity Kylie Jenner for advertising to push the devices into the mainstream, but the Ray-Bans and the flood of cheap versions of the same technology have concerned privacy advocates.

“Smartglasses with cameras are a privacy nightmare that illustrate how Australian privacy laws haven’t kept up with technology changes,” said Tom Sulston, head of policy at Digital Rights Watch.

“We shouldn’t have elevated expectations of personal privacy when out in public, but we should have some.”

Sulston said it was particularly problematic when in the hands of misogynist social media influencers who use the glasses to make content “of them harassing women – typically in places where we have higher expectations of more sensitive use of video cameras, like the beach”.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner said the privacy regulator was aware of the community concerns and was monitoring the rollout of the new technology.

“Organisations that collect, use or disclose personal information through products or services are subject to obligations under the act and the Australian Privacy Principles where the act applies,” the spokesperson said.

“People concerned about being photographed or recorded by another individual may also wish to seek independent legal advice about whether other commonwealth, state or territory laws may be relevant in the circumstances.”

A spokesperson for Kmart said the Anko glasses “are part of an established and increasingly mainstream category of wearable technology, with similar products available globally from major technology and eyewear brands”.

“As with any device capable of recording images, we expect customers to use the product responsibly, respectfully and in accordance with applicable laws and community expectations around privacy.”

Sulston said that due to the ongoing privacy issues, including how the collected data may be used by the companies producing the glasses, the social backlash would likely continue.

“The best way to lose friends and alienate people will be to be a public specs offender.”

One reviewer on TechRadar said of the Meta glasses this week that although it is his favourite tech of the year so far, he was afraid to wear them in public due to the growing backlash.

“I haven’t been worried about going around wearing my Meta Ray-Ban and Oakley specs in the past, but with growing public anger over the way smart specs are being misused, I have a genuine concern someone will see me wearing them and act violently towards me,” he said.

body_text:
Handful of tollroads to get one-off price cuts but WestConnex toll to keep rising at least 4% a year

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The cost of using Sydney’s biggest toll road will continue to rise at least 4% a year after the multinational private operator was accused of blocking the state government’s push for sweeping reforms.

Only a handful of Sydney’s motorways will receive one-off toll cuts under a deal announced by the state Labor government on Monday, as the tolling bill footed by taxpayers surpasses $1bn.

Eleven of Sydney’s toll roads are run by Transurban, a $47bn company with operations in Victoria, Queensland and the US, with most under contracts granting exclusive operating rights into the 2040s or later.

The deal will see the state pay $850m to widen the M2-M7 tollway, boosting traffic flows, which Transurban expects will increase its toll revenue. The government will separately spend $143m to settle the deal, negotiated over two years.

Under Monday’s deal, Transurban will cut some fares by 10% on the Lane Cove Tunnel and the M2 in July 2027 and the M7 in 2028. The cross-city tunnel toll will be cut by a one-off 20% in 2028 while the eastern distributor’s northbound fare will be cut and a southbound fare added.

Those highways accounted for less than half of the 1m trips recorded each day on average across Transurban’s Sydney network, suggesting most tollway trips would not see a toll reduction.

The Westconnex highway, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, and the NorthConnex will not get a reduction.

The premier, Chris Minns, told reporters on Monday the government had failed to negotiate a deal for the excluded highways at an appropriate cost with Transurban.

“We weren’t able to get the rate of the dollars that we wanted in exchange for, I guess, what we had to give up,” Minns said.

“We need toll relief now and it’s better to have it at a lower base given the multiple increases that they have through the year.”

Transurban’s chief executive, Michelle Jablko, told investors on Monday the state would have had to spend significant amounts to fund a WestConnex toll reduction.

“Even a small change in WestConnex could cost taxpayers quite a lot,” Jablko said.

Transurban data indicates the average Sydney customer spends nearly $650 a year on tolls. It costs $12.74 for a car to travel the full length of WestConnex and the motorway’s tolls increase by at least 4% each year.

Allan Fels, a former chief of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, led the state’s 2024 tolling review and called for the different roads’ tolls to be standardised so toll burdens would be balanced between Sydney’s west and its wealthier north and east. Jabklo on Monday said sweeping reforms could worsen congestion.

Fels, who was not directly involved in the government’s negotiations, said Monday’s toll reductions represented a “good start”.
 But he said Transurban had blocked reform and put profits over public interest. The company declined to comment.

“It’s essentially a financial vehicle, that receives an enormous amount of money, and that’s what it’s all about,” Fels told Guardian Australia.

“[Transurban’s demands] were excessive, completely out of the ballpark … Their whole approach to compensation ruled out some public interest reforms, including on WestConnex.”

NSW taxpayers already pay Transurban more than $100m a year to cover Labor’s cap on tolls introduced in January 2024, covering the difference for motorists spending more than $60 each week.

That figure will more than double to $211m in 2026-27 after the state budget temporarily lowered the cap to $50.

Fels said commuter anger at growing toll bills would force the state to revisit the contracts in future.

“The government deemed it was just too tough politically in the face of resistance by Transurban to deliver the whole package … [but] they hinted they might come back to this,” he said.

Jablko did not directly answer when asked on Monday whether the government had promised it would not amend the contracts in future.

“By working constructively with the government, we were able to deal into what was important to them today and protect the value of the contracts,” she said.

“What government wants to do in the future is always going to be a question for them, but it was really important for us to show up in the right way.”

title: Alan Jones argues ‘rivalry’ and ‘treachery’ but after decades wielding the sword of public opinion, he’s the one on trial
excerpt:
His legal strategy was apparent from the very first. Jones will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the ‘credibility and reliability’ of his accusers

Get our breaking news email, free app or...
body_text:
His legal strategy was apparent from the very first. Jones will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the ‘credibility and reliability’ of his accusers

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Alan Jones has enjoyed decades as the centre of attention, as the wielder of power.

The booming voice, the vast radio audience, the bully pulpit of an eponymous TV show, the great and the good on speed-dial, a staffer in the prime ministerial office dubbed the “minister for Alan Jones”: these were not ancillaries peripheral to the Jones empire, they were central to it.

Even walking into court on Monday, at the epicentre of a glacially moving press pack, it was all about Alan.

That evaporated as soon as he stepped inside the claustrophobic confines of court 3.1.

Stripped of his dominance, his control and his voice, Jones is forced instead to listen, as 22 separate allegations are detailed against him.

Jones has pleaded not guilty. He is – as he has consistently asserted – entitled to the presumption of innocence.

At first, Jones sat not in the dock but behind his lawyers, with whom he quietly conversed and occasionally showed handwritten notes, recorded with a silver pen in a black notebook.

At one point, Jones was asked to move to another seat across the courtroom.

He would have been in the eyeline of the first witness – Complainant J – and the court wanted Jones moved to a place where he could not be seen by the man who would be the first to detail his charges against him.

From his silence, Jones’s legal strategy was apparent from the very first. He will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the “credibility and reliability” of those who accuse him.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” his barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, told the court, the first thundering sentence of her opening submission.

“Rumours and innuendo have been thrown at Alan Jones for years.”

Jones’s defence would expose, the court heard, “what [the complainants] did not tell the police, what they left out of their statements … but that we have discovered: concoction, contamination and reconstruction”.

“Mr Jones since day one has said he was not guilty of all these charges,” Bashir told the court.

“Mr Jones will have the opportunity to test the evidence in the prosecution case including the credibility and the reliability of the complainants.”

This is a trial over 22 alleged indecent assault and sexual touching offences..

In opening submissions, the prosecution argued a common thread emerged, of people too afraid, too indebted, too ashamed, to speak up in their own defence.

The court heard that Jones had allegedly been financially supporting the family of Complainant A. The then-17-year-old was invited to stay at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls property. There, in a bedroom, he alleges Jones forced himself on him, kissing him and grabbing his penis.

The teenager told no one about it but 10 days later wrote, in a letter to his mother, “Someone in power did something they should not have and I was so worried because of all the help they had offered”, according to the prosecution’s opening.

Another teenager, a star schoolboy athlete from a similarly impecunious background, was given a weekly stipend by Jones, a mobile phone “to keep in contact” and later, a car. Jones allegedly grabbed him on the penis as he drove Jones to his country property, the court heard.

After an alleged incident in which Jones kissed him – un-consented, on the mouth “with a chomping motion … smothering” – Jones is alleged to have told Complainant J “you’ve been a really good boy, I’m going to give you some more money”.

Complainant C worked for Jones at a radio station, and was repeatedly groped by Jones, the court heard. The court heard that, as C drove Jones home from work, Jones would grab C on the penis, rubbing his hand up and down.

The prosecution alleged Jones would talk about C’s penis, “calling him ‘Donkey’ and saying things like ‘It’s not really that big is it?’ and ‘when can I see it?’”

The court was told the prosecution would present as evidence text messages sent by Jones to C, commenting on the “size of his penis, dismay at never having seen C’s penis” and declarations of love.

The court heard C did not invite, nor want to receive, the messages, but felt he had to reply, “concerned about his position in the media industry if he overtly rejected” Jones’s propositions.

Complainant F, who was 17 when he alleges Jones squeezed his buttocks at a public event, told his mother of the assault, but did not report it to police because he “felt nobody would believe his word over the defendant’s”.

Complainant J was the first witness to take the stand. A record-breaking junior athlete when he fell into Jones’s orbit, he is now a middle-aged man, but retains a sportsman’s build and singular focus.

Asked to relive his allegations against Jones, J repeatedly took time to compose himself, closing his eyes and asking the court for a moment while he sought to replay in his mind the specifics of incidents, some of them more than two decades old.

J told the court Jones grabbed and squeezed his penis as he drove Jones to his country property, the older man asking “does it feel good?”. In another incident at Jones’s Circular Quay apartment, J gave evidence Jones allegedly hugged him and kissed him without his consent. J’s coach was waiting downstairs in a car for him.

Prosecutor Georgina Wright asked why J didn’t tell his coach what had just happened.

“If I told someone … all of a sudden I would lose everything. I come from a small family, we struggled our whole lives, and I was getting everything handed to me, it was a wonderful life.

“I thought if I told someone what was happening, I would lose everything.”

J told the court he was conflicted by his friendship with Jones.

Jones was generous and supportive, he says, Jones had given him a financial security he’d not known in his life. But there was a price to pay, J said.

“I was fearful of him, but I was also accepting these things from him. And I didn’t want to lose those things.

“The friendship, I would say, was tainted by the things that were going on.

title: Nancy Guthrie ransom notes release follows Unabomber ‘precedent' that cracked case, expert says
excerpt: Retired FBI agent Jason Pack exposes critical errors in the Pima County Sheriff's Department's investigation into the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie. Pack highlights early mistakes, including a failur...
body_text:
Retired FBI agent Jason Pack exposes critical errors in the Pima County Sheriff's Department's investigation into the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie. Pack highlights early mistakes, including a failure to properly secure the crime scene from reporters and delivery drivers. He analyzes newly released, chilling ransom notes that suggest a deeply troubling timeline in the active kidnapping case.

A veteran retired investigator following the Nancy Guthrie case said the release of two purported ransom notes echoes the investigative strategy that helped identify the Unabomber, as authorities hope the messages will generate new tips six months after her suspected kidnapping in Tucson, Arizona.

"Law enforcement rarely makes the deliberate call to release an offender's own words to the public," said Lisa Miller, a retired investigator from the Colorado Attorney General's Office.

While she's not connected to the Guthrie investigation, she's been following it closely for the past six months.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMANDS RELEASED BY PIMA COUNTY SHERIFF'S DEPARTMENT IN BID TO IDENTIFY SENDER

Nancy Guthrie disappeared from her Tucson home in the early morning hours of Feb. 1, with investigators treating the case as an apparent abduction. (Fox Flight Team; Courtesy of NBC)

"The last major precedent: 1995, the Unabomber manifesto…published on the FBI’s recommendation, betting someone would recognize the writing," she noted in an X post over the weekend. "It worked."

David Kaczynski and his wife, Linda Patrik, recognized Ted Kaczynski's writing style and alerted authorities. Ted Kaczynski was arrested in 1996 and pleaded guilty two years later to avoid the death penalty. He spent most of his time behind bars at the ADX Florence Supermax prison in Colorado.

According to FBI records, Kaczynski sent a 35,000-word manifesto outlining his motives "and views of the ills of modern society."

NANCY GUTHRIE CASE COULD HINGE ON MYSTERY TIPSTER WHO EMAILED TMZ

Then-FBI Director Louis Freeh and then-U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno signed off on a plan to publish the document. After it ran in national news, the task force investigating that case received thousands of tips — including a note from David Kaczynski, who included other writing samples that linguistic analysts used to compare against the manifesto.

NANCY GUTHRIE SHERIFF SAYS INVESTIGATORS MAY HAVE MORE VIDEO EVIDENCE AS THEY REVIEW THOUSANDS OF CLIPS

On Friday, the Pima County Sheriff's Department released two notes that have been deemed potentially credible in the abduction of the 84-year-old mother of "Today" co-host Savannah Guthrie.

Authorities said the two notes share a "unique linguistic style" and are believed to have been sent by the same person.

Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos, left, said there is "nothing to indicate" a recent Tucson home invasion and sexual assault is connected to the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie. At right is an image released by the FBI showing a masked person seen outside Guthrie's Tucson-area home before she vanished. (Reuters ; FBI)

"There are a number of pieces of information in these notes that just might jar someone to say, 'You know, I've heard that,' or the wording, the style of the writing," Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos said in a video posted to X Saturday. "We hope that by releasing the actual note, we'll get some response from the community."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

They are much shorter than the Unabomber's lengthy essay and less useful for linguistics analysis, Miller said, but they still contain clues and consistent phrasing that could stand out to someone who knows the writer.

The clearest habit appears to be the sender's tendency to write a statement and then immediately follow it with a comma-spliced reinforcing statement, she said.

For example, she gave the following lines:

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"You will not be able to contact me from here on out, there will be no negotiation."

"We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention."

Police officers bring Theodore Kaczynski, aka the Unabomber, to court for arraignment. Kaczynski later pleaded guilty to the mail bomb attacks that killed three people and injured 23. (Ralf-Finn Hestoft/CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images       )

Miller said she doesn't believe the notes were written by artificial intelligence. The notes include "uneven grammar and syntax," emotionally charged repetitions and awkward phrasing, she said.

Authorities are looking for help identifying the masked intruder who appeared on Guthrie's Nest doorbell camera on the night of her abduction as well as the sender of the notes.

Anyone with information in the case is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI or, to remain anonymous, call 520-88-CRIME.

The sum of all rewards in the case is over $1.2 million. The money remained unclaimed as of Friday, a day before the six-month mark since Guthrie's kidnapping.

title: Sunday Times and Sun columnist Rod Liddle dies aged 66
excerpt:
Tributes paid across industry to provocative journalist who died after short illness

The writer and broadcaster Rod Liddle, a prominent columnist for the Sunday Times and the Sun, has died after a sh...
body_text:
Tributes paid across industry to provocative journalist who died after short illness

The writer and broadcaster Rod Liddle, a prominent columnist for the Sunday Times and the Sun, has died after a short illness.

Liddle, whose provocative style attracted both praise and criticism, also wrote for the Spectator magazine and earlier in his career edited BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. He was 66.

While Liddle worked as a speechwriter for the Labour party in the 1980s, his later writing often critiqued and criticised the left.

Tributes to Liddle were immediately paid by Piers Morgan, former Sunday Times editor Andrew Neil and BBC Today presenter Justin Webb, who described Liddle as brilliant, kind and funny.

David Yelland, a former editor of the Sun, said Liddle “morphed into a brilliant and gifted writer who I could rarely agree with but always turned to first”.

“It was because he was so talented he was able to behave so badly and write so (it has to said) abhorrently on many occasions,” he said. “And he knew this. It was his essence. RIP Rod.”

Liddle died at the James Cook university hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening. His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said in a statement: “We’re all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.

“He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous. Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.

“He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life.”

Liddle’s irreverent style meant he was no stranger to controversy. In 2010, he became the first blogger to be censured by the former Press Complaints Commission for incorrectly stating in a Spectator piece that the “overwhelming majority” of violent crime in London was carried out by young African-Caribbean men.

Liddle left as editor of the BBC’s Today programme, its flagship political show in 2002. At the time, it was reported that his departure followed a disagreement with the BBC’s then director general, Greg Dyke, about a regular column he wrote for the Guardian.

It followed a column in which Liddle had criticised Countryside Alliance marchers as “Mill on the Floss extras” and “those who own the countryside, or run it, together with a forelock-tugging menagerie of their better-paid servants”.

It was during his tenure at Today that Liddle hired Andrew Gilligan, the journalist whose 2003 report claimed the UK government had “sexed up” its dossier on Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction. Liddle left the BBC before Gilligan’s report was broadcast.

Liddle also presented a programme about infidelity, arguing that men were genetically pre-programmed to be unfaithful. His former wife had written about his adultery in a series of newspaper features.

Rebekah Brooks, the chief executive of News UK, which publishes the Sunday Times and the Sun, said everyone at the company had been “deeply shocked and saddened” to learn of his sudden death.

“Rod was an inimitable journalistic force, brilliant, provocative and immensely talented, whose sharp wit and uncompromising voice graced our pages and airwaves for decades,” she said. “He challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism.”

Ben Taylor, editor of the Sunday Times, said: “Rod Liddle had a wonderful way with words and used his unique talent to speak for the readers, highlighting the cant and absurdity that bedevils modern life. He was also supremely entertaining and for years his column was the first that many turned to every Sunday. We will miss him desperately.”

Victoria Newton, editor-in-chief of the Sun, said: “A champion of press freedom, no topic was off-limits, and his writing – as funny as it was excoriating – was simply exceptional. A terrific observer of the frailties of our political class, he will be remembered for his razor sharp wit and for his huge intellect.”

title: Pentagon boosts Patriot, THAAD interceptor output amid stockpile strain
excerpt: The United States Department of Defense penned a new deal with defence giants Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman in an effort to ramp up production capacity for parts used in missile defence systems...
body_text:
The United States Department of Defense penned a new deal with defence giants Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman in an effort to ramp up production capacity for parts used in missile defence systems.

The deal, which will impact the Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD missile interceptor systems, was announced on Monday.

“Building the Arsenal of Freedom requires robust, dynamic supply chains at every level of the industrial base,” said Michael P. Duffey, Undersecretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment, in a release.

The deal will triple Patriot production and quadruple THAAD system production. While the agency did not release the terms of the agreement, the US Army on Wednesday awarded Lockheed Martin a contract worth more than $58bn to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

That deal converted a previous one-year, $4.7bn contract the Pentagon issued in April into a seven-year agreement for interceptors.

Northrop Grumman announced that its share of the agreement exceeds $3bn.

“Our long-term investments in breakthrough manufacturing technologies and resilient supply chains let us pivot from steady production to a production surge in record time,” Ben Davies, corporate vice president of Northrop Grumman, said in a media release.

The company said that, because of investments made in 2021, the Falls Church, Virginia-based defence giant has nearly tripled production capacity at its Allegany Ballistics Laboratory in West Virginia, while production at its Maryland facility has increased by 25 percent.

The new deal comes as Pentagon negotiators have pushed to accelerate production agreements, as US involvement in several conflicts, including with Iran, and its continued military assistance to Ukraine, have put pressure on US stockpiles.

Ukraine, a key US ally, is running low on Patriot interceptors, the country’s only weapon capable of intercepting ballistic missiles.

On Wall Street, both companies’ stocks surged as US markets opened for the week. Northrop Grumman rose more than 1 percent in early trading, while Lockheed Martin gained 0.7 per cent.

title: Romania blasts rock to divert water from drought-hit Danube to nuclear reactor
excerpt:
Hungary and Romania face energy crisis as record-low river levels force atomic power plants to reduce output

Romanian naval forces carried out a controlled explosion to help redirect vital cooling wa...
body_text:
Hungary and Romania face energy crisis as record-low river levels force atomic power plants to reduce output

Romanian naval forces carried out a controlled explosion to help redirect vital cooling water from the drought-hit Danube to the country’s last working nuclear ⁠reactor, while neighbouring Hungary ​said it may be able to eke out two more days of power from its only atomic plant.

Hungary and Romania have been forced to shut down nuclear reactors cooled by the Danube for the first time, as record-low water levels deepen fears of an energy crisis across the region.

Romania has declared a nationwide state of emergency throughout August stemming from a decline in electricity production after record low Danube river levels led to the shutdown at the Cernavodǎ nuclear plant.

The Danube operation used 180kg of explosives, the Adevărul newspaper reported, to move a large rock restricting the flow of water in a blast that sent a tower of water ⁠into the air. The extraordinary measure underlined the scale of the crisis in Europe, where heat and drought have lowered river levels and raised concerns about water supplies, river transport and power generation.

“Any day past Wednesday or Thursday that the nuclear power plant functions is a gain,” Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruțǎ, said on Monday. “A day of it functioning is three times more efficient than the costs of this operation.”

Experts said the controlled explosion would allow authorities to build a temporary dam, diverting more water into the channel serving Cernavodǎ’s remaining reactor.

With both countries’ sole nuclear plants at reduced ⁠capacity, Hungary and Romania are increasingly relying on expensive power imports as heatwave conditions increase demand for electricity. Both countries use water ​from the Danube as coolant for their reactors.

At Paks, Hungary’s Soviet-era nuclear power station, output has been reduced. The 44-year-old plant, which normally generates almost half of the country’s electricity, is operating at less than half its capacity. Authorities ‌earlier said they might have to ‌shut Paks as early as Sunday, but later said it could operate at its reduced capacity until Monday ‌or Tuesday, offering a small reprieve for the power supply.

Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, said the plant was expected to be fully shut down next week. With the Danube forecast to remain too shallow for the reactors’ cooling systems, the closure could last for several weeks.

“An energy crisis situation could arise beginning Monday,” he posted on X. “Coordinated steps and restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences. We are counting on everyone!”

He added: “Today and maybe tomorrow the last turbine producing 240 megawatts can keep working. This is very good news, as the complete shutdown of the plant can be avoided on one of the days with the ‌highest consumption.”

Magyar earlier said voluntary ​cuts in power usage had reduced ​demand by 700MW on Sunday, significantly easing pressure on the grid.

Adding to voluntary cuts by other companies, the pharmaceuticals company Richter said on Mondayit would reduce its electricity consumption by more than 50% in the next three weeks.

In Serbia, record-low Danube levels have pushed the country’s key hydroelectric plant to operate with only 20% of its capacity, prompting the prime minister, Djuro Macut, to preside over an emergency meeting on Monday focusing on energy problems.

Water levels are not expected to rise on the Danube in the coming days or even weeks as no significant rainfall is forecast. The river passes through 10 countries. In some stretches it has fallen to levels never previously recorded. The river’s retreat has revealed rocks, shipwrecks, a second world war bomb and the remains of a woolly mammoth.

The prehistoric bones were discovered on the exposed riverbed by a resident of Ryahovo, a village in northern Bulgaria. Experts from the regional history museum in the nearby city of Ruse were sent to examine the rare find.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

title: Rhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's rivers
excerpt:
The Rhine fell to its lowest ever levels at points in Germany and the Netherlands as heatwave conditions continue

The River Rhine has fallen to record low levels in several locations in Germany and t...
body_text:
The Rhine fell to its lowest ever levels at points in Germany and the Netherlands as heatwave conditions continue

The River Rhine has fallen to record low levels in several locations in Germany and the Netherlands as prolonged heatwaves continue across Europe.

Last week, levels were measured in Cologne in western Germany and in Lobith, where the Rhine crosses from Germany into the Netherlands, that were lower than at any point since records began.

Other major European rivers with important transport, industrial and agricultural functions have also seen record low levels, including the Danube, which flows through 10 countries, and Italy's Po river.

Drought conditions remained stable and critical in most of Europe and worsened in central-western Europe in mid-July, according to the EU's Drought Observatories.

Renewed heatwave conditions are due to continue for at least another week, pushing temperatures above 40C in many central and southern European countries.

Germany's Low Water Information System (NIWIS) said that 44% of the Rhine measuring stations and 78% of those on the Danube had recorded extremely low water levels at the end of July.

The Rhine - which starts in the Swiss Alps and empties in the North Sea - is one of Europe's busiest waterways. Decreasing water levels have sparked concerns about the economic fallout of having to limit navigation and shipping.

On Friday, the navigable water depth at the chokepoint of Kaub near Koblenz hit the 2018 record low of 25cm, before recovering slightly on Monday.

The Kaub gauging station in western Germany is a key indicator of navigability on the Rhine because it measures how heavily cargo vessels can be loaded. Low water levels measured there can severely restrict inland shipping.

Martin Wolters of the Rhine Waterways and Shipping Authority told German outlet WDR that although shipping on the Rhine was unlikely to be suspended altogether, precautions would have to be taken, such as spreading out cargo among more vessels to make them less heavy.

In time, this can result in higher transport costs and supply bottlenecks, Wolters said.

"There comes a time when loads are too small to be worthwhile or vessel owners are worried about damaging their ships," one commodity trader told Reuters.

Last week, the waters of the Danube fell to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including Serbia and Romania, forcing Hungary to shut down its only nuclear power plant.

"We don't know when we will be able to restart [the plant]," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Monday. "We hope that it will happen as soon as possible and we hope that the cooling, liberating rain that the forecasters do not yet see coming will arrive."

The drought of the Danube is also causing serious disruption to power supplies in Serbia and Romania.

Serbia cut output at its coal-fired power plants due to the lack of water disrupting cooling systems, while Romania carried out a controlled explosion on a large rock on the banks of the Danube to increase waterflow to the Cernavoda nuclear power plant.

Italy's longest river, the Po, hit a historic low near the northern city of Cremona in late July. Authorities raised the drought alert level to "high" across the entire Po Valley, while experts have issued warnings about potential disruption to the drinking water supply.

Lower river flows at the mouth of the Po have also pushed saltwater from the sea into the riverbed, disrupting the ecosystem and causing serious issues for farmers who use water from the Po to irrigate their crops.

A recent study by scientists at the World Weather Attribution group found that there had been no clear long-term trend towards lower rainfall across much of Europe.

But the researchers said that human-caused climate change was increasing evaporation of moisture through higher temperatures, making drought conditions more likely.

The hot, dry weather also increased the demand for water for household, agricultural and industrial use.

Prolonged periods of drought can also affect the water levels of lakes, impacting availability of freshwater resources.

The EU's Copernicus climate service said the 2022 drought in Europe contributed to increased wildfire activity - which in drove higher than average carbon emissions.

Why temperature records are being not only broken but smashed
