If a committee is trying to hold Democrats accountable for government overreach, the networks avoid it like … a deadly bat virus. On July 25, Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul released more than 1,100 pages of COVID-19 czar Dr. Anthony Fauci's personal diary (from his government computer) spanning 2019 to 2022.

Two days later, "CBS Evening News" broke the network silence with a 24-second report. Then there was nothing for another two days until the morning Fauci was scheduled to appear before Paul’s committee.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

It's not like there was nothing newsworthy in Fauci’s diary entries. For example, he admitted early on that COVID did not emerge from the Wuhan wet markets, but he spent 2020 aggressively denouncing the lab-leak thesis as a fringy conspiracy theory – with much media amplification.

Dr. Anthony Fauci had chummy relationships with several members of the press, including CNN anchors Jake Tapper and Dana Bash, according to his newly-publicized diary entries. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images; )

Surely, the entries the networks hated the most were the references to the fawning friendships he developed with TV anchors and hosts. ABC’s George Stephanopoulos texted, "Thank you, Tony, so impressive" after one interview. He recounted a warm conversation with then-NBC anchor Chuck Todd about how to deal with the cantankerous conservative media.

In July 2020, Fauci gushed that he was forming a friendship with CNN’s Jake Tapper. "Had dinner over Jake Tapper and Jen Tapper’s home in DC. Terrific couple. Friendship building," Fauci wrote. Later that month, Fauci wrote that he "gave Jake some questions to ask" Trump adviser and pediatrician Brett Giroir during a very hostile interview on CNN’s "State of the Union."

INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

Then on Oct. 23, 2020, there was more: "Had dinner at my home with Jake and Jennifer Tapper. Relaxed, good time. Jake clearly believes that Trump is totally nuts." These dinners came at a time when this kind of socializing was strongly discouraged between family members, but clearly the elitist media and government officials were exempt from these orders.

Once the networks began covering the Fauci hearing, it became clear they were like Fauci’s unpaid defense lawyers. Before the hearing, ABC reporter Jay O’Brien fretted on "Good Morning America" that it would be a "fiery hearing" for poor Fauci at "85 years old," who "has long been a target" of Sen. Paul, noting his lawyer said Paul’s conducted a "years-long public crusade against the doctor, not a genuine quest for information." That sounds like ABC’s reporting on Trump.

"CBS Mornings" previewed the hearing with Biden transition-team adviser Dr. Celine Gounder, who bizarrely claimed Fauci never had authority to close the country down, even as Fauci bragged about all the politicians taking his advice. WATCH: FAUCI ATTORNEY EJECTED FROM SENATE HEARING AFTER CHAOTIC EXCHANGE: ‘YOU ARE NOT RECOGNIZED!’

On both NBC’s morning and evening news shows on hearing day, reporter Monica Alba actually quoted from Fauci’s writings, including the part reveling in his fame. But the networks repeatedly made it sound like Paul did something wrong or impolite in releasing Fauci’s "private diaries," which were composed on a government computer as preparation for his impending book deal.

"CBS Evening News" harped on the "angry Senate hearing" where Paul "kicked one of Fauci’s lawyers out" (for trying to answer for Fauci) while "Democrats accused the GOP of conducting a biased investigation." At least fill-in anchor Matt Gutman aired excerpts of his interview with National Institutes of Health Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, a longtime Fauci critic, who explained there was American support for "gain-of-function" research to engineer a more dangerous virus in China.

Then on Oct. 23, 2020, there was more: "Had dinner at my home with Jake and Jennifer Tapper. Relaxed, good time. Jake clearly believes that Trump is totally nuts."

On both Wednesday night and Thursday morning, ABC’s Jay O’Brien touted Fauci as "the man millions of Americans turned to for answers during the COVID pandemic." His refusal to answer was presented as merely sad: "The 85-year-old Fauci, who served in government for 54 years and has testified in more than 200 hearings, sitting stone-faced as Republicans needled him." Republicans pounced on The Science was the gist of it.

The drop-dead funniest proclamation came the next morning from ABC "Good Morning America" co-host George "so impressive, Tony" Stephanopoulos. He mourned it was "a sign of the times" that the Fauci hearing was "about as partisan as it gets." But there was somehow no partisanship during the January 6 hearings, as Stephanopoulos touted former Rep. Liz Cheney’s "lonely path" as a Republican serving Pelosi’s purposes.

So Republican hearings, when they’re actually mentioned on the news, are spun as angry partisan spectacles, but Democrat hearings are presented as the noblest expressions of democracy and accountability. This blatantly partisan spin is why public trust in the elitist media is so low.

title: Florida mail carrier accused of snatching pets on route, trapping 100-plus cats and dogs in ‘hoarding’ house
excerpt: Bodycam video shows investigators responding to a Florida home where they rescued more than 100 animals from what police said were "deplorable" conditions in a woman’s home. (Martin County Sheriff’s O...
body_text:
Bodycam video shows investigators responding to a Florida home where they rescued more than 100 animals from what police said were "deplorable" conditions in a woman’s home. (Martin County Sheriff’s Office)

The "worst animal hoarding case" a Florida sheriff has ever seen is now expanding as more animals are being recovered.

Some of the rescued animals already have been reunited with owners who said they’d given up hope of ever seeing them again.

Gail Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, was arrested July 20 after authorities found more than 100 animals held in feces-filled cages in her Stuart home. She’d been "collecting cats" she found along her mail route, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said.

Gail Giustino, 77, has been charged with one count of animal cruelty and one count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)

RIDGLAN FARMS RESCUE BEAGLES FIND NEW LIFE HELPING VETERANS OVERCOME WAR TRAUMA WITH PAWS OF WAR

With no air conditioning or ventilation, the home was "probably 110 degrees" on the late July day when the animals were removed, Budensiek said in a news conference on July 20 outside Giustino’s home.

"We were coming out here thinking maybe 15, 20, 30 cats," he told reporters, as people wearing white hazmat suits carried out cages holding dozens of cats and at least a dozen small dogs. There was "a foot of animal feces" in parts of the house, Budensiek said.

Some of the caged cats were held fast in feces that had hardened like concrete. Staffers had to smash bricks of feces from around the cats’ legs to allow them to move, Sarah Fisher, spokeswoman for the Humane Society of Treasure Coast, told Fox News Digital.

"When we cracked the door…the stench was unreal," Budensiek said. "The air was stifling hot." He went on to say, "She never walks the pets. She never brings them outside of the house. They've been confined to that animal jail really for however long she's been hoarding these pets."

Investigators recovered animals from inside the home of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)

PARTNER OF WOMAN KILLED BY DOGS RECENTLY SAVED NEIGHBOR WOUNDED IN SIMILAR ATTACK: COURT RECORDS

Investigators faced an "overwhelming" smell of "animal urine, feces, and ammonia," an odor that wafted outside the house, authorities said. The "deplorable" conditions inside the house left "no safe path of entry due to excessive debris, animal feces, and urine," investigators reported.

The odor inside the residence was so severe that it "presented a potential health hazard to responding personnel," arrest records show.

Since 2014, local animal control had issued "up to 65 civil citations" to Giustino for the conditions she’s kept animals, the sheriff said.

DOG SAVED FROM ISIS BY ARMY VETERAN 'KIDNAPPED' FROM FAMILY YARD BY LOCAL AUTHORITIES

And code enforcement officers helped her add air-conditioning units, Budensiek said. But investigators found that those units were not working. And "we haven’t been out here checking on her for the last 10 years," he said.

Giustino could have been charged with up to 160 counts of animal cruelty, Budensiek said. Instead, she was charged with one misdemeanor count of animal cruelty and one misdemeanor count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. She was released on a $50,000 bond.

"We truly believe that Gail thinks she's doing the right thing," he said. "But she's doing it the wrong way."

Investigators recovered dogs and cats from inside the house of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)

He said, "The goal of arresting her was to be able to seize the animals, to save them from death and try to get them the help that they need."

They also hoped the process would lead to mental health treatment for Giustino, he said. She did not respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.

Giustino started working for the U.S. Postal Service in 1997 and is still employed, said Debra Jean Fetterly, a USPS spokesperson for South Florida.

"We are aware of the situation," Fetterly told Fox News Digital. "The Postal Service does not publicly discuss personnel matters."

Days after the arrest, Martin County officials were able to trap and bring in three of four cats that escaped during the rescue effort at Giustino’s home.

And a friend surrendered five more small dogs Giustino allegedly left in her care, Fisher said. By July 29, the humane society had received 108 animals from Giustino’s home.

"We unfortunately are anticipating more of Gail's animals to be coming in the coming weeks" from her friends’ homes, Fisher said. "The sheriff's looking into that right now."

"We don't know really what to expect, but we're prepared."

Meanwhile, staffers have struggled emotionally, she said, because the animals "were in pretty terrible shape."

Two dogs removed from the home of Gail Giustino receive care at the Humane Society of Treasure Coast. (Courtesy of Sarah Fisher)

"They were really just shut down. Some of the cats were catatonic; they wouldn't even move. They were traumatized."

But now, they’ve started showing signs of healing.

"It's actually filling our hearts right now because they have been coming out of their shells," Fisher said. "These cats that weren’t even lifting their heads up are now meowing and seeking attention, and I think they know they're safe."

The 12 tiny dogs recovered from Giustino’s home showed signs of improvement faster, she said.

They were thin, flea-covered, missing hair because of neglect, and were suffering with dental disease, Fisher said. They range in age from 2 to 8, she said, and many appear to be Yorkshire terriers, also known as Yorkies.

"Dogs are just different," Fisher said. "They were happy as could be. They knew they were saved and they were happy. … It's really giving us hope at the shelter."

Further bolstering spirits is the enthusiastic support from locals, Fisher said.

They’ve flooded the shelter with requests to adopt the neglected animals. They’ve brought pizzas, pastries and other treats for workers.

A big part of the project involves trying to arrange for reunions with potential owners.

On Friday morning, July 24, hearts overflowed with hope outside the shelter.

Dozens of people from all walks of life queued up in the blazing Florida heat, all waiting to see if their missing pets were among those rescued.

Jisel Leon reunites with her cat, Blizzard, at the Humane Society of Treasure Coast in Palm City, Fla., on July 24, 2026. (Courtesy of Sarah Fisher)

"We had 50-plus people, very, very eager right when the doors opened at 10 o’clock," she said.

"They were very wonderful and patient. And one by one, they were all walking out crying because their animals weren't with us."

Shelter employees had hoped for joyful reunions.

"There were grown men crying; there were kids crying. It was so emotional," Fisher said. "It was really, really hard."

By the end of that Friday, two more pet owners rejoiced over their unexpected reunions.

And staffers hope there will be more in the coming days as word spreads about the recovered animals, she said.

Any of the dogs and cats not claimed eventually will be available for adoption. There’s no timeline yet for that.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"We want to make sure that any of these owned animals are going to be going home with their owners, and we're not accidentally going to be adopting them out."

Linh Nguyen called her reunion with 6-year-old Patchy a clear answer to prayer.

Linh Nguyen and Patchy walk by the water in Stuart, Fla., on July 24, 2026. (Courtesy of Linh Nguyen)

He’d disappeared from her yard in early January.

"I’d been praying for his return for seven months," Nguyen told Fox News Digital.

As she prayed, she said she told God she knew it was just "a little thing, just a cat."

But her faith told her that anything was possible.

She posted fliers offering a $5,000 reward for Patchy’s return. She rode her bike through the neighborhood late at night calling his name until she was hoarse. And she kept praying.

"If You do a miracle and bring my cat home," she pleaded in faith, "I will tell everyone it is You."

Then she saw a news report about the rescued cats. She had a strong feeling her missing pet might be among them. And when she stepped into the Humane Society, he saw her right away, she said. She heard meowing that got progressively louder.

"I couldn’t see him, but I recognized his voice."

Now, Nguyen said, Patchy is thriving at home again and is enjoying walks on a leash.

She’s relieved to know that others are being reunited with their pets, she said. And she’s glad to know that Giustino "will get the help that she needs."

"This," Nguyen said, "is a pure miracle."

title: Skin condition under the eyes goes viral as doctors warn it could signal hidden health issue
excerpt:
Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name "ferritin face."

Dark u...
body_text:
Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name "ferritin face."

Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores — a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name "ferritin face."

Experts say there's some truth behind the trend — with important caveats.

Ferritin can be thought of as the body's "iron storage vault," according to Dr. Josef Hadeed, a double board-certified plastic surgeon at Hadeed Plastic Surgery in Beverly Hills, California. It is a protein that stores iron inside the body's cells and releases it when needed.

LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW

"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," Hadeed told Fox News Digital.

Low iron levels can compromise skin elasticity, which can make the tissue appear thinner and less resilient, the doctor said.

Dark under-eye circles can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media with the name "ferritin face." (iStock)

When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable, Hadeed noted.

Besides pale skin and dark under-eye circles, other symptoms may signal that someone is lacking iron.

CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS

"The severity of these symptoms generally increases as ferritin decreases," Dane Thomas, a Texas-based hematology/oncology physician associate who specializes in the care of patients with hematologic disorders and cancer, told Fox News Digital.

Low energy, fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches, fainting, brittle or thin nails, hair loss, cravings to chew ice, and restless legs syndrome are a few signs, according to Thomas.

"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," an expert told Fox News Digital. (iStock)

"Some patients also experience decreased exercise tolerance, difficulty concentrating or shortness of breath with exertion," he said.

Other symptoms can include pounding or "whooshing" in the ears, a sore or smooth tongue, rapid heartbeat, intolerance to cold and poor sleep, according to the American Society of Hematology.

Beyond cosmetic concerns, ferritin face may signal an underlying medical condition, including chronic bleeding, gastrointestinal disorders or cancers, or malabsorption, according to hematological experts.

With the rise in bariatric surgery, more patients are developing iron deficiency due to impaired iron absorption, Thomas said. Certain over-the-counter acid-suppressing medications, including proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2-receptor blockers, may also contribute to low iron.

"This is not something that someone should self-treat."

While treating iron deficiency is important, identifying and addressing its underlying cause is equally critical, he said.

"Whenever possible, I work with my patients to determine why their iron deficiency developed so we can reduce the likelihood that it will recur," Thomas told Fox News Digital. "This often involves collaboration with gastroenterologists, gynecologists or other specialists to evaluate for sources of blood loss or malabsorption."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Pregnancy, heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent blood donation can also contribute to lower iron levels. Vegetarians, vegans and those who follow diets that do not include iron-rich foods may also be at risk, according to the American Society of Hematologists.

If a person thinks they may have low ferritin, it is important to see a physician.

"This is not something that someone should self-treat, and I always advise them to seek professional help," Hadeed advised. "Unlike water-soluble vitamins, the body has no easy mechanism to excrete excess iron, and over-supplementation can lead to increased levels of iron in the body, which can affect the liver and heart."

When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable. (iStock)

A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. Further evaluation may include stool and urine tests to look for blood, along with endoscopy to examine the esophagus, stomach and colon. Women may also undergo a gynecological evaluation, according to experts.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Treatment for iron deficiency may include oral supplementation and, in cases of severe anemia, intravenous (IV) iron or blood transfusions.

"The biggest drawback of oral iron is gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and stomach upset," Thomas noted.

"These side effects can often be minimized by taking iron every other day rather than daily, a strategy that also maintains excellent absorption for many patients."

He also recommends spacing them apart from calcium supplements, dairy products and antacids, which can affect absorption.

A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. (iStock)

Following a diet that includes iron-rich foods can also help, according to the American Society of Hematology website.

Some examples include beef, pork, or lamb; organ meats like liver, chicken, turkey, duck and fish (especially shellfish, sardines and anchovies); leafy greens, such as broccoli, kale, turnip greens and collard greens; legumes, including lima beans, peas, pinto beans and black-eyed peas; and iron-enriched pastas, grains, rice and cereals.

Ferritin face is reversible, Hadeed emphasized.

Once iron stores are safely restored and hemoglobin levels rebound, the skin recovers its healthy capillary flush, and dark under-eye circles tend to fade over several months.

Amy McGorry is a contributing health writer for Fox News Digital. Follow her on Twitter @amymcgorry.

title: Spain says migrants leaving Ceuta after mass influx in which 67 died
excerpt:
Spain says “virtually all” of the estimated 60,000 migrants who stormed its North African enclave of Ceuta by land and sea in recent days have already left again voluntarily.

The number of people who...
body_text:
Spain says “virtually all” of the estimated 60,000 migrants who stormed its North African enclave of Ceuta by land and sea in recent days have already left again voluntarily.

The number of people who had died trying to enter Ceuta was raised to at least 67 on Saturday, Spanish officials said, adding there could be additional casualties on the Moroccan side of the border. Some of the confirmed dead had drowned, and ⁠some were crushed while trying to climb the breakwater that holds the border fence.

“Virtually all those who entered Ceuta have now returned to Morocco,” Spain’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Jose Manuel Albares, wrote on X on Friday night.

The mass influx of migrants had dismayed European Union governments, and particularly those in the Schengen area – 29 countries that have abolished border controls for travel between them.

European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen on Friday described the images from Ceuta as “unacceptable”, while French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said France would tighten its borders with Spain.

In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni threatened to suspend Italy’s open-border Schengen agreement with Spain “to defend our borders and ensure the safety of our citizens”, though Italy does not share a border with Spain.

Spain’s Interior Ministry said about 50,000 people had crossed the border since Thursday morning, and estimated that 48,300 had returned by 6pm (16:00 GMT) on Friday. Juan Jesus Vivas, head of Ceuta’s local government, said as many as 60,000 people had pushed across over the past couple of days.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who travelled to Ceuta on Friday, said the mass crossing represented “a violation of Spain’s territorial sovereignty”.

Spain announced it was installing a containment barrier along the breakwater fence into the sea.

Moroccan police in riot gear used tear gas and water cannon trucks at the enclave’s border on Friday night to disperse people gathered near the fences and push them back.

“Honestly, I don’t even know why I came, and now I’m going back,” a young Moroccan man, who said he was from Tangier, told Reuters. “I haven’t eaten since lunch yesterday, even though I brought some money with me … What we’re doing is neither good nor enjoyable.”

Ceuta, together with Melilla – another autonomous ‌Spanish city in North Africa – represents the European Union’s only land border with Africa. Both cities often experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to migrate to Europe.

To reach Ceuta, migrants often swim from the Moroccan town of Fnideq, covering about 5km (3 miles) to reach Spanish territory. Others attempt the crossing from the nearby town of Belyounech, where the distance is shorter.

Ceuta authorities linked the surge in attempted crossings to a Spanish Supreme Court ruling earlier this month that prevented authorities from immediately returning migrants who arrive by sea. The ruling does not apply to migrants who enter Spain by land, including by climbing over the border fence.

Sanchez said on Friday that the influx of migrants was caused by mafias spreading rumours about this court ruling. But activists in Morocco expressed doubt that the ruling was behind the surge, arguing most migrants would have been unaware of such legal decisions.

Although the crossing appeared blocked later on Friday, many migrants still moved along the coast, seeking routes around the fence.

“I was late,” said Brahim, 32, who had arrived from Tangier hoping to cross through the gate, but found it effectively shut.

title: Iran warns against ‘flames of war’ amid US strike threats on energy sites
excerpt: Tehran, Iran – Iran’s authorities have promised retaliation in case of threatened attacks by the United States against critical energy infrastructure, while military strikes continue across the region...
body_text:
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s authorities have promised retaliation in case of threatened attacks by the United States against critical energy infrastructure, while military strikes continue across the region.

“The United States is moving at an accelerating pace to fan the flames of a full-scale regional war,” Major General Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran’s wartime military command, said in a statement on Saturday.

Addressing regional neighbours, he said the US was using their capital, resources and infrastructure as a shield for its own interests while strengthening Israel’s war machine.

“It is hereby stated explicitly: Muslim countries must, with foresight, monitor America’s crimes and reconsider their cooperation and alignment with the US. Otherwise, any country that makes itself a defensive shield for criminal, aggressor America will burn in the fire of war,” said Abdollahi.

The warning comes in reaction to reports by major US media outlets that the US and Israel may be imminently launching an extensive wave of attacks against Iran’s civilian infrastructure, including power plants and petrochemical manufacturers.

President Donald Trump has yet to give final authorisation on an operation that could potentially last up to two weeks and aim to cut electricity across Iran’s capital, Tehran, and create disruptions across the country, the reports said, citing unnamed sources.

The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies said earlier this week that US air defences have performed largely well, but persistent combat operations have reduced the inventory of missile interceptors in the US military’s arsenal, with Patriot inventories now under 1,000 and THAAD at about 250.

The Iranian state-linked Tasnim news website on Saturday cited an unnamed source as saying armed forces have prepared an extensive plan of retaliation to the “potential madness” of the US by hitting “vital infrastructure” linked with the US and Israel.

On Tuesday, Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz said “we very much want to strike Iran’s energy targets.

“The United States is not approving it at present, because of concern that Iran would strike neighbouring countries and there would be a global oil crisis,” he told a security conference broadcast by Channel 14, adding that Israel was ready to “set Iran back 40 years”.

Since the start of the war on February 28, the US and Israel have hit military bases and leaders across Iran, but also targeted the country’s civilian infrastructure, parts of which will require years and extensive investments to rebuild. The bombing has only exacerbated Iran’s internal woes, including a contracting economy and a major energy imbalance that are squeezing more than 90 million Iranians.

In response, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Iran’s regular army have launched ballistic missiles and drones at US and Israeli military bases across the region, but have also responded to energy attacks by striking energy infrastructure in Israel, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman.

Amid the threats of escalation, strikes have intensified across the region in recent days.

The US military attacked at least five Iranian provinces overnight into Thursday, saying the targets were IRGC command centres, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and air-defence sites, and maritime capabilities. Several soldiers and multiple civilians were among the casualties, including a two-year-old boy who was killed when his home was hit in the southern island of Qeshm.

On Saturday, Kuwait’s army said its air defences destroyed multiple Iranian drones within the country’s airspace, with some damage reported to government facilities and civilian vehicles.

At least two vessels were hit off the coast of Oman, with one suffering damage to its engine room, according to Western maritime authorities.

Iranian state media on Saturday broadcast footage from proximity to the missile-struck ship, warning others that this was “the smoke of mistakenly trusting the US” promises of safe passage through the southern corridor of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran also said four other ships were turned back, as the waterway remains closed to traffic not approved by the IRGC.

In Iraq, sporadic drone attacks have targeted Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, which have raised the idea of entering the conflict to topple the Islamic Republic in Iran. Two Kurdish armed groups separately claimed they were targeted on Friday. Pro-Iran media in Iraq on Saturday released footage purporting to show a refinery in Iraqi Kurdistan’s Erbil on fire after being targeted by an unnamed actor.

The latest attacks in Iraq come days after the US and Saudi Arabia jointly attacked bases belonging to Iraqi armed forces who are aligned with Tehran, killing at least 20 fighters and multiple IRGC advisers.

Those attacks came in response to attacks on Saudi energy facilities and disruptions created in the Bab al-Mandeb and the Red Sea by the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen. Riyadh is attempting to form an international coalition to counter disruptions in the Red Sea, which links with the Suez Canal.

In southern Lebanon, the Israeli army continues to occupy large areas of land, destroying villages and infrastructure, while also detonating structures purportedly belonging to Iran-backed Hezbollah.

Iran has emphasised that it does not intend to let go of the Strait of Hormuz as strategic leverage in dealing with the US offensive.

Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, said in a brief message on Saturday that continued military strikes and a naval blockade by the US only deteriorate the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and other waterways.

“The global economy, and US energy market and voters will pay the price,” he said.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs says it has not sent any requests for negotiations to Washington amid the latest attacks, but messages have been relayed through mediators, and discussions are ongoing over how to handle an eventual reopening of the strait.

Speaking on Saturday, Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf again appeared to signal a need to reach a negotiated resolution that would formalise perceived gains from military action.

“We have been victorious. But the victories of this war must be solidified, we must be able to register this victory,” he said during a meeting with hardline lawmakers, adding that the country needs to have hope for a clear future.

Ghalibaf said authorities must aim to give the office of the supreme leader in Iran greater latitude in making decisions about the future, but did not elaborate.

In Tehran on Saturday, the first day of the week in Iran, the public message being broadcast by the authorities was still one of vengeance for Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on the first day of the US-Israel war on Iran, along with dozens of other officials.

A huge banner in central Tehran’s Valiasr Square depicted a boy with a red headband carrying a flag of blood revenge.

“Trump, his advisers and allies are frustrated by Iran’s steadfastness,” read the headline from Keyhan, a hardline daily newspaper.

title: Democrats’ ‘climate hushing’ prompts activists to turn up the volume
excerpt:
Nationwide actions seek to counter view that talking about climate crisis distracts from affordability messaging

This summer, torrential rains have washed away Texas neighborhoods, dangerous heat has...
body_text:
Nationwide actions seek to counter view that talking about climate crisis distracts from affordability messaging

This summer, torrential rains have washed away Texas neighborhoods, dangerous heat has blanketed swaths of the country, and smoke from Canadian wildfires has choked communities as far south as Florida.

Research makes clear that global warming is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe. Yet the climate crisis has largely disappeared from the political agenda, with many Democrats who once described it as an existential threat now shying away from talking about it.

Now US activists are pushing back against this trend of “climate hushing”, arguing it is misguided. During the summer’s federal recess, during which lawmakers leave the nation’s capital to work directly within their home states or districts, demonstrators organized by the environmental advocacy coalition Climate Action Campaign are calling on representatives to put climate back on the political agenda.

“The long history of the climate movement proves that we move fastest when there’s real pressure from the grassroots,” said Bill McKibben, the environmental author and activist who co-founded climate non-profit 350.org, “All the evidence shows those grassroots are as worried about [the] climate crisis as they ever were.”

The events, set to take place over the next month in at least 20 states during the House and Senate recess periods, will mobilize members of groups including local Sierra Club chapters, the senior citizen-led climate organization Third Act, which McKibben founded, and local affiliates of the racial justice group the NAACP.

“It’s the broadest brush that we are working with,” said Margie Alt, director of the Climate Action Campaign. “The message is, talk about climate, climate can’t wait, and we want to see action.”

Actions began on Thursday and will take a variety of forms. In Michigan, participants will demonstrate against the Republican representative Bill Huizenga who voted for Trump’s so-called big beautiful bill, which boosted planet-heating fossil fuels.

In Arizona, young activists will meet with the Democratic representative Adelita Shirley Grijalva, a climate champion, and encourage her to continue talking about global warming. In other districts, organizers have circulated petitions calling on the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, to prioritize climate issues or plan to call on their representatives to connect the climate crisis to recent heatwaves.

The activists’ campaign comes as new polling challenges the need for “climate hushing”, a trend that took off as some policy wonks argued that talking about global warming could alienate voters and distract from the message of affordability. July research from the University of California, Santa Barbara found that emphasizing climate change was neutral to beneficial for Democratic candidates, suggesting that talking more about the issue does not alienate voters and can even increase support in competitive races.

Though the Trump administration frequently derides climate policy as a “scam” and a “hoax”, polling indicates most Americans are not onboard with that view. Another July poll from Data for Progress found that 61% of likely voters believe extreme weather has become more frequent over the past five years, including nearly half of Republicans. And one month earlier, a Yale survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming.

“Smart politicians will grab on this issue,” said McKibben. “There’s perhaps no other question where the gulf between Maga and the general public is higher.”

Alt said she saw climate-hushing as “the climate denial of 2026”.

“I don’t think that ignoring the climate crisis is smart politics,” she said. “I think that it is dropping the ball on the biggest threat the US and the world faces.”

title: Purple reign: how shade became British gardeners’ favourite
excerpt:
Britons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choice

If you manage to spot a garden in bloom this summer, beyond the strips of bleached a...
body_text:
Britons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choice

If you manage to spot a garden in bloom this summer, beyond the strips of bleached and torched grass, there may be one colour you see more than any other: purple, the horticultural hue of the season.

Plants such as lavender, salvias and catmint are in vogue, according to the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS), which conducted extensive research into the colours Britons best love to see in their gardens.

In one experiment at RHS Garden Wisley’s Hilltop, more than 11,000 visitors were asked to choose their preferred shades. Purple flower hues accounted for the strongest preference (26.67%), closely followed by red (25.24%).

The purple patch has surprised garden trend watchers and marks a departure from recent less dramatic trends. Grey hues have been very popular in home and garden design over the last few years.

Tom Massey, an award-winning garden designer based in London, said clients wanted bright colours, particularly purples. He said: “We’ve moved away from the era of large expanses of decking, paving and lawn towards richer, more naturalistic planting inspired by meadows and natural plant communities.”

Laura Carey, who co-owns Carey garden designs with her husband, Joe, has found that purple is the most popular colour with her clients, too. She said: “Purple is a favourite across the board with all of our clients. There are so many purple flowering plants to choose from, including national favourites like lavender, alliums and geraniums.”

Massey added: “Purple has always been a hugely important colour in gardens because it combines beautifully with greens, silvers and the buff tones of ornamental grasses. It also attracts pollinators and tends to have a calming quality. Plants like salvias, nepetas, alliums and lavender remain incredibly popular for exactly those reasons.”

The popularity of the colour may be related to the emotions it evokes in humans. Other research found that purples and blues evoke a sense of calm and relaxation, and yellows and oranges bring joy.

Massey said: “I think people are becoming much more confident with colour generally. You can see this in high-profile public landscapes that have proved hugely popular, such as Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in London, parts of the High Line in New York, and the seasonal displays and borders at RHS gardens like Wisley, where bold combinations of colour are used to create planting schemes that are both beautiful and ecologically rich.”

The findings were published in the study Flower Power: How favourite flower colours shape how we feel in Acta Psychologica.

Dr Ashby Sachs, a wellbeing fellow at the RHS, said: “Colour is a key consideration when it comes to garden design, but little is known about how it interacts with our sense of wellbeing. That different shades of colour can elicit an anticipated emotional response in people is incredibly useful when it comes to designing spaces for specific purposes and people such as in schools and hospitals.”

title: The dinner candle you're actually supposed to eat as restaurants chase memorable experiences
excerpt:
South Florida entrepreneur Claudia Mosley says her edible melting candles are made in savory and sweet varieties, with plans to bring the interactive concept from the home to restaurant dining rooms.
...
body_text:
South Florida entrepreneur Claudia Mosley says her edible melting candles are made in savory and sweet varieties, with plans to bring the interactive concept from the home to restaurant dining rooms.

A South Florida entrepreneur believes the next big innovation in entertaining isn't another kitchen gadget or smartphone app. It's a candle you can eat.

Claudia Mosley, founder of CeraViva, has created handcrafted edible candles that melt into warm dipping sauces and dessert spreads, transforming an ordinary meal into what she calls "an experience."

"The product is not really the candle," Mosley told Fox News Digital. "The candle is the vehicle. The product is the experience that you're giving your guests."

CHEF WHO FLED COMMUNIST COUNTRY OPENS WORLD'S FIRST MICHELIN-STARRED CUBAN RESTAURANT

Made with organic and premium ingredients, the candles are designed to pair with bread, vegetables, seafood, meats or desserts, Mosley said.

Savory flavors include chimichurri, shrimp scampi and parmesan cream, while sweet varieties include raspberry cream, apple pie and a new Key lime pie flavor.

Claudia Mosley is the founder of CeraVida edible candles. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

Mosley said her sweet candles contain no added sugar.

AMERICA'S MOST-SEARCHED ICE CREAM BRAND MAY SURPRISE YOU — AND THERE'S A HEALTHY REASON WHY

"They're sweet, but they're not super sweet," she said. "They have the perfect balance."

Each candle is crafted to encourage people to put away their phones and spend time connecting around the dinner table, Mosley said.

CeraVida edible melting candles come in a variety of flavors, both sweet and savory. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

The business represents more than culinary creativity for Mosley. Born in Colombia, the 50-year-old mother of four immigrated to the United States as a teenager and built a successful merchant services company with her identical twin sister before launching CeraViva.

Mosley said she's been living the "true American dream."

That entrepreneurial mindset has shaped every step of the venture. Mosley said she has invested more than $20,000 to launch the business, obtaining the necessary state licenses, moving production into a commercial kitchen and developing a patented formula designed to withstand shipping and refrigeration.

A CeraVida raspberry-flavored edible candle melts on top of vanilla ice cream in a martini glass. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

Consumers can purchase the candles directly from CeraViva's website for $38, but Mosley said her bigger goal is getting them onto restaurant tables.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Every restaurant is looking for an experience," she said.

Mosley told Fox News Digital she hopes her candles create a restaurant experience, encouraging more conversations at the dinner table. (Peter Burke/Fox News Digital)

Diners would order the edible candle as an appetizer before their meal, giving it 20 to 25 minutes to melt into a warm dipping sauce while they talk, she said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Mosley's edible candles are meant to create conversation, encourage families to unplug and give restaurants a memorable experience customers can't get at home.

Whether the edible candle becomes the next viral dining trend remains to be seen, but Mosley is betting the simple act of lighting a flame can help rekindle something she believes many families have lost — meaningful time together.

Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

title: Unearthed posts show Heartland Dem candidate rallying in favor of child gender surgery: 'Radical as it gets'
excerpt:
Lawmakers hear from witnesses as the committee examines standards of care, medical practices, and the broader debate surrounding gender transition procedures for minors.

FIRST ON FOX: Nebraska Democr...
body_text:
Lawmakers hear from witnesses as the committee examines standards of care, medical practices, and the broader debate surrounding gender transition procedures for minors.

FIRST ON FOX: Nebraska Democratic congressional nominee Denise Powell publicly opposed Nebraska's 2023 law restricting gender transition procedures for minors, calling it "discriminatory and hateful" and urging supporters to contact lawmakers, according to unearthed social media posts that are generating pushback from critics.

Before becoming her party's nominee, Powell made multiple Facebook and TikTok posts opposing LB 574, Nebraska's "Let Them Grow Act," which prohibits gender transition procedures for minors and regulates the use of puberty blockers and hormone treatments for those under 19.

In a March 2023 Facebook post, Powell, listed as an administrator on The Bellwether Initiative Nebraska page, urged Nebraskans to contact their state senators and join her at the Capitol on the final day of the first round of floor debate over the bill while wearing a shirt that read "PROTECT TRANS KIDS."

"Today is the final day of the first round of floor debate on LB 574, a bill that would prohibit and punish healthcare providers from providing gender affirming care to children under the age of 19," she wrote.

WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN

Denise Powell, Democratic candidate for Nebraska's second congressional district, speaks during a campaign event at Metro Community College's Center for Advanced Manufacturing in Omaha, Neb., on Tuesday, July 14, 2026. Powell was joined by former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. (Nikos Frazier/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images)

"Laws like this one are passing all over the country — Iowa, Kentucky, Tennessee, to name a few. Nebraska has the opportunity to set an example; to show trans kids and families around the country that we won't stand for this discriminatory and hateful behavior."

Powell also praised lawmakers "fighting this on the front line" and urged supporters to "call or tweet at your senators TODAY."

"Trans people belong in Nebraska and everywhere and we will never ever stop fighting for their right to exist and thrive," she wrote.

SEN HAWLEY WARNS IT WOULD BE 'UNCONSCIONABLE' IF BILLIONS OF TAXPAYER FUNDS FLOW TO TRANS KIDS’ SEX CHANGES

People gather in Union Square for the Together We Win rally in support of transgender youth held in New York City, N.Y., on Jan. 10, 2026. (Jason Alpert-Wisnia / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)

Powell also took to TikTok under the username "dbpinomaha" to oppose the legislation.

In a video posted Feb. 8, 2023, Powell wrote, "Aaaaand we're back, this time to oppose LB 574, a bill that would make it illegal for kids to access gender-affirming care," before the video showed her sipping from a mug beneath the words, "Lord it's too early for the garbage."

The video then showed a photo of the Nebraska State Capitol exterior with the words, "Democracy happens here. Sometimes," before cutting to footage of protesters holding signs reading, "Trans Nebraskans Belong."

The video also included photos appearing to show Powell in her car holding one of the protest signs herself.

DEMOCRATS STAY QUIET ON NEXT STEPS AFTER SUPREME COURT TRANSGENDER SPORTS RULING

Denise Powell, candidate for the Democratic nomination to the House of Representatives in Nebraska's second district, right, hugs Jennifer Reyna, chair of Latino Caucus for the Democratic Party of Nebraska, during an election night watch party Wednesday, May 13, 2026, in Omaha, Neb. (Rebecca S. Gratz/AP Photo)

"LB 574 hurt kids," she wrote in the caption. "Call your senator and tell them TRANS NEBRASKANS BELONG."

In a separate TikTok posted on March 31, 2023, Powell shared a video of student walkouts at high schools around Omaha and Lincoln, writing that students had walked out in support of transgender youth and adding, "we are here for it!"

The Nebraska Legislature passed LB 574 by a 33-15 vote, and Gov. Jim Pillen later signed it into law.

That same year, Nebraska First PAC poll found that 61% of likely Nebraska voters supported prohibiting "gender altering procedures like surgeries, puberty blockers, or hormone therapies" for those under 19, while 78% agreed children should wait until adulthood before undergoing "irreversible, sex-change surgeries."

In April, a bill from Republican state Sen. Kathleen Kauth to expand LB 574 by banning puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for those under 19 failed to advance, according to the Nebraska Examiner .

"NE-2 is a swing district known for electing moderates, but Denise Powell is about as radical as it gets," Jon Schweppe, former Trump official at the FTC and senior advisor at American Principles Project, told Fox News Digital.

"Not only has she been an advocate for transgender sex changes for kids, but she served on the board of an organization which opposes parental rights in education and promotes an 'LGBTQ liberation' curriculum for fifth graders. These are the issues she clearly cares about the most."

Zach Bannon, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) told Fox News Digital that Powell is a "rubber stamp for the radical far-left, supporting their most extreme policies, including sex change surgeries for kids."

"Denise Powell continues to prove that she rejects common sense and is completely out of touch with Nebraska values," Bannon added.

Powell is challenging Republican Omaha City Councilman Brinker Harding for Nebraska's open 2nd Congressional District, a seat Democrats are seeking to flip as Republicans try to hold on to their razor-thin majority in the House of Representatives.

According to her campaign website, Powell says her priorities are lowering costs, protecting healthcare access and abortion rights, supporting workers, and opposing President Donald Trump's "abuse of power and attacks on our democracy."

Fox News Digital reached out to Powell's campaign multiple times for comment.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Democratic Socialists awarded $5.2M in inheritance dispute despite family's objections
excerpt: Alexandria Hoff reports on the escalating threat of socialism as big-name donors increasingly back Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates. Author Evan Barker, in her book "Nothing Left," re...
body_text:
Alexandria Hoff reports on the escalating threat of socialism as big-name donors increasingly back Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates. Author Evan Barker, in her book "Nothing Left," reveals how wealthy contributors disguise themselves as "grassroots" supporters through DSA backing, utilizing unpaid labor to save millions. The DSA now boasts over 120,000 members.

The Democratic Socialists of America just won $5.2 million in an inheritance dispute, according to a new legal filing, handing the organization a major financial boost as it seeks to expand its influence within the Democratic Party.

The $5.2 million award is serious money for the Democratic Socialists of America, amounting to nearly an entire year of revenue for the organization, according to its tax filings.

For a little over a year, the Democratic Socialists of America had been embroiled in a legal dispute over the will of New York University professor David Greenberg, who died in July 2024. Greenberg stipulated in his will that the contents of his New York University retirement account should be transferred to the New American Movement, a now-defunct left-wing activist group, or "any successor thereof" upon his death.

The New American Movement merged with the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee to form the Democratic Socialists of America in 1982, according to contemporary coverage in left-wing media outlets. Greenberg, a sociology professor, spent much of his life involved with left-wing movements, with his NYU obituary describing him as "a prominent figure in America's radical criminology movement."

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

The Democratic Socialists of America just won $5.2 million in an inheritance dispute, according to a new legal filing.  (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Martin Hecht, Greenberg's nephew, contended that the Democratic Socialists of America failed to file the proper paperwork to be considered the legal successor and that New York University failed to fulfill its fiduciary duty to Greenberg by not making sure his will accurately reflected his wishes before his death.

The judge presiding over the case ultimately sided with the Democratic Socialists of America, handing it the multimillion-dollar sum. Hecht initiated his lawsuit in April 2025 and the case was ultimately decided Monday.

The $5.2 million constituted the majority of Greenberg's wealth, with a separate account worth $1.3 million being transferred to his estate without dispute, per a legal filing.

FAR-LEFT SURGE: MAMDANI-BACKED CANDIDATES OUST DEM ESTABLISHMENT INCUMBENTS

On Inauguration Day on Jan. 20, 2025, Democratic Socialists of America members marched in Washington, D.C., carrying signs that said, "SOCIALISM BEATS FASCISM," equating the incoming Trump administration to "fascism."  (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

This cash comes at an opportune time for the organization.

Candidates affiliated with or backed by the Democratic Socialists of America have enjoyed a string of victories in recent months, beginning with Zohran Mamdani’s election as New York City mayor in 2025 and continuing with 2026 primary wins by candidates such as Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, who bested establishment-backed opponents in New York’s congressional primaries.

Socialist candidates have also won primary races in Philadelphia, the District of Columbia and Colorado.

REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER FAR-LEFT GROUP'S PUSH TO TRANSFORM AMERICA INTO 'CUBAN DICTATORSHIP'

Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside of a Trump owned building during a May Day rally in New York City in 2019. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

The victories, several of which came against Democratic incumbents, have expanded the Democratic Socialists of America's foothold in government and given the group greater influence over the party, particularly in heavily Democratic urban districts.

What the Democratic Socialists of America ultimately will use its newfound wealth to do has not been disclosed, but its past spending behavior may provide some clues.

The organization, for instance, regularly spends big on advertisements meant to convince people to vote for Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates. In an August 2024 blog post, one New York Democratic Socialists of America member floated paying for advertisements to support the organization’s recruitment efforts.

Tax documents filed by the Democratic Socialists of America in November 2025 show that the organization distributes cash to its local chapters and aligned groups while also spending big on community mobilization and messaging campaigns.

These efforts appear to have borne some fruit. In early July, the Democratic Socialists of America announced that it had grown to 120,000 members, claiming that it had become the "largest socialist organization in United States history."

The Democratic Socialists of America and Hecht's attorneys did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital.

title: Marilyn Monroe role leaves actresses 'set up to fail': experts
excerpt:
Melissa Stevens, granddaughter of late photographer Sam Shaw, discusses the new book, "Dear Marilyn: The Unseen Letters and Photographs."

Dakota Johnson's reported turn as Marilyn Monroe is already r...
body_text:
Melissa Stevens, granddaughter of late photographer Sam Shaw, discusses the new book, "Dear Marilyn: The Unseen Letters and Photographs."

Dakota Johnson's reported turn as Marilyn Monroe is already reigniting a familiar Hollywood debate: Can anyone successfully step into the shoes of one of the world's most enduring cultural icons?

Instead of a traditional biopic, Maggie Gyllenhaal's "Flesh Impact" imagines Monroe beyond the platinum hair and red lipstick, exploring the woman behind one of pop culture's most enduring personas.

Branding experts say the reaction is part of a decades-long pattern. Every generation produces another actress willing to portray Monroe, but few escape comparisons to the Hollywood icon, whose glamour, mystique and tragic legacy have made her one of the entertainment industry's most untouchable figures. The fresh premise did little to quiet critics online, many of whom argued Hollywood should stop revisiting Monroe altogether.

"i think we have enough movies about her," a social media user wrote online as a first look of Johnson was shared.

DAKOTA JOHNSON STUNS AS MARILYN MONROE IN FIRST LOOK AFTER DIRECTOR DOUBTED CASTING

More than six decades after her death, Marilyn Monroe remains one of Hollywood's most enduring cultural icons, with experts saying the actress's legacy makes her one of the industry's most difficult figures to portray. (Baron/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

"Please leave Marilyn alone," another added. "Let her rest in peace."

"How many f---ing times y'all gonna reheat the Marilyn Monroe nachos supreme?" one user questioned.

The backlash doesn't come as a surprise to branding experts, who say Monroe occupies a rare place in American pop culture that makes her one of Hollywood's most difficult figures to portray. Decades after her death, they argue, audiences still feel a personal connection to the screen legend.

"Marilyn Monroe is this irreplaceable icon that embodied glamor, mystique and tragedy. We all feel like we know Marilyn Monroe and any actress that portrays her almost seems like an imposter," strategic communications expert Kelcey Kintner explained to Fox News Digital. "So it's almost as if these actresses are set up to fail, even thought it's an incredibly dynamic person to play."

Dakota Johnson's reported casting as Marilyn Monroe in the upcoming film "Flesh Impact" has sparked debate online, with some fans questioning whether Hollywood should revisit the late screen legend. (Courtesy of Genesis)

One expert likened modern Monroe portrayals to an overcomplicated twist on a classic.

"Ever go to a restaurant and hear the server say ’this is the chef’s take on a cheeseburger’ but you don’t want an interpretation, you just want a cheeseburger?" branding expert Doug Eldridge told Fox News Digital.

"It’s Res Ipsa Loquitur. ‘The thing speaks for itself,’" he explained. "The same holds true for other iconic staples, such as Marilyn Monroe: often imitated, never duplicated."

MARILYN MONROE'S ICONIC SUBWAY GRATE PHOTO HAS SURPRISING WWII ROOTS AND HIDDEN HISTORY

Dakota Johnson will play Marilyn Monroe at age 36 in "Flesh Impact." (Matt Winkelmeyer/GA/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)

Hollywood's continued fascination with Monroe is symptomatic of a much larger problem: an industry increasingly driven by reboots, remakes and familiar intellectual property rather than original storytelling.

"Paradoxically, Hollywood is often thought to be the home of ‘creativity’ yet much of the content being produced these days, hinges on reboots and extensions of past successes," Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, said. "How deep are we in the comic book catalog at this point – producers are chasing that lightning in the bottle moment, but it comes with fatigue; it starts with sagging box office numbers, but eventually, it ends when viewers become ambivalent and ratings head off a cliff."

"Creating something fresh and truly unique is an incredibly difficult endeavor, but rehashing the same narrative and storyline also comes at a price."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Marilyn Monroe's glamour, mystique and enduring cultural legacy continue to inspire new film projects, even as each portrayal draws intense scrutiny from fans and critics alike. (M. Garrett/Murray Garrett/Getty Images)

Hollywood's repeated return to Monroe is no accident. The continued fascination with Monroe reflects a broader yearning for the glamour and larger-than-life movie stars of cinema's Golden Age.

"In our age of AI and technology, it draws back to a simpler time when Hollywood icons could command so much singular attention," Kintner, Senior VP at Red Banyan PR, explained. "However, I think an artist can find a new way of approaching a much covered topic or person that brings fresh insights and makes an impact."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Despite Monroe's enduring appeal, one question continues to shadow every new project: Can anyone truly play the Hollywood legend?

"Maybe not, because at the end of the day, they aren't Marilyn and can't be, no matter their talent," Kintner mused.

"There is a longing when a celebrity has died way too young to recreate them in some way," she added. "But it always falls short because the true individual who captured the attention of the world – has been lost."

One branding expert chose Sydney Sweeney as an actress that could portray Marilyn Monroe. (Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for Lionsgate)

If anyone could do it, Eldridge picked this generation's blonde bombshell – Sydney Sweeney.

"She would be impervious to the criticism and her gargantuan audience would translate to a box office bonanza," he explained. "It might not be critically received, but it would be a commercial juggernaut. Not only is she the logical choice – she’s arguably the only choice."

title: Election security at center of California Republicans' push to win over fed-up voters
excerpt: California GOP Chair Corrin Rankin tells Fox News Digital Democrats have embraced the "extremism of socialism," blaming Gov. Gavin Newsom for California's affordability crisis as Republicans push vote...
body_text:
California GOP Chair Corrin Rankin tells Fox News Digital Democrats have embraced the "extremism of socialism," blaming Gov. Gavin Newsom for California's affordability crisis as Republicans push voter ID and seek to flip the governor's mansion.

Republicans in California are making a voter ID ballot initiative the centerpiece of their 2026 strategy as Americans' frustration grows over affordability and education issues.

"Californians need to feel secure in our elections," California GOP Chairwoman Corrin Rankin told Fox News Digital in an interview. "The way it is now, there's so much room for uncertainty and confusion. What Proposition 39 is going to do is it's going to sort of close the loopholes. It's a commonsense solution that will strengthen our democracy."

Beyond the ballot measure, Rankin argues the initiative reflects broader voter frustration that Republicans hope to capitalize on in the 2026 midterms. She claims California voters are primarily concerned about affordability, education and confidence in state government.

SEN MARK WARNER CALLED OUT IN ABC INTERVIEW FOR INACCURATE VOTER ID CLAIMS

California Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, who is term-limited, spoke this week in California. (Reuters)

"Californians need to feel like we can trust our election systems, and trust is not given. Trust is earned and this will allow Californians to feel more like they can trust our election system," she added.

The Golden State’s primary race on June 2 garnered national attention and widespread criticism after it took weeks to deliver results. California election officials continued to count ballots postmarked by Election Day even if they arrived within seven days — and they are permitted up to 30 days to certify results.

In the primaries, the Los Angeles mayoral race became the center of controversy as President Donald Trump was among the chorus of voices challenging the runoff election results, alleging irregularities as the count continued past Election Day.

Spencer Pratt ultimately lost the race with far-left City Council Member Nithya Raman advancing to face incumbent Democrat Mayor Karen Bass in the general election in November. The race was called six days after the June 2 elections.

"There's so many other states throughout our country and throughout the world actually that seem to be able to have a winner on election night," said Rankin. "It'd be wonderful if California could do the same."

CALIFORNIA’S SLUGGISH VOTE COUNTING RIPPED ACROSS THE POLITICAL SPECTRUM: 'EXTREMELY EMBARRASSING'

A fuel pump as a driver refuels a vehicle with diesel fuel at a Shell gas station in Seattle, Washington, US, on Monday, March 9, 2026. (M. Scott Brauer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

While election reform is the party's signature ballot effort, Rankin says kitchen-table issues will determine whether Republicans make gains in November.

She said affordability is the number one concern among voters with California recently landing in the top five most expensive states, according to The Missouri Economic Research and Information Center's quarterly Cost of Living Index.

"A lot of parents want their adult children to stay in California, to be a part of and contribute to the same California dream that was so great for our grandparents and our parents," said Rankin. "We want it to be great for us and for our children. Affordability is the top issue."

NEWSOM UNDER FIRE AS CALIFORNIA GAS TAX HIKE SENDS PUMP PRICES EVEN HIGHER

California drivers are paying about $5.65 per gallon for regular gasoline—roughly $1.25 more, or about 28% higher, than they were at this time last year, according to AAA and federal energy data.

Rankin also said that Californians are concerned about their school systems with zip codes determining the quality of educations students receive, which has long been an argument in the Republican push for school choice.

"When [candidates] keep their race focused on their district, focused on the voters in their district and the issues that matter most to those voters, stay focused on issues like affordability, children's education, the prices of gas and groceries, things like that," said Rankin. "That's what voters want to hear. That's what they care about. They care about what happens locally."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during a press conference for a housing affordability reform bill signing on July 13, 2026, in Oakland, Calif. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is serving his second and final term, fueling speculation about a 2028 presidential bid and creating what Rankin believes is an opportunity for Republicans to win back voters disillusioned with Democratic leadership.

Pointing to the state's troubled high-speed rail project, Rankin argued California has become a cautionary tale of government waste under one-party rule.

"We've got a bullet train that he's been funding with billions of dollars for years, yet we have no train. So where's the money going to?" Rankin asked.

Critics have long scrutinized the project, which was approved by voters in 2008 with an estimated $33 billion price tag but is now projected to cost more than $200 billion.

Rankin said the spending reflects what she views as a broader ideological shift within the Democratic Party, arguing California has embraced policies that are now spreading nationwide.

"I think that the Democrats have gone so far to the left that many Californians just don't see themselves... many Democrats in California just don't relate to the current flow of the Democrat party,"Rankin said."They're moving way too far into the extremism of socialism. I think a lot of people have red flags and just don't want to be part of it."

Fox News Digital reached out to Gov. Gavin Newsom for comment.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Jewish community in Denver on high alert over rise of democratic socialist Melat Kiros
excerpt: Democratic socialist Melat Kiros' primary victory in Colorado has prompted a political counter from members of the state's Jewish community, who say they feel afraid and unheard as debates over antise...
body_text:
Democratic socialist Melat Kiros' primary victory in Colorado has prompted a political counter from members of the state's Jewish community, who say they feel afraid and unheard as debates over antisemitism and party politics intensify.

Progressive groups celebrated a major victory when 29-year-old Democratic Socialist Melat Kiros ousted 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado’s 1st Congressional District in June. But the Democratic primary upset heightened safety concerns among Denver’s Jewish leaders, who warn her sharp rhetoric will fuel antisemitic hostility and violence in their city.

Local Jewish leaders told Fox News Digital that Kiros has left many in the community on edge because of her controversial comments — including describing the Oct. 7 attacks as "inevitable," refusing to label a local firebombing as antisemitic, and accusing Israel of genocide and apartheid.

In the hours after Kiros claimed victory, Rabbi Menachem Lehrfield, director of the Jewish Outreach Initiative in Denver, wrote on social media that he felt fearful knowing that many of his neighbors seemed to support the kind of anti-Israel rhetoric Kiros campaigned on. After his post was met with a barrage of antisemitic comments, Lehrfield published an op-ed explaining how for observant Jews like himself, just wearing a yarmulke down the streets in Denver now feels like a dangerous thing to do.

Just 24 hours after publishing his op-ed, those fears became a reality.

Democratic congressional candidate Melat Kiros speaks to supporters at an election-night watch party after winning the Colorado primary on June 30, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. Kiros defeated incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette, D-Colo., in the Democratic primary. (Michael Ciaglo/Getty Images)

SOCIALIST COLORADO CANDIDATE BLAMES ISRAEL FOR 'PUTTING JEWISH PEOPLE IN GREAT DANGER'

"I was walking down the street right here, right outside this building, and somebody rolled down their window and yelled, ‘dirty Jew,’ to me," Lehrfield told Fox News Digital during an interview at his Denver office. "I don't know what's going to happen next time. I don't know if next time, instead of hurling vile words, they'll be hurling an explosive like the person who killed Karen Diamond in Boulder. I don't know if they're going to do something to me or my family or my community. There's a real fear that we're living with."

"What I'm most afraid of is the fact that so many of the people in my community, so many people in the district, voted for her," he added.

Rabbi Menachem Lehrfield, director of the Jewish Outreach Initiative in Denver, speaks about rising security concerns following Colorado's 1st Congressional District primary election in an interview with Fox News Digital on Monday, July 13, 2026.  (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

Many residents are still reeling from the deadly antisemitic attack in Boulder last year.

In June 2025, an 82-year-old woman, Karen Diamond, was killed and a dozen others were injured when a man threw Molotov cocktails into a peaceful pro-Israel gathering on Boulder’s Pearl Street Mall. Prosecutors charged 45-year-old illegal immigrant Mohamed Sabry Soliman with murder and hate crimes, noting he yelled "Free Palestine" and spent a year planning the attack to "kill all Zionist people."

When asked about the attack during a 9News interview, Kiros condemned the violence but refused to call it antisemitic, saying she didn’t "know what was in the heart of the perpetrator."

A few weeks after the 9News interview, Kiros clarified that the attack in Boulder was indeed "a horrific attack on a group of Jewish people that were peacefully protesting," but she blamed Israel for rising antisemitism in the U.S.

Melat Kiros participated in a League of Women Voters Congressional District 1 candidate forum at Montview Presbyterian Church in Denver, Colo., on May 28, 2026. (RJ Sangosti/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post)

THE GREAT BETRAYAL: HOW RADICAL PROGRESSIVES ARE DYNAMITING THE BLACK-JEWISH ALLIANCE

"We are seeing that the actions of Israel are putting Jewish people in great danger," she continued, while vowing to prioritize combating "hate and antisemitism" if elected.

For some advocates in Denver’s Jewish community, her refusal to label the attack as antisemitic was seen as a slap in the face.

"Kiros's inability to call the Boulder firebombing an antisemitic attack was extremely frustrating and difficult for our community to hear," Brandon Rattiner, senior director of the Jewish Community Relations Council (JCRC), told Fox News Digital. "First and foremost, she's a lawyer, and the judge said it was an antisemitic attack, so this is not something that’s really still being debated."

"The impact here was pretty clear: A Jewish person was killed, over a dozen were hurt, and it was one of the biggest and most prominent antisemitic attacks on Jews throughout the world," he continued. "So the inability to see and to hear our community when we are asking for level of care and empathy was incredibly hurtful to hear."

Brandon Rattiner, senior director of the Jewish Community Relations Council (JCRC), addresses community reactions to the Colorado primary election results during an interview with Fox News Digital in Denver, Colorado on Tuesday, July 14, 2026.  (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

Rattiner met with Kiros ahead of the primary to share his community’s concerns. While he thought they had a good conversation, Rattiner said he felt betrayed when Kiros appeared on anti-Israel podcaster Hasan Piker’s livestream two weeks later and "did the opposite of everything that we had discussed."

"I had asked for nuance and she spoke in absolutist positions," Rattiner said. "I had asked for empathy and compassion, and she seemed to only allow that for one side of the conflict."

Kiros, a former attorney turned doctoral student and barista, launched her campaign on progressive promises like universal healthcare, housing reform, and universal child and elder care. But her positions on Israel became a polarizing flashpoint.

While national progressives view her win as proof that voters want bolder policies, local Jewish leaders say that normalizing extreme language makes everyday life less safe for their community.

Susan Rona, regional director of the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) Mountain States Region, discusses tracking antisemitic incidents in Colorado during an interview with Fox News Digital in Denver, Colorado on Thursday, July 16, 2026.  (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

Susan Rona, regional director for the Anti-Defamation League (ADL), told Fox News Digital that this rhetoric fuels violence against Jewish people.

"When political leaders refuse to name something as a targeted antisemitic attack, it creates some distrust of leadership and causes additional fear because it minimizes and causes dehumanization of Jews, which leads to violence," Rona said.

"We’re seeing that pretty clearly in Colorado," she continued. "There’s a direct line to all this antisemitic rhetoric we’re hearing and violence happening toward the Jewish community."

Antisemitic incidents are skyrocketing in Colorado, according to the advocacy group, having reached the third-highest on record since ADL began tracking them in 1979.

ADL’s most recent report tallied 167 incidents in 2025 — a massive jump from ten years ago when the region saw fewer than 12 cases in a year.

What makes 2026 particularly alarming, Rona said, is the rise in the violent nature of these attacks. She cited the Boulder firebombing, a child being physically assaulted with a makeshift lasso and subject to antisemitic slurs, and a visibly Jewish woman being assaulted in a laundromat.

The ADL says that criticism of Zionism and the state of Israel is central to the Democratic Socialists of America’s platform.

Anti-Israel protesters gather at a "Stop the Sale of Stolen Palestinian Land" protest at the Park East Synagogue in Manhattan on Tuesday, May 5, 2026, in New York City. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The ADL released an update to its report on the DSA political movement after its wave of primary wins this year, highlighting the DSA’s "explicitly anti-Israel platform." The report noted the DSA’s formal endorsement of Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) against Israel, and declaration that Zionism is equivalent to racism. According to ADL, at its national convention, the DSA also passed a resolution mandating that its candidates refuse any affiliation with "Zionist lobby groups" or the Israeli government.

"I'm concerned that antisemitism is becoming mainstreamed in politics. It's becoming institutionalized [and] normalized," Rona said.

Community leaders stressed that their issue isn't simply disagreeing with someone over their criticism of Israel or its leadership.

"It is always OK to criticize Israel the same way it's OK to criticize any country; that is part of the democratic process," Rabbi Lehrfield said. "There's nobody more critical of Israel than Israelis… But there's a big distinction between criticizing Israel and demonizing it and saying it doesn't have a right to exist."

"When it turns into hate speech and starts this normalization of targeting and dehumanizing Jews, it's where we really [cross] a line, and we have to call it out for what it is," Rona agreed.

Not everyone agrees that Kiros’ rhetoric is anti-Jewish. Ian Zuckerman, an associate professor of history at Regis University who says he’s a "proudly Jewish Coloradan," published an op-ed in Colorado Newsline saying he was "thrilled" by Kiros’ primary win.

Melat Kiros on the night of her primary victory.

He adamantly disagreed with those who called her rhetoric antisemitic, using examples from history to say that a rejection of political Zionism is not equivalent to antisemitism. He accused the candidate's critics of "splitting hairs," arguing Kiros did ultimately condemn the violent attack against individuals over their beliefs.

"Kiros got it right: Respect for basic human dignity means that no one should be subjected to violence because of their beliefs or their ascriptive identity," he wrote. "Though the scale is incomparable, our condemnation of the attacks in Boulder and our horror at the genocide in Gaza stem from the same moral principle."

In response to Kiros’ victory, a Jewish independent candidate, Dr. Shimon Blau, quickly gathered signatures to get on the ballot for the general election. While winning a third-party campaign in Denver is an uphill battle, Rattiner said his candidacy speaks volumes about the mood of the electorate.

"The best way to understand his candidacy is this is a community that is feeling isolated, vilified, and in pain," Rattiner said.

Blau called Kiros’ campaign a danger to the Jewish community. He also suggested he was entering the race to stand up against socialist policies.

"I believe in human rights for everyone," Blau told the Denverite. "I believe in healthcare reform, in fiscal responsibility. I believe in a certain level of personal responsibility, and I'm a little bit wary of government overreach if it's a little bit too far. I am absolutely not a socialist."
